DEDICATION.
TO E. M. C., MY COMRADE IN THIS UNDERTAKING.

FOREWORD.
T his book is a record of the work and the life of the craftsman in a feudal society
not unlike that of Early Medieval Europe. It deals, not with a period of great
attainment in fine art, but with a beautiful and Signified scheme of peasant
decoration, based upon the traditions of Indian art and craft. Sinhalese art is essentially
Indian, but possesses this especial interest, that it is in many ways of an earlier character,
and more truly Hindu—though Buddhist in intention,—than any Indian art surviving
on the mainland so late as the beginning of the nineteenth century. The minor arts, and
the painting, are such as we might expect to have been associated with the culture of
Asoka’s time, and the builders of Barahat.
The period dealt with I have called Medireval; but it must be understood that changes of
style in decorative art take place comparatively slowly, and that it is generally impossible
to say at a glance whether a given piece of work be of the sixteenth, seventeenth, eighteenth
century, or even older or later. Most of the specimens here figured or described date from
the latter part of the eighteenth century. Mediseval conditions survived in full force until
the British occupation of Kandy in 1815, and what is actually described in this book is the
work of Sinhalese craftsmen under mediaeval conditions, mainly as these survived in the
eighteenth century, .and, in a- less degree, even to the present day.
Mediaeval Sinhalese Art was the art of a people for whom husbandry was the most honour­
able of all occupations, amongst whom the landless man was a nobody, and whose ploughmen
spoke as elegantly as courtiers; It was a religious art, and so a popular art. It was also
essentially a national art; the craftsmen, forming an integral part of the Civil Service,
were rewarded with grants of State land, no less than soldiers or husbandmen. It was the
art of a people whose kings were ‘one with the religion and the people,’—perhaps the most
Significant phrage in the whole of that magnificent chronicle, the Mahavaipsa, from which
I have so often quoted,— a phrase embodying an ideal hopeless of attainment by a foreign
ruler.
It was the aft of a poor people, the annual income of whose kings did not in the eighteenth
century exceed ¿zooo in money, beside revenue in kind. It was very different from the
sumptuary art of the great courts and wealthy cities of India, of which we trace but a faint
reflection here and there in the use of Indian materials, and the importation of Indian
craftsmen. But it is the only true art discoverable in Ceylon to-day. In a few years it may
be gone for ever.. I have tried to make a picture of it, before it was too late.
If we would understand the significance and the history of the arts and crafts in India,
it will be needful to begin with Such survivals of them as we can study readily, and work
back from these to earlier times. Hence, even from a wider point of view, I make no
apology for writing a large book about a time when the traditions of fine art were stereo­
typed, and even the traditions of the crafts intensely formalised and. rigid. Such an art is,
as- it were, an outlier, left by long continued denudation, in extent severely limited, yet
evidence unmistakcable of a former continuity which it helps us to understand. Even
so considered, the .intrinsic value of the art is great; the capacity for certain types of
designing survives even to this day amongst a few craftsmen almost perfectly developed;
and whatevef limitations even late Sinhalese art possessed, it is at least immeasurably
superior to anything produced by any would-be-modern Sinhalese artists of the present day.
An eighteenth century jataka painting is as much superior to a modern Low-country book
illustration, as a Kandyan jewel is to a modern imitation of a design borrowed from a
Birmingham catalogue, or a Kandyan temple to a modern structure such as that described
on p. 13a. ,
as •. Y

This book is not primarily intended as a work of scholarship, but is written first of all for
the Sinhalese people, as a memorial of a period which at present they are not willing
to understand. fThe ‘educated’ Sinhalese of to-day, after, on the one hand, a century of
foreign government, and of education in which the national culture has been completely
ignored, and, on the other hand, jn equal Jjeriod of subservient and obsequious imitation
of foreign manners, have little reason to be proud of their present achievement in the Art
of Living. Evidence of shallow thought is everywhere to be seen in an exaltation of the
present age at the expense of the past. It is, however, only in an effort to realise the ideals
of this very past, and of the past of India, that there lies the possibility of a true regeneration
and revitalising of the national life of the Sinhalese people. This book, then, is written
first of all as a contribution to the understanding of this past.
Secondly, it is meant for those in East or West who are interested in the reorganization
of life, and especially of the arts and crafts under modern conditions.
Thirdly, an endeavour has been made to render it as far as possible of value to the anthro­
pologist, and to students of sociology and folk-lore. Criticism, only too easy from several
points of view, should take into account the actual purpose of the book, and the fact that
such a detailed account of the arts and crafts of a small area in the East, is really pioneer work.
In Ceylon, as in India, the direct and indirect influence of contact with the West has been
fatal to the arts. The two most direct causes of this adverse influence have been the destruc­
tion of the organization of state-craftsmen, following upon the British occupation; and the
subsequent systematic neglect, by British and Sinhalese alike, of a local architectural
tradition. A less direct, but equally sure and certain, cause of the decline of the arts has
been the growth of commercialism,— that system of production under which the work of
European machines and machine-like men has in the East driven the village weaver from
his loom,* the craftsman from his tools, the ploughman from his songs, and has divorced art
from labour. In the words of Blake,
“When nations grow old
The arts grow cold,
And commerce settles on every tree.”
In such grim fashion has commerce settled in the East'
The Sinhalese people are not, in my opinion, happier 'or better than they were in the
eighteenth century. Talk of progress, and the reality, are not the same. Civilisation is
supposed to advance by the creation of new desires, to gratify which the individual must
endeavour to improve his position. But in reality it is not quantity, but quality of wants
that may be taken as evidence of progress in the Art of Living. No one acquainted with
modern Sinhalese taste will pretend that it gives evidence of any improvement in the quality
of wants. Indeed, it is sufficiently obvious that quantity, variety, and novelty are not really
compatible with quality.
From a study of the arts and crafts under mediæval conditions in East and West: under
modern conditions in the West: and under conditions resulting from the influence of West
on East, something may be learnt of the true and false relations between art and life. What
are the conditions necessary to the existence of a worthy art ? Let us first enquire what
conditions forbid its existence in the modern West. They may be summed up in the words
commercialism and irréligion.
* In euphemistic language, '■ '■ successfully contested the village weaver s market.”

The essential method of commercialism is to create a want in order to have the opportunity
of profiting by the filling of it. Under the commercial system, it is no longer demand
that regulates supply, but production that ‘forces a market.’’ Machinery has enabled the
capitalist to do this to the fullest extent. The promise of labour-saving machinery was:
a millenium for the worker, shorter hours and easier work; its result have been merely
increased production, increased profit to the capitalist, and not less, but less intelligent, work
for the producer. Not merely is the workman through division of labour no longer able
to make any whole thing, not only is he confined to making small parts of things, but it is
impossible for him to improve his position or to win reward for excellence in the craft itself.
Under guild conditions, it was possible and usual for the apprentice to rise through all
grades of knowledge and experience to the position of a master-craftsman. But take any
such trade as carpet making under modern conditions, by powei-looms. "fhe operator has
no longer to design or to weave in and out the threads with his own fingers. He is employed
in reality, not as a carpet weaver, but as the tender of a machine. He may rise to a higher
place it is true,— but it is the place of a man responsible for the successful running of many
machines by many men. He can never rise in virtue of his knowledge or experience in the
craft itself. That craft is for him destroyed as a means of culture, aud the community has
lost one more man’s intelligence,—for it is obviously futile to attempt to build up by evening
classes and free libraries, what the whole of a man’s work is for ever breaking down. It is no
longer possible for culture and refinement to come to the craftsman through his work; it
must be won, if won at all, in spite of his work; he must seek them in a brief hour snatched
from rest and sleep, at the expense of life itself. It is not strange that he does not seek them,
nor that their expression is lacking in his work. He has not even the capacity for idling,
but must continually seek amusement and excitement. There can be no quality of leisure
in his work., In short, commercial production absolutely forbids a union of art with labour^
*t@Llt is instructive to compare the still surviving, but fast disappearing, relics of this union
in the East, .with the results of Western endeavours through education and free libraries
to restore that general culture which cannot undef commercialism exist; not there does
the ploughman speak as elegantly as the courtier, not there are riches little valued ; nor can
these things be where life is lived, not as an art, but as a wild beast fight.*
The conditions of labour affect not merely the producer, but also the consumer, who under
modern conditions must put up with the lack of temperament in the mechanical work
composing his environment; and must suffer economically also, inasmuch as work in which
the worker is not interested, or of which he cannot be proud, generally costs the consumer
more in the long run than the initial cheapness saves.
But the primary importance of all that is meant by craftsmanship relates to the life of the
producer. .Cheap work, cheap men ; and the community suffers accordingly, A society
which sees wealth in things rather than in men, is ultimately doomed. It appears, therefore,
that it is absolutely essential that mechanical production should in the future be, not
abandoned, but controlled in the real interests of humanity. If this appears to be impossible,
as I am unwilling to believe, it must be admitted that civilization is not much better than a
failure; for it is not much good being more ingenious than our forefathers if we cannot be
either happier or better.
One of the most interesting and difficult distinctions that can be drawn is that between a
* “ The Burman, if asked to give his candid opinion after a year's experience of English life, would
probably say that the position of the vast majority of Englishmen was not much better than that of

tool and a machine. It is, however, one that the craftsman can always draw for himself,
when he is free to do so. Thus the carpet loom is a tool, a contrivance for holding warp
threads at a stretch, for the pile to be woven round them by the craftsman’s fingers; but the
power loom is a machine, for it does the essential part of the work, and in so doing imposes
limitations on the spontaneity and freedom of the design and on the intelligence of the
worker. The gouge and chisel are tools, but the mechanical carver is a machine, perhaps
the most stupid yet invented. It is essential, then, for a re-union of art with labour, that
machinery should be controlled ; and this control can be properly exercised only by the
craftsman himself. The place of machinery in a true civilisation will be that of a hewer of
wood and drawer of water, a servant, not a master; its concern will be rather with the
■ preparation than with the subsequent manipulation of materials. Its purpose will be, not
to rob the craftsmen of that part of labour which is his very craft itself, but to save him
from the heaviest and least interesting work, and to carry out only the simpler and most
mechanical processes of manufacture. It is, of course, true that even in the preparation of
materials, and the execution of monotonous labour, the machine is in many cases inferior to
the hand. Thus, to take a single example, the hand-woven textile is, ceteris paribus, more
durable than the machine woven, owing to the regularity and mechanical character of the
strains put upon the threads of the latter; and the surface, even if quite unornamented, is
artistically superior. So again, a machine-stamped binding, or a machine-planed table, or
a lathe-spun bowl, lack the peculiar surface characteristic of each material, and developed
by hand-work on it ; the technical perfection of the surface in the one case is simply
uninteresting, in the other varied. The machine, however, has come to stay, and, rightly
used, may be transformed from a curse into a blessing. The problem is not how to abolish
machinery, but how so to regulate it that it shall serve without enslaving man ; how to stop
competition between machine and hand-work, by defining and delimiting intelligently the
proper spheres of each. The community cannot afford to dispense with the intellectual and'
imaginative forces, the educational and ethical factors which go with the existence of
skilled craftsmen and small workshops. It must, therefore, protect these in their proper
sphere. This can be done only by restoring the entire control of production to the actual
workers, as in the old guild systems; or by the endowment of craftsmanship as in Ceylon, in
the feudal manner, but substituting for the king or overlord the democratic community as
patron. The first method may perhaps be achieved through a development of the trade-
unions of the West, historically the representatives of the old guild associations of
producers.* The second may be achieved by the action of the community in appointing as
its servants, for life or good conduct, its craftsmen and its artists, just as it now appoints its
judges, its preachers, its professors and medical officers.
A community, convinced of the desirability of possessing within itself a body of skilled
craftsmen, and of benefiting from the educational influence and actual productions of such
workmen, could attain these ends by appointing master-craftsmen as servants of the com­
munity, endowing them with a salary, or with a house or other security from want, on
• condition of performance of work for the community. Such Public Craftsmen should be
required to keep apprentices, and choose from these one to be their successor in office.
Such a system would effect the object in view more certainly and more economically than
much larger sums spent on technical education, or the encouragement of competitive
designs for large public works. Without some such solution of the problem, humanity
* Works of thefirst importance on this subject are : A. f. Penty, ‘ Restoration of the Guild System,'
London, 1906; C. R. Ashbee, ‘ Craftsmanship in Competitive Industryj Campden, 1908.

will in the future have to face a complete alienation of art from labour, resulting in a civilisa­
tion “divorced from Nature, but unreclaimed by Art.”
Side by side with commercialism, the growth of irréligion has been destructive of the arts.
Needless to say that by irréligion I do not refer to the decline of one or another particular
form of dogmatic belief, but to the prevalence of that superficial view of life which concen­
trates the attention solely upon outward things, and not at all upon things of the imagination,
real things. The distinction between naturalism and idealism in art is one that is funda­
mentally religious. It is the lack of a metaphysic in modern materialistic culture that
makes it possible for the artist to find sufficient satisfaction in the imitation of beautiful
appearances, and a sufficient aim for art in the giving of pleasure. This reduction of the
highest aim of art from prophecy to amusement strikes at the root of any possible revival
of true art,— which has to do, not with imitation, but imagination. Art that is driven to
save its life, as in modern Europe, by emancipation from all metaphysical and subjective
conceptions, is bound in the end to lose that life ; it becomes, in fact, the work of amateurs
lacking equally in inspiration and tradition. To reunite imagination with technique is as
necessary as to reassociate art with labour.
So far as Ceylon is concerned, it is of course true, that as in later India, a “too conclusive
reliance on traditional practice has led to a mental stagnation which deprives Indian art of
its former vitality.” The true impulse to a wider and fuller life must come once more, as in
Ceylon it has always come, from India. If this book in any way contributes towards the
preparation of the ground for the reception of such impulses, the labour spent upon it will
be repaid in full.
It is of interest to record, in connection with the arts and crafts aspect of the questions just
discussed, that this book has been printed by hand, upon the press used by William Morris
for printing the Kelmscott Chaucer. The printing, carried on in the Norman Chapel at
Broad Campden, has occupied some fifteen months. I cannot help seeing in these very
facts an illustration of the way in which the East and the West may together be united in an
endeavour to restore that true Art of Living which has for so long been neglected by
humanity.

The English reader is recommended to ignore all diacritical marks on consonants, pronounce
consonants as in English, and vowels as in French, except V’ which is like '■ a' in man.
The n in Sinhalese (sinihald) is pronounced like the n in pink, or, more exactly, like the n in
the French word, bon. The A should be distinctly pronounced, like the ^'in pin-head. A
few fully anglicised words such as adigar for adikarama, are printed without diacritical
marks. In Sinhalese words the common contraction ‘e’ (or ‘^’) for aydis, used side by side
with the full termination, as in dange, dangaya. The ending ya is also often omitted, as in
vihara, for vihdraya, a Buddhist temple. The corruption ‘e’ for aya in devale {deva + alaya,
god-mansion) is also used. Sinhalese words in the plural are usually given in the Sinhalese
form, as tuppop, plural of tuppofiya-, but the English ‘s’ is sometimes added instead.

and Kandy Museum; belonging to the Dajada Maligava and Maha Dcvale, jCandy; and
in my own collection. A majority of the objects illustrated are of eighteenth century date.

CHAPTER I. THE SINHALESE PEOPLE.
“ The Mahavamsa, composed equally for the delight and amazement of good men."
T he Sinhalese people are inhabitants of Ceylon, but not all the people of The Sinha-
Ceylon are Sinhalese. The etymologically identical word ‘ Ceylonese,’ however, lesepeople.
is used to describe all persons born in Ceylon, whether Sinhalese, Tamil,
Eurasian or otherwise, except Europeans. The word Cingalese is an old-fashioned
and less correct spelling of Sinhalese. Of the three and a half millions forming, in
round numbers, the population of Ceylon, two and a third million are Sinhalese inhabiting
the southern two-thirds of the island, and rather less than one million are Tamils,
living mostly in the north, on the east coast, and in Colombo. -The remaining population
consists of Moormen (Muhammedans of Tamil extraction for the most part). Burghers
(mixed descendants of Dutch settlers), Malays, Eurasians, Europeans and a few others.
Of the influence exerted by these groups of people on Sinhalese art, we shall need to
consider only the Tamil,' for on the one hand Ceylon lies outside the range of the
Muhammedan conquests and influence, and for the rest, we must carefully avoid the
manifestations of European influence if we are to see Sinhalese art at its best and purest.
Fortunately, in the 18th.century this influence had scarcely at all affected the art of the
Kandyan province, although well marked in ,the low-country. As an introduction to
the study of Sinhalese art as it existed in the latter half of the 19th century, the present
chapter provides a brief history of the Sinhalese people, especially in respect of the
history of the arts and cfafts amongst them.
Almost the earliest Indian tradition of Ceylon is found in the Ramayaija, that beautiful Rdmayaifa
and romantic love-story, which has for so long been to India all and more than was the
tale of Troy to Greece, or Volsunga to the Scandinavians. It relates the capture of Srta,
a queen of Northern India, by Ravaija the Lord of Lanka (Ceylon) ; and the invasion of
Ceylon by Rama, aided by his brother Lakshman and by Hanuman and his monkey
army ; the defeat and death of Ravapa, and recovery of Sita. Lanka is also mentioned
in the Mahabharata.
Another reference to LaAka is found in the Skanda Puraija^ the story of a great and Skanda
malignant demon, for whose overthrow Skanda or Kartikeya was incarnated as a god of PurStfa
war and wisdom. This Kartikeya is still revered, particularly at his shrine at Katara-
gama in the feverish forests of the south-east of Ceylon, whence pilgrims resort from
even the distant parts of India ; Kataragam DeviyO, as he is generally known, was the
patron god of Elala ; and many devales of his are found elsewhere, although the one
just referred to is of peculiar sanctity.
These two stories afford some evidence of the existence of more or less civilised peo- Vijaya
pi es in Ceylon previous to the arrival of Vijaya ancj his companions. The details of
the account of Vijaya’s reception and settlement afford later and further indications of
the existence of an earlier civilisation in Ceylon; reference is found to cities, spinning,
sumptuous beds, etc. In any case it is clear that, according to the legends, the Sinhalese
cannot be of pure Aryan blood, as the first settlers married either the aborigines, or
women from Southern India, and there has been a very large amount of Tamil blood
introduced at many subsequent periods. Their civilisation and art are nevertheless dis­
tinctly Aryan and distinguished from, though closely resembling, that of Southern
India.
b I I

The Sinha- Professor Geiger says, “ There is hardly a corner of the Indian continent of whose his­
Ifse people tory we know so much as we do of that of the island of Ceylon.”* He here refers
to the history recorded in two Pali chronicles, the Dipavarpsa and Mahavarpsa, written in
the 4th and 5th centuries a.d., respectively, and the latter from time to time added to,
and continued up to the time of the British occupation of the Kandyan Provinces in 1815.
There are also other verse chronicles and historical ballads of various dates.
Vijaya The Mahavarpsa in Chapters VI.— Vlll. records the landing T of the first Aryan settlers
in Ceylon under the leadership of Vijaya. These w^ere the founders of the Sinhalese
race, so called because Vijaya’s father sprang from, and was the slayer of, a lion {simha).
The story is briefly as follows :— The King of Vahga, a principality of Magadha, had
a beautiful daughter, of whom it had been prophesied that a lion would be her mate.
To avoid this she was carefully guarded, but of course in vain. She escaped, and while
passing through a wilderness, was carried off by the ‘ lion,’ probably a chieftain of the
‘ Lion-race.’ They had a son (Sirphabahu) and a daughter. The son, when he grew
up became ashamed of and finally slew his father ; and marrying his sister established
himself as a king in Laja rata. Their eldest son was Vijaya, who, being expelled from
the kingdom on account of his lawless behaviour, took ship with 700 followers and
ultimately reached Ceylon. Landing here his followers went in search of food, but
Kuveni were one by one imprisoned by a Yakkhipi named Kuveni (just as was done by Kirke
to the followers of Odysseus). Vijaya himself, provided with a charmed thread, alone
was able to withstand Kuvepi’s sorcery and compel her to restore his imprisoned com­
panions ; she further provided them with rice and a vast variety of other articles which
she had obtained from the ships of mariners who had fallen a prey to her. Kuveni
enabled Vijaya to destroy the other Yakkhas and their city, and herself bore him three
children. But when his followers had settled in the layid and wished him to assume
the sovereignty, he repudiated Kuvepi as beneath him in rank, and sent to Madura to
the Papdiyan king to ask for a royal virgin to be his consort,— a custom followed by most
Sinhalese kings thereafter. Kuveni returned to the Yakkhas and was destroyed by them
for her treachery. It is mentioned that 1000 artisans were sent over in the Papejiyan
Princess’s retinue. According to tradition mentioned by Valentyn these were gold­
smiths, blacksmiths, brass-founders, -carpenters and stone-cutters (evidently the five
sections of the Kammalar, see below. Chap. III). Vijaya and his successors were of the
Buddhism Brahman faith, and it was not till 307 b.c. that Buddhism was established in Ceylon as
iniroduced’ the result of the preaching of Afeka’s son.“]: Mahinda, and later, of his daughter, Sangha-
mitta. The King at that time, Devanam Piyatissa, the most renowned of the Buddhist
kings of Ceylon [307-267 b.c.] was Mahinda’s first convert. Far reaching and many
sided were the results of this conversion. A period of immense religious fervour and
artistic activity followed. In 288 B.c. Sanghamitta landed in Ceylon with a branch of
The samd the sacred Bo tree beneath which the Buddha had attained enlightenment. We are
Bo-trei told that she brought with her eighteen personages of the royal blood, eighteen mem­
plan ted at bers of noble families, eight of the Brahman and eight of the setthi (trading) caste ; and
Anuradha~ eight each of the herdsman, goldsmith and ‘ kalihga ’ castes, as well as of weavers and
pura potters. The branch was planted with great ceremony in the Mahamegha garden at

Anuradhapura, where it still flourishes as the oldest historical tree in the world, com- T“he Sinha-,
memorating the noble life and teaching of Gotama Buddha, who attained enlightenment lesepeople
beneath the parent tree. The religious enthusiasm of the royal adherents of the new
faith, led to the erection at successive periods of the great series of buildings whose
remains still cover many square miles of town and forest land. The oldest of these
are found at Mihintale, where a great stupa was erected over Mahinda’s ashes.
Wars with the Tamils began in 237 b.c., when the throne was seized by Tamil mercenaries. TLlala
Twenty-two years later it was recovered by Asela, but retaken by the Tamils under Elaja
in 205 B.c. Elala was the greatest of the Tamil rulers; He “ruled the kingdom for
forty-four years, administering justice with impartiality to friends and foes” (Mahavaipsa
Ch. XXI).* The dethroned dynasty took refuge at Magampattu on the south coast, the
great tank and dagaba remaining at Tissamaharama still. At last one of the princes, named
Duttha GamanI (Gamani the disobedient—because he would not be held back from war
at his father’s wish) engaged in a long and finally successful war, recovering Anurad­
hapura and killing Elaja in single combat, both being mounted upon elephants.-f- Elala
was buried with every honour. His tomb was so honoured that it was the custom for
even kings, when nearing it, to silence all music and pass on foot; this homage was
paid as late as a.d. 1818 when, on the suppression of the rebellion, the defeated aspirant
to the throne approaching the place in his escape, “although weary and almost incapable
of exertion, not knowing the exact spot,’^ dismounted and continued on foot till assured
that he had passed far beyond, the ancient memorial (Forbes I. 233).
Duffha Gamani (161-137 succeeded to the throne he had so hardly won, and
proved no less great as a ruler than as a warrior. He was a great patron of the church
and builder of dagabas and temples.
He erected the nine-storied brazen palace (Lohapasada) and built also the great T!he Brazen
Ruvanveli and Mirisavetiya dagabas. The Mahavaipsa accounts J of the hnWAing Palace,An-
operations and furniture of these are of the greatest interest, if only for comparison uradhapura
with the descriptions of buildings erected and offerings made by later kings, up to the
beginning of the nineteenth century itself. “ The monarch Duftha Gamani . . . con­
vening the priesthood, thus addressed them, ‘I will build for you a palace like unto
that of the devas ; send to the world of the devas,- and procure for me a plan of their,
palace.’ Accordingly they dispatched thither eight priests. . . .” On their way to the
Tavatirpsa heavens they saw a certain palace “having nine stories, provided with a
thousand apartments and a thousand sleeping rooms. It had four faces, each having
windows to the number of a thousand, like so many eyes; and the eaves of the roof
were decorated with a fringe tinkling (with gems). . . . The aforesaid eight theras,
seeing this palace, immediately made a drawing of it on a cloth with vermilion ;
and returning thence, presented the drawing to the priests who sent it to the court of
the king. The monarch on examining the same, and delighted therewith, repaired to
the celebrated gardens (Mahamegha) and there built the glorious Lohapasada according
to the plan of that renowned palace.”

The Sin/m- he passed away “while yet gazing on the Mahathupa, stretched on his bed.” So died
lese people this great man ; but his spirit lived on, and manifested itself continually in the religious

morials of its love and fear and hope.
GajaBahu We have seen that wars with the Tamils began in 237 b.c., the Sinhalese throne
being on several occasions thereafter occupied by Tamil usurpers. In a.d. 113 Gaja
Bahu turned the tables by invading southern India; he brought back 1200 Tamil cap­
tives (of whom some were no doubt craftsmen) and settled them in different parts of
his kingdom. The annual perahfra of the Maha Devale in Kandy still commemorates
his victory; it is said that the tooth-relic which now heads the procession was not con­
nected with it before the time of Kirti Sri. At this festival a high place has always been
held by the goddess Pattini. Gaja Bahu had brought back from India her halamba
or golden anklet and introduced her worship into Ceylon. Bronze copies of the anklets
are kept in Pattini Devales, and an oath taken on them is particularly binding. The
national game of amkeliya established in her honour, is still resorted to in times of
sickness.-b
The Tooth- In the ninth year of the reign of Sri Meghavaitna {t.e. a.d. 313) “ a certain Brahman
relic princess brought thither from Kalinga the Dathadhatu, or tooth-relic of Buddha, under
circumstances set forth in the Dathadhatuvamsa.% The monarch taking charge of it
himself and rendering the highest honours to it, in the most reverential manner deposited
it in a casket . . . and placed it in the building called the Dhammacakka built by
Devanam Piyatissa in the royal park.” This was at Anuradhapura. The relic was
afterwards enshrined at Polonnaruva, which was made the capital in a.d. 769, when
AnurS-dhapura was abandoned to the Tamils. Subsequently the tooth-relic was removed
successively to Beligala (Vijaya Bahu III., a.d. 1236), Dambadeijiya (Parakrama Bahu
II., a.d. 1240), and again to Polonnaruva. In the time of Bhuvaneka Bahu I. (a.d.
1277) Ceylon was invaded by Arya Cakravarti and the tooth relic carried away to India.
It was soon recovered by Parakrama III. (a.d. 1288) and brought back to Polonnaruwa.
Thereafter it was hidden for safety in various places, until it passed into the hands of
the Tamil Kings of Jaffna. It was taken from them by the Portuguese, who carried it to
Goa and there reduced it to ashes. But this (it is said) was merely a counterfeit. The real
tooth-relic was enshrined in Kandy by Vimala Dharma Suriya II. (a.d. 1679), who built
a temple for its reception; and his son Narendra Sirjiha, the last Sinhalese king, when
this fell into disrepair, built the present Dalada Maligava. It is to be hoped that the
late talk of completely remodelling this historic building so as to make it more com­
modious will be heard no more of.
The relic is now preserved in a series of elaborate jewelled caskets (dedicated by suc-
successive kings) one within the other, fastened by three keys kept by the Diva Nilame,
and the high priests of the Asgiriya and Malvatte. With the caskets is kept a quantity
of beautiful jewellery which has been dedicated from time to time. The tooth is only
exhibited upon rare occasions, perhaps once or twice a year, for some great personage,
and at the same time is shown to crowds of pilgrims from different parts of the country.

The process ot removing the tooth* from its various coverings is an impressive cere- The Sinha-
mony. There are present in the small upper room of the Maligava the Diva Nilame lese people
in full dress, the two High Priests and some other priests. The modern and ugly iron-
barred cage is unlocked, and the golden chains and jewels lifted off the outer casket;
the caskets are removed one by one, three being unlocked by the aforesaid keys ; finally
the smallest casket containing the relic itself is reached ; from this it is removed with
trembling fingers and great reverence by one of the aged High Priests, and set in a silver
holder under a glass case for exhibition to the people.
But it is necessary to return to the history. In a.d. 332, Jetthatissa II. succeeded Jefthatissa
èri Mèghavaijpa, who was king when the relic first came to Ceylon. Jetthatissa “was
a skilful carver. This monarch, having carried out several arduous undertakings in
painting and carving, himself taught the art to many of his subjects. He sculptured
a beautiful image of the Bodhisatta, so perfect that it seemed as if it had been executed
by supernatural power ; and also a throne, a parasol, and a state room with some beau­
tiful works in ivory made for it ; and having administered the Government of Lanka for
nine years, he also fulfilled the destiny due to him” (Mahavaipsa, Ch. XXXVIII).
His successor, Buddhadasa (a.d. 339) was himself a great physician, and “ out of' Buddhadasa
benevolence towards the inhabitants of the island, the sovereign provided hospitals for
all villages, and appointed physicians to them. The Raja having composed the work
Saratthasangaha, containing the substance of all medical science, ordained that there
should be a physician for every twice five villages, and set apart one twentieth of the
produce of fields for the maintenance of these physicians” (Mahavarpsa, Ch. XXXVIII).
Thus he followed in the footsteps of the great Duttha Gamanl, who on his death-bed
was able to say, “ I have daily maintained at eighteen different places, hospitals with
suitable diet and medicines prepared by medical practitioners for the infirm” (Maha-
vatpsa, Ch. XXXII). The great Parakrama Bahu I. pursued the same policy eight
hundred years later.
Two distinguished foreigners visited Ceylon early in the fifth century. The first of Buddha­
these was the learned Brahman Buddhaghosa, who came to Ceylon from Northern ghosa
India about a.d. 400, to consult and copy the commentaries on the Tripitaka or Buddhist
canon. He further composed new commentaries, which are still regarded as authori­
tative. His influence led to what may be called a Buddhist revival.
In A.D. 412 the Chinese monk Fa Hian landed in Ceylon and remained two years Fa Hian
at Anuradhapura, copying the sacred books. He has left on record a detailed account
of the glories of Anuradhapura and the prosperity of Buddhism. J-
The great Mahavatpsa chronicle was compiled in the reign of King Dhatusena (a.d. Mahdvam-
461-479). Both the Dipavaipsa and the Mahavarpsa are based on the historical material sa comp iled
contained in the Sinhalese Atthakathas, no longer extant, and on legends and traditions
amongst the people. It is really an epic work with Duftha GamanI for its hero. It
covers the period 543-301 b.c. Continuations were added at various times, a final
supplement bringing the record up to the British occupation of Kandy in 1815.

The existing remains at Sigiri are amongst the most interesting and remarkable in Ceylon.
Especially noteworthy are the cave paintings, of which further mention is made in a

Polonna- In the eighth century the Sinhalese were forced by the Tamils to abandon Anuradha-
ruva pura, and founded a new capital at Pulatthi (Polonnaruva). But even here they were
not safe, although they were sometimes able to reoccupy even Anuradhapura temporarily.
In the eleventh century, in the reign of the weak king Mahinda V., Lanka was altogether
overrun by the Tamils who destroyed the country and occupied Polonnaruva. The
warlike Vijaya Bahu I. restored the Sinhalese rule, and it was at Polonnaruva that Para-
krama Bahu the Great reigned from a.d. 1164 to 1197. This great man was at once
a warrior and statesman; he succeeded in bringing the whole country beneath his sway
and in driving out the Tamils; after which he ruled so firmly and justly that, as the
Dambulla inscription informs us, “even a woman might traverse the island with a pre­
cious jewel and not be asked what it was.” After peace was thus established, Parakrama
Bahu rebuilt and restored the harassed city of Polonnaruva, and also the buildings of
Anuradhapura “which had been wholly destroyed by the hosts of the Colians (Tamils).”
Thereafter “ Parakrama Bahu, the conqueror of kings, dwelt in the beautiful city of
Pulatthi (Polonnaruva), far from the strife of foes. A faithful and wise man, blessed
with the dawn of fortune, and a leader of those that love music and poetry, he passed
his time in the enjoyment of quiet pleasures and enjoyments” (Mahavaipsa, Chapter
LXXIV). He purged and purified the Buddhist church and erected noble buildings
for the church and the priesthood ; as “a round temple of the tooth-relic built wholly of
stone and adorned with beautiful pillars, staircases, walls and such like, and ornamented
with rows of figures of the lion, the kinnara and the hamsa^' and “ a beautiful image
house with five stories, that contained images of Gods and Brahmas and other beings,
and workmanship of flowers and plants, and adorned with pinnacles and eaves and inner
rooms, halls and chambers— an image house which bore worthily the name of Lanka
Tilaka (‘Brow-gem of Ceylon’; but not the present temple in Udanuvara).” Like so
many other kings before and after him, “this most excellent of men caused many tanks
and channels to be built in divers places, so that he might put an end to the calamity
of famine among men” (Mahavarpsa, Chap. LXXIX). Such was Parakrama Bahu the
Great; of English kings there is surely none but Alfred the Great with whom he may
be justly compared.
Tamil in­ After his death there was much unpeace in the land. During the apparently beneficent
vasions reign of a Tamil (Pandiyan) usurper named Parakrama, Ceylon was invaded by Tamils
from Kalinga, led by Magha. If the Papdiyan and Colian Tamils chastised the Sinha­
lese with whips, the men of Kalinga did so with scorpions. “ They robbed the inhabit­
ants of their garments and their jewels and everything that they had. . . . The rich
men they tied up with cloths and tortured and took possession of all their wealth. . . .
They broke down the image houses and destroyed many cetiyas. They took up their
dwelling in the viharas. . . . Many books also of great excellence they loosed from the
cords that bound them, and cast them away in divers places. . . . Alas, alas ! even so
did those Tamil giants, like the giants of Mara, destroy the kingdom and the religion
of the land” (Mahavarpsa, Chap. LXXX).
Troubled times continued, the capital being shifted from place to place, to Datuba-

deijiya, Yapahuva (whence was brought the beautiful pierced stone window now 'The Sinha-
in the Colombo Museum) Kurunegala, Gampola, Kotte, Sitavaka and Kandy. Yet ksepeople
many brave and patriotic kings made strenuous efforts for their people’s good. Of
Vijaya Bahu III. (a.d. 1236) it is said in the Raja-ratnakara that he “ established a
school in every village and charged the priests who superintended the same to take
nothing from the learners, promising that they should be rewarded for their trouble by
himself. His son Parakrama Bahu II. (a.d. 1240-1275) temporarily drove out the Pamkrama
Tamils and brought the whole country under his rule. At this time it is said that Bdhu II.
there were nearly one and a half million villages in the three districts of Ceylon (Pihifi
Rata, Ruhunu Rata, and Maya Rata) corresponding at a very moderate estimate to a
population of ten millions, about three times as great as the present. The distribu­
tion of the population, too, is now very different from what it was in the thirteenth
century. At that time the population was densest in the eastern and north central dis­
tricts, dense also in the north, but scanty on the western coast. In the eighteenth
century the north central districts, including the ancient capitals of Anuradhapura and
Polonnaruva had long been deserted, chiefly in consequence of the Tamil wars and the
disorganisation of the great irrigation systems which alone enabled those dry regions to
support a large population. Now, as Mr. Arunachalam points out* “ The most striking
change is the advance, by over 100 per cent, of the population of the western sea coast
and its vicinity, and the decline by almost as much of the populations of the ancient
kingdoms. . . . The change indicates clearly the difference caused in the condition of
the island by the disorganisation of its great irrigation system, and the consequent decay
of the great national industry, rice cultivation, and by the advent of Europeans. Popu­
lation and wealth have faded away from their ancient seats and gathered towards the
coast. The Island, no longer self-sufficient or self-centred, is dependent for its pros­
perity mainly on foreign enterprise, on the European capitalist and planter, and the South
Indian labourer and tradesttian.”

From this period dated the division of what had been one people, into ‘Kandyan’ and Division in­
‘ Low-country’ Sinhalese. The Sinhalese in the immediate vicinity of Colombo and along to Kandyan
the coast were soon driven to make peace, and even allied themselves with the Portu­ and Low-
guese, often turning nominal Christians and adopting Portuguese names to curry favour, country
or under compulsion. The same process was continued in the time of the Dutch suc­ Sinhalese
cessors of the Portuguese. But the greater part of the Sinhalese people, the hardy
mountaineers of the interior, preserved their independence, keeping the foreigner at bay
for more than 200 years after, the first landing of the Portuguese. They have had their
reward; for in spite of the progress of denationalisation even amongst these, there are
still preserved amongst them sufficient traces of the old national life, sufficient remains
of skilful craftsmen’s handiwork, to enable us to form an estimate of the Sinhalese as a
live and individual people, with a national character and national art; an individuality
and art which it is more difficult and often impossible to trace in the low-country districts
long subjected to western influence.
Mayadunne and his son Raja Sirpha I. waged continual, and on the whole successful, war Raja Simha
against the Portuguese, from the Sinhalese capital at Sitavaka. Raja Sitpha’s successor, I.
Vimala Dharma Süriya I. (a.d. 1592) established his capital once more in Kandy, which

In the long reign of Raja Sirpha II. (a.d. 1633-1687) the Portuguese wars were con­ Raja Simha
tinued ; an alliance was made with the Dutch, and the Portuguese finally expelled in II.
A.D. 1658, but the Dutch did not prove more faithful allies, although theirs was a policy
more purely commercial; there is a Sinhalese proverb, spoken when a man makes
a bad exchange and used in reference to the Dutch succeeding the Portuguese, “I
have given pepper and got ginger.” Raja Sirpha seems to have been a very cruel
and capricious monarch. One Robert Knox was a prisoner at his court for twenty RobertKnox
years, escaping then to write one of the most truthful, and at the same time fascinating
books of travel ever set down. His “ Historical Relation of the Island Ceylon ” (a.d.
1681) is a compendium of invaluable information, written in spirited and idiomatic
English; it is still the most interesting work on Ceylon and the Sinhalese, and is often
quoted in the present volume. Ribeiro’s “Fatalidade Histórica de Ceilao,” written a few
years later, gives a valuable account of the low-country at the same period.

Asgiriya crowd of priests and chiefs, of whom Nugavela Basnayaka Nilame of the Mahâ Dévale

Çhelepola died in exile, Pilima Talava by an executioner, many others by the sword
or the gallows, and not a few were put to death by the English Government in the cruel
times of the rebellion of 1818. The king, then only twenty-one, in the days of his
youth and popularity, worshipped Buddha with his mother and sister, and, after causing
Ehelepola to read the contents of an ola dedicating Kahawatta and Udasgiriya to the
new vihara, he offered the writing by laying it on the table before the image. He said
that Udasgiriya was his mother’s village, and she joined in the offering. Then the royal
party walked round the vihara, and the king seeing the bare surface of the rock which
formed part of the back wall, ordered that the contents of the writing should be there
inscribed. About two months afterwards the king, with his mother and sister, again
visited the vihara. Ehelepola Adigar read the ola writing, which was compared with
the inscription by the king in presence of the chief priests, and praising the stone­
cutters he ordered them to be paid from the treasury” (Lawrie’s Gazetteer, p. 74).
Beginning But the king’s mind became deranged ; he lived in perpetual fear of his life, and com­
of the end mitted great cruelties on those whom he feared. From 1800-1804 there was continuous
warfare between the Kandyan king and the English in the low-country. From that
time to 1815 there was no open war, but destructive raids were made by either party
when opportunity afforded to destroy a village or to burn a harvest. In 1812 Pilima
Talava attempted a rebellion, but failed, and was beheaded with several members of his
family. He was succeeded by Ehelapola, who in 1814 also revolted, and was forced to
flee to Colombo, while the king revenged himself upon his wife and family.
British rule About this time ten native merchants who were British subjects were barbarously treated
begins by the king, and seven died as a result ; this was made the chief pretext for an invasion
of Kandy by the British in 1815. Unsupported by his ill-used subjects, Vikrama Siipha
was easily overcome and captured, after which the Sinhalese voluntarily surrendered the
Government to the British, but with full Teservation of their rights and liberties.
Uva Rebel­ The Sinhalese soon regretted this surrender, though glad tt> be rid of the tyrant.
lion The chiefs especially disliked the curtailment of their powers. In 1817 a rebellion
broke out in Uva, developing into a war of independence with some chance of success ;
but the harassed people were unable to hold out, and the rebels were put down with
great severity in the following year. The results of foreign rule and of the insur­
rection and its suppression were disastrous. It was many years before thé country began
to recover its prosperity, while the breach in the continuity of national tradition and culture
has never been spanned. But with the exception of a small rising in 1848, this was the
last struggle, and the year 1815 may be taken as that of the final extinction of an indepen­
dence which had lasted with few interruptions for more than twenty-three centuries.
Had the British, instead of attempting to rule directly a people with whose religion and
traditions they were entirely out of sympathy, established a Sinhalese upon the throne as

Into the details of a century of British rule we need not enter. At the beginning of it Disijitegra-
the Kandyap Sinhalese were still an independent and self-contained community, with a tion of reli-
culture and art which had for all an equal appeal, and a state religion which was also gion and
the religion of the people. Now however, the old spirit has departed, and though the society
unspoilt villager is still a man worth knowing well, the ‘ educated ’ classes are sadly
degenerate and de-nationalised. Impoverished by the change from a society based on
personal relations to one based on the exchange of coin and free'T:rade in land, the aris­
tocracy are unable, even if willing, to support the old traditions ; nor, breaking with
these, have they in any adequate way acquired the culture of the west. By many, the
old life and old culture are despised, and all interest in the country and its past is dead.
The priesthood suffers ako from lack of the vigorous support of the kings ; temples are
allowed to fall into decay, and valuable and beautiful memorials of the past allowed to
disappear, or to be cheaply restored away by thaae who do not understand or care for
them.* As an example of the disintegration of society and of the general disorganisa­

What the temples were really entitled to was the usufruct of lands dedicated to them ;

another reasonably, especially when of a different religion, and when the rulers have
no permanent personal interest in the land. No ruler who was really “ one with the
religion and the people,” could have borne for a year with the -situation which a suc­
cession of Christian rulers has merely aggravated.
Education The people take but little interest in education; it is left to others, whose interests are not
always identical with those of the people themselves, to provide what they will. The
officially recognised system of education, based on examinations such as the Cambridge
locals and London University courses, has no place for any aspect of the national
culture*—history, music, art or religion. It appeals only to the material interests.

Something must be said of the history of the arts during the last century. That history Decline of
has been one of continuous decline. Those who read the following chapters and per- art
ceive how the religious, artistic and national life of the people formed together the
expression of one culture which all classes shared, will understand how impossible it
was that the arts should continue to flourish under foreign rulers, ignorant of, and in
the main opposed, to the perpetuation of that culture and religion. What befell the
royal craftsmen when the Buddhist king was replaced by the Christian Governor ? How
could there continue that identification of sentiment between ruler and craftsmen which
made possible the building of Gangarama, the Dalada Maligava, or the last festival
at Asgiriya ? Imagine the effect on English art if English independence had ceased
in the reign of Henry III., and the Government had passed into the hands of a nation
of materialists *— Westminster Abbey left unfinished. Gothic art no more the vehicle
of the national religious sentiment. One of the most sympathetic and cultured of
recent Colonial Secretaries of Ceylon, was able to enquire after two years in Ceylon,
what a Jataka might be. Now it is quite natural that an ordinary educated English­
man should lack that knowledge, but for the ruler of a Buddhist people to do so is
altogether incongruous and improper. Such an one cannot enter into the life of the
people, or be a guide or father to them; at the worst they will imitate him for interested
reasons, at the best they will ignore him altogether.
Even accepting the situation, we find that most injury is done to art through the
departmental notions of architecture prevailing.-f- A majority of official buildings are
ugly, and all are unrelated to the national style of art and architecture. Even in the ‘
few cases where an eflibrt has been made to build in the style of the country, the result
has been a fiasco ; the Ruvanveli ambalam for instance, is merely a contractor’s structure
masquerading as a Kandyan building.^
Government support of an institution like the Kandy Art Association § however
excellent in its degree, is totally inadequate to save the arts and crafts of the country
from gradual decay; from that only the people themselves can ultimately save them.
But the responsibility of Government (as the inheritors of the great traditions of the
Sinhalese kings) to support the culture and ar£6 of the land is none the less real. The
hereditary skill and taste of the ¿aste craftsmen might be preserved for the future
generations, if the Government gave directly to craftsmen even a quarter of the support
given by the later Sinhalese kings; which might be done in many ways, but especially
by the employment of craftsmen in all lesser building operations, placing the whole
design and execution in their hands (subject to the nature of actual requirements) and
not in that of engineers, untrained in art, least of all in Sinhalese art, and also by the
c ommissioning of more elaborate works of art than those now undertaken, and the
purchase of these without regard to the possibility or otherwise of immediate re-sale.

Ihe Sinha- If England chooses to assume the rule of other peoples, she has a responsibility towards
lese people their culture, no less than in respect of their material interests. If this responsibility
is shirked, her rule may not always be favourably compared with that of the Sinhalese
and Tamil kings who preceded her.
The arts, however, can only be saved in the long run by the people themselves. How
are the people to be saved? How shall they be re-energised and re-inspired, how become
once more socially constructive, how learn to re-express the national emotion in literature
and art? The answer is, by love of India. There is scarcely any part of Sinhalese life,
or religion, or art, which is quite comprehensible without reference to India; the
Sinhalese themselves are Indians ; the greatness of their civilization dates from the wave
of Indian influences that reach Ceylon through Atoka’s missionaries; the air and soil
in which the nation has grown and borne good fruit are Indian ; how should another
soil and atmosphere be suited to it now? India without Ceylon is incomplete, for in
many ways, Ceylon is a more perfect window through which to gaze on India’s past,
than any that can be found in India herself. Much more is Ceylon incomplete if alienated
from the Motherland. The most remarkable and significant of the awakenings to
national self-consciousness which have taken place in modern times, is the recognition
by the people of India of their fundamental unity. Of this unity Ceylon is economically,
mentally and spiritually, a part; and with its culture and its life, must her own survive
or perish.
i©k We have reviewed in the briefest possible space, the culture-history of the Sinhalese
people, as recorded in one of the most interesting chronicles known to the world. We
have seen something of the earth whence they sprang, and the waters that gave them
drink. At all times the national life was reflected in the national culture. The art
expression of that culture in the eighteenth century can only be understood and appreciated,
when the people themselves and the ideals of their religion and civilization are understood
and respected. An attitude of sympathy is essential also to the comprehension of much
that seems strange or repulsive in an alien culture. No aspect of Eastern art. can be
rightly appreciated by those who approach it only with the intention of discovering what
it has not accomplished. A study of what it has done will serve us better. Towards
that study the present work is a small contribution. In the light of the past and for
the help of the future, it is offered to the Sinhalese people as a monument to a part of
their departed glory.

CHAPTER II. SOCIAL ECONOMY OF THE
KANDYAN SINHALESE IN THE EIGH­
TEENTH CENTURY.
Riches are not here valued, nor make any the more Honourable" (Knox).
T h e first chapter of this book is intended to provide an historical background
for the mental picture of the Sinhalese people which will be formed in the
reader’s mind. In the present chapter will be found a more detailed account
of the constitution of the Kandyan kingdom, and of the social economy of the Kandyans
in the 18th century. Sinhalese craftsmanship flourished exceedingly in the Kandyan
districts up to the very end of that century and even later, and almost the whole extent
of its decline coincides with the succeeding period of foreign rule and resulting decay
of the social organism; hence the importance of considering the social conditions of
the 18th century, if we are rightly to understand the craftsman and his art. If the
present chapter should appear at all superfluous, it should be remembered that the object
of this book is not merely to figure specimens of the work of Sinhalese craftsmen, but
to provide, if it be possible, some faint picture of a land and a time of which, even as
of Medisval Europe, it could be said ‘that in those times there was no such thing as
a piece of handicraft being ugly’; and this faint picture would be fainter still if we
should speak only of the craftsman’s handiwork and forget the man himself and his out­
look upon life.
At the close of the eighteenth century, the Kandyan kingdom consisted of ten disdvana or ..
districts, each in charge of a Dissva (earl), and nine other districts {rata) each in charge
of a chief usually known as the Ratemahdtmaya. All these districts together correspond
more or less with the area occupied by the present Central, Sabaragamuwa, Uva, North
Central, North Western (part), and Eastern (part) provinces, i.e., the whole of the
mountainous districts and some part of the low-country commanded by the mountains,
or which the Kandyan kings were otherwise able to protect.
The King ruled as an absolute monarch; his ministers could advise, but not control his Government
actions ; with him rested all decisions as to peace and war; he also promulgated edicts.
But the acts of his Government were presumed to be guided by the institutions of his
kingdom. Before innovations of importance were carried into effect, it was usual to
consult the principal chiefs and often also the principal priests, and such persohs were
usually called to councils when important matters were afoot. The King’s authority
was exercised through certain officers of State, of whom the two Adigars (‘Viziers’),
the Disavas, aijd the Ratemahatmayas were chief: the officers attached to the King’s
ho usehold (keepers of the robes, treasurer, armourer, etc.), the chiefs of departments
employed in his personal service (such as the Koftalbadde Nilame mentioned below) and
the principals of impi>rtant temples (the Diva Nilama of viharas and the Basnayaka Nilama
of devales) attended also on many public occasions.
The two Adigars possessed a general jurisdiction over the whole of the Kandyan
provinces; by them the King’s orders were communicated to the public and to the
chief residents in Kandy. The King’s orders to the chiefs resident in the provinces
were conveyed by olas (palm leaf mss.) written in the name of the first Adigar,
or in his absence from Kandy, in the name of the second. The Adigars were
c 2 19

Social charged with the conduct of public festivals, the repair of temples on behalf of the
economy King, and the catching of elephants in Kandy, and were expected to personally super­
intend all public works; they had charge also of the repair of the streets and of every
work contributing to the beauty and cleanliness of the capital. They had many other
duties, as well as various privileges and honours. Their staff of office consisted of
a lac-painted cane (vevela) curved at the top, which was delivered into their hands upon
their appointment; in former times the cane had merely a silver he^d and ferrule, but
a cane cased entirely in silver was introduced by the last king. For the better support
of their dignity, a disdvanaya was usually conferred upon each Adigar, in addition to
his own duties and offices. Under the Disavas and Ratemahatmayas were various minor
officers, such as Koralas, Vidanes, Araccis, etc. Independent of them were the officers
of public departments, and the principals of large temples.
’Justice The dispensation of justice was organized in a way that would not have been unsatisfactory,
had it been always purely administered; every person was at liberty to seek redress,
first by application to the headman of the village, next to the chief of the province, to
the Adigar, the ‘Great Court’ and finally to the King. But as (i) bribes were often
resorted to by both parties in a dispute, (2) fines levied belonged to the chiefs who levied
them, and these chiefs received no salary for their services, (3) the chiefs were occasionally
required by the King to make extraordinary contributions, necessarily exacted from the
people, and (4) the chief, as is the case in the Indian Civil Service to-day, combined
judicial and executive functions, it will be seen that opportunities for the miscarriage
of justice were not lacking. But the villager is scarcely less at the mercy of the headman
now than he was then. Nevertheless in many cases there can be no doubt that substantial
justice was obtained; it is said that there were some Kandyan chiefs reputed no less
for their ability in the investigation of suits than their integrity in the decision of them.
The customary laws regarding marriage, inheritance, crime, slaves, and the like are
detailed in the Nitinighaijduva (translation, Colombo, 1888), a work of fascinating interest
for the study of Sinhalese society.
The law’s delays were as proverbial as in England. One who appealed to the great court
or to the King might get immediate redress or might have to remain in Kandy for
months or years. Recourse was often had to swearing by ordeal of hot oil or red-hot
iron.* Litigation is now a much greater burden on the people than it was then, when
touting proctors had not been invented. It must be taken into consideration that the
people were naturally honest and law-abiding, and that even to-day the crime so prevalent
in the low-country districts long subjected to European influence is much less in the
interior; a more honest and trustworthy man than the unspoilt Kandyan villager it would
be hard to find. In illustration of his character I quote from a Government Agent’s
report of 1870, the following:
Character “ There is annually a gathering from all parts of the Island at Anuradhapura to visit
what are called sacred places. I suppose about 20,000 people come hefe, remain for a
few days, and then leave. There are no houses for their reception, but under the grand
umbrageous trees of our park-like environs they erect their little booths and picnic in
. the open air. As the height of the festival approaches, the place becomes instinct with
life; and when there is no room left to camp in, the later comers unceremoniously take
possession of the verandahs of the public buildings. So orderly is their conduct, however,
that no one thinks of disturbing them. The old Kacceri stands, a detached building
not far from the bazaar, and about one-eighth of a mile from the Assistant Agent’s house.

Mention must be made of Caste, especially as the caste system of Ceylon is similar to Caste
the Dravidian in South India and differs from the well-known four-fold caste division
of the Hindus generally. Vijaya himself could hardly have found a place in the
Brahmanical caste system. The Sinhalese people from an early date had constant and
intimate relations with the Tamils in Southern India. So it is that we find the Dravidian
and not the Aryan caste system amongst the Sinhalese. In this system the cultivator
ranked highest. With the spread of Aryan civilization came the Brahmanical system,
which was superimposed upon the Dravidian, so that the Brahman and Kshattriya
ranked above the cultivator. Hence the order of castes in Ceylon came to be—
I. Bamurfu (Brahmans); 2. Baja (the ruling caste); 3. Govt (cultivators); subsequently
the Velenda or merchant was added. But as there was no place for Brahmans in a
Buddhist country, and the royal family formed a caste by itself, and merchants were
few or none, the goviyo have remained to this day of chief importance from the caste
point of view. That is, the goviya, or veUala as he is often called, is the man of high
caste. The goviyn included three ranks, the chiefs {radala or mudali peruvd), the nobles
or titled men (sifanc), and the rest of the goviyS; and these together formed as we have
seen over ninety per cent, of the community.
Authorities differ somewhat as to the order of precedence of the remaining classes.
They are given in the following order by the Janavamsa, a most interesting Sinhalese
poem of the fifteenth century, often regarded as an authoritative work, especially by
the artificers, but according to others it has been adapted in their interests. The jana-
vamsa, by one Siipha of Kessellena, purports to be founded on a Pali original.* It gives
interesting but mainly fanciful accounts of the origin of the different castes and endeavours
to show that all men are really of one race though occupied in different ways; stress
being laid upon the well-known saying of Buddha, “Not by birth does one become
a Vasala (outcaste), not by birth does he become a Brahman. By deed does one become a
Vasala, by deed does he become a Brahman.” In spite of the recognition of such
teaching as truly Buddhist, the strength of caste feeling is but little less than in India; nor
is it otherwise even amongst the converts to Christianity.

Of all these, only Nos. i, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 13, 20, are really important elements in the

Slaves There were also a certain number of slaves {vdllu) but not very many, beihg persons born
so or who had become so in various ways, as by inability to pay a debt, by being sold as
children, or cast into slavery by. the king. Slavery was an economic institution and
did not interfere with caste distinctions. A man could not possess slaves of higher
caste than his own. Slaves could be freed or become free in various ways. Praedial
and domestic slavery of a mild form seems to have been an institution in most parts
of India from very remote times, although Megasthenes affirmed it “ a great thing that
no Indian slave existed.”

place regarding the relative rank of different castes; neither Buddhisrri nor Christianity
have greatly weakened the power of caste.

This is looking at the matter from the Western point of view. As a matter of fact, the idea Overlord-
is one rather of overlordship or dominion, than ownership of land as understood in the ship
modern west. It is probable that Sinhalese society “ developed itself, clearing by clearing,
in separate village communities, isolated from each other, and scattered over the land very
much as they evert now still are in the existing condition of the North Central Province. . .
The aggregation of a plurality of villages together under a common head . . . very soon
followed” (Phear). Thus arose the petty chieftain, who developed by a process of con­
solidation into a regulus or kinglet, becoming finally the king of the whole land. The
original chieftain did not own land ; what he possessed was the right to cultivate his own
share of village land, and also a right to certain contributions and services due to him from
the other shareholders. The King’s right arose by the gradual consolidation of such
rights into the hands of a central authority, and is therefore rather one of dominion than of
ownership. The point does not much affect the present issues, but reference in the text to
ownership of land should be taken as subject to this qualification of the implied idea. Even
praveiji lands dedicated to temples, were not absolute freeholds which the trustees could
dispose of as they liked; the land was still the King’s, and through him the people’s ; the
services only were dedicated for ever to the temple.

The kinds of villages were as follows :
1. Gabaiagam, or royal villages ; these usually contained lands which were cultivated Royal
entirely for the benefit of the crown, supplying all the requirements of the palace ; and manors
other lands which the tenants cultivated entirely for themselves ; or the crown land was
cultivated on the ayde (half share) system. Crown villages much resembled early English
royal manors ; they included original crown lands, and lands which had fallen in to the
crown by failure of the tenant to perform his service or by the death of a grantee.
2. Vihàregam, or villages belonging to a temple of Buddha. The tenants owed personal Religious
service to the temple or made payment in kind to the incumbent priests.* manors
3. Devalegam, or villages belonging to the temple of some deity.*
4. Nindagam, or villages which for the time being were the entire property of the grantee Private
or temporary chief ; if definitely granted by the King with a sannasa it became heredit- manors
able personal property and was called praveyi. The inhabitants in consideration for their
lands cultivated gratuitously for the benefit of the grantee and owed him other services. A
nindagama was to the proprietor what a gabadtlgama was to the king. Nindagam were
naturally highly prized by the grarrtees; they were usually bestowed as a reward for
eminent public services or bravery in battle, a policy followed by even the English as late
as iSao.j- Nindagam granted upon a sannasa are now the hereditary property of the
descendants of the original grantees.^
5. VidanSgam, villages under the orders of a Vidane, and containing usually people of low
caste liable to public service.
It will be clear from the account of the land system just given that both husbandmen and
craftsmen of all sorts worked either for the King, a religious foundation, or a chieftain, as
well as for themselves or their neighbours. Most of these services were themselves a
payment for lands held by the family, and so were not otherwise remunerated; and
even when work was done to order for a consideration, payment was made in kind,
usually shares of paddy from the threshing floor. It will be seen that there was very
little use of money, it was indeed so scarce that it •‘could hardly be said to be in circulation ;

Interdepen- No man was independent of another. Take the case of a nindagama-, the villagers held
dence of all lands of the proprietor for their Own use, on condition of cultivating the muttettuva, or
men proprietor’s special field; for this, one tenant, in respect of his panguva or share, had to
supply cattle for ploughing and threshing, or perhaps one gave cattle for ploughing and
another for threshing ; there might be others to attend to the irrigation ; others for plough-
ing,sowing and watching; others for threshing-floor service; and others for storing the crop;
and so in every case, there was a remarkable inter-relation of parts of the social organism.
The Sinhalese are now supposed to be incapable of concerted action and unfitted for
self-government; and perhaps the ‘educated’ (which usually means denationalised) classes
are so; but it may well be doubted whether the men who were capable of working together
successfully so complex an arrangement, and indeed, ordering all the details of their culti­
vation by mutual arrangement, and who have possessed their Parish Councils from a time
antedating the witanagcmots of England, are not as capable of self-government as are a
people whose Parish Councils are but a thing of yesterday and who seem to have lost the
sense of communal interests and capacity for concerted action in small matters. The
capacity has now been half destroyed, with the destruction of the society through which it
was expressed; but surely it is there still. Observe how remarkably the different parts
of the social organism were fitted and dovetailed together; there was a place for every
man, and no man could be spared; class distinctions were not invidious, nor emphasized
The Plough- by difference of culture. “Their ordinary Plowmen and Husbandmen do speak elegantly,
man fit to and are full of complement. And there is no difference between the ability and speech of
rule a king- a Couniry-man and a Courtier." A Sinhalese proverb runs, ‘Take a Ploughman from the
dom Plough and wash off his dirt, and he is fit to rule a kingdom.’ “This was spoken,” says
Knox, “of the People of Cande TJda . . . because of the Civility, Understanding and
Gravity of the poorest men among them.” This, in the words of Okakura,* is the “ spiritual
feudalism whereby caste makes a peasant in all his poverty one of the aristocrats of
humanity.” Honour, pride, noblesse oblige, are of the caste idea. But Buddha saw all
men as one and proclaimed the equality and brotherhood of all. Christ’s position in the
West was similar. In neither place has-ihe teaching been accepted. The Western forms
of caste are less rigid but more sordid thfan the Eastern; that is all that can be said.
Such an organization of society seems strange already, even in the East, so rapid has been
the ‘progress’ of the nineteenth century. There was no trade in land, nor did agricultural
labourers work for hire. Craftsmen made no goods for sale and kept no shops.-f “ Riches
were little valued nor made any the more honourable.” Yet there flourished a prosperous
agricultural community, a pure and intellectual religion, and a highly skilled and intelligent
race of craftsmen. It is probable that in respect of most real advantages, the Kandyan
villager was better off in the eighteenth century than he is now.

The villages were to a great degree isolated and self-contained, dependent on the outside Social
world for little but salt. A small external trade in Indian cloth and such things may have economy
been carried on by the Muhammedan ‘tavalam merchants’ who carried goods on pack
bulls along the steep and narrow jungle paths that led from village to village. No Villages
doubt Hindu and Muhammedan traders resided in Kandy. South Indian printed cot­ self-con
tons and gold woven cloths and brocades were purchased by the well-to-do for use as tained
ladies’ robes arrd for jackets for the chiefs; good specimens of such Ihdian textiles are
even now to be found in the possession of old families. For the dévale, printed ceiling
cloths with scenes from the purânas were needed ; these must have come from S. India,
or at least from Jaffna, which has still a small trade in printed cotton with the Sinhalese
provinces. Trade with the Dutch was a Royal monopoly. Cinnamon, elephants, areca Dutch
nut, other spices and arrack were the chief items of the trade ; money, metals (copper, Trade
lead, brass, iron and steel), Indian piece goods, china-ware (sent as presents to the King
and his officers of distinction) were the corresponding imports.
Reference must be made to the Muhammedan element in the population. Before the Muhamme-
fifteenth century the trade of the island had passed almost entirely into the hands of Arabs dans
who traded on the Indian seas. The trade included pearls, gems, spices, and elephants.
Later, there was much rivalry between these people and the Dutch. Arab adventurers
settled on the Indian and Ceylon coasts, intermarried with the inhabitants and became
important elements in the population. They were reinforced by coast Moormen from
Southern India, most of whom were actually converts ; at present a majority of Ceylon
Moormen are certainly of Tamil extraction.* A few of the Muhammedan communities
were settled in the interior, and owed services to the King, chieftains, or even to
Buddhist temples, chiefly the conveyance of grain on pack bulls.
It cannot be too well realised that the Sinhalese society was a community based on rice. Rice
Land was not the luxury of a few, but the daily occupation and livelihood of the majority ;
not to own land is still felt to be scarcely respectable. Every man from the King
down had an immediate interest in the cultivation of the land ; almost every man cultivated
the soil with his own hands. How markedly the same conditions still persist is shown
by the census of 1901 ; out of a thousand persons in the Central Province nine hundred
and six subsist by agriculture, thirty-two by the preparation and supply of material
substances, eighteen by personal service, ten by some profession, and nine by trade ; in
this tale craftsmen are included partly in the thirty-two who live by the supply of
material substances and partly in the ten professional, forming thus less than the 4‘2 per
cent, of the whole people which these two classes represent ; the proportion was probably
higher in the eighteenth century when artistic and literary production was more
appreciated.
'■ '■ Husbandry’’ says Knox, “is the great employment of the country. ... In this the best
men labour. Nor is it held any disgrace for Men of the greatest Quality to do any
work either at home or in the Field, if it be for themselves; but to work for hire with
th em is reckoned for a great shame : and vepy few are here to be found that will work so.”
Great chiefs were not ashamed to hold the plough in their own hands, and it was thought
becoming for the young men to reap at least a part of the harvest every year; for which
damascened and ivory-handled sickles were sometimes used. The great majority of men,
and amongst the village folk, of women also, were continually brought into close touch
with the soil and with each other by working together in the fields; even the crafts­
men did not as a body rely upon their craft as a direct means of livelihood, and used
