Social themselves to lay aside their tools to do a share of field work when need was, as at sowing
economy or harvest time. The structure of the regular Indian village community is every­
where apparent, more or less veiled or modified by later developments; the scattered
villages of the North Central Province show it best. It is true that the rice lands were
held individually and not as common property, but this did not remove the need for
communal action in cultivation, each shareholder or tenant or land-owner, as one may
prefer to call him, doing an amount of work proportional to the extent of his holding.
In such matters as fencing, water-supply and night-watching it would have been
absurd to deal with each field separately, and no-one ever thought of doing so. The
cultivators decided together in any year whether conditions allowed of the cultivation
of the whole or only a part of the fields, the water supply being thus treated as
common property due to each in the proportion of his holding. “At reaping they
are excellent good,” says Knox, “just after the English manner. The whole Town,
as I said before, as they joyn together in Tilling, so in their Harvest also; For all fall
in together in reaping one man’s Field, and so to the next, till every man’s Corn be
down. And the Custome is, that every man, during the reaping of his Corn, finds
all the rest with Victuals.” How strongly we are reminded of mediseval England, and
Langland’s “faire field ful of folke ... of alle maner of men, the mene and the riche.”
A great part of the cultivation was looked after by women, the custom varying in different
districts. But the presence of women at certain times and places was strictly taboo.
The ceremonial purity of the threshing floor was guarded with special care. A special
euphemistic vocabulary is made use of while threshing is going on ; women are prohibited
from entering, as are persons who have attended a funeral, or come from an ‘unclean’
house* (unless after bathing and putting on clean clothes), or have eaten unclean food.
Manorial An official named Gamerdla (like the bailiff of an English manor) was concerned with
organization the administrative organization needed to secure to the head of the village the rents and
services due to him; the office was usually hereditary in one of the wealthier families.
But as there was also much matter for internal administration in the village, in the interests
of the landholders themselves, they elected a Vel-viddne (like the praspositus of an English
manor) to control and carry out the system of fencing, ploughing, sowing, etc.
Village The village court, or gansabhdva, consisted of the principal and experienced men of
court the village who met at an ambalam or shady tree or other central place and gave doom
on civil and criminal disputes relating to boundaries, debts, thefts, and quarrels; they
were wont to aim at an amicable settlement, and directed their endeavours rather to
compromising a case than to the infliction of punishment. It will be seen that, as in
India, beneath the outward form of a despotic rule lay the democratic and communistic
organization of the villages. ,
Concerted The capacity for communal action is shown in the frequent cases of combination amongst
action villagers, to erect and endow viharas. This proof of the possibility of united action even
apart from Royal or viceregal patronage, is of particular promise for the future. Thus,
in Tumpane, the western division of the Central province, there were but few viharas
before the British accession, and the majority now existing have been built by villagers
since 1815, and endowed by them with small parcels of land. The villagers in such cases
had the right of selecting the incumbent on a vacancy, and also of ousting one who failed to
perform his duties. Thus, to take a special case, Yafivavala viharain Harispattuva, was
built in Kirti 8rl’s reign by the villagers, who dedicated small pieces of land consisting of
nine fields and four gardens. The King is said to have given an ivory image of Buddha

There is great charm as one walks along the narrow village paths, in coming suddenly Agricul-
upon some hillside clearing where twenty or thirty men are at work, singing in chorus turaJsongs
with an old man leading them; or a party of women weeding and singing as they work
across a field with stooping backs in the hot sun. They say that the singing makes
the labour less arduous and irksome; no doubt it does. There is a verse in the Makha
Deva Jataka, a Sinhalese poem of the thirteenth century, referring to such scenes—
“ Hundreds of girls he saw, tending the earladen fields of hill-rice, singing sweet songs
without fault, wherein his own life was praised.” Of agricultural songs I give a few
specimens. “In Rayigam Korale renowned there grew a famous /«/a-palm, fairer than
speech can tell, with various beauty crowned, from village unto village known; fair
of hue this palm flower bloomed, as it were lotus petals expanded on the tree.” This
is part of a reaping song in praise of a tala tree (talipot, Corypha umbraculifera), a tall
and beautiful flowering palm. A sowing song begins as follows: “ When the fields are
well prepared, which lie round Balagala hill, right quickly then the seed is sown by
the four Regents of the Earth.” A threshing song contains the following verses: “ O
bull-king leader of the team, O Veriya going next him, and Kalata the bull-calf, make
haste to get the threshing ended; I will get your twin horns gilt, deck your pair of ears
with pearls, your dew-claws likewise; thus I shall adorn you. Ye bulls that wander
by the hillside, yoked together by a woodbine, wearing pearls and coral beads, and eating
tender leaves, draw the grain into this threshing floor” ; and in another version, “This
is not our threshing floor, ’tis the Moon-god’s threshing floor; this is not our threshing
floor, ’tis the Sun-god’s threshing floor . . . etc.” The semi-religious character of many
of the agricultural songs is very noteworthy. Some, like the last quoted, are associated
with elaborate and often beautiful ceremonies, intended to avert disaster, and to secure
the growth and successful ingathering of the crop, others belong to that ‘ pagan ’ conception
of all life as a sacrament, which gives so much beauty and dignity to common things.
The great simplicity of ordinary life must always be kept in mind. The house was a Domestic
one-storied timber and mud wall building with thatched roof, and if belonging to a man architecture
of some importance consisted of a number of rooms arranged about an inner square
verandah (the floors being daubed with cow-dung to keep them clean and smooth), within
which, again, was a square yard {hatares-midula') open to the sky, where sometimes a
few potherbs might be grown. The rooms were rather dark, having unglazed windows
on the inside only, for the sake of privacy. The poorest house, however, had but one
room, few more than two or three, except the valavva or ‘manor house’ of a great man.
Ordinary houses were not often made by the craftsmen, but each man put up his own,
the kapurala performing the necessary ceremonies. A verse from a Cambridgeshire
traditional song, ‘ Ground for the Floor,’ exactly describes the situation within :
As for grates. I’ve got none, for my fire’s on the ground.
And chairs I’ve got none to set myself down;
I’ve a three-legged stool, it’s the chief of my store.
In my neat little cottage with ground for the floor.
Household work was done by the women on the inside verandah ; here they pounded
31

Social rice and kurakkan, and wove their mats. One room was set apart as a kitchen. A granary
economy (atuvd) was built up on stone pillars as a protection against white ants, on the inner
verandah, or formed a separate building outside. The house could be enlarged by the
addition of other courtyards surrounded by their own set of rooms, and in this way there
often grew up quite a large house, consisting of several associated but independent parts,
occupied by the families of near relations or of married sons or daughters. This is, of
course, a feature of the well-known joint family system.
Furniture Furniture was of the simplest. Three-legged stools, or shaped logs {kolombu) afforded
seats according to rank; none but the King might sit upon a stool with a back. Four­
legged beds were in general use, but often only by the master of the house, the women,
children and servants sleeping on mats on the floor ; some beds were elaborately and
beautifully carved. For the kitchen a set of earthern pots, a vegetable sheer, a coconut
scraper (hiramanaya'), a stone for grinding curry-stuffs (miris-gald), a water dipper {kinissa),
baskets for corn, wooden spoons, and a spoon rack {henditlna) were the principal require­
ments. Three stones (lig-gal) formed a cooking hearth, supporting an earthen pot over
a wood fire; but in some districts an earthen hearth in the form of a ring open at one
side served the same purpose. Earthern or brass coconut oil lamps afforded a dim light.
Agricultural implements, including the yoke {kada) for carrying burdens were also stored
in the house. Clothing, books (if any) and valuables were kept in wooden chests.
Cloths were also stored in earthen pots for their better protection against insects. Cot­
shaped wooden cradles were suspended from the roof. For eating purposes, those who
could afford it, had silver, brass or china dishes (resp., tfti, pingand) on which to lay the
plantain leaf from which the food was directly taken. The king’s plantain leaf was laid
on a gold plate. Honorable persons used a low brass stand (serak-kalé) as a small table for
eating from, being seated on a stool themselves ; others ate upon the ground, the plantain
leaf being laid on an elegantly plaited grass tray or dish (atulpata). All, of course, ate
with the fingers ; the women separately and after the men had been served. Beef was
wholly avoided, and flesh and fish but very little used, rice being the staple food ; but
the diet of well-to-do persons was sufficiently varied with numerous curries, rice and other
corn cakes and sweetmeats skilfully prepared by the women of the household, who, how­
ever high in rank, took pride in culinary operations. The common drink was water.
When drinking from a vessel the people avoided soiling it, by holding the pot at a distance
and pouring water into the mouth, or the hand held as a cup against the mouth.
Costume Together with this simplicity of life and general absence of luxury went a well-considered
love of beautiful dress, affording a remarkable contrast to the modern tendency to combine
every sort of personal luxury with gloomy European costume in its extremest forms.
There could hardly be imagined a more beautiful sight than a Kandyan lady (PI. II.)
wearing her embroidered bodice covered with a sari of old Indian brocade, bare-footed,
and covered with delicate tinkling chains and pendants, rings and bracelets, of which
profusion one feels that nothing could be spared. The full dress of chiefs (PI. III.) is
equally striking, but less beautiful.

Sumptuary The details of costume and many other matters were regulated by well-defined sumptuary
laws ‘laws. Artificers, according to Knox, wore the same apparel as the goviyB. Of the
barbers, both men and women might wear doublets, but not sit on stools. Potters might
not wear any doublet, nor the cloth below the knee, or sit on stools. The mal-gaha or
flower ornament on the hat, the eight-cornered hat, shoes, stockings, trousers and all
regalia such as the sword of state, umbrella of dominion, and royal jewellery none but the
king might use. So, too, plastered walls, tiled roofs, finials and two-storied buildings
were forbidden to all save the King, temples, and the highest officers. The modes of
salutation, and even the language employed, varied according to the rank of the person
addressed. Great nicety in the employment of the proper titles for any occasion was
used.
Speaking of the difference in costume of the classes, Knox says of the ‘ Hondrews ’ {goviyd):
“These are distinguished from others by their names, and the wearing of their cloth, which
the Men wear down half their Legs, and the Women to their Heels: one end of which
Cloth the Women fling over their Shoulders, and with the very end carelesly cover their
Breasts; whereas the other sort of Women must go naked from the wast upwards, and
their Cloaths not hang down much below their Knees: except it be for cold; for then
either Women or Men may throw their Cloth over their Backs. But then they do excuse
it to the Hondrews, when they meet them, saying. Excuse me, it is for warmth.
They are distinguished also by their own Countrey Caps, which are of the fashion of
Mitres; there are two flaps tied up over the top of the Crown. If they be Hondrews, their
Caps are all of one Colour, either White or Blew : if of inferior quality, then the Cap
and the flaps on each side be of different Colours, whereof the Flaps are always Red.”
These caps are no longer worn, and were already out of fashion in the eighteenth century.
Their appearance is illustrated on Plate XXX., in figure 3. I do not know what the
knitted caps made by Knox and his fellow-prisoners in such quantities (Knox, p. 129)
were like, probably there are none of these in existence now. It is now usual, and
probably was so in the eighteenth century also, for any but officers on duty, to wear no
hat, or only a kerchief arranged turband-wise ; or in some districts, when engaged in field
work, enormous hats of bamboo leaf (bafa kola toppiya) or smaller low-crowned hats of
plaited grass.
One other garment must be mentioned, the diya-kacciya, described more fully in the
chapter on Weaving. It was the dress of runners and watchmen or guards (murakdraya),
(see PI. V.); and also a bathing costume generally; it is said also to have been regularly
worn as an undergarment. Those worn by persons of rank were elaborately and beauti­
fully ornamented.

The women’s costume at the present day, in the low-country consists of a loose, low-cut
bodice, and a cloth round the lower part of the body, and is said to be of Malay origin,
like the tortoise-shell combs worn by low-country men.
The position of women, as usual in Buddhist countries, was good in many respects. The Position of
property of husband and wife remained distinct, the husband having no power over his •women
wife’s estate,—-an advantage very newly won in England, but of long standing in the
East, despite the supposed slavery of women there. Women could inherit service lands
and could exercise much influence. Seclusion was not customary, unless amongst the
aristocracy ; it is probably more fashionable now than in the middle ages. According
to Knox, there was rather too great freedom than the reverse, parents regarding their
daughters’ lovers with favour, on account of the services they were willing to render when
need was. What spirit and character Kandyan women could show is illustrated by more
than one anecdote. In the early days of British rule, Miyanadeijiya Lekam of Degaldoruva
was robbed in his own house by Malay desperadoes, and such wounds inflicted that his
bowels gushed out ; but such was his firmness, that he bound up his bowels with his
waistcloth and found time before his death to leave his property to his only daughter,
whose subsequent evidence led to the conviction and execution of the robbers ; so
courageous had been her behaviour throughout, that a grant of land was specially made
to her by the Government (Lawrie’s Gazetteer, p. 137). One heroic tale sounds more
like a story of the Rajputs than one of the Sinhalese. It relates the history of a woman
trained in arms, whose prowess so delighted the king (sixteenth or seventeenth century)
that he rewarded her with gifts of elephants and lands, and made her Disava of the Four
Korales (Bell, Kegalla Report, p. 50).

garden Hevanetenne Megodavatte with the one pela ând five lâhas extent of Darandra;

Women Religious dedications by women were not unusual. For example, Lat Etana, grand­
daughter of Abeyakon Mudiyanse of Medivaka Minuvangomuva, ‘did many meritorious
acts with a view of obtaining the other world.’ Her daughter, Kuda Etana, offered
to the Dalada Maligava certain lands, ‘ reserving her right to possess on giving one bag
of rice to the Maligava each year,’ and made other offerings of robes, books, mats and
cloths, and ‘for a general almsgiving,’ twenty-two cloths, three cows with calves, five
bill-hooks, five axes, five sickles, two areca-nut slicers and lime boxes, two sets ear-flowers,
and six silver bangles.” The merits of these offerings were to be shared by the gods,
the king, the ministers, the incumbent of both viharas, the low and high inhabitants
of the world, her ancestors, herself, and her dead relations, ‘and may I obtain such blessings
as to see the future Buddha’ (Lawrie’s Gazetteer, p. 586).
Knox’s account of Kandyan women is as follows :
“They are in their gate and behaviour very high, stately in their carriage after the Portugal
manner, of whom I think they have learned : yet they hold it no scorn to admit the
meanest to come to speech of them. They are very thrifty, and it is a disgrace to them
to be prodigal, and their Pride and Glory to be accounted near and saving. And to
praise themselves they will sometimes say. That scraps and parings mil serve them; but
that the best is for their Husbands. The Men are not jealous of their Wives, for the greatest
Ladies in the Land will frequently talk and discourse with any Men they please, altho
their Husbands be in presence. And altho they be so stately, they will lay their hand
to such work as is necessary to be done in the House, notwithstanding they have Slaves
and Servants enough to do it.”
Character Of the character and manners of Kandyans generally, Knox remarks (pp. 63-5, and 97)
(Knox) “They are a people proper and very well favoured. . . . They are very active and nimble
in their limbs and very ingenious. . . . They are crafty and treacherous, not to be trusted
upon any protestations : for their manner of speaking is very smooth and courteous,
insomuch that they who are unacquainted with their dispositions and manners, may
easily be deceived by them. For they make no account nor conscience of lying, neither
is it any shame or disgrace to them, if they be catched in telling lies ; it is so customary.*
They are very vigilant and wakeful, sufficed with very little sleep : very hardy both for
diet and weather, very proud and self conceited. . . . They are not very malitious one
towards another ; and their anger doth not last long ; seldom or never any blood shed
among them in their quarrels. It is not customary to strike ; and it is very rare that
they give a blow so much as to their Slaves; who may very familiarly talk and dis­
course with their Masters. They are very near and covetous, and will pinch their own
bellies for profit ; very few spendthrifts or bad husbands are to be met with here. ... Of
all Vices they are least addicted to stealing, the which they do exceedingly hate and abhor ;
so that there are but few Robberies committed among them. They do much extol and
commend Chastity, Temperance, and Truth in words and actions; and confess that it
* Largely a matter of politeness, and without expectation of the person addressed being really
deceived, as in England ^ Not at home' stands for ‘ Will not see you.' A Kandyan will promise
anything, rather than appear ill mannered; it is your own fault if you look for performance.

is out of weakness and infirmity, that they cannot practice the same, acknowledging Social
that the contrary Vices are to be abhorred, being abomination both in the sight of God economy
and Man. . . . When they travel together a great many of them, the Roads are so narrow,
that but one can go abreast, and if there be Twenty of them, there is but one Argument
or Matter discoursed of among them all from the first to the last. And so they go talking
along all together, and every one carrieth his Provisions on his back for his whole Journey.
. . . At their leisure when their affairs will permit, they commonly meet at places built
for strangers and way-faring men to lodge in, in their Language called Amblomb, where
they sit chewing Betel, and looking one upon the other very gravely and solidly, discoursing
concerning the Affairs at Court, between the King and the great men; and what Employ­
ment the People of the City are busied about. For as it is the chief of their business
to serve the King, so the chief of their discourse is concerning such matters. Also they
talk of their own affairs, about Cattel and Husbandry. And when they meet with
Outlandish-men they enquire about the Laws and Government of their Countrey, and
if it be like theirs; and what Taxes and Duties we are bound to pay, and perform to
our King, &c.
“In short, in Carriage and Behaviour they are very grave and stately like unto the l!hey are
Portugals, in under standing quick and apprehensive, in design subtil and crafty, in grave and
discourse courteous but full of Flatteries, naturally inclined to temperance both in meat stately
and drink, but not to Chastity, near and Provident in their Families, commending good [Knox)
Husbandry. In their dispositions not passionate, neither hard to be reconciled again
when angry. In their Promises very unfaithful, approving lying in themselves, but
misliking it in others; delighting in sloath, deferring labour till urgent necessity con­
strain them, neat in apparel, nice in eating; and not given to much sleep.”
The four great annual festivals [mangalya*) are the Avurudu (New Year) in Vesak Fouinannual
(May), the Perahera in Ehala (July), the Karti or feast of lights (Hindu Dipavali) in festivals
II (November), and the Alutsal (harvest-home) in Duruffa (January). The great annual
holidays occupied two or three weeks previous to the New Year; at this time the fields
do not require much attention, the craftsmen are idle, and the people engage in games,
such as atfikeliya. Before the New Year, it was the duty of the astrologers to prepare a
notice, giving information of (i) the day and precise minute of its commencement; (2) the
auspicious hour for the NSnumura mangalya; (3) the auspicious hour for taking the first
cooked food ; (4) the hour for taking the first bath; (5) the hour for commencing business;
and (6) the auspicious hour for making presents. The Nanumura mangalya is a purification
ceremony immediately following the New Year, in which use is made of a composition

Alutsal The Alutsal mangalya or harvest-home took place in January; the astrologers fixed two
mafigalya auspicious hours, one for bringing in the new rice, the other for dressing and eating it.
It was brought into Kandy from the royal and temple villages, the ears of rice in earthern
pots and the grain in clean white bags. The grain for the Maligava was conveyed on
an elephant, that for the devales and the palace was carried by men on yokes under covers
{gahoni) of white or clean cloth; they were met on the way by the Adigars and chiefs,
who attended them to the great square, and there the auspicious hour was awaited, after
which the grain was taken to its various destinations. At the same time the chiefs and
people in the country brought home the new rice in a similar fashion. Two or three days
afterwards occurred the auspicious hour for eating the first new rice of the season, dressed
in a particular manner.
Buddhism Some mention of religion must be made. The universal and state religion even under
most of the Tamil kings* was Buddhism. Any detailed account of Buddhism would be
out of place here; and the information is easily obtained elsewhere. But this much
should be understood, that it is a moral philosophy, founded by the great reformer,
Gotama Buddha (d. 543 b.c.), and distinguished more or less clearly from the Brahmanical
Hinduism on which it is founded, by its condemnation of ritual observances and sacrifices,
its rejection of all kinds of animism, its insistence on the equality and brotherhood of
all men, and by its monastic institutions. The existence of gods and heavens is not denied,
but they,' like man and earth, are not eternal, and do not give the highest unchanging
bliss; those whose merits bring them even to the highest heavens are not freed from
the necessity for rebirth in this or other worlds. The existence of individual souls is
denied, as is also that of a God or creator. Personal existence is an evil; the goal before
all humanity is the attainment of an unconditional state free from the operation of causality,
and called Nirvaria; this state is beyond the range of perception of gods and unenlightened
men. It corresponds to the fourth state of the Vedantist, of union with Brahma, that
is Being, of which nought else can be predicated save existence. But many Southern
Buddhists hold Nirvaija to be strictly annihilation, there being no remainder when the
elements composing individuality are dispersed.
Nirvaija is to be obtained not by prayer or by sacrifices, but by freeing the mind from
all attachment and desire. Rapid spiritual progress is only possible to the ascetic; but
extreme ascetism and self-torture are condemned as much as sensuous self-indulgence,
both hindering progress. But the simple mode of salvation, the ‘middle way’ for those
who remain in the world, and in^whom the immediate desire for emancipation has not
become intense, is self-restraint, and the performance of good actions without regard to
reward, and without thought of .ah Imrja'My. This means of salvation thus corresponds
to the karma-yoga of Hinduism, and is that which makes the rhost general appeal to
good men everywhere.
In practice. Buddhism is a religion of love and pity shown to all living beings; and affords
a sufficient sanction for morality in its recognition of the immutable laws of cause and effect,
or karma, the d.ue recompense, in this world or the next, inevitably attending upon every
action. But a great part of the secret of the success of Buddhism lay in the dynamic force
of the Buddha’s own personality, and the intensity of his love for all living beings. It

It is quite impossible to summarise all the stories of the jatakas usually painted on
vihara walls. The Vessantara story is given by way of example. But the variety is
infinite; the Bodhisat* was born not only as a man, but very often as an animal or a deva.
The whole series of stories forms not merely a collection of edifying fables, of which
many are very beautiful, but is the most valuable collection of early folk-lore extant.
The stories are accessible in English, in the translation edited by Prof. Cowell, and
published at Cambridge (1895—1907); the last of the six volumes of this work has
just been issued.-f- The jatakas most usually illustrated are the Vessantara, Sattubhatta,

Maitri Representations of '■ Maitri' Buddha are often the subject of Vihara paintings, as at
Buddha Degaldoruva or Ridi Vihara on the rock ceilings. Maitri Buddha, the ‘loving one,’
is that bodhisatva or Buddha-elect who is to be next in the order of succession of these
great beings. The love of Buddhists turns naturally to such an one, still personal and
‘human,’ since the Buddha himself having reached nirvaija, has reached an unconditioned
state, unrelated to the world of men. In Ceylon, Nata deviyo is regarded as the Maitri
Buddha. At present he is in Divyaloka, where he awaits the time of his last incarnation,
and the attainment of Buddhahood.
Goiama Certain events in the actual life of Gotama Buddha must be related here, as they are so
Buddha often illustrated on vihara walls. The enlightenment (attaining of Buddhahood) took
place beneath the Bo-tree where the Prince had remained during the terrible mental
struggle symbolized in the descriptions and representations of his conflict with Mara,
the ‘devil’ of this temptation in the wilderness. The Prince was seated upon a throne
beneath the tree; the powers of evil, led by Mara, made repeated and terrific attacks
upon his person, accompanied by portents and horrors of every description (PI. XIV., 2).

These powers are depicted as material beings, fiends and devils of every kind, brandishing Social

The conflict is spoken of as Mara yuddhaya, Mara’s battle. yuddhaya
The less philosophical Buddhists no doubt believe in the real material conflict thus repre­
sented ; for others it is merely a symbol. As such it is most suggestive. The serenity
of the seated figure is powerfully contrasted with the vain efforts of the loathsome and
horrible devils around ; the devotion of the Earth Goddess is the crowning touch.
Ere the sun set, Mara abandoned the vain contest, and withdrew ; but the daughters
of Mara in the forms of beautiful women now approached and tempted him; but he
remained indifferent; and so the struggle ended. Hour by hour the divine insight of
the Prince grew, till by dawn came perfect knowledge, and the long-sought Buddhahood
was attained. The event was accompanied by many portents, of which one was the
spreading of the six-coloured aura (Budures) emanating from his body, throughout
all the spheres. In many seated figures of Buddha, this aura is represented as a halo
of coloured rays (Pis. XVIII, XIX). Also the Buddha broke into triumphant song, using
as a parable of life, the simple wood and clay-built house which in his time must have
differed little from the ordinary houses of the Sinhalese in the eighteenth century.
Then followed the period known as the satsatiya,* seven weeks. During the first he ^Satsatiya'
remained seated in the spot where the victory was won ; during the second he remained
in contemplation, with eyes fixed on the sacred tree beneath which he had been seated;
then he walked to and fro between that spot and the throne for seven days; then for
seven days he remained in a golden palace erected by the Devas, and as he sat here, the
whole of the Dharma, or truth, revealed presented itself to his mind, from the first words
spoken after enlightenment and quoted above to the last before his death. During the fifth
week he rested beneath a tree named Ajapkla. In the sixth week he sat by the lake
Mucalinda, and during a terrific storm was sheltered by the Naga Mucalinda, who erected
his hood as a canopy above him. During the last week he dwelt in a certain grove of
Khlrapala trees. Throughout this time he ate no food. On the fiftieth day two Brahman
merchants approached the place, and guided by a Devi who appeared in the sky, went
towards the Buddha, desiring to make offerings of honey. The story goes on to relate
that as it was not right for Buddha to receive anything in the hands, the Regent Gods
of the Four Quarters appeared, having each an almsbowl of emerald; but he would not
accept this. They then offered four bowls of stone, and when each entreated him to
accept the one offered by himself, Buddha received them all, and formed them into one
bowl, the fourfold origin of which appeared at the upper rim. In this bowl he received
the offering. Subsequently Buddha proceeded to Benares, and there began his mission,
preaching to all men the Dharma, and founding the order of Buddhist monks.
The following five precepts {pan-sil) are binding on the laity in general: not to destroy Pan-sil, the
life , not to steal, to refrain from adultery, falsehood, and intoxicants. Three other Jive precepts
precepts are observed on special occasions: not to eat at unseasonable hours, to abstain

and broad beds, and from sexual intercourse of any kind. The eight precepts {ata-sil) Ata-sil

Social thus indicated, are observed for twenty-four hours on the four pohoya or sabbath days

Giving of A beautiful aspect of Buddhist belief is the ‘giving of merit.’ This is the giving to
merit others of a share in the merit acquired by one’s own acts. The original merit is not
diminished, any more than a lamp from which a hundred lamps have been lighted burns
the dimmer. A Buddhist mother will take her child by the hand, when she goes with her
offerings of food or flowers to the Vihara, not merely that he may be trained in the path
of love and charity, but that he may share the merit of her actions. The great pilgrimage
to Adam’s Peak is similarly a means both of acquiring merit, and an opporunity of
bestowing it on others. The pilgrimage to Adam’s Peak is the outing of the year.
Parties of men, women, and children are made up and they trudge afoot from their own
villages to the summit of the peak, there lay their offerings upon the great footmark,
and so return home. A good deal of rough living is involved, but the whole expedition
is a delight, as one may judge who has met such a party of pilgrims on the narrow tracks
beyond Ratnapura, or even on the main roads below, singing almost continuously, carrying
their little store of luggage in a double bag (ploguvd) slung over the shoulder. The songs
show clearly that great sympathy which the people feel for one striving to become a
Buddha, and show also the spell which the great forest and high mountain cast upon them.
Very magnificent and very tender is the idea of helping the god by sharing with him the
merit of the pilgrimage; not that the merit is thereby lessened to the pilgrim, though
it is areal gift to the divinity. A few verses from the ^rl Paga Mana, one of the most
popular songs, are as follows :
Entering the forest of the god.
Beholding the god’s auspicious forest.
Bestowing merit on the god with cheerful heart.
Ever making him our refuge;
Buddha first all men adore.
They travel many a yodun in the forest.
Thinking of Saman DeviyO as they come,
‘By virtue of these merits (that we give) the Buddhahood thou shalt attain.’
Go we all to worship Samanala,
And overcome the ocean of rebirth.
Let us offer all these flowers and lamps.
Let us sing all through the forest!
Even very old and infirm people undertake this pilgrimage; it was undertaken by more
than one king. Lawrie (p. 119) mentions that Kapuvatte Kumarihami, a very wealthy
lady, ‘in old age and extreme weakness . . . undertook a pilgrimage to Adam’s Peak,
and died in February, 1884, when she was being carried down the mountain on the back
of one of her vassals.’

The object of the institution of the priesthood was “to cause the most virtuous, intelligent, Social
unselfish and spiritual-minded persons in a country to withdraw from the social surroundings economy
where their sensual and other selfish desires were naturally strengthened, devote their
lives to the acquisition of the highest wisdom, and fit themselves to teach and guide others Buddhist
out of the pleasant path leading towards misery, into the harder path that leads towards priesthood
true happiness and liberation.” No vow of obedience bound the monk ; “mental culture,
not mental death was the aim set before the Buddhist ascetic by the founder of his order.
Each one is to conquer self by himself” (Rhys Davids, ‘Buddhism’). A monk was always
free to cast off his robes and return to the world if he wished.
The principal duties of a Buddhist priest, beside the observance of the ten precepts, are to
care for the vihâra (Buddhist temple), keep it clean, and offer flowers daily, meditate and
study ; receive the offerings of worshippers, administer pansil and ata-sil on pahoya days ;
explain the teachings of Buddha when required ; read and expound the scriptures (bana)
on special occasions (particularly during Vas season) ; perform pirit service when required ;
superintend repairs to the vihâra buildings, and generally oversee the service of tenants;
often also they taught the children and practised medicine ; the priest in fact should be,
often was, and still sometimes is, the intellectual centre of the village. Of the relations
between priest and people the Temple Lands Commissioners speak as follows:
“ Besides the relation in which the priests stand to their tenants as landlords, and the
religious influence of their possession, they have other holds on the affection of the people.
Their pansalas are the schools for village children, and the sons of even the superior head­
men are very generally educated at them. They have also, frequently, some knowledge
of medicine, and when this is the case they generally give the benefit of their advice
gratuitously, which the vedarala seldom do. Add to this that, as every revenue officer
who has ever attempted to induce the natives to exert themselves for their own good
knows, the priests are generally, when properly applied to, foremost with their money,
if rich, or with their influence or both, in furthering every scheme for local improvement ;
and from what has been stated, it will be evident that not only is it their interest to be
kind and considerate to their tenants, but that they generally are so, and that their influence
among the people is, in a social point of view, usefully employed ” (quoted S.T. Report,
1872), p. 448. There was thus a close parallel between the position of the incumbent
of the village vihâra, and that of the parish priest of mediæval England; he, too, had
tithes and rents to gather in, and he taught the children at the church door, as the Buddhist
priest did in the pansala. Each at his best’, represented to the community the true ideal
of the man of religion
Buddhism was itself already founded on Hinduism, and close akin to some of the higher
forms of it ; and the outward forms of popular Hinduism have in later times been mixed Devales
with it, a fact not surprising when we consider the lóng continued Tamil influence on
Sinhalese religion, exerted through the Tamil queens and sometimes through actual Tamil
rulers, and in countless other ways. Hence it is that we find attached to almost every
vi hâra, a dévâle (devâlaya) where some Hindu god is worshipped, often under the same
roof, though not officially recognized by the Buddhist priest. The dëvâles are generally
endowed with lands after the manner of Buddhist temples ; the lay trustee [Basnayaka
Nilame), often a personage of political importance Corresponding to the Diva Nilame of a
Buddhist temple, and having jurisdiction over inhabitants of dévâle villages, while the
priest {kapurala or kapuva) was usually the principal tenant of the dévâle. Offerings
are commonly made by worshippers at both vihàras and dëvâles, the one with a view to
purely spiritual benefits, the other with a view to material ones. But the dévâles were
almost as much political as religious institutions.
45

Social The principal dévales are dedicated to the following five Hindu gods: {i)Vishnu; not
economy much resembling the Hindu Vishpu, but a Buddhist archangel, a candidate for Buddha-
hood and a tutelary deity of Lanka : (2) Nata deviyo, who is to the Buddhist no other
'Principal than the Maitri Buddha^ or Buddha of the next epoch, at present in the world of
gods of gods: (3) Kataragam deviya (see p. i) : (4) Pattini, goddess of chastity (see p. 6) : and
devales (5) Saman (Lakshmand), half-brother of Rama, who, with Vishiju and Kartikeya accepted
the general trust of guarding Lanka for Gotama Buddha ; Saman is the special deity and
guardian ofârl Pàda (Adam’s Peak), called after him, Samanaja.
Nature Beside these great Hindu gods thus worshipped in a somewhat altered form, a number
spirits of lesser beneficent divinities are also worshipped upon special occasions, as for example
Gana deviyo (Ganèéa), Bhomi devi (goddess of the earth, who alone remained by Buddha
when all other gods fled in terror of Mara’s attack) ; minor deities (devatavo) and nature
spirits, such as the guardians of the threshold and the door ; spirits dwelling in trees,
who should be propitiated before the tree is felled, and the like. The sun and moon
are regularly spoken of as gods, but are not worshipped with offerings, though often
invoked or mentioned with others in religious songs.
Demonism A very large element of demonism or devil propitiation also enters into popular religion,
and represents a survival of pre-Buddhist devil-dread ; the rites, carried out by priests
known as Kaffafya or Takdessa {ivomyaka, a demon), are directed to the cure or infliction
of disease by the aid of the demons.
Planet There is also planet worship to be mentioned, as well as the ordinary widespread reliance
worship upon astrology. Planet worship consists in the propitiation of planetary gods by bali
ceremonies. In connection with some of these the most elaborate temporary images
are made in wet clay ; some are repulsive, but certain of those representing gods are
dignified and even beautiful (PI. IV., 2). The rites are usually performed only by men
of low caste, especially beravayO.
Buddhism The attitude of Buddhism to the arts demands some consideration here. Buddhism
and art holds the one great aim of life, the goal for which all should strive, to be salvation from
the round of repeated or individual existence ; and considers rapid spiritual progress to
be compatible only with an ascetic life. By those that seek to follow the path that leads
to such salvation, even the highest intellectual and emotional pleasures must be renounced.
The priesthood accordingly were required, amongst other things to abstain from dancing,
singing, music and stage plays, not to use ornaments, nor to sleep on high or broad beds.
They were allowed to possess personally only their robes, a loin girdle, an alms-bowl,
a razor, a needle, a water strainer, a fan, and a pair of sandals, eight articles in all. The
robes were to be of dull orange colour (originally selected as a colour regarded with con­
tempt) and made of material first torn to pieces and then sewn together, so as to be of
no commercial value. But the priestly community as a whole could be endowed with
books, lands and houses, and so became at various times quite wealthy ; the houses were
often by no means lacking in adornment of carving and metal work ; also it often happened
that presents of beautifully adorned examples of one or other of the eight requisites were
made to individual priests, and were handed down by them in pupillary succession ; as
for example ivory-handled fans, beautifully decorated books and silk robes ; but all such
possessions made but a small item, and the vow of individual poverty has been for the
most part well kept, except at times of admitted degeneracy in the church. But it
appears that priests were sometimes wealthy enough to build or repair viharas and make
gifts (Lawrie’s Gazetteer, p. 688, Palkutubure Unnànse) ; for an example of the in­
heritance of land, books, fan, bowl, etc., in pupillary succession see the same, p. 856;
but the goods are to be in charge of certain lay trustees, who were to be responsible.
46

‘Form, sound, taste, smell, touch, these intoxicate beings; cut off the yearning which Social
is inherent in them’ says the Dhammika Sutta, addressed to priests. Again, the first of economy
the ten ‘objects’ on which the thoughts of an ordained priest should dwell runs thus:
‘Beauty is nothing to me,— neither the beauty of the body nor that that comes of dress’ Asceticism
(Dasa Dhamma Suttam) ; but of course the beauty of Buddha’s own person is frequently
insisted on in Buddhist literature. As example of the ascetic attitude may be quoted the
story of Citta Gutta and the cave with the painted roof, from the Viiuddhi Marggaya
(first quarter of the fifth century a.d.) : —“Once on a time a number of monks were walking
from cave to cave, inspecting in them various paintings which were found to charm
the eye, and so came to the rock cave, Karanda Maha Lena. Seeing in this cave the
representations in paint of the seven Buddhas, Vipassiya, Sikhiya, Vessabhuya, Kakusand-
haya, Konagamanaya, Kassapaya and Gautamaya in the act of departing (renonucing
worldly pleasures) to become monks preparatory to attaining Buddhahood, they remarked
to the great monk (Citta Gutta Thera) who had been dwelling in it, ‘These paintings
are attractive’; and he addressing them, ‘Evetni (long life !), I who am living in this cave
have passed sixty years (in it), but no such paintings have ever come under my notice.
However, now because of you who have eyes, I have come to know of the existence of
the paintings.’ This great monk who has been dwelling in this rock cave for so long a
time, never opened his eyes and looked up, as he was wont to look about him only within
the distance of a yoke (about eight feet). Opposite this rock cave there is a huge na-tree.
This great monk, however, did not see (the top of) it. But when every year it flowered
in season, he saw the pollen, etc., of the flowers on the ground, and had thus discovered
that the tree had blossomed.”
This attitude is logical in the case of one who believes that rapid spiritual progress can Asceticism
thus only be made, and who is in haste. But it is admitted that spiritual progress pan be notf or all
made in other ways, and perhaps not much less quickly, for example, by the performance
of right action without attachment to the fruit. And for those who tread such paths art
is a means and an aid to spiritual progress, but it is important that it should be so used,
and not as an hindrance. And so like everything else, it has been made a part of religion.
The ascetic path has never been for all men, and all occasions. The citizen or ‘house­
holder’ is first, as without him the race would not continue and the purpose of the cosmos
would fail. Art is of the first importance as the form of culture which most easily
humanises his toil and spiritualizes his ideas. So long as man is related to the world
of phenomenal appearance, whether real or not, art of some kind is the necessary means
of spiritualizing that relation. This applies as much to the ornament of utilitarian objects
and to architecture, as to the purely substantive and ideal art which definitely aims at
the revelation of the divine. All art is a very essential part of culture, an integral and
inseparable part of any noble ‘ civilization.’ The ornament added lightly by the craftsman
to an every-day utensil, is at once the humanization of his labour, and the witness that man
does not live by bread alone.
B uddhism became indeed the chief patron rather than the opponent of fine arts, which Buddhism
spread with it from India to Ceylon, Burma, Siam, and Java in the south, and to China patron of
and Japan in the north. It thus came to pass that it was important for even the priests arts
to have some knowledge of the theoretical side of craftsmanship at least, and this was often ,
the case ; they were rather expected to explain such works as Sariputra to the less learned
craftsman than to learn from him. In the eighteenth century there were even craftsmen
amongst the priesthood; but unordained, as the Siamese sect which alone existed then
admitted only men of high caste to the priesthood itself (quite contrary to true Buddhism);
such a man was Silvatenna, who painted at Degaldoruva and Ridi vihara.
47

Social With regard to the conventionalism of Buddhist (and Hindu) art, and the strict rules of
economy proportion for the figure, we shall see that these probably originated (in India) amongst a
class of more or less priestly crattsmen perhaps, indeed probably, before the decay of
Convention Buddhism in India, not among the monks themselves. Just how long ago the rules were
in Buddhist formulated is uncertain (to hazard a guess, by the fifth century a.d., before the final decline
art of Buddhism in India, and when the craftsmen were still required to satisfy the require­
ments both of Buddhists and of Hindus), but no doubt one object of them was to make
possible the reproduction of images in suiHcient quantity by average workmen at all times.
This, rightly, I think, sets religious above ‘artistic’ considerations; but, art having thus
sought first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, the rest was added to it. For
such convention is a far greater help than hindrance to real art. It does not prevent the
man of genius from producing the most beautiful work possible, though ensuring that
it shall so far conform to an accepted standard as to be immediate and universal in its
appeal; at the same time it does prevent the possibility of“ the holy and elevating subjects
being treated absurdly or stupidly, so as to wound tbe feelings of serious men”; which
happens every day now that the old tradition is generally broken with. It is true that
present-day painters and imagers have no feeling for the human figure, and images of
Buddha are usually wooden and unrefined, sometimes even repulsive in aspect; yet even
the worst traditional work is preferable to the weak, effeminate and sensuous drawing
of low-country workmen, who under Western influence have attempted a more naturalistic
style, without any training whatever, and certainly without taste. The Burmese alabaster
Buddhas now so fashionable are equally offensive. The old tradition did really ensure a
certain dignity of treatment, however blindly and unfeelingly its rules were followed.
What is now needed is for men who do understand the human figure (— as the makers of
the tradition must have done—) and whose faith is real, to work willingly and consciously
on traditional lines, welcoming the tradition as a help, not rejecting it as a hindrance;
for the artist cannot again command the hearts of men, without some relation to the
symbols that have for so long appealed to them, and with which are bound up such
manifold and complex associations, and so much that is changeless and eternal.
Buddhism Buddhism in practice has also been the patron of the lesser arts, as every vihara and library
and the testifies. Kings, and others according to their means, made gifts of gold and silver plate,
lesser arts books with painted or carved ivory or chased metal covers, to the viharas, and ornamented
furniture (from pottery to beds) to the priesthood, and such things as writing styles and
fans to individual priests. Kirti ^rl gave so much, that he has now the credit of having
given almost everything of value now to be found in Kandyan Viharas. In a tudapata
of 1803 A.D., regarding the Kotabogofla Vihara, it is mentioned that Kirti 8rl ‘built the
Dalada temple in Kandy anew . . . and . . . did likewise make offerings of his own orna­
ments of gold and set with gems, pearls and diamonds, high and low lands, men slaves and
women slaves, elephants, horses, white and black cattle’ (Lawrie’s Gazetteer, p. 472).
In 1815 A.D. one Upasaka Ranhoti Duraya (a lay preacher) of Haputale made offerings
to a vihara, of a “flag, beds, sheets, pillows, mattresses, brooms, iron walking-sticks,
blank ola leaves for writing, daitdisana, pitchers, cans, spittoons, and tom-toms.” An
image was made by subscription ; an ambalam was erected and several idai}4u (log bridges)
placed in position; note the practical charity. The temple itself “ was built by the
villagers, who joined in asweddumizing (reclaiming) a number of little deoiyas throughout
the hena” (Lawrie’s Gazetteer, p. 328). Artificers were regularly employed for years
together on religious buildings, and well rewarded for their work. Craftsmen holding
temple lands were required to supply the requisites for the upkeep and service of the
temple. In such countless ways was art bound up with the religious life of the people.
48

Were it not, indeed, for the work lavished on Buddhist temples in Ceylon, and the offerings Social
made to the priesthood, this book might have been left unwritten. We shall see that economy
the landholding craftsmen were practically state-endowed ; and in return their work was
done essentially for the people themselves, whose palaces and picture galleries were the
viharas and dévales where they worshipped, and with which their festivals were associated.
Luxury was little, and the amount of fine art absorbed and hidden away by royalty and
other wealthy persons was small compared with that belonging to the Church and so
to the whole folk. Just so was it in mediæval Europe; art was for the people, and no
lack of it. Now it is otherwise, and art is for the rich only, and hard to come by.
APPENDIX TO CHAPTER II.
I. EDUCATION.
In times past the education of boys was carried on by Buddhist priests at the village pansala, Reading
the home of the incumbent of the nearest vihara, just as the village priest taught at the and writing
church door in mediaeval England. This system has been already referred to, on p. 45
above. At about the age of six the boy was taken to the pansala with an offering for
the teacher. At an auspicious hour the teacher took his seat and recited the first line of
vowels, beginning with the words svasti siddham, ‘let prosperity attend’; the alphabet
continues, ayanu, ayanu, etc., . . . ending with the words iti siddhi astu, ‘so let there be
success !’ The alphabet first given to the pupil was written in large characters, in three
lines on an ola leaf; afterwards a book was given containing the complete alphabet,
including combinations of letters. The letters were learnt by loud repetition in a singsong
tone; the pupil stood before the teacher holding the closed book to his forehead and so
repeated his lesson. Nothing else was taught until the alphabet could be repeated without
fault or hesitation. The form of the letters had next to be systematically learnt, the
teacher pointed to the letters and read; ‘the letter ‘a’ is read '■ ayanu” and so on.
Writing was only taught after this descriptive repetition was perfectly mastered. Writing
was learnt on a narrow board, called velipila, spread with sand; it stood on four legs, which
were sometimes turned and lacquered; the teacher had a carved ivory style {velipata) with
which he traced the sign sva, after which he guided the boy’s hand in copying : the boy
wrote with his middle finger, supported by the fore-finger and thumb; in this way,
little by little, the boy learnt to write the whole alphabet, and by that time he could read
short sentences : this might take six months or a year. Ola writing was taught afterwards.
The boy was given a long strip of ola, untrimmed, and the teacher wrote large letters
on this: the boy was given an ulkapiva, i.e., a blunt writing style, and with this he traced
the letters over and over again till the leaf was cut through; this was called safahan
kfplma ; the boy learnt in this way to exercise a very even pressure. Afterwards he used
karakola (talipot leaf) not tracing but copying the guru akuru (letters written by the
teacher) as in a copybook, writing smaller and smaller by degrees : finally he was allowed
to use a sharp style {panhiudd) and to write on puskola (prepared talipot leaf).
As an example of good handwriting (on paper) may be shown the script of Fig, 3, two
pages of an eighteenth century paper ‘prayer book,’ a breviary said to have been used by
Narendra Siipha himself. The book is further illustrated on Pis. XVII. and XX.

The standard of good writing (on olas) is conveyed in a corrupt Sanskrit verse current in
pansala schools:
Samani samapaddni, Samansani samah sirah
Akshardifi pratishtavyah, Mriduni lalitani ca
Lesson books ‘Well-formed letters should be similar in size, similar in their tails, and in their heads,
and (written) with a light pressure.’
The first book read and learnt after the alphabet was the Nampota, a list of important places
and temples, practically an elementary geography of Ceylon; next came Mangul-lakutfu,
a description of the 216 auspicious marks on the soles of the feet of Buddha, in which
book Sanskrit words appear, followed by sentences in Pali. Everything had to be learnt
by heart and repeated perfectly; much or all of the material so learnt was not understood
at the time, but laid a sure foundation for more advanced studies. The books next read
were Gana-devi-hHla (account of the youth and education of Ganeid), Vadan-kavi-pota
(grammar, orthography, &c.), Buddha-gajja (praise of Buddha in Sanskrit), Sakas-ka^a
(prose with difficult combinations of words; there is a saying “the tongue that hadi not
SO

uttered Sakas-ka^a is like a white ant’s”). After these came Namas/ifa (Sanskrit ilokas Education
on Buddha, and Sinhalese paraphrase); Navaratna (‘nine gems,’nine verses of high value
uttered by nine Pandits at the court of Vikrama); Vyasakara, Pratyaiataka, Anuruddha Curriculum
iataka, Bauddha Sataka (or Bhakti iataka), Surya Sataka, Vfittamalava, Vj-ittamaiakhyava,
Amara Simha (i.e., AmarakBsha,ths Sanskrit vocabulary), all in Sanskrit: these works com­
pleted a thorough general education; a majority of students did not, of course, proceed so
far. If, however, the student was in tended for a learned profession, as astrology or medicine,
or for the priesthood, he now proceeded to specialise ; he would read, for example, Toga-
Sataka (Arishta iataka) as his first hook in medicine. If intended for the priesthood he
would study Pali.
Teaching was not always carried on at the pansala : the child might be taught at home by a
priest or by his own father. In the case of aristocratic families, the incumbent of the
family vihara became the child’s tutor. Otherwise, and especially if there were no pansala
near, the father taught his own children in the same way.
Children were taught to be silent in the presence of their elders, and very obedient, and
remain so even when grown up. They were also expected to do their own share of house­
hold or other work at an early age, and so became capable and responsible much sooner
than in Europe, where children expect all their wants attended to by their elders.
The relation between pupil and teacher in the East is one of affectionate respect, almost
of reverence. This is marked in many gracious ways; I shall not easily forget the action
of a craftsman’s apprentice (a man full-grown) to whom I paid money in the presence
of his teacher and of another master craftsman ; taking the money in both hands he salaamed
to his gurunnanse" and gave it to him; he received the money and then gravely returned
both money and salute; and so also with the other master craftsmen there.
The old system of education above described could not have been preserved in its entirety ; ‘Progress’
it is in many respects unsuited to modern requirements, besides having intrinsic faults; hut
it is very unfortunate that so many of its real advantages are lacking in the modern system,
and especially unfortunate that an “ English education” such as the Royal College provides,
leaves the “educated” ignorant of everything that would appear to be of special interest
and value to him, and unable to hand on to others even that knowledge which he possesses
of the great world beyond, and the lesson he has learnt from a study of the history and
manners of other peoples. Most stupid of all is the affectation of despising everything
Sinhalese and thoughtlessly admiring everything English ; reminding one of that time in
England when ‘Falsehood in a Ciceronian dialect had no opposers; truth in patois no
listeners.’
II. BOOKS.
Sinhalese books are written on ‘olas,’ or strips of the leaf of the talipot palm, Corypha Preparation
umbraculifera. The leaves are prepared as follows: a leaf bud of the palm is cut down of olas
just before it opens; the leaf segments are separated and the midrib removed, dividing
each segment into two strips. 'These are loosely rolled and placed in a copper cauldron
with cold water and then boiled for an hour, and afterwards dried in the sun for three
days. The leaves are then again rolled, this time not singly, but in rolls a foot or so in
diameter. The rolls are exposed to the dew for three successive nights, after which they
become pliable. In this state they can be preserved a long time, especially if kept in a
smoky place, such as the loft in a kitchen. When required for use, the rolls are taken
one by one and smoothed by rubbing on a polished areca stump; the trunk is tied across
e 2 51

Books two posts and the ola laid across it with a weight attached to the stalk end ; the ola is then
pulled up and down across the trunk until it is smooth on both sides. The leaves are
Preparation next cut up into various standard sizes, the largest three spans in length, the next and
of leaves most usual length for valuable books being two spans and four fingers; smaller sizes vary
from eighteen inches downwards. Care is taken to make the strips of even breadth. All
the leaves are then punched with the two string holes in accordance with the following
rule:
Ayamena catur bhagam, Trihhdgam punar eva ca,
TJbhayoh satra-madhyena, Tatha kuryat chidra-lakshanam.
“Fold the leaf in three and again in four and perforate between the pairs of lines formed
by the folding.” The leaves are next strung on smooth rounded sticks passed through
the string holes, in thick parcels between wooden covers; the four sides of the leaves are
singed with a hot iron; the packet, now called pot-gefya, is so stored until required
for use. Each leaf is a. pat-iruva\ a ‘gathering’ of eight or sixteen leaves, lettered
alphabetically, is a pat-katfuva [Clough].
The leaves are removed from the packet one by one and written on with a sharp style
{panhiuda): after the writing and revision an ink composed of dummala oil and lamp
black is lightly rubbed on {kalu-madinavd) with a rag and wiped with clean chaff, after
which the writing stands out clearly.
The completed book consists of the written leaves, enclosed between two wooden covers
[pot-kambi) of the same size and shape which are painted, lacquered, carved or quite plain.
Book covers are also made of ivory, and silver. A string {pot-lanuva), composed sometimes
of cotton, sometimes of niyanda fibre, and often with different colored strands, passes
through one set of holes and through holes in the covers, and is wound round the, book
when not in use. One end of the string is attached to a flat button {pot-sakiya), ivory,
horn or metal, which prevents the string from slipping through the cover. The correct
rule for thus tying up the book is given in the verse;
Prathame daia-sOtraifi, PaBca-sOtraf maddhyame
Pripanam tripanam bandham, Mata mata vidhiyate.
“Ten strings at the top, five strings in the middle, three and three, and the cross strings
in pairs is the rule.” The Sanskrit is apparently corrupt.
The actual leaves of the book are rarely ornamented. The full stops, however, are some­
times rubricated, and the small space around the string-hole, which is liable to become
frayed and should not be written upon, has also occasionally some decoration in red. Books
of magic, such as Bali songs, charms and spells, are illustrated with pictures of demons,
diagrams, etc., in plain black; but only such as can be scratched with the style upon the
leaf. Horoscopes are written on full-length strips of leaf and are elaborately ornamented
Lette rs with geometrical decoration similarly incised. Letters were sent on strips of ola, neatly
folded, and bound with narrow strips of ola, passing once or several times round, in
accordance with etiquette, as given in a verse current in the pansalas:
Ekani iatru dvayatp. mitram, Trlf bandhum catur prabhurn

CHAPTER III. PARTICULAR ACCOUNT
OF THE ARTIFICERS.
‘To the craftsman his reward'
A MORE particular account of the Atari, Navandanns, or caste or guild of artificers
proper, will be necessary. The subdivisions of the caste, according to Valentyn,
are eleven in number, viz., atari, blacksmiths; badallu, silversmiths; va4uv0,
carpenters; liyana vaduva, turners; ridiketayankarayo, damasceners ; etdatkefayankarayo, ivory
carvers and cabinet makers; galvaduvo, stone cutters; ratne endra karayO (?), jewellers;
fwi/awij, arrow makers (lac workers); r/r/tfr«, painters; founders. But Valentyn’s
divisions are rather a list of names given to men who follow particular branches of their
craft, than actual caste divisions. The Janavaipsa merely distinguishes two principal
divisions of the caste, viz., (i) kamburs, navandanno or atari, divided into lokaruvO, workers
in copper, bronze and brass; sittaru, painters ; and svarriakdrayo, goldsmiths ; and including
also turners and blacksmiths: and, (2) vaduvs, carpenters, blacksmiths and masons,
including housebuilders, agricultural implement makers (who are also mentioned in the
first section) and arrow makers {ivaduvo, including all lac workers). The existence of
a confusion between the two classes is admitted, and appears to have been inevitable as
the work of the two to some extent overlapped. It seems likely that the kamburo (also
spoken of in the Janavarpsa as Kammara Brahmans') were strictly speaking the imported
kammalar workmen from the coast, who did fine work as goldsmiths, painters, etc., and
that the vaduvo were the indigenous artificers accustomed only to the ordinary work of
building, tool making, etc. Just in the same way there were two groups of weavers,
the who made country cloth (home-spun, so to say) and the ‘chalias’ (salagamayo)
who were brought over from South India to make fine and gold-woven cloths. Con­
fusion also results from the use of terms in a particular as well as in a general sense.
At the present day two main divisions, corresponding in the main with those of the Jana-
vamsa form the only real caste division. Those in the higher division (architects, painters,
gold and silversmiths, brass repoussers, ivory and wood carvers) called galladdo, do not
eat or intermarry with those in the lower division, called vaduvo (ordinary carpenters
and turners of wood and ivory, blacksmiths, damasceners, stone carvers and lac workers).
The term vaduva now has the general meaning of‘carpenter,’ and would hardly be used
in speaking of a blacksmith, still less of a goldsmith, but is used in the Mayamataya in
the sense of ‘architect,’ and together with sittaruva, ‘painter,’ refers to men of the superior
division. The tailors and embroiderers {hannali) and leather workers (hommarayo), potters
(badahelayo), weavers of country cloth {beravayd), mat-makers {kinharayo), and makers of
whips, cords, and preparers of hides (rofyo) were of other and inferior caste. These last
are only incidentally referred to in the present chapter.

Craftsmen at the present day require a daily wage of Rs. i to Rs. 3 if working in Kandy;
good painters at the Maligava receive Rs. 2. The difference in amount depends more
on the feeling of the craftsman for his employer than upon his superiority or otherwise.
If executing a commission at home, he prefers to leave the amount of his reward to the
patron’s judgment, to fixing a price beforehand, but he is likely to be weeks or months

The blacksmiths had occasional dealings with the veddas, or wild men of the woods. Smiths work
“ The wilder sort of them, when they want Arrows, will carry their load of Flesh in for Vfidas
the night, and hang it up in a Smith's shop, also a Leaf cut in the form they will have
their Arrows made, and hang by it. Which if the Smith do make according to their
Pattern they will requite, and bring him more Flesh : but if he make them not, they
will do him a mischief one time or another by shooting in the night. . . . They are so
curious of their Arrows that no Smith can please them. The King once to gratifie them
for a great Present they brought him, gave all of them of his best made Arrow-blades :
which nevertheless would not please their humour. For they went all of them to a Rock
by a River and ground them into another form” (Knox, pp. 62, 63).
Thus, in spite of the fact that the artificers were already paid for their services more or Payment of
less adequately by the lands they held, they were liberally rewarded for ecclesiastical craftsmen
work, and not infrequently also for special excellence or skill in craftsmanship otherwise
applied. But they were never paid a daily wage, nor required to work a given number
of hours a day. I have had craftsmen working at my house in Kandy for weeks together ;
just as they once worked in the royal workshop. They had no idea of‘making money’
or ‘bettering themselves’; they wanted only money sufficient to buy food for themselves
and their families ; they had no wish to save money. When a large piece of work was
completed they would expect some special gift, such as a good cloth. They rarely worked
a week without having to go home for a few days to find some strayed buffalo, or to take
part in the cultivation of their fields. Yet they were always most consciencious in money
matters, such as expenditure on materials ; and though they would have hated fixed hours
of work, often worked far into the night by lamp-light, purely by their own wish, and
because they so much loved the work itself. Their pride in real capacity was most naïve
and unaffected. Their greatest possible ambition was that I should buy them some small
piece of land and reward them with it, as did the kings of old.
The reason for the special payments for ecclesiastical work was that it was felt unbecoming
for the patron to obtain the credit for a meritorious action, unless the cost was really
borne by him ; unless, indeed, he did so bear it, there was no real merit acquired. The
feeling came out as strongly when the Ruvanveli dâgaba was built (see Chapter I.,p. 4),
and Duttha GamaijI deemed it unmeet that such work should be executed by unpaid
labour, and took extraordinary precautions to prevent any voluntary work being done,
lest any of the merit should be lost to himself ; he could share the merit by deliberate
gift, without loss to himself, but if voluntary work were done secretly, only the doer
obtained the merit. The lamp of sacrifice burned as steadily in India as in mediæval
Europe. There is no more evidence that in the religious architecture of the East any
saving of cost was attempted or desired, than there is of any such thing in mediæval
Eng lish building of church and shrine.*

It will be observed that in this way the chief families of smiths possessed what was really Devlndra

The iron cubit rule {riyan Mid) used by him is still preserved by his descendants (‘Ceylon
National Review,’ No. II., 1906, p. 235).

Penalties We gather an idea of the reasons and manner of punishment of craftsmen from an incident
for bad’work connected with the building of the parapet of the Kandy lake, about a.d. 1806 ; although
the work was carried out as rajokariya by ordinary villagers, and was not (except as
regards the design), done by the craftsmen themselves. One Gannoruve Tikiri Gammahe
of Gannoruva had charge of part of the work, which was allotted to his people, and those
of Parakatavela Aracci. When the king came to inspect the work, the gammahe’s part
was still unfinished, but the rest completed. He was taken to prison by the kankanama
(overseer) of the V edakarayO people, and his certificate of office forfeited. He was eighteen
days in prison, but ‘got released,’ after which other adventures befel him.
A story is told of the goldsmith, Ratnavalli Navaratna Abharaija of Nilavala, already
mentioned, that seeing the King (Kirti Sri) one day asleep he conceived the idea of setting
a gem in the royal great toe nail; which he succeeded in doing without awakening the
sleeping monarch. His awakening was awaited with some trepidation, lest he should
have presumed too far; but the King was delighted at his skill, and rewarded him with
liberality.
Rewards Amongst the rewards and marks of favour bestowed by the Kings on artificers, were
portions of the royal dress; when the Gangarama Vihara was completed an entire costume
was presented. In the ordinary way no one would have been allowed to wear such
garments, the sumptuary laws being very definite; but probably the smiths could use them
as the kumara ^nduma at nstra mangalya (see Appendix to this Chapter); in the meanwhile
these gifts were, and still are in a few cases, greatly treasured. It is also said that the maker
of the crown might try it on his own head; which would have been horrible treason for
any other to do. Thepatabendi decoration was sometimes conferred on eminent craftsmen ;
it was a pafa-tahaduva or gold frontlet, tied on by the king himself as a mark of honour.
High spirit The high spirit of the craftsmen is sufficiently indicated in Knox’s account of them. He
of the crafts- says: “ Next after the degree of Hondrews may be placed Goldsmiths, Blacksmiths,
men Carpenters and Painters. Who are all of one degree and quality. But the Hondrews
will not eat with them: however in Apparel there is no difference; and they are also
privileged to sit on stools, which none of the inferior ranks of People hereafter mentioned,
may do. Heretofore they were accounted almost equal to the Inferior sort of Hondrews,
and they would eat in these Artificers’ Houses, but afterwards they were degraded upon
this occasion. It chanced some Hondrews came to a Smith’s Shop to have their Tools
mended, when it came to be Dinner time, the Smith leaves work, and goes in to his
House to dine, leaving the Hondrews in his Shop: who had waited there a great while
to have their work done. Now whether the Smith fearing lest their hunger might move
them to be so impudent or desperate as to partake with him of his Dinner, clapt to his
Door after him; Which was taken so hainously by those hungry people in his Shop,
that immediately they all went and declared abroad what an affront the Smith had put
upon them. Whereupon it was decreed and confirmed, that for ever all the people of
that rank should be deposed, and deprived of the Honour of having the Hondrews to
eat in their Houses. Which Decree has stood in force ever since.
Nevertheless these Smiths take much upon them, especially those who are the King’s
Smiths (i.e., pattal hatara men) ; that is, such who live in the King’s Towns, and do
his work. These have this Privilege, that each has a parcel of Towns belonging to them,
whom none but they are to work for. The ordinary work they do for them is mending

their Tools, for which every man pays to his Smith a certain Rate of Corn in Harvest Artificers
time according to ancient Custom. But if any has work extraordinary, as making new
Tools or the like, besides the aforesaid rate of Corn, he must pay him for it. In order
to this, they come in an humble manner to the Smith with a Present, being Rice, Hens,
and other sorts of Provision, or a bottle of Rack, desiring him to appoint his time, when
they shall come to have their work done. Which when he hath appointed them, they
come at the set time, and bring both {char-) Coals and Iron with them. The Smith
sits very gravely upon his Stool, his Anvil before him, with his left hand towards the
forge, and a little Hammer in his Right. They themselves who come with their work
must blow the Bellows, and when the Iron is to be beaten with the great Maul, he holds
it, still sitting upon his Stool, and they must hammer it themselves, he only with his
little Hammer knocking it sometimes into fashion. And if it be anything to be filed,
he makes them go themselves and grind it upon a Stone, that his labour of fileing may
be tbe less; and when they have done it as well as they can, he goes over it again with
his file and finisheth it. That which makes these Smiths thus stately is, because the Towns
People are compelled to go to their own Smith, and none else. And if they should,
that Smith is liable to pay Damages that should work for any in another Smith’s Juris­
diction.”
We have seen that less than four per cent, of the Kandyan population now appear to ‘Their
belong to the artificers’ caste. But in the census report, on which this estimate is based, number
statistics are given of occupation, and not of caste; for in this social institution. Govern­
ment aifects a blindness which in actual administration it cannot maintain.* The number
of persons belonging to the craftsman castes greatly exceeds the number of those still
practising their craft, so that we may suppose that quite as many as ten per cent, of the
population in the eighteenth century, consisted of craftsmen and their dependents. Of
these, not more than half can have been navandanns (p. 54), the superior artificers which
alone are spoken of in the present chapter. It is necessary to say a few words as to their
origin.
At first sight it seems strange to suppose that many of them were of Indian origin; yet Indian
this is a point on which no doubt can be entertained. Numerous references to the origin of
importation of artificers from Southern India have been given in Chapter I.; that the some crafts-
practice continued even into the eighteenth century is attested by contemporary records men
and sannas. The navandanno at any one time, speaking of the eighteenth and immediately
preceding centuries at least, consisted partly of indigenous craftsmen, and partly of newly-
settled Tamil artificers, coming from Southern India, to work for the king, who showed
them favour and made them grants of land. Hence it is that not only do we find the
closest correspondence in detail and technique between South Indian (Tamil) and Sinhalese
work; but also that the artificer families have often Hindu names (such as Rajeivara
Devasurendra), they preserve traces of biva worship (such as Sanskrit ilokas written in
his praise), and of other Hindu ceremonies {nitra mangalya, etc.); their technical works are
obviously a part of the Indian Silpaiastra; some of their technical terms are corruptions
of Tamil words; they make use of Hindu mantrams (cf. p. 74); they are occasionally
referred to as Kammdlar; and so forth. The community of design elements would not
