thus from time to time imported, very soon became part and parcel of the Kandyan
Sinhalese people, Buddhist by faith ; the style and feeling of their work was modified,
under the influence of the living local tradition, something of the Hindu-Dravidian
element being lost, and the Buddhist-Aryan acquired. It is remarkable indeed, that the
local tradition should have so successfully and continuously preserved its vitality and
individuality.
The The indigenous craftsmen, it will be perceived, represented both the original Sinhalese
indigenous stock, and the later immigrant craftsmen incorporated from time to time into their com-
tradition munity. It would be difficult to say how far an original Sinhalese element is represented
in the body of superior craftsmen; for we do not know much of the state of the arts in
very early times, and we have the record of the introduction of Indian craftsmen with
Buddhist missionaries from the North (p. 2), and again at the time of Gaja Bahu’s
invasion of Southern India (p. 6). The inferior craftsmen, potters, weavers (except
salagamayd), mat makers, etc., on the other hand no doubt represent an integral part of
the Sinhalese population, perhaps even carrying on the remote traditions of the pre-
Sinhalese inhabitants, who may have been by no means uncivilised.
In a general way it may be stated that the indigenous craftsmen of all sorts, integrally
a part of the Sinhalese population, were makers of the plainer and most necessary articles
normally required by a simple agricultural people, and the imported craftsmen were more
especially sumptuary artists from the big cities and craftsguilds of Southern India, making
the more elaborate and costly goods required by tbe Court and the capital. The distinction
is clearly marked in the case of weavers, the indigenous beravayo making country cloth,
good but not fine, and the imported salagamayS making the gold-woven muslins worn
by royalty and nobility. So, too, the dye-painting of cloth, the more elaborate sorts of
embroidery (with gold), and tailoring and sandal making and so forth were crafts practised
almost exclusively by foreign craftsmen, at the Court only. The king, sometimes himself
a Tamil, and always with Tamil queens, naturally favoured Tamil fashions, and the results
are seen in the Tamil influence upon jewellery and dress in the eighteenth century. India
was the source of sumptuous cloths and skilled craftsmen for the Sinhalese, much as Paris
sets the fashion in London. Even at the present day, those who require silk brocades or
gold-woven turbans in Ceylon, are obliged to import them from Southern India, and
dye-painted kerchiefs are made in Jaffna for sale in Kandy. It will thus be seen how
intimately connected was the art of Southern India and Ceylon; but while thus recognizing
the influence of the Tamil craftsmen, it is necessary to remember also the continuity
and vitality of the indigenous tradition, and to give to the Sinhalese people the full credit
for the fact that their art, taken as a whole, is perfectly distinct in style and feeling from
that of Southern India, and preserves clearer and more numerous traces of the Early Indian,
and especially of the Early Buddhist style, than can easily be found in India itself.
It is desirable to trace a little more fully the history of the kammslar, the South Indian
craftsmen who thus came to Ceylon from time to time, and there joined their fellows
already settled there and practising their craft. The Kammular in South India are the
62

craftsmen par excellence, the builders and sculptors of the great Hindu temples. The Artificers
following account of the Kammalar in South India is mainly condensed from Dr. Pulney
Andy’s paper in No. 50 of ‘The Journal of Indian Art and Industry’:
The kammalar are descendants of a race of Aryans who entered India across the Panjab Origin of
long before Vyasa began the collection and arrangement of the Vedas. They were known craftsmen
in early times as Viiva Brahmans, Deva Brahmans or Deva Kammalar, in contradistinction
to the modern Brahmans who are descendants of Vashishta. They spread gradually towards
the south and appear to have gone thence to Ceylon, Burma, Siam and Java, the art of
all which lands is closely related to that of South India. They reject the authority of
the Brahmans, having priests of their own caste, and perform many rites after the manner
of Brahmans. The Kammalar claim to have been at one time spiritual guides and
priests to the whole people, of which a trace survives in the proverb, ‘The Kammalan is
guru to the world,’ which is said to be current in Southern India. They still perform
priestly rites in connection with the consecration of images. They both claim and possess
various special privileges which they have always upheld with much vigour. Their
priests are or were learned in the Silpaiastra. The majority are Saivites. They trace
their ancestry to the five sons of Viivakarma, of whom the first-born Manu, worked in
iron; the second, Maya, in wood; the third, Tvastra, in brass, copper, and alloys; the
fourth, Silpi, in stone; and the fifth, Viivajna, was a gold and silversmith and jeweller.
Even to-day the blacksmith is said to take precedence amongst the artificers— a point
of difference from Ceylon. In former times the artisans had their own guilds, which
protected the interests of their own trades; but as these institutions gradually declined,
the Kammalar were driven to seek the aid of capitalists of other castes, and now they
are, in a majority of instances, reduced to mere paid workmen, earning daily wages.
The five occupations are not mutually exclusive; for example, the son of a goldsmith
may, if he likes, follow any of the other crafts, or vice-versa. We have seen this is only
partially the case in Ceylon, as there is a general division into two groups which do
not intermarry. In India the five sects form one compact community; as indeed they
do in Ceylon, though partly divided as remarked.
Some part of the foregoing history of the Kammalar is mythical. A critical examination
of the history and traditions of the Kammalar, and of their technical literature is greatly
to be desired, and may be expected to throw light on the general history of art, of guilds,
and perhaps of freemasonry. Will not the Vi^vakarma Kulabhimana Sabha in Madras
begin this much-needed investigation before the opportunities are lost for good and all ?
It is probably true that there existed a caste or guild of artificers at a time long ante­
cedent to the Christian era, and that they had spread all over India, perhaps as far as
the extreme south at the time of the founding of the Sinhalese nation by Vijaya. Later,
they passed to Ceylon, Java and other places. There is a remarkable unity underlying
the diverse developments of Indian art (including the art of Ceylon, Burma, Slam, and
Java), not merely as regards the persistence in time of elements of decoration, but also
ge ographically; here I refer to the present peculiar isolation of particular trades and
techniques which survive, so to say, in scattered ‘islands’ all over India (cf. ‘Indian Art
at Delhi,’ 1904, pp. 112, 154, 158, 179, 206, 221, 233, and also this work, in various
places). The argument from distribution is, that a knowledge of these crafts was once
more widely spread and continuous; it is also fairly clear that it was once very much more
extensive and thorough.
The greatest interest attaches to the system of apprenticeship and instruction found Apprenttce-
amongst the Kandyan craftsmen. From the social and guild point of view, the same ship
method may be said to be characteristic of all the craftsmen, both of the artificers’ caste
63

Artificers and also potters and weavers, etc. That is, the trade was hereditary, and the sons are
brought up to it as a matter of course,* and trained in the actual workshop, being given
Apprentice- easy or monotonous work at first (as grinding colours) and little by little picking up a
ship knowledge of the craft by precept, example, and practice; and so the tradition was
perpetuated. Thus from the very beginning, the disciple absorbed together, technique,
tradition and metaphysic. No technical education of the future can replace the workshop
training of the old craftsmen; for technical education supplies only technique, and that
inferior; the imagination it takes no account at all! When the son married and set up
for himself, he would be given tools, but would still very probably continue to work
with and for his father. We see here the working of the joint family system. Very
often also the craftsman trained up with his own sons those of other men of the same
caste. In either case the relation between master and pupil was one of lasting reverence
and affection; especially where the period of instruction was prolonged, and the informa­
tion imparted of great value, as amongst the higher craftsmen.
Such was the general type of apprenticeship amongst the craftsmen; but the teaching
of drawing and design was confined to the superior division of the artificer’s caste, the
galladdo from whom the paftal-hatara men were drawn. The lower division of craftsmen
had also some knowledge of design, but in the main relied upon the others to set out
their work.

I. TEACHING OF DRAWING.
As architects, painters and designers, a thorough knowledge of drawing was essential
to the superior craftsmen, and we find a highly systematic course of instruction in use
for the education of apprentices. These were usually the sons of master craftsmen; but
the sons of relations and even of outsiders were also received. A man of the proper caste,
wishing to apprentice his son to a master-craftsman, would first find a'fortunate hour
{nckat balanavd), and then proceed to the craftsman’s house with his son of about six
years old, and one or more servants carrying presents of food and betel leaves on a yoke.

As it was usual for one man to practise several of the higher crafts at the same time (as
painting and ivory carving together, or with others as well), the pupils also had practice
in several crafts, but usually selected one or more as their special work. A galladda
proficient in five crafts was called silpacariya.
Workshop It should be pointed out that in the case of such pupils as we are considering, a general
education and religious education was imparted at the same time, similar to that given in pansala
schools. Reading, writing and arithmetic were thus taught; the latter was essential for
the purpose of the astrological calculations required to determine favourable times for
the commencement of important works, and for the understanding of the measurements
given in the technical books referred to. The rules for drawing figures necessitated the
construction and use of scales. A good deal of geometry of a practical character was
also learnt in connection with the construction of repeating patterns. The master crafts­
man had thus a small school where technical instruction was given in addition to an
ordinary education. The relation between master and pupil remained to the last, one
of affectionate reverence. It was customary for the pupil to offer whatever he earned
to his teacher, who, unless specially asked, returned the greeting and the gift with the
same grave courtesy with which it was offered. A friend of mine, now over fifty, tells
me that he always observes this custom with his father (now over eighty), who was his
teacher. The whole system was indeed mainly one of hereditary transmission of a craft
or ‘mystery’; and though other pupils were admitted, the master was loth to reveal his
last secrets save to a son, or perhaps to a faithful pupil at the completion of his course.
If the pupil was an outsider, his father from time to time made presents to the teacher,
and at the conclusion of the period of instruction some more substantial gift, such as a
buffalo. As the pupil grew up, he continued to work for and with his teacher, and thus
the tradition was perfectly transmitted. It is indeed a strange thing for anyone used to
the ecclecticism of modern Europe to be brought face to face with strong living traditions
in this way; for in Europe “whatever of art is left which is in any sense the result
of continuous tradition is, and long has been, so degraded as to have lost any claim to
be considered art at all”; while the only art existing in Ceylon, worthy the name of
art, is strictly traditional.
'Teaching in Before leaving the subject of teaching drawing, it may be noted that it is one worthy
English of close study in India and the East generally. The information gained from a com-
schools parative study of the methods employed in different parts of India would be of the utmost
historical, artistic and anthropological value. Since Indian craftsmen are admittedly
masters of design, their methods of instruction should be of permanent interest and value
to all interested in the teaching of drawing; and a proper and rational system of instruction
might be introduced into English schools in Ceylon, where at present the poor learner
is put through the old-fashioned South Kensington mill, and may ‘learn drawing’ without
acquiring any knowledge of Indian traditional design, or in any way connecting the subject
with his ordinary life or the past history of his country. The object of teaching drawing
should surely be educational, and not merely utilitarian! I have not space to enter into
the subject at length; but the points which I consider of greatest importance are, (i) a
greater recognition of the value of drawing from memory; (2) instruction in the use
68

of ruler and compasses at an early stage, the drawing of curves to be taught first of all, ‘Teaching of
leaving the straight lines to take care of themselves later. Anyone who can draw drawing
accurately a sensitive curve could also draw a straight line; (3) the postponement of
model drawing to a late stage; (4) the elimination of scientific perspective from the
ordinary drawing course; (5) recognition of local tradition, by a large use of Eastern
decorative forms for freehand work, and of brass and earthenware for model drawing;
and (6) cultivation of taste in, by explanation of, the principles of design, and exhibition
of examples or pictures of good work, mainly oriental. I do not wish to condemn direct
drawing from nature, but rather to postpone it to a late stage in the actual drawing course ;
at an earlier stage I would introduce it only in connection with nature study and not as a
part of the actual instruction in drawing. A logical contrast would thus be drawn between
drawing as a means of recording observations of scientific interest or practical value, and
drawing as an art, i.e., as a means of interpretation of nature; and both points of view
would be of interest.
The first thing to do in this investigation, would be to compare the South Indian methods
with those of Ceylon, and with one another, and from these observations to reconstruct
as it were a perfect text, exhibiting the instruction as a connected scheme. In this
direction I have made some enquiries at Tanjore, from an old master-craftsman named
Annasami Stapati Rayar. Drawing was taught as in Ceylon, upon a wooden board,
prepared by covering with a lime and rice, or charcoal, lime and rice paste, and drawn
upon with a leaden pencil. The forms first drawn were the simplified but comparatively
naturalistic outlines of certain fruits and vegetables (can this really be a part of the tradition,
or is it of modern origin ?); and certain double curves or conventional leaf forms, called
kadaikaddu, kurippu and akatti karukku (Fig. 10), which
apparently correspond to the Sinhalese vaka deka (an
example of the latter (Fig. 5) was recognized by the
Stapati as kadaikadiT)- Copy or sketch books, called
kaduttam pustakam, were used as in Ceylon. One such
in my possession, about a century old, consists mainly
of sketches or memory notes of images of the principal
deities and their attributes as detailed in the &stra.

II. NETRA MANGALYA.
Netra The Netra Mangalya ceremony is one of great interest in itself, and important from our
Mangalya point of view as showing the craftsman in his sacerdotal capacity (see p. 63) and as
illustrating the relation between him and his patron. The ceremony was really the
dedication of the temple (more exactly, the image in it); and it will be well for the sake
of completeness to trace very briefly the whole course of events connected with the
building of a new vihara, before laying special stress on the nstra mangalya. The patron
was almost always the King, who had, of course, the state workmen at his disposal.
But in many cases the patron was a layman or group of laymen*; or might be a priest
who made himself responsible for the construction or restoration of a temple.-)' Having
determined to build and endow a new vihara, the King sent presents of betel, etc., by
yoke, to the artificer (whom hereafter I speak of as the foreman) in thz paffal-hatara who
was to be entrusted with the work, and requested him to undertake it. Any lesser man
than the King would on such an occasion go himself with the presents to the smith’s
house. The foreman appointed a meeting with the patron (as I shall call the King
hereafter) on the spot, after determining an auspicious moment for beginning the work
{nekat balanavd). He there received presents of clothing and rice, and performed various
prelimary ceremonies analogous to those proper to the building of a house, but more
elaborate. An altar to Gaija DeviyO (Gariesha) and bulat tatwva to Bhuma Devi were
erected and an atamagala diagram drawn (see glossary), after which the work on the
foundation was begun.
The artificers were provided with food and clothing while the work continued. Presents
were made to the foreman from time to time, especially when the image was first plastered
and whitened preliminary to painting, and again later as described below.
By far the most important ceremony connected with the building and decoration of a
vihara or with its renovation {jara-ves-arinava) was the actual netra mangalya or Eye
ceremonial. The ceremony had to be performed in the case of any image, whether set up
in a vihara or not. Even in the case of flat paintings it was necessary. D. S. Muhandiram
when making for me a book of drawings of gods according to the Rupavaliya, left the
eyes to be subsequently inserted on a suitable auspicious occasion, with some simpler
form of the ceremony described. Knox has a reference to the subject as follows: “Some
being devoutly disposed, will make the Image of this God (Buddha) at their own charge.
For the making whereof they must bountifully reward the Founder. Before the Eyes
are made, it is not accounted a God, but a lump of ordinary Metal, and thrown about
the Shop with no more regard than any thing else. But when the Eyes are to be made,
the Artificer is to have a good gratification, besides the first agreed upon reward. The
Eyes being formed, it is thenceforward a God.J And then, being brought with honour
from the Workman’s Shop, it is dedicated by Solemnities and Sacrifices, and carried
with great state into its shrine or little house, which is before built and prepared for it.
Sometimes a man will order the Smith to make this Idol, and then after it is made will
go about with it to well-disposed people to contribute towards the Wages the Smith

is to have for making it. And men will give freely towards the charge. And this is N^tra

Almost in the same way, the medieval guilds in Europe, wishing to make offerings to
the parish church, would sometimes undertake a work beyond their means, and raise
money for it by a popular entertainment or ‘Ale,’ which nowadays has degenerated into
a bazaar. But the Sinhalese made use of no such inducements; they had only to ask,
and the money was gladly given, by those who were eager to share in the merit of the work!
The ceremony would seem to be rather Hindu than Buddhist in origin; the underlying
idea seems to be an endeavour to secure good ‘conditions’ at the time of definitely
consecrating the image as a medium which shall put the worshipper in touch with the
unseen god whose symbol is thus set forth, and this is rather a Hindu than a Buddhist
idea; for Southern Buddhism does not regard Buddha as a still existent personal God,
and would not have been likely to originate such a ceremonial, in connection with a
mere memorial. But the ceremony no doubt dates back to the time when Buddhism
and Hinduism were more distinctly recognized as two aspects of one faith, which
historically and fundamentally they are. Some idea of danger (as of‘playing with fire,’
or ‘calling down lightning from heaven’) appears to attach to this consecration of the
image, whereby it is made a medium between the worshipper and his god (which would
be a Hindu not a Buddhist idea) ; and the object of the ceremonial is, in this connection,
to avert misfortunes, akin to those resulting from a glance of the‘evil eye,’which might
otherwise afflict the presumptuous builder and artist. Something of the same feeling
is shown in other cases, where images are held to be the vehicle of power. A golden
image at Morapaya vihara, is said to have possessed such power, that when a priest
attempted to repair its head, his own. head became leprous and withered away.* The-
image appears to be regarded as charged with power, like a Leyden jar, and similarly,
when dealing with it, means should be taken to avoid a shock ; but all this is rather foreign
to the spirit of Southern Buddhism, and belongs to the Hindu stratum in it.
The first essential was, as always, to find out a suitable day and hour for the ceremony How it is
{nekat balanavd). As the eyes had to be painted about five a.m. in memory of the fact begun
that Buddha attained enlightenment at that hour, a nfkata that falls at that time must
be waited for. Till then the ceremony had to be postponed, even if for a whole year,
as auspicious nekat falling at other times were of no use.
The preparations for the ceremony were elaborate. At about six p.m. the previous
evening, a beginning was made with the recitation of Kosala-bimba-vari}anava-\ ; at eight
or nine the arrangement of the kalasthapanaya was begun; about three a.m. the offerings
{pidinnd) at the altars were made; and about five the eyes were painted. Outside

Netra the vihara were erected eight altars (dibba-gl, lit., god’s houses) to Indra, Agni, Yama,
Mangalya Nairrita, Varuija, Vaijavya, Uttara and Isanah*; alternating with these were eight others
for the attendants of these gods. On each side of the door were prepared altars to the
guardian devatavO {dvdrapala), whose images (doratu-pala-rUpd) were carved at the base
of the door jambs (often on ivory plaques, as at the Dalada Maligava, Kandy); and on
the threshold an altar to the guardian (kshetrapald) of the site. One altar, for the Kadgapala
devatava was prepared outside the vihara, beyond the limits of the pansala grounds.
A kalasthapanaya was prepared, i.e., a collection of eighty pots [mutti), in which were
placed rice, coconuts, jaggery and money (a fanam in each); each pot was covered by a
napkin. A kanya nul (thread spun by a virgin) was drawn round, and the pots covered
with a cloth of five colours.
The details of the preparation of the kalasihdpanaya were as follows : rice {hal) was spread
on the ground, and an atamagala diagram [see glossary] drawn in it with the finger.
The area was next covered with mats over which five kinds of paddy had been thinly
spread, and the space was then divided into eighty parts by strips of coconut leaf. The
eighty pots were arranged in the places thus indicated, separated into two groups of
forty each, forming the Brahma Garbbhaya and the Vishifu Garbbhaya, A special pot set
in the middle of those of the former group, containing gold, silver, pearls and the nine
gems, was called Brahma Kalaya, and another pot set in the middle of the other group
and containing rice was called the Vishnu Kalaya. These chief pots were elevated on
stools above the others. The whole collection formed the kalasthapanaya.
Inside the vihara was prepared an altar to Gat}a Deviya (Gaoesha); also the indraklla.
This was a figure made of rags, supported on a rukattana stick (Alstonia scholaris) set up
in a kalage<}iya (earthen pot) in which the nine gems, gold, rice, etc., had been placed.
It was set in the middle of an atamagala diagram drawn in rice on the vihara floor, in
front of the image and facing it.
All the foregoing arrangements were made by two or more men or youths dressed as
Brahmans; the costume (brahmaiia endumd) consisted of dhofi, shawl, turban, ear-rings,
and thread. When completed another man, dressed in red clothing, called ratu (vduma
(red tuppofiya, heffaya, handkerchief, and tall pointed jagalat toppiya), and provided with
a sword, took a dummala kabala and a kotalaya and went before each of the altars offering
incense and water and reciting Sanskrit ilokas; he walked round the vihara ten times
(keeping always to the right), and finally proceeded with drums and music to the
Kadgapala altar and made offerings there, then returned to the vihara. The purpose
of the drum was to attract the attention of those to whom offerings were made. Offerings
were also made at the Gatja deviyo dibba-gi inside the vihare.
All was now ready for the second and most essential part of the ceremony. The foreman
dressed up as a prince, and had further a fine cloth (called vahantarava) over his head.
The costume (kumara ^ndumd) consisted of tuppotiya, hettaya, toppiya, sword and jewellery.
It would appear from the Mahavarpsa (Ch. LXXIII.) and other references that the eyes
were at one time regularly painted by the King himself. The chronicle states that
an ecclesiastical building (Dhammagdra) was erected by Parakrama Bahu I. “ It was
adorned with many images of the Conqueror made of gold and the other precious
substances, and decorated with an array of pictures of the Omniscient wrought on cloth.
And whenever the great king entered the house to paint with his own hands the eyes
of the images of the Conqueror, or to make offerings to the Tathagata, or to hear the

preaching of his doctrines that have never been surpassed, the nautch girls danced and Netra

the ceremony of placing pots full of water and of other rites; and on the completion
of the Netra Pinkama, his hands having been washed, he was graciously pleased to bestow
on the two artists, with the object of satisfying them and to enable them to make offerings
to Buddha, fields ... to be held absolutely from generation to generation.” Here the
King himself painted the eyes, as the reference to the washing of his hands shows ; and
this appears to have been the usual custom. It is stated likewise of Kirti ^rl, that on the
completion of the Gangarama Vihara, and all preparations had been duly made, that “he
set the eyes of the image amidst great rejoicing, and the sound of musical instruments.”
On the other hand, the eyes were sometimes painted by the craftsmen themselves, even
in the days of kings. A deed of a.d. 1753 makes mention of a land which had been
‘granted to Hamadi Bacjala for painting the eyes of Buddha’ (Lawrie’s Gazetteer, p. 937).
Evidently the ceremony was performed by the king if possible; just as in modern times,
great men are availed of to lay foundation stones; but when the king was not available
(and, of course, always after 1815, when the rule of the Kandyan kings came to an end)
the chief painter, in royal garb, performed the ceremony himself; and it is thus that
the ritual has been described to me by present-day craftsmen.
The painter of the eyes, whether the King or craftsman, was accompanied by a second
man, also robed, and with a cloth over his head, but less elaborately; both, and also
the ‘Brahmans’ if not very youthful, entered the vihara, but all other men, and still
more, women, stood afar off. The second man carried a mirror [kannaiiya : originally, no
doubt, of metal) and the brushes and black paint for painting the eyes. On opening
the door, mantrams were said, and the dhoby spread a white cloth to walk upon (or
perhaps this was done at an earlier stage). Proceeding to the image, before which stood
the indraktla above described, the second man held the mirror in front of it while the
first man painted in the eyes. The second man repeated mantrams * the while. If there

On such occasions, king, chiefs and people were brought near together, taking part in
joint dedications. At Ovisa, for instance, in 1775, on the occasion of eye painting, the
King dedicated lands to the Nallegoda Vihara, and many dedications of praveifi Imàs by
villagers were also made, the chiefs and others being witnesses (Lawrie’s Gazetteer, p. 671).
In the case of communal or private dedications, the Royal consent was required, and
readily given, often with the addition of further gifts. And so, to quote again the words
of the chronicle, the king was ‘one with the religion and the people.’-f-
After such almsgivings had been completed, the curtains before the image were drawn
back, and all the people entered with loud cries of‘Sadhu! Sadhul’ For some days
the festival {netra pinkama) continued, when many further presents were given to the
craftsmen, and the temple was formally endowed with lands.

III. ARTIFICER TENANT HOLDINGS.
The system of land tenure, by which certain services were to be rendered in return for
land held from the king, a religious foundation, or a chieftain, has been explained above
(p. 25), and the general character of the craftsmen’s services indicated. Some examples of
the holdings of artificers are here quoted in greater detail, from Lawrie’s Gazetteer.
The Dalada Maligava had a Badal Panguva at Çmbulpure, Hârispattuva; tenant,Vijëndragë
Punci Nayide, holding ij acre fields and i| acre garden. Services, commutable for
Rs. I‘So: to go to the Mâligâva and polish the gold and silver vessels and implements
of the temple during six days in a year; to give either an arecanut-cutter or two rings of
silver wire to the Diva Nilame after the New Year. When on duty at the Maligava, the
tenant received gruel in the morning, curry and rice in the afternoon, and a hun^uva of
raw rice in the evening.
The Gadaladeijiya Dévale had a Badal Panguva (goldsmith’s holding) at Gadalâdeijiya ;
tenant holding half an acre field. Services (commutable for Rs. y 3 5) : to supply a silver
sura and polish and repair the ran-avuda for the perahera ; put up an anamlstraya and
decorate it ; join in weeding the majuva ; supply one hutfifuva oil for Karti ; at each of
the festivals to give to the Basnayaka Nilame and the Vidane two silver rings each.
Also a Navan Panguva (smith’s holding) of the same extent. Services (commutable for
Rs. 5'85) : to give iron utensils for the multen-ge; work as a blacksmith ; clean ran-doliznà
pandan for the perahera ; nail laths ; give a pair of scissors and an arecanut-cutter for the
dalumura tatuva ; clear maluva, and put up an anamestraya and decorate it ; give a hurt4uva
of oil for Karti\ at each of the festivals to present to the Basnayaka Nilame and Vidane
an arecanut-cutter each.
At Etipola, a tenant held one acre field and 2I acres hena, and his service (commutable for
Rs. 2) was to appear before the proprietor at the New Year with forty betel leaves; and
to make billhooks for the proprietor, by whom iron and food were supplied, for six days
in the year.
At Embekke, the Kataragama Dévale possessed a Navan Panguva held by two goldsmiths
and a Buddhist priest. The area held was la. 3p. fields and la. 2p. gardens. The services
(commutable for Rs. 53'6o a year) were : to polish the gold, silver, brass, &c., vessels ; to
work in gold, silver, copper, and iron work ; to make and repair the hinges and keys ;
to join in repairs; to make a silver sura for the ehela tree; to maintain, whitewash, and
decorate an anamestra-ge -, to present the Basnayaka Nilame at each of the festivals with
a ring and an arecanut-cutter ; to make iron implements for the tenants for three months,
iron and charcoal being supplied.
So much for the services due to chieftains, or the proprietors of Ninda villages. The
service of the various Royal Artificer Tenants, as we have seen, consisted in supplying
craftsmen as members of the Koftal-badda and Pattal-hatara, the former for a part of the
year, the latter more continuously working for the king in Kandy.

V. VISVAKARMA.
Viávakarma, already referred to as the mythical ancestor of the Kammalar, is the patron
deity of arts and crafts, the great Over-craftsman of the Universe. He is the architect
of the gods, and revealer of the"Sthapatya Veda, or science of architecture and mechanics.
He is described in the Mahabharata as ‘ Lord of the arts, the carpenter of the Gods, the
fashioner of all ornaments. Who formed the celestial chariots of the deities, on whose
craft men subsist, and whom, a great and immortal God, they continually worship.’ He
is known in India also as Karu, the workman; Takshaka, the woodcutter; and Deva-
vardhika, the builder of the Gods. In the last capacity he is frequently referred to in
the Mahavarpsa, and as assisting human undertakings at the command of the Gods; as in
Ch. XXVIII., where by his aid, bricks are miraculously produced. In Ch. XXX., when
the King enquired of a certain bricklayer, “ In what form dost thou propose to construct
78

the cetiya?”, it is stated that Viivakarma in that instant inspired him. The bricklayer, FiJva-
filling a golden dish with water, and taking some water in the palm of his hand, dashed iarma
it against the water (in the dish); a great globule, like unto a ball of crystal rose to the
surface ; and he said, ‘I will construct it in this form.’ The delighted monarch bestowed
on him a suit of clothes worth a thousand, a splendid pair of slippers, and 12,000 kahapaifam
(coins) ” (Mahavairisa, Ch. XXX). It would be easy to quote any number of such stories
from Indian literature.
The Indian craftsman, indeed, conceives of his art not as the accumulated knowledge
of ages, but as originating in the divine skill of Viivakarma, and revealed by him. Beauty,
rhythm, proportion, idea, have an absolute existence on an ideal plane, where all who
seek may find. The reality of things exists in the mind, not in the detail of their appearance
to the eye. This inward inspiration upon which the Indian artist is taught to rely,
appearing like the still small voice of a god, that god was conceived of as Viivakarma.
He may be thought of as that part of Divinity which is conditioned by a special relation
to artistic expression. In another way, again, he may be conceived of as the sum total
of consciousness of individual craftsmen of all ages and places, composing a ‘group soul’
of a higher order of consciousness. These philosophical conceptions are not consciously
present in the minds of modern craftsmen, but they are not foreign to Indian thought.
Vi^vakarma, like the other divinities, is represented as possessing a certain form and
attributes. These are detailed in v. 149 of the Rupavaliya: “Salutation I give to Viiva-
karma, the fair and great, who is renowned and free, who hath five tilaka-muked. faces,
ten arms, holding a book and writing style, a sword, an adze (lit. a club), a citron, a cup,
a water-pot, a rosary, a cobra.(about his neck), a noose, hands betokening sternness and
beneficence (one closed and one open) and wearing a golden sacred thread.”
On PI. XXL will be found a representation of Vilvakarma, drawn to scale and with the
proper attributes as directed in the canon, prepared for me by Devasurendra Muhandirama
of Embekke.*
Viivakarma is not worshipped by craftsmen or others with offerings or ritual, but is often
referred to in charms and songs connected with building operations, where he is invoked
to ward off disasters and assist the craftsmen. An example of such a charm is the Vluvahu
Pfntma, “The Jump from the Threshold,” detailing ceremonies and offerings necessary
to hallow and protect a newly completed building, at the close of which the officiating
craftsman or kattafiya has to ‘spring from the threshold.’ Of this-work there is a printed
version, giving, beside the song itself, the auspicious mantrams that are chanted. This
Uluvahu Penima, after the manner of such works, recites the origin of the matter in hand,
in this case, the revelation of building and arts and crafts generally, by Viivakarma in the
time of the mythical Maha Sammata, and concludes with auspicious mantrams.
* “The initials [D.S.M.] attached to figures in this book, indicate the work of a craftsman named
Devasurendra Muhandirama of F-tnhekke.

Kandyan Sinhalese design are named and explained,-)- the elements, that is to say, of the
strictly decorative art, distinguished from the more pictorial and sculpturesque art of the
jataka paintings and images. The motifs in Sinhalese decorative art may be tabulated as
follows, using, as far as possible, the names employed by the craftsmen themselves :

SUN and MOON. The symbols of the sun and moon, the physical vestures of the great Design and
beings that control them, may be mentioned here. They are cut on sannas and on boundary ornament
stones as symbols of eternity, and are represented as a plain disc and crescent, the circle
sometimes with human features. Used as a charm or protection, on a divi-niya-pota Sun and
(cheetah’s claws mounted as a child’s pendant), they are seen in the example of PI. Moon
XLVIII., 9. But the circles in Figs. 15 and 17 (same PI.) represent not the sun, but
the disc of Vishnu, a weapon resembling the Sikh quoit. When used on a larger scale
in painted decoration, the sun has always a full round face with human features (as in
PI. XVI.; and the moon has in it the figure of a hare (see below, p. 89). The symbols
of the sun and moon are among the 108 magul-lakunu (Fig. 69). The sun and moon are
never worshipped with offerings, but are often invoked as guardians and protectors,
especially in religious agricultural songs.
KINDURA, KINNARA. The kindurO of Sinhalese painters, are beings, human above Kindura
and bird-like below; like a siren or a harpy, but with human arms and shoulders, and the
wings not large enough for flight (Fig. 10). Like
other mythical creatures, they are thought to dwell
in the Himalayas, that Indian forest of Broceliande,
where the boundary between the common world
and the ideal world of the imagination may at any
moment vanish. There has been some confusion as
to the meaning of the word kindura. The meaning
given by Monier Williams (Skt. Diet.) is a being of
the centaur type, half horse, half man; and he is, pre­
sumably, followed by Dawson (Hindu Mythology, Fig. 10. Kindura ; from a modern
p. 158), and Pincott (Prema Sagara, 1897, pp. 16, drawing [D. S. M.].
232). I do not know how the confusion arose. In
the man-bird form they are represented at Barahat (third century b.c.), at Ajanta (fifth
century a .d.), and mentioned by Aelian (second century a .d.) as follows; “These arq.
matchless for the melodious notes of their throat and tongue, so that . . . they are sirens,
or nearly so, for the mythical maidens so named are represented alike in the song of the
poet and the picture of the artist, as winged and having the legs of birds.” In the Prema
Sagara (loc. cit., p. 310) they are described as ‘playing away on pipes and kettle-drums.’
Griinwedel (‘Buddhist Art in India’) reproduces a rather graceful modern Siamese drawing
of the bird-woman form.*
The type of kindura known to Kandyan artists is, then, the true one. It is often called
liya~ or ‘ woman-i?Sif«ri7,’just as a mermaid is oftener spoken of than a merman. The
form is found not only in purely decorative work, but of necessity also in pictures of the
Canda Kinnara Jataka, as at Kelaijiya (PI. VIIa.). The story of the jataka is briefly thus:
The Bodhisat was incarnated as a Kinnara and lived with his wife Canda in the Himalayas.
The king of Benares committed his Government to his ministers and went alone to
th e Himalayas on a hunting expedition. The two Kinnaras, whose home was on the
Mountains of the Moon, had come down from them and were playing and singing by
a stream, Canda dancing to the sound of her fellow’s flute. The king heard the sound,
and creeping near, was smitten with love for Canda. ‘I will shoot the husband,’ thought
he, ‘and kill him, and I will live here with his wife.’ He shot and slew the Kinnara;
his mate fled in fear and sorrow to the top of the mountain, and a dialogue ensued between

Makara MAKARA. The makara resembles a dolphin or crocodile ; the snout ends in a trunk like
an elephant’s, but shorter and often curled up so as to be inconspicuous ; the body and tail
are bird-like; but the Early Indian forms (Fig. i8) had a distinctly fishy tail; as also in
PI. XLVII., 8. Fig. 17 is from an old drawing by a pupil of Devaragampola Silvatenna.
The makara is one of the signs of the zodiac ; one of the 108 mangul-lakui}u ; it is also the
banner of the Indian god of love. A special form of necklace, called tnakara-malaya, is
shown in PI. XLIX., 11. But its only common use in eighteenth century Sinhalese art is in
the makara toran which abound in Sinhalese architecture above doorways and images, as in
Pis. VII., I ; VIIa, above the image : PI. XXXVIII., 9 shows a modern, debased rendering
in ivory. The makara torana is an ornamental arch springing from two profile makara
facing each other, and with a ‘ kibihi’ face in the position of the keystone ; the intermediate
space on either side is variously treated. In PI. VIIa. it is filled with flying sanda kindura.
The makara face is never used by itself ; Mr. Bell’s ‘•makara quadrifrons’ of the Medagoda
Dévale stone pillar is really a ‘kibihi quadrifrons.’ He also mentions makara faces in
error on p. 20. Almost all full-face detached heads are kibihi \ all profile, içrapendiya.
Mr. Bell finds the prototype of the curious ornamental arches (makara toran') in the chaitya
window of the early Buddhist cave temples of India (Kegalla Report, p. 21).
The makara is described as follows in v. 148 of the Rûpâvaliya; “The makara has the
trunk of an elephant, the feet of a lion, the ears of a pig, the body of a fish living in water,
the teeth turned outwards, eyes like Hanuman’s, and a splendid tail.”

BHERUNDA PAKSH A YA. A ‘ double-headed eagle,’ like Design and
the eagle in the arms of Russia and Austria. Fig. i 8 a , repre- ornament
senting the flag of the Three Korales, shows very well its

very commonly in modern brass trays and plates. As a jewelled pakshaya

It may be noted here, that there can be little doubt of the
eastern origin of heraldry. The heroes of the Mahabharata
had each his own device. We have seen in the description of
the great perahera, how each district of the Kandyan kingdom
had its own flag and device ; also that the makara is the device
on the banner of the Indian Eros. So there need be no occasion
for surprise at recognizing in the arms of Austria and of
Russia, the very ‘double-headed eagle,’ an Indian form which
we find in Ceylon as the device of the Three Korales. The
historic evidence for the migration of this particular symbol,
by direct contact, is regarded as complete.*
Heraldry was introduced into Europe by the Crusaders. When

Sitpha SIMHA. The lion is the mythical ancestor, and totem animal of the Sinhalese, standing
for majesty and power, as in the case of Buddha’s name of Sakya-sirfiha, or the royal
name Rlja-siipha. A typical representation of the Sinhalese lion is given in Fig. 22,
from a modern drawing; see also Pis. XXVI., i ; XXIX., 7 ; XXXVIII., i and 5 ; and
XLV., 3. The full face detached, caWcA.kibihi-mana, shown in Fig. 23, is most often seen
in makara-toran, where it forms the central feature in the position of keystone of the arch ;
and it is used in design as the starting point of sprays and branches of foliaceous ornament.
Some sixteen, or thirty-two kinds of sitpha are recognized by Sinhalese artists; there are
three kinds beside the kesara sirnha, or lion proper; and the others are not really lions at
all, but other beasts, the word ‘lion’ being used generically for ‘animal,’ as the word ‘deer’
is used in speaking of ‘ mice, and such small deer,’ and regularly in the same way in older

;©klt may be remarked that the title of king or lord is often given to representations of the
hamsa, lion or cobra—it is the hamsa raja, simha raja or naga raja whose form is represented,
rather than individual animals. This is but another way of saying that all Indian art is
idealistic, representing types rather than individuals.
i@,The Rupavaliya accounts of the lion (above), nara simha (overleaf), and horse (p. 90)
should be carefully noted. For comparison Lquote the description of a lion from an old
Chinese canon. “ With a form like that of the tiger, and with a colour tawny or sometimes
blue, the lion looks like the Muku-inu, a shaggy dog. It has a huge head hard as bronze,
a long tail, a forehead firm as iron, hook-like fangs, eyes like bended bows, and raised ears.
The eyes flash like lightning, and the roar is like thunder.”* It is only in the light of
descriptions that the aim of Eastern art in representing animal forms can be rightly
understood. A tendency to naturalism is but rarely found, and it is rather the expression
of a mental conception than a realistic picture that is aimed at. It is this point of view
which has preserved Oriental art from such paltry and emasculated realism as the lions of
Trafalgar Square. The artist’s lion need be like no lion on earth or in any Zoological
Garden; he is not illustrating a work on natural history; it is rather for him to express
through it the whole theory of his national existence and the strength of his individual and
national idiosyncracy. It is this possibility which explains the vitality and expressiveness
* Quoted by Sei-ichi Taki, '■ Ti'he Kokka,' igo'6, No. 198, p. 486.

in the handiwork of the English painter of domestic pets.

Naga NAGA. The naga, or cobra, in relation to Indian religion and art is sufficiently well known
to need no long description. We do not find in the later Sinhalese art the semi-human
forms seen at Barahat, Ajanta, or Anuradhapura. The Naga Raja, Ananta, is often referred
to in Sinhalese poetry; the Naga Mucalinda who sheltered the Buddha is often depicted
or wrought (see PI. XVIII.). In decoration we find the naga as a simple cobra, e.g., on
woven cloths, embroidered on betel bags; in architecture as a protective symbol, e.g., the
naga bandha or ‘cobra knop’ marking the transition from the square to the octagonal part of
a wooden pillar.* The naga paruva is a whorl of cobras interlocked in succession, often
seen on modern brass trays; the simple naga paffuva, or pair of cobras with heads only
entwined I have only once seen and then not quite obvious; but the naga dapgaya (darapa
or dangarayd) an elaborate entwining of two cobras is not very rare (Pis. VII., 6, and LII.,
3); it is probably the same as Mr. Bell’s naga-putuwa (for pattuvd) and naga vpiksha; if so,
it may also be called nagapoffava, though I have never heard it. The form is well known in
widely separated parts of India (see Journal of Indian Art, Vol V., PI. 84), it is of interest
as corresponding to, and perhaps the origin of the classical caduceus. The cobra’s hood
is one of the 108 magul-lakunu.
Fish FISH. The mythical fish called matsya, an incarnation of Vishiju, is one of the 108
magul-lakupu. Fish are not often used in pure decoration ; but examples are to be found
in the ornament of earthenware, as in PI. XXV., 2. It may be remarked that fish
and wavy lines are symbolical of water, as in PI. I., where fishes are shown in the river,
preventing any possible mistake as to what is intended, much as ships and fishes are often
shown on the sea in old maps. The seven great rivers of India, in the magul-lakupu
(Fig. 69), are represented by seven squares, each containing a wavy line and a fish.

Brass or bronze hanging lamps have frequently the form of birds (PI. XLIV., 4). A

MRIGA. The deer is rarely found in decoration. One appears amongst the flowers in Mriga

HARE. A legend often depicted on vihara walls is that of the Hare in the Moon. The Hare
story is briefly as follows: The Bodhisatta was born as a hare who one day observed that
other animals provided themselves with stores of food, from which, if need were, they
would have something to offer to a beggar ; reflecting that he himself had nothing suitable,
and could hardly offer grass, he determined to offer his own flesh if the occasion arose.
Perceiving this splendid display of virtue, áakra descended to the forest and appeared to
th e hare in the form of a Brahman, who addressed the hare thus: “Wise Sir, if I could
get something to eat, after keeping the fast, I would perform all my priestly duties.” To
which the hare replied, “Brahman, you have done well in coming to me for food. This
day I will grant you a boon that I have never granted before, but you shall not break the
moral law by taking animal life. Go, friend, and when you have piled together logs of
wood and kindled a fire, come and let me know, and I will sacrifice myself by falling into
the midst of the flames, and when my body is roasted, you shall eat my flesh and fulfil
all your priestly duties.” áakra did accordingly, though the fire was but a feigned one.
The Bodhisatta came, and offering his whole body as a free gift, he sprang up, and like
89

Design and a royal swan alighting on a cluster of lotuses, in an ecstacy of joy he fell on the heap of
ornament live coals. He was not burnt by the feigned fire ; éakra revealed himself as having
come to put the hare’s virtue to the test, and saying, “ O wise hare, be thy virtue known
throughout a whole æon,” he took up the hare and painted the figure of it on the moon,
then replaced it on a bed of grass in the same forest and returned to his own place in
heaven. This story is told in the Sasajâtaka (ed., Cowell, Cambridge, Vol. III., p. 34).
The hare is used decoratively in the forest scene shown on PI. XVI.; (ceiling painting)
the hares are arranged in pairs, face to face, or in heraldic language ‘affronted’. The
hare does not appear to be used with conscious symbolism in Sinhalese art ; in Hindu
mythology it stands for mildness and speed. In simple representations of the moon,
which like those of the sun, are a common vihara decoration, the hare is usually represented
on the moon’s disc. Other paintings show áakra with a brush in one hand, and the hare
under his left arm, painting its form on the moon’s disk.

scene, PI. XVI. ; there is also a squirrel amongst the birds in the ceiling painting of PI. XV.,
and they are also found on a painted box in my possession. Their use is purely decorative.

Horse HORSE. The horse {aSvayi) is but rarely met with in Kandyan decoration. The

Hog, Crow DOG, CROW. These marks of degradation were occasionally inscribed on stones in

chàrters as symbols of the degradation awaiting those who should contravene them ; but
these instances can only by a stretch be included in the discussion of decorative art.

The following story is a translation of an extract from the Kathavastu Prakaraifa kindly
forwarded by Mr. T. B. Parajiatella. It is here given in order to further illustrate the
nature of the mythical nari lata v(la.
“ Long ago when a Raja named Barribadat ruled according to the four good rules in Baranas
Nuvara (Benares) in Kasirafa on the plain of Dambadiva, enjoying regal luxuries, there
dwelt a young Brahman in Pasalgama. At the death of his parents becoming master of all
their property, as he was living in enjoyment of the comforts of a layman, many hermits
92

during the rainy season came from the Himalaya forest to Benares to the abodes of men Design and
and dwelt in ease in places such as the royal gardens and went too and fro in the city streets, ornament
Thereupon when the townspeople saw the hermits they prepared eatables and drinkables
and gave to them and made arrangements for them to remain there till the end of the wet
season, the hermits yeasaying them, dwelt in the royal gardens and such places. The
townspeople began to treat them with food consisting of delicious dishes of every kind.
At that time the aforesaid Brahmaija Kumara one day entering the city observing the
people very eagerly treating the hermits and himself also going near the hermits remained
Fig. 31. Nari lata, from a painted earthen pot.
a few days, thinking “I also follow the calling of a hermit and adopt the holy life, I too
shall be similarly treated.” Accordingly resolving that it was well to don the hermit’s
robes, returning home, he gave over to his relatives and friends all his moveables and
immovables, and adopted the life of a hermit, eating jungle roots and fruits and the like
food, he dwelt in a certain rock cave. Having attained dhyana in a short time, and able to
travel in the sky,one day when near his cave, he saw in a creeper called Nari Lata, a full
blown flower having the appearance of a woman, in all wise of perfect beauty, glorious in
grace. At that very moment he lost the power of dhyana which he had so long successfully
practised by great self control; his dhyana disappeared at the thought of indulgence, his
passions were let loose. Feeling very sorrowful thereat (bethought) ‘Now what shall I
do? What is the use of taking all this trouble and living in the jungle’, and returning
to the abodes of men, taking a wife and thinking to live in comfort, he went to his village,
cas t off his hermit’s robes and became a layman and begot children; following industrial
and commercial pursuits he with difficulty supported his wife and children, and at the
end of his life died in accordance with karma, having forfeited the privilege of birth in
Brahma Loka. Thus even for those who have successfully attained dhyana the power of
levitation is destroyed by the strength of lust and they are subject to samara's woe. To
those that heed this fact, that desire is as a thorn in the flesh, like a thief stealing away
the holy life, like a great fire to burn the holy forest (of hermits) and reduce to ashes;
considering those most evil consequences, drive away evil lusts and adopt a holy life.” This
story of the consequences of lust is taken from the Kathavastu Prakarana.

and his companions had sorrowfully to resume their travels” (Philpot, loc. cit.).'

NELUN-MALA. The lotus is to oriental art all that the rose was to medieval English Nelun-mala
art. It underlies many forms not at first sight traceable to it. The most characteristic {Lotus)
simple lotus forms in use are the ‘rosettes,’ used to fill space (PI. XVIII.) or as
independent ornament, as in the case of pottery stamps (PI. XXV., 3), or in series,
especially on the beams of painted ceilings, as in PI. XV.; also typically at Kelaniya).
All circular objects, such as round boxes, lend themselves to simple lotus ornament.
We never observe that tendency to naturalism sometimes noticeable at Anuradhapura,
Ajanta, etc., but the simple rosette is capable of almost infinite variation; some of the
forms are shown in Fig. 34, others on PI. XX., 2; PI. XXIII., 2; PI. XXV., 3; PI.

Palä-peti PALA-PETI. Pala-peti is a form of ornament derived directly from the lotus; it is much
employed in Sinhalese art, and in all Indian art; it is a border or moulding (Fig. 37),
consisting of lotus petals, the petals fully seen, alternating with petals three-parts hidden by
those on either side of them, precisely as in the ordinary representations of the whole flower.
In the case of circular objects, such as metal dishes and vessels, sandal-wood grinding
stones, etc., the form at once suggests the lotus flower, and the petal ornament follows;
thence it has been adapted as a border applicable to straight work of every description,
particularly architectural mouldings. Innumerable examples of its use are illustrated in
the present book (PI. XLIL, i and 3, etc., etc.) It is sometimes greatly elaborated with
Hya-pata ornament (Fig. 39, m), but the simple forms are the most beautiful.

Malaya MALAYA. The ‘garland’ plays an important part in all Indian decoration. Its use in
ornament is derived from the actual use of garlands of flowers used to decorate the person
or offered to an image, or hung round a building. In jewellery this idea is very evident;
neck chains are called garlands, and named after particular flowers. The motif is seen
only rarely in Sinhalese architecture, and chiefly in the carving of wooden pillars, where
a garland of pearls is often represented round the top. In ceiling paintings the garland
motif is sometimes used as a frame (PI. XIV., 4) as in South Indian palampores, or hung,
as it were, along the very top of the wall, just under the ceiling; both may be seen at
K?laijiya. The garland motif in Indian art is one that often at first sight suggests
Renaissance influence, but there can be no doubt of its indigenous character, from its
constant occurrence on the most ancient monuments. But it is often used in India in a
very rococo and insincere way, even combined with ribands tied in bows. In such matters
Sinhalese art tends to be somewhat more pure and severe than other Indian art.
Pine-apple' ‘PINE-APPLE’ : this form (Fig. 33, ix.) is not distinguished by a separate name by the
Sinhalese, to whom it is one of many kinds of conventional flower ; neither do I think that
it has any real connection with the pine-apple, the resemblance being quite illusory; but
the cross-hatching of the middle part of the flower deserves notice ; it represents,! suppose,
rather the central florets of such flowers of those of the Composite, than any real fruit: it
is of further interest as recalling Assyrian forms. The cross-hatching is associated with
several different flower forms; some common types are shown in Fig. 59.

and West, rather than of a borrowing of East from West. In using this term for either

BINDUVA. The‘dot ’ is used singly, or in groups or series (PI. XXIV., various instances ; Binduva

IRI, line. There is not much to tell of the use of the simple line, except to note that Straight
the teaching of drawing does not begin with straight lines, but with curves. The use of line
firm black outline, drawn with the fine stiff telitaifa brush, is very characteristic. Clearness
and definition belong to all Eastern decorative art, and this is emphasized by the defined
outlining. The line as such is often used in the ornament of pottery.
VAKA, curve. Perhaps the most marked feature of Indian decorative art, and the arts Curve
derived from it, in Ceylon, Burma and Siam, and China lies in the character of its abstract
curved forms. I shall digress for a moment to discuss the general treatment of curved
forms in Sinhalese and other Eastern ornament.
The curved boundary of leaf or stem or scroll has always a peculiar character of life and
crispness, not often sinking into mere roundness or softness. Curves of this character are
well illustrated in Fig. 69, vi. and xiii. (Sinhalese), and in Fig. 47 (Siamese). This
type of abstract curve is not confined to recognizedly vegetable ornament; it appears as
much in the Siamese ‘flame ornament’ and the outline of a Siamese gable, as every stem
and leaf of liya vela ornament in Ceylon, and in the details of South Indian architectural
decoration. The reason for this universality is that Indian art at its best is never realistic,
but is based on abstractions or ideal forms; hence the ideal curved form which exists
as the prototype of all curved forms, if rightly apprehended, must inevitably reappear in
all idealized forms of ornament. This is what we find to be the case. The type of
curve I speak of is best described as temperate, or disciplined, but is capable of degeneration
into rococo forms. By such standards must the quality of Indian craftsmanship at various
periods be criticised.
The point is well illustrated by a quotation from Ruskin: “Our first constituents of
orn ament will therefore be abstract lines, that is to say, the most frequent contours of
n atural objects, transferred to architectural forms when it is not right or possible to render
such forms distinctly imitative. For instance, the line or curve of the edge of a leaf may
be accurately given to the edge of a stone, without rendering the stone in the least like
a leaf, or suggestive of a leaf; and this the more fully, because the lines of nature are alike
in all her works; simpler or richer in combination, but the same in character; and when
they are taken out of their combinations it is impossible to say from which of her works
they have been borrowed, their universal property being that of ever-varying curvature
in the most subtle and subdued transitions, with peculiar expresssons of motion, elasticity,
h 4 103

Design and or dependence.”* As also remarked by him, curves of this type not only mark the force
ornament and vigour of vegetable growth, “ but some among the most beautiful of them are described
■ by bodies variously in motion, or subjected to-force; as by projectiles in the air, by the
Ideal curves particles of water in a gentle current, by planets in motion in an orbit, by their satellites,
if the actual path of the satellite in space be considered instead of its relation to the planet;
s- by boats, or birds, turning in the water or air, by clouds in various action upon the wind,
■ by sails in the curvatures they assume under its force, and by thousands of other objects
. moving or bearing force.” They appear also in the forms of flame. Disciplined spiral
forms suggest the curling of a tendril or the involution of a shell. Spiral and continuous
curve together give the simplest form of‘branch’ or vine.
Observe that these ideal and disciplined curves are as characteristic of Indian as of Gothic
art. The fact is, that the quality which had been looked upon as Gothicness, and which
Ruskin called Christian, is not a thing peculiar to Gothic art, but is found in all great and
ideal art. Hindu or Buddhist, ornament is often intensely and surprisingly Gothic in
feeling; and cannot fail to be so, since both agree in the recognition of abstract natural
form, or ideal form, as the true basis of all noble ornament, and the purpose of art to be the
revelation of a deeper reality than that of phenomenal appearance. And this applies only
to Gothic art of the thirteenth century; it is the essential character of all Indian art from
the beginning. Sinhalese art sometimes falls away from this ideal and becomes rococo.
It is not by chance that the Sinhalese craftsman comes to have these disciplined or temperate
curves at his command; for the most essential part of his artistic apprenticeship and
training consists of instruction calculated to impress their character indelibly upon his
mind, so that his hand cannot fail to trace them, whether he will or no. Hence the great
ease with which he repeats ornamental forms based on the fundamental curves, and the
certainty and freedom of his touch. The whole character of his later work depends on
the education in the use of flattened curves with which his training begins.
The first and most thorough part of the Sinhalese craftsman’s education in design consists
in the close study of the ideal curved form of the vaka deka, or double curve, and from this
point— the spiral being evolved by the reflexion of the simple curve upon itself—he is
carried on until he has such command of curved form as to design easily such forms as the
most elaborate tiringi tale; and the subtle sense of curvature thus ingrained in him expresses
itself ever after in whatso form of leaf or stem or feather that he may devise. Anyone
who has spent time copying much Sinhalese or similar Eastern ornament, or has critically
examined reproductions of original work drawn by untrained men will know how extremely
difficult it is to preserve the sensitive types of curvature consistently ; especially in repeating
patterns, it is fatally easy to allow the forms to degenerate and weaken. But the trained
craftsman never falters, because the curve is second nature to him; he could not draw
it wrong without deliberate effort. Such is the curve of energy and growth ; rhythmic
and disciplined, but unsatisfied, ever striving towards an end not yet attained; as of a vine
climbing upwards vigorously, or restless flames of fire. Contrasted with it is the rounded
curve, or circle; as of the lotus, expressing peace and balance. The circular form is
complete, without beginning or end; it is a form at perfect rest. Not wdthout reason
has the circular been chosen to typify the Law {Dharma). These facts seem to have been
unconsciously realised by the best designers.
Study the vihara ceiling reproduced on PI. XV., and analysed in Fig 52, The floral
ornament of the painted boards is overflowing with life and energy, almost restless in its
vigour, though the vigour is always a disciplined vigour of growth. But tiirn to the great
Stones of Venice^ ed. 2, p. 215.

TRIANGLE. Triangles in Kandyan art are of three sorts. First, the chevron border 'Triangle
(Fig. 56, a) is equivalent to a series of alternating upright and inverted triangles; if one
series be shaded or coloured, the other left plain, this is at once apparent, as in Figs.
56, B and c, and in Pis. XXXIII., 1-3, and XLIX., 10. Borders thus originating are
105

Design and distinguished by the presence of the two boundary lines, passing through the bases and
ornament apices of the triangles.
A second type of triangle is derived from the is-leaf (q.v.) and is used as a border of the
same general character (PI. XLIV., 3), but recognised by the absence of the line passing
through the apices of the triangle ; there is further generally some small star or projection
at the apex, corresponding to the drip-tip of the real leaf (PI. XXX., i, and Fig. 41, g).
On some woven cloths, pairs of these triangles are set point to point, forming an hour-glass
pattern, but still called bc-kola by the weavers.
The two triangles already mentioned are usually equilateral. A third kind is isosceles
and much elongated. It appears typically on lacquered sticks, and is called patura (wedge
or wing). It is also common on South Indian and Malayan printed cloths worn in Ceylon
(see PI. XXII., royal costume of 1603). It is considered by Rouffaer and Juynboll
(Indische Batikunst, III., 163) to be of Malay-Polynesian origin. The ‘¿ff-leaf triangle,’
on the other hand, is the one referred to by the same authors as similar to, but less
pronounced than the Malay-Polynesian type, and as probably of Buddhist origin.
Diya-r(la DIYA-R^LA. The chevron, ‘zig-zag’ or wave is often met with; as on PI. XL, 4,
outer ring of ornament on seat: and often on woven cloths and mats, as PI. XXVIII.,
1,15, also in paintings of textiles (PI. XIV., 5). The use of a zig-zag line to symbolize
water is of hoary antiquity, and now world wide. It is interesting to find the name diya
reía, ‘wave,’ still employed by Sinhalese craftsmen to denote chevron or zig-zag pattern.

mouth ’ A very characteristic and fanciful motif is the setting of a branch or spray from the mouth
of an animal [Figs. 12, (15) and 68] or bird (PI. XXIII., 2). A common example is the

idea in such cases is probably that of flower offering, as in many Barahat sculptures. I
have myself used this motif in the cover design of the ‘Ceylon National Review.’

APPENDIX TO CHAPTER IV.:
THE RUPAVALIYA.
A part of the artistic canon of Sinhalese painters is found in a Sanskrit work called the
R upavaliya, which is much relied on in Kandyan painters of the best sort. The versions
procurable are usually very corrupt and imperfect. Nothing is known of the date of the
work, which is clearly of Hindu origin. The learned Mudaliyar, E. R. Gooneratne, to
whom I am indebted for a revised text and a translation based on my own and other copies
of the work collated by Sllakkhandha Thera of Simbali Avasa, thinks that from the
language the work may have been written in the eleventh century. I proceed to give an
analysis of the contents, with translations of verses of interest in connection witn Sinhalese
art; which reservation it is necessary to make, because the figures of many of the gods

RafUvaliya necessary to represent them, and can do so when required. The verses are in the form
of an invocation to, or meditation {dhyana) on, the beings described.

CHAPTER V. ARCHITECTURE.
"■ Dhe T'emples of their Gods are of rare and 'Exquisite Work” (Knox).
IT is not meant here to give any exhaustive account of late Mediaeval Sinhalese
architecture, but only such a general account of it as shall enable the reader to
understand its relation to the fine and lesser arts, and to comprehend the arrangement
of such temples as he may have the opportunity to visit. It must not be supposed that
Medieval Sinhalese architecture can compare either in extent or magnificence with that
of Southern India or with that of earlier times in Ceylon, to which the well-known remains
at Anuradhapura and Polonnaruva testify. But it will be found that the typical Kandyan
wooden architecture has a distinct character of its own, and that it responds directly to
the needs of a small agricultural people, not luxurious, and rather prosperous than wealthy.
In spite of the great remains at Anuradhapura it should be fully realised that the truly
national and indigenous architecture has always been one of wooden building; the great
stone buildings whose remains attract so many visitors to the ‘buried cities,’ were probably
erected with Indian assistance and partly by Indian workmen; so were many later stone
buildings (especially when for the worship of Hindu gods) such as the sixteenth century
Beretidi Kovil and the unmistakeable Hindu temple at Ridi Vihara. Other buildings
such as Lankatilaka, the Dalada Maligava and Gaijegoda vihara (Sab.) having more or
less stone work in their construction were probably made by native or long naturalised
gal-va4uv0\ but a majority of viharas are without stone construction, or have only a stone
doorstep or ‘moonstone,’ as at Degaldoruva; stone steps and plain balustrade are also
met with.
It should be remembered that in India, stone building was not practised until a little
before Aioka’s time (third century b.c.), and no doubt a knowledge of it came to Ceylon
from Northern India along with the Buddhist missionaries; but a wooden style was already
well established, and while serving as the model for the work in stone, has never been
itself displaced. Buddhist wooden architecture of the same general type is still to be
found in Nepal; in most other parts of India it has been replaced by stone.
At a later time, when a knowledge of stone building had spread to Southern India and
the great Dravidian building tradition sprang up, it was easy for the Sinhalese kings to
get such masons as they required thence; and it is probable that most of the gal-va4uvo
actually living in Ceylon as subjects of the Sinhalese kings in later times, were of South'
Indian blood.
Domestic We have already seen that the dwelling house was a simple framed one-storied building
building of timber and wattle and daub, like an English half-timbered cottage, with thatched
roof and small central courtyard. Each man built his own home, except a few noblemen
whose manor-houses were better and more pretentious than the wood and daub cottages
of the ordinary people. Nails were not used in ordinary building, but everything was
fastened with rattans and other jungle ropes. The solid timbers of royal buildings were
morticed and tenoned together in a very substantial manner. The use of stone was
confined to royal and religious buildings.
The house itself was built on a stone and mud foundation raised above the ground level;
this foundation, smoothly plastered and cowdunged, formed the floor and inner verandah,
and projected outside the walls as a narrow ledge or outer verandah {pila), used to sleep
or sit on. The houses of great persons only differed from those of lesser men by having
more rooms and courtyards, better timber, the beam ends and verandah pillars and their
brackets sometimes carved, and in a very few cases only, a tiled roof. Fig. 70 shows the

Granaries Two other kinds of buildings may be mentioned before speaking of religious ones. The
[Atii) granary {atuvo), always raised on low stone pillars as a protection against white ants, was
if small, built over some part of the inner verandah of the house ; if large, as in the case
of a royal store {maha gabaiâvd), a pansala, or the home of a well-to-do or powerful man,
it formed a separate building. But in the Kegalla district a special type of small granary
is found, a cask-shaped wattle-and-daub erection on stone pillars, whitened with kaolin,
and covered with a heavy thatch, standing near the house but not forming a part of it ;
this type (called bissa, pi. bihi) is noteworthy as being often ornamented with paintings
of elephants, etc. (PI. VII., 9). The outer walls of even quite small houses are sometimes
similarly painted with conventional designs (PI. VII., 6). The granaries were usually
sealed in clay with a wooden seal, of which a specimen is figured on PI. XIII., 5.
Best Houses The second building to be mentioned is the ambalama or wayside shelter. Of these there
{Ambalam) were many at no great distance apart on frequented paths, and better ones in each village,
erected by all the villagers, or by some one man (or even a woman), anxious to perform
so meritorious an act.* A beautiful ambalam of moderate size at Mangalagama (Four
Korales) is shown on PI. VII. The pillars are of stone, supporting on carved wooden
brackets an open timbered roof (Fig. 76) covered with tiles, and with two earthen finíais
at the end of the roof ridge. The smallest ambalam consisted of a foundation of four beams
to sit upon, with four posts at the corners and a thatched roof ; the better ones had more
pillars and were sometimes divided into compartments for the convenience of those desirous
of spending the night there. But a single-roomed ambalama could be sub-divided for the
sake of privacy by means of a pili-vela (‘clothes-line,’ made by Rodiyas,) consisting of
two cords of niyauda fibre passed through a central block ; the four ends of the cords being
fastened in the four corners of the room, and cloths hung over the cords themselves,
the room was conveniently divided into four separate compartments.
Ambalam were sometimes well carved, and even painted ; hut no provision was made for
the entertainment of the strangers, who usually carried their own food and cooking utensils.
But near to an ambalama, and elsewhere along the roads are to be seen ‘drinking fountains,’ ,
that is, stone or earthen pots kept supplied by the neighbours with pure water, covered
with a lid and provided with a dipper {kinissa).

We have already seen (p. 37) ‘that the ambalama served not only as a halting place for

One of the principal routes was from Hambantota to Kandy, passing through Vellavaya
and up’ on to the Uva patanas ; through {ittalapitiya, Dambevinne (Velimada), Paraijagama
(Fort MacDonald) to Maturafa and thence through Hanguranketa, Mirupe, Talatuoya
and Ampitiya to Kandy. The longest stage between two iiarti was not more than fifteen
miles. From Kandy, a main track proceeded to Anuradhapura. There was also a track
which passed down through the Three and Four Korales to Sitavaka and Colombo.-j'
The present-day Government Rest House, or Dak bungalow as it would be called in India,
4
may be regarded as the descendant of the old i am, but accommodates a very different type
of traveller. Rest-houses of the old type, in a debased Kandyan style, have in recent times
been built at Ratnapura, Ruvanveli, and Kegalla.
Wayfarers were of the following sorts, viz.; persons going to Kandy to perform their Services
or take in their produce-rent; officials on tour, who travelled with a great retinue and were
sometimes a grievous burden ; king’s messengers; traders, not many ; and parties of pilgrims,
especially on the way to Adam’s Peak or other shrines. Neither men nor women thought
much of walking long distances. Women of rank, and sometimes men, were borne in
palanquins. Carts were known, but few roads were practicable for wheeled traffic.

But viharas are often built on bare rock, especially when such is found on the top of some
low hill overlooking the surrounding hills and villages. The need for raising the buildings
on stone pillars is then avoided. The situation of such viharas is often most romantic,
as at Lankatilaka, where the beautiful temple buildings are visible from many points across
wide stretches of rice-field. But viharas are also sometimes built on an artificial stone, or
stone and mud, foundation, as the Dajada Maligava itself.
Viharas are rarely of two stories, as at Dodantale, where the ground floor serves as a
preaching hall [baija maiuva) and the upper floor for the image house [pilima-gi) and its
verandah ; or at the Dalada Maligava, where the tooth-relic is enshrined in an upper room.
Sometimes the roof over the image house is raised high above the verandah roof, the image
room being proportionately high within (as at Gangarama, PI. VII., 5) and if, as atGaijegoda
(Sab.) there is a small window in the wall high up, the effect of a clerestory is produced.
The ceiling is usually boarded, and the boards painted passing finely (PI. XV., Ganegoda
vihara ceiling); the verandah roof may be similarly treated (PI. XVI., Dalada Maligava
verandah ceiling,— now altered, and for the worse). Where the ceiling of the verandah or
inner room is left open, the handsome timbering is ample compensation, as in the upper
verandah, PI. VIII., Dalada Maligava. Observe here also the ‘rayled banister,’ as Knox
would have called it.
There is almost invariably a verandah (in the tiniest viharas merely a portico), the roof of
which is pitched at a lower angle than that of the roof of the main part of the building.
The verandah and main roof are structurally distinct, as indicated in the diagram (Fig. 72).
To this fact is due the pagoda-like appearance of many viharas (as in the Buddhist
architecture of Nepal and Burma, where Chinese influence may have carried the tendency
further); for the roof seems occasionally almost to turn up
at the edge, as contrasted in the slope of the inner and
outer parts of it. The constructive distinction between
verandah and main roof is probably due to the influence
of the cave temple, which forms the actual image house
{pilima-gi) and corresponds to the interior of the construe- .
tional vihara and against which a lean-to verandah is built,
as at Ridi Vihara.
Dagabas in particular were covered with pure white lime

amongst the green rice-fields is often most beautiful. But
it is now usual to mix a large proportion of Ricketts’ blue
with the white, which thus loses all its purity and beauty.

The pohoya-ge]\s&t referred to is a rectangular building, erected on a solid foundation within

Fortifica- Forts and fortifications were few or none, the Kandyans trusting rather to the woods and
tions hills as their natural protection. But watches were kept. The guard-house (mura-gi)
at the top of Malabar Street, in Kandy, a small house covered with flat tiles, still remains.
There were also certain kadavat or guarded entrances to the inner circle of the Kandyan
kingdom, as at Ambuluva, where part of a wall still remains. In the Jud. Com. Diary
for 6th October, 1819, there is a notice that a man in the last king’s reign was sent to
Moragammana to teach the people there how to pound rice for the king, according
to a new method, and on returning, found the gravets at Ambuluva shut (Lawrie’s
Gazetteer, p. 43).
