APPENDIX TO CHAPTER V.
MAYAMATAYA.
The Mayamataya is, according to the account which the unknown writer gives of his work,
a translation into Sinhalese of an original work written in Sanskrit ilokas, made in 8aka
1756 (a.d. 1837). The authorship of the original work is ascribed to the fishis-, its
date is quite uncertain, but it is probably not less than several centuries old, and contains
matter that may be much older. The work is intended for architects, but it is rather
120

an astrological handbook and guide to the reading of omens than a manual of craftsmanship Mayä-
like the Säriputra or the Vaijayantaya. The work is badly arranged, and full of contra- mataya
dictions and redundancies, and even considered apart from these defects, appears to
contain much that is puerile and superstitious. The chief subjects dealt with are the
propitiation of nature spirits who may be injured or offended at various stages of the work,
practical advice as to the planning of a house and laying out of a town, and information
as to auspicious and inauspicious omens, and astrological information as to what are
favourable times for beginning the different kinds of work. The Sinhalese builder is
still careful to begin his work at an auspicious hour, and believes that the neglect of this
precaution would be disastrous. But the elaborate ceremonies connected with the felling
of the ‘auspicious post’ {maguí kapa) are never now observed in the case of ordinary houses,
and even in the eighteenth century they would only have been observed in the case of
very important buildings, and when felling the ?hala gaha for the perahfraJ*
The injunction to avoid a hollow tree for the maguí kapa reminds us of the beautiful story
in the jataka book, the Kusanaji Jataka,-!- of which the gist is as follows;
The Bödhisat was born once as a deva that dwelt in a clump of kusa grass in the king’s Kusanäli
garden at Benares. In the same garden there grew a beautiful Wishing-tree, with a ‘Jaiaka
straight stem and spreading branches, and the king loved it. In it dwelt one who had
been a king of devas and was now reborn as a tree-devl; and the Bödhisat was her great
friend. Now the palace roof was a king-post roof, and the main pillar had grown
shaky. The royal carpenters were ordered to replace it with another; but they could
find no tree good enough, except the beautiful Wishing-tree. They came to the king
and told him that they feared to fell this sacred tree. But he ordered them to set about
it at once. So they went to the garden, and made offerings to the tree, meaning to fell
it the next day. But the tree devi was plunged into the deepest sorrow when she heard
their words and knew that her dear tree was to be destroyed. No one of the other forest
devas could offer help, when at last the Bödhisat came thither, and being told of the
news, answered hopefully, ‘ Have no fear, I will see that the tree is not cut down.’
Next day, when the carpenters came, the Bödhisat assumed the form of a chameleon and
ran up and down the tree, in and out, so that it seemed to be a hollow tree, and full of holes.
Then he rested on the branches and wagged his head to and fro. Seeing this, the master-
craftsman, thinking it was a hollow tree, laid his hand on it and exclaimed, ‘The tree is
rotten, we were too hasty last night in making our offerings, let us be off to find another.’
And so they went off full of scorn for the great tree which had been saved by the wisdom
of the Bödhisat.

their hands. When they were come back to the great tree, they hung upon it a garland
of five branches, and girt it with a cord, fastened a knop of flowers against it and lit a
lamp, and so honouring the tree, they spoke thus before it, ‘ On the seventh day from this
we shall fell this tree, for this is the king’s command. Let those devas who may be dwelling
in the tree depart elsewhither, and not unto us be the blame.’
The deva that dwelt in that tree heard their words, and thought to himself, ‘These
craftsmen are agreed to fell my tree, and to destroy my home. I myself shall perish
when my place of habitation is destroyed. Also the young iai trees that are all about me
will be destroyed; and in them there dwell many devas of my kith and kin. My own
death touches me not so near as the destruction of my children, let me then save their lives
if I may avail thereto.’ So at the hour of midnight, the tree-deva, in the radiance of his
divinity, entered the king’s resplendent chamber, and stood beside the royal pillow
sobbing, his glory lighting up the whole room. At which the king was overcome with
fear and surprise, and stammered out, ‘ What god art thou, that dost appear floating in
the air, wearing an angel’s garb; what is thy grief, why dost thou weep so heavily?’
To which the deva-prince replied, ‘I am called in thy realm, O king, the Lucky-tree;
for sixty-thousand years all men have loved and worshipped me. Many a house and
town, many a palace too they made, yet never did me wrong; honour thou me, even as
they did, O king.’ But the king answered, ‘Never have I yet seen a trunk so fine, so tall
and great of girth, so thick and strong. I shall raise a glorious palace, resting on a single
column; there shalt thou long endure.’ The deva-prince answered, ‘ Since thou are set
on my destruction, one thing I ask, to cut me small, cut me piecemeal and limb from limb,
0 king, if thou must cut at all. Cut first the top, the middle next, and then the root of me—
and if so thou fellest me, O king, death will not give me grievous pain.’ The king said
then, ‘This is a painful death—to sever from the living frame first the hands and feet, then
nose and ears, and last of all the head. O Lucky-tree, O forest-lord, why will thou thus
be cut piecemeal, what gain is thine thereby ? ’ To which the Lucky-tree replied, ‘ Hearken
now while I reveal the meaning of my wish to be felled in pieces— there is a sufficient and
a worthy reason for it: my kith and kin have grown up around me, and beneath my shade,
1 should crush them if I fell entire upon them, and very great would be their sorrow.’
The king was greatly moved at these words and thought within himself, ‘This is a noble-
minded god that would save the dwellings of his fellows despite the destruction of his
own ; and he broke into these words, ‘ O Lucky-tree, O forest lord, thy thought is noble
indeed; as thou wouldst save thy kindred, so I shall spare thee, have no more fear.’
Then the deva-prince spake to the king, and counselled him and left him. And the king
took to heart his words, and gave generous gifts and alms, until the time came for his
departure to join the hosts of heaven.”*
It must not be thought that the only idea in this so-called ‘ tree-worship’ is one of propitiation
of a feared unseen power; combined with and softening this feeling, is the old Hindu
1
* ‘ ‘The Jataka^ ed. Cowell: No. 465, Voi. IV. have endeavoured to put the unsympathetic

feeling of sympathy for everything that has life, and desire to avoid injury to living things. Mdyd-
It has everywhere been held that, apart from the little organized life of the tree itself, mataya
trees and forests are the abode of nature spirits (nymphs, dryads, devas, nats, etc.)
approximating to, but scarcely reaching the human plane of evolution. Nowhere has
this been more the case than in India, where, moreover, a logical perception of the unity
of all life is expressed in a repugnance to the destruction of life in any form.
“A true Hindu would not heedlessly injure the slightest object that has life. A tree is
as much a manifestation of the Divine Wisdom and Power as the man himself, and the
Devas engaged in the building up of a flower, love their work with as much fond regard
as the artist, who paints its picture, loves the semblance. The man, who, through
thoughtlessness or ignorance, injures these divine works, incurs the anger and ill-will of
these elemental workers. Therefore a Hindu in plucking a flower or cutting a twig prays
to the Supreme, and asks permission of the industrious ones who have made it. By the
very fact that he recognizes their labour and appreciates their actions he propitiates these
Sylvan Devas and gets their good-will and blessing.”*
There is thus a double strand in ‘tree-worship’—a desire to avert revenge by due
propitiation ; and a shrinking from the infliction of injury. In its extremest form, and
when the tree-deva is conceived to be malignant, the first feeling has led even to human
sacrifices offered to trees, and this, as it is clear from the literature,-j- must have been a
custom at some long past stage of social development; the other feeling finds expression
in the gentle consideration and beautiful ceremonial of the Mayamataya, verses 20— 27,
and in the universal Hindu love of trees and forests.
The idea of the actual relation between the deva and the tree is of a mystical character.
The anti-realism of Indian philosophy makes it possible for the most intellectual minds
to accept the possibility of other worlds and other beings than those we call material;
for even to the material world a merely relative reality is granted,— the phenomenal world
exists at all, only in so far as it exists in relation to a mind, and to none of us is it the same
identically. Hence the impossibility of questioning the ‘reality’ of another man’s sub­
jective experience, or denying the possible existence of beings of many orders, having a
reality as great, but no greater than that of this phenomenal world.
The relation between tree and deva is symbolically represented in art and literature in
various ways. Often a face is drawn amidst the branches.| to suggest rather than to show
the indwelling deva, whose life is, in a strange way, the tree’s life, or bound up with it,
,yet is not the tree itself. At other times the tree deva is represented as dwelling in a
mansion which is in, or perhaps rather ‘at’ or ‘through,’ the tree, and which is not
ordinarily visible to human beings.§ This is a form of the well-known folk-lore conception
of the ‘invisible house.’
The tree-deva is able to leave the tree, and has its own divine form, conceived as anthropo­
morphic, yet can assume other forms at will, and on returning, ‘enters’ the tree and
becomes invisible; the deva’s life is ended with that of the tree. Tree devas may be
e ither malignant or beneficent. In Alavakadamanaya the tree-spirit is a man-eating
devil; in the Sutasoma Jataka, a gentle dryad, to whom the man-eating raja endeavours
to make human offerings, in complete misunderstanding of her true character. But
otherwise, the tree-spirit is realised as gentle and beneficent, and honoured as such by

MilyJ- offerings of flowers and sandal paste, and the love of the people; his or her home must
mataya be kept clean and pure. There is a wonderful delicacy and beauty in these pagan ideas.
There is nothing more characteristic of paganism, than its ideal conception of the purity
and delicacy of the personified powers of nature, and of the local habitations of the gods.
Just as in Iceland Thorolf Mostbeard laid down that ‘no man unwashed should turn his
eyes to Holyfell, and that nought should he done to death there, either man or beast,’*
so in Ceylon, even the Kapurala may not enter the dévale sanctum unless free from
ceremonial defilement, the threshing floor is a sacred and pure place, and the worshipper
in a Hindu temple must bathe and put on a clean cloth washed by his own hands ere
worshipping, and the inner precincts are closed to those of lower caste who are eaters of
meat and otherwise follow the less spiritual modes of life.
c©^. Whatever views may be held as to the real meaning of these things, which some would
call superstition, and some would call poetry, I am sure at least of this, that no good will is
ever wasted, and that in the selfish or the loving attitude of men towards even a tree, there
is some actual meaning, some real truth, some impulse, which has, in its own way, its
own effect. It would be easy to say more, but this will perhaps suffice. Before turning,
however, from this subject, to me of such great interest, I will throw a sop to the philistine,
as follows: these feelings and ideas, whether they be regarded as ‘superstitious’ or not,
have nevertheless a practical aspect; for the Indian objection to the unnecessary destruc­
tion of trees and forests, however sentimental, would have checked or prevented such a
wholesale destruction of forest as has now, for example, turned whole districts in Ceylon
into nightmare prospects of unending tea plantations, reduced the rainfall, and increased
both the rate of soil erosion in the hills, and the liability of the lowlands to disastrous
floods, at the same time necessitating so strict a preservation of the remaining timber that
the husbandman is hard put to it to get the wood needed for fences, ploughs and the
like, and the householder to get the timber needed for the massive construction of houses
such as those of a century ago.
It is time to return from this digression to the MaySmataya itself.
Of particular interest are the verses speaking of good and evil craftsmen, and their fate
in this life and in lives to come. It must be understood that in the old days a man’s trade
was the heaven-ordained work of his caste or guild, and the resulting idea of noblesse oblige,
together with the sanction for morality which the doctrine of karma carries with it, had
something to do with the excellence of the old craftsmen’s work.
Some of the verses devoted to practical advice are shrewd and even obvious, as the
warning not to build on a site which is wet even in dry weather (v. 243) ; the recom­
mendation to grow such fruits as jak, coconut, mango, and sugar-cane about the house
(v. 266). The work, in fact, appears to contain a practical nucleus of sound advice, now
much corrupted, misunderstood and overlaid by meaningless superstition. It is, never­
theless, of interest as revealing some of the ideas associated by the architect with his
work, and giving details of methods of construction and social customs of which mention
might not be readily found elsewhere. A summary now follows :

CHAPTER VI. WOODWORK.
‘ He taketfi i3f crooked piece of wood, and full of knots, and carveth it with the diligence of his idleness,
and ihapeth it by the skill of his indolence'—E cclesiastes.
WE have seen that Kandyan architecture is one typically of wooden, not of stone
construction. It should be remembered that the general use of wood for
building domestic utensils is a survival from very early times, and that while
on the Indian continent wood was very largely superseded by stone as a building material,
jn Ceylon the indigenous style remained to the last one of wooden architecture. It is
therefore natural that much of the best Kandyan woodwork should be architectural, and that
*it should derive a special charm from its architectural adaptation. The timbered hall and
roof at their best are such as any people might be proud of, compafkble with the lesser sort
of Gothic timbered hall and roof ; the carved doors and windows are at once decorative and
constructional ; and every detail is of artistic and historic interest. The constant richness
and variety of carving, and its close relation to the nature of the material are always pleasing ;
and we never find it so disposed as to interfere with the utility of beam or frame ; it appears
almost always as if it were an essential and necessary part of the constructional work.

Ther^ is usually a verandah to all important buildings, in which case a characteristic Roofs
pectiliarity of the roof appears, viz., the change of slope which gives a pagoda-like
appearance to many Kandyan buildings. This results from the separate construction and
different slope of the main roof and the verandah roof. In some cases the latter is a good
deal lower than the main roof, so that the verandah is practically a lean-to against the wall
of the main building (PL VII., 5) giving the false appearance of a two-storied building;
if a window is pierced, the effect of a clerestory is produced. The change of slope is
Sometimes emphasized by different tiling of the two parts of the roof.
'In the case of open buildings having a double series of pillars, but no walls, the change
of slope of the roof takes place naturally and constructionally over the inner series of pillars.
In this case, then, the ‘verandah’ becomes part of the main building related to the central
space as aisle to nave in a church. The Kandy ‘Audience Hall’ illustrates this type of
building well. It is described by Mr. Lewis* as follows:
“The audience hall of the kings, which is now used as a court-house, consists of a high-
pitched roof supported by four rows of wooden pillars arranged so as to form a nave with
its aisles, supported on a stone platform and without walls, the building being open on
all sides. The pillars . -. support heavy beams and a king-post roof. The wall plates
are elaborately carved and support carved terminals. The roof projects considerably over
the pillars. The slope of the roof over the aisles is at a less acute angle than that of the
roof over the main part of the building.”
The change of slope is also frequently seen in walled
buildings lacking a verandah, and is then the result of
special construction of the main roof; into which the
verandah roof is, as it were, absorbed (PI. VII., 1,2). We
seem to have the following pedigree;—lean-to verandah of
a cave-temple; lean-to verandah of constructional vihara;
verandah raised to roof level (PI. VII., 7) retaining difference
of slope ; adoption of same form in main roof even
when verandah is absent (PI. VII., i, 2); and to that an
historically speaking secondary lean-to verandah may be
added (PI. VII., 5).' The principles are easily applied in
the further elaborated case of buildings of two or more
stories, such as devales, and a few viharas (Dalada
Maligava, etc.)

The projection of the roofs of Kandyan buildings to a con­
siderable distance beyond the pillars or walls is a noticeable
feature. This is an adaptive character. As Mr. Lewis
remarks, the “ overhanging eaves are specially suited to a
rainy climate like that of most of the Kandyan country,
and serve to protect the walls from becoming sodden.
They have, therefore, instinctively been adopted by the
Kandyans, and in this the native builders show more sense of vihara garth at GaijegOiJa,
than European architects in Kandy and Colombo, who are Sab., showing timbering of
fond of erecting buildings with elaborate cement or plaster roof. The tiles are missing
façades which speedily look weather-beaten and shabby, on one side. The triangular
and the walls of which get soaked through annually and niches in the wall are for
therefore soon deteriorate.” The characteristic eaves tiles lamps at the karti maftgalya.
also serve as a ‘weather-boarding’ to protect the walls,
and are thus constructional as well as decorative. It is
needless to remark that Government, as in India, have consistently ignored the local
building traditions, thus at the same time striking at the foundation of the arts and crafts
of the country, and incurring needless trouble and expense through ignorance. Yet they
have been told more than once of their errors. In 1868, Mr. Russell, Government Agent
at Jaffna, wrote to Government regarding the preservation of ancient buildings, observing
at the same time, “the study of such works might possibly produce a beneficial effect on
the draughtsmen of the Public Works Department, who appear to me to have much to
learn in respect of adapting a building to the use for which it is intended and to the
conditions of climate under which it must be occupied.”*
But the Government remains equally blind to the artistic and the practical value of the
traditional crafts ; and the Europeanised Sinhalese are, if possible, more ignorant and
deluded. To take one instance only; at the Musæus Buddhist School in Colombo, it*
was decided to build a little temple for the use of the girls. Here, if anywhere, one might
have looked for some appreciation of tradition, some elementary conception of fitness and
the association of ideas; but no—the local paper informs us that the building “is a very
pretty structure, a vaulted roof with a fine dome, gothic windows, doors and a porch,
with parapet battlements of classic design, being very effective.”
As Mr. Lewis remarks, “It is lamentable to see everywhere this process taking place ;
old and artistic Kandyan work is being removed and replaced by nondescript and hideous
modern work after the style of the petty masons and contractors of the low country. The
new temples are adorned with plaster masonry, sometimes representing sham Venetian
blinds, bastard and attenuated Gothic pointed arches are introduced ; the Kandyan wooden
pillars give way to round ones of brick plastered over, of the stock quasi-classical pattern
that was introduced into the bungalows of the early English occupation ; the doorways
have semicircular arches with poor mouldings ; the door panels and mouldings are painted
in ugly loud colours which with the panels and mouldings have a Dutch character, but
lack the massiveness and picturesqueness of their Dutch originals ; and the pretty quaint
* Manual oj the North Central Province, p- 215.

little windows are being replaced by rectangular openings filled in with ugly wooden Woodwork

Doors were framed wooden structures, fitted and pegged together, and built into the Doors
substance of the wall; but some viharas had door-frames of stone. The doors were
either one or two-leaved, having tenons above and below, turning in sockets in the
frame; hinges are very rarely seen in old work. The parts of a complete door and
frame included the two uluvahu-kanu or kanda (door , padi-kasda (threshold), haras-
kadaya (lintel), ba-pata (horizontal plank at lintel level, to carry upper tenon of leaf), agul-
kanuva (‘bolt-post,’ upright carrying wood bolt), agula (bolt), and the door leaf itself
{dora hifind iflld). An additional horizontal, above the haras-kadaya and between an
upward extension of the jambs, is called uttara Iflla, and is generally decorated.
Door jambs are almost always carved, sometimes very elaborately, as in the example from
Dippitiya Vihara figured by Mr. Bell (Kegalla Report). The usual arrangement shows a
moulding at the inner angle, and liya v^la (‘branch’) ornament on the front; at
the base on either side, a carved representation of a guardian deity in low relief, or a figure
of a dancer, or an elephant or other form, above which come the ‘asana kadaya’ incisions
so characteristic of Kandyan woodwork (e.g. Fig. 74, n),then ^g(ta liyapotaoxnagabandha,
from which the rest of the carved jamb begins and continues. The lintel may be straight
or arched, and plain or carved. In some cases all the carving referred to is executed in ivory
and thus applied in lieu of carving the jamb itself (PI. XXXVIIL, i).
There are some good examples of Kandyan doors in the Colombo Museum. Mr. Bell
describes the leaves and one jamb of a door from Devanagala in the following words : “The
carving of the borders is exceedingly delicate. The framework of the panels is in high
relief, the ten panels themselves being plain. . The outer borders, upper and lower, are
carved in the universal foliage scroll with inner bevelled edges of paid peti: the centre
border (overlapping the right side plank so as to hide the line of junction when the door
is closed) has a perpendicular band of tiny ndri-latd. The door swung on tenons in a
socketed sill and lintel. The carving of the jamb is equally tasteful. Behind an outer
beading and inner splayed edge of lotus petals runs a long narrow panel with gracefully
intertwined double scroll of creeper— separating four figures, all different from each other.
'A space half moulded, half panelled, in flower design, intervenes between it and the base
panel, in which is placed besides a tree an elephant with head and right forefoot raised,
and curled trunk. The disappearance of the fellow jamb, lintel, and sill are much to be
ffegretted.’*
Another fine door remains at Devanagala; it is illustrated on PI. VII., Fig. 8, and is thus
described by Mr. Bell: “The present vihare is a modern tiled building of brick and clay,
35 ft. 5 in. by 16 ft. 4 in., unplastered and ugly. Into the outer wall have been fitted the
wooden doorframes and double-winged doors taken from an older vihare. The door on
the east side, which is much weatherworn, is panelled in six elongated compartments
containing figures of dancers and animals, bevelled in lotus-petal pattern and framed by
tiri y pitting and wide border of lotuses.” Another doorway, that of the Dippitiya Vihara,
is figured in the K^galla Report.

Bridges The simplest form of wooden bridge (edari^d) now everywhere seen is a single tree-trunk
passing from bank to bank of a small stream. If the stream is too wide to be spanned by
a single trunk, piles are driven and two or more trunks laid across them.
The chief forms of architectural woodwork have now been noted. The construction is
very massive, and would endure indefinitely were it not for the activity of white ants,
which is such that it may be doubted if any woodwork really ancient now survives, while
such as remains is so generally neglected that it cannot last very much longer. Only last
4
year the ancient Pohoya M uva Vihara in Kandy had to be pulled down and rebuilt from
this cause, as prophecied in “An Open Letter to the Kandyan Chiefs,” an appeal for the
better preservation of ancient buildings in Ceylon, published in 1905 ; a little regular care
would have prevented the necessity for this; needless to say no modern work can in any
real sense replace the old (for the same reasons that modern Gothic restoration in England
cannot replace Mediæval work) ; which if any one should doubt let him examine the
modern ‘Kandyan’ ambalams built by District Engineers at Kegalla, Ruvanvela and
Ratnapura.
The foregoing observations on architectural woodwork have a general application to all
buildings, such as viharas, dévales, palaces, and ambalams, in the construction of which
craftsmen are concerned, but only in a much reduced form to ordinary dwelling houses,
which each man made for himself. These were constructed of smaller timber tied with
jungle ropes, and the walls of wattle and daub, the roof thatched.
The sumptuary laws forbade any elaborate domestic architecture. Major Forbes* states
that “ the king did not permit any person to have a house two storeys high, nor to build
one with windows, nor even to roof with tiles nor whitewash mud walls, without obtaining
the royal sanction.” Davyj- remarks that “The dwellings of the people in general . . .
are invariably thatched ; only those of the highest rank being permitted to have tiled roofs.”
Only the king’s palace and religious building were allowed to have doors with ornamental
tops, or finials to the roofs, or to be plastered with lime.
Domestic i^W e pass now to the consideration of domestic and other woodwork not architectural.
woodwork The plain four-legged bed {?nda) is an ancient and wide-spread Indian form, consisting
of a frame of netted rope or rattan, supported by four feet. In Ceylon it is essentially a
Beds wooden frame (fÿda viyald) of four parts, and with four legs [kakut) ; usually with a low
head-rest in addition, morticed into the two upper legs, the tops of which project above
the frame for this purpose (PL IX., 7). In the most characteristic types, the influence
of architectural forms is evident, the legs being thirmed, and chamfered as are wooden
pillars (PI. XII., 4-7) ; turned and lacquered legs are also met with. The now commoner
turned and carved four-post beds in general use owe their form to European influence,
mainly Dutch ; it is curious that there still exists a real style in furniture, based on
eighteenth century European ; a more dignified and massive architectural style is that
really proper to the country, but so little furniture of any kind was formerly used, as to
make it natural for the European forms to come in with the Europeart habit; to say
nothing of the prevalent mania for the imitation of all things European ; though the
semi-Dutch style of furniture was arrived at before that mania reached its present height.
The mattress was formed of rope or rattan netting ; over this were laid a few cloths and
mats and a pillow, the sleeper covering himself from head to foot with cloth or cotton

Turning now to stools and chairs, we remark at once that the ancient hour-glass form of Stools

None but the king was allowed to sit upon a chair with a back; as remarked by Sir

It is noteworthy that rare woods, such as ebony and calamander, were most sparingly
used by Kandyan carpenters. Ebony is sometimes used as inlay, often associated with
ivory, as at RidI Vihâra, with a fine eifect ; for ‘ raylings,’ as we are told by Knox ; but rare
woods are not used for the construction of large objects, such as boxes and doors. It is
really a misuse of material to attempt such work : the wood is rare (calamander now
almost -extinct as a result of the increased demand) and should be used as such, with
restraint and dignity ; it is difficult to get large pieces of it, and it readily cracks, as if
intended only for inlay. There is a Certain vulgarity associated with the use of rare materials
in large quantities where not required.
Turned circular wooden boxes, rarely more than a foot in diameter, are in general use, ’Jewel boxes
either for betel leaves and the accessories of chewing, or for jewellery or valuables ; they
were especially used in devales to hold valuable insignia, as the halamba of Pattini ; and
were thence called abharai^a-pefti (regalia-boxes: PI. XIII., 3). Like much other turned
work, these boxes are usually adorned with lac applied on the lathe.
Another type of box used for jewels is the vfl-petfiya, or cane box, fitted with brass hinge
and lock (PI. XLIIIa., 8) ; a stronger round form, with shallow detachable lid, is used for
storing grain, carrying food, or generally as a box of any kind ; one form is divided internally
to serve as a food-basket for rice and curries for a number of persons travelling.

Stonework Perhaps the most remarkablfc eighteenth century stonework building in the Kandyan
District is the peculiar vihara at Galma^uva. This, the ‘most Hindu-looking Buddhist
temple in existence,’ or at least in Ceylon, was never finished. It is said to have been
built by Kirti èri, but that while it was in progress he heard of the cave at Degaldoruva,
he abandoned the scheme and set to work on the cave-temple at Degaldoruva. This,
however, seems improbable, considering the great difference in style of the two temples,
and the fact that the massive masonry and brickwork at Galmaduva were finished, nothing
remaining to be done but to set up the image and decorate the temple. The plan of the
building is a square stone chamber, covered by a pyramidal tower of stone and brick
masonry, reminding one of the gopuram of a Hindu temple. Around this building and
a little removed from it is a massive wall with an overhanging cornice, with five windows
on each of three of its sides, and a doorway in place of the central window on the other side.
The arches of the doorways and windows is remarkable. They are semi-circular cusped
arches with a keystone ; the door has six of these cusps, the windows two. In the image
room there is an asana, or throne for the image. The whole building contrasts markedly
with all other ‘Kandyan’ architecture.
Speaking now generally of Kandyan stonework, it will be found that stone masonry plays a
very small part in the construction of typical Kandyan buildings; in viharas there is fairly
often a carved stone doorstep (‘moonstone’) and no other work in stone. In the Kegalla
District “elaborately carved monolithic pillars are rare. . . . Basement revetments in
worked stone, where found, follow one recognized plan. First a low socle, next the
plinth, then a narrow fillet slightly retired, Lesbian cyma moulding of shallow lotus leaves
{pala peti) running back to the inner plane, a vertical block broken half way by a bold
torus, a second fillet slightly projecting, finished by ogee and rectangular cornice coping.

Practically all stonework was intended to be covered with plaster of milky whiteness,
just as the brickwork at Lankatilaka is only the foundation for work in modelled plaster
[see PI. VII., I, and description]. The Kandy bo maluva wall, so beautifully described by
the chronicler as resembling the necklet of a fair woman that was the city of Kandy,
must have been lovely indeed when the delicate mouldings were perfected in form, and
snowy white. The common whitewashing of the carved stone doors of temples, to which
objection is often taken, is not a modern fashion, but a somewhat careless continuation of
an old one. There can be no doubt that all architectural stonework was intended to be
plastered or painted, or both. This old Buddhist method does not survive so markedly in

Before finally leaving the subject of stonework it is necessary to refer to the smaller Domestic
domestic and religious purposes for which stone articles are employed. The commonest stonework
of these perhaps is the curry stone (ku4u-miris-gald), a plain slab and roller for compounding
the ingredients of ‘ sambol,’ a preparation of condiments eaten with curry. Somewhat
more elaborate are medicine stones {bet-gal) used in the preparation of herb and mineral
medicines, and for the grinding of colours by painters. In form and use these bet-gal
resemble the pestle and mortar of Europe, but the mortar is flatter. The pestle is often
grotesquely carved. Two bet-gal are shown in PI. LII., 6, the pestles carved into heads
and the four angles of the mortar with cobra hoods. Somewhat similar in purpose are
the sandal wood grinding stones {handun-gal), on which sandal wood is rubbed down
with water to prepare the fragrant paste so often referred to in Indian poetry. The stones
are circular in outline, something like a bread platter, but having the upper side, on which
the wood is rubbed, quite smooth but carved below with three low legs, an elaborate
central pattern, and pala peti chamfer (see PI. LII., 7). The kurukkan-gala is a quern or
hand mill for grinding kurakkan, the grain chiefly grown in hillside cultivation.
In connection with viharas and bo-ma¡u, stone lamps, altars (for flower offerings), bowls
{patra)- and stone troughs for dyeing robes are sometimes to be found; there is one of

The stone pestle used by the potters will be described in the chapter on Pottery.

to the ivory turner’s lathe of PI. VI., 4, but worked by a bow, and having a copper plate
set with corundum powder.

CHAPTER VIII. FIGURE SCULPTURE.
'"■ The sound of the tools that are raising the image of Buddha, let it reverberate in Heaven!"
—Empress Komio of Japan.
IN this chapter I speak of all sorts of images, whether in the round or in low relief,
and whatever the materials of which they are made.
The most primitive images made are the impermanent images made for use in yak
and bali ceremonies, and wax images of Ririyaka used in huniyan ceremonies. These are
made by the professional astrologers and dancers of the weaver [beravdya) caste, not by
the regular artists. The mud images of devils, and planetary or other gods are prepared
in low relief on a wooden foundation, or in the round, on a wicker construction; PI. IV., 2,
shows an elaborate erection of the first kind, which required fully two days for its construc­
tion by several men. The devils, it will be seen, are intentionally hideous; the gods’
faces, however, are refined and even beautiful. These gods’ heads were made separately
by the modellers, the rest of the work done on the spot. The smoothed clay is whitened
and painted with earths, and the figures decorated with cut leaves of coconut and plantain.
It is probable that in work of this kind, executed in impermanent materials we see a
survival of the most primitive form of Indo-Aryan plastic art.
More important from every other point of view are the images of Buddha, and of gods
and men. Images of Buddha and of gods are made according to certain canons laid down
in the work called Sariputra, which will subsequently be summarised. Images, says the
canon, may be made of gold, copper, clay, stone, wood, burnt clay (brick), and lime. Images
of silver, bronze, brass, and ivory were also made. Small images were most often made of
metal—brass, silver, and even gold. A majority of these belonging to the later times
are ill-formed and even grotesque, but earlier examples of a very superior character are
sometimes seen.
A few references to metal images are given in various places. Thus when the last king’s
favourite astrologer built a Vihara at Tibbotumulla, the king presented him with a gold
image, which he deposited in the vihara, which the king also endowed with lands.* The
golden image at Morapaya Vihara has been referred to above (p. 71). A golden image
valued at ^1,000 was stolen not long since from Niyangampaha Vihara atGampola. There
is a bronze-gilt Buddha at Danagirigala.-f- But bronze images do not appear to have been
often made in the later times. Very beautiful examples are occasionally met with which
may well date from the fifth century or earlier. Brass images of poor quality are still
commonly made.
There are many references in the chronicles and elsewhere, to images made of stone, brick,
mud and other materials. Thus, we learn from the Mahavaijisa, that at Gañgarima, Klrtl
árl “caused a fair statue of the Conqueror, nine cubits high, to be hewn out by cunning
workmen, skilled in the art of cutting stone and the like crafts. And he covered that
beautiful and graceful statue with leaf of gold, so that it looked like the living Buddha.”
At Ridi Vihara he had “a great sleeping image made with fine brick and mortar and clay,
and many other images of Buddha also, seated and erect. ... At the foot of the sleeping
image he let make in order, fair images of Ananda, the constant attendant of Buddha and
the preserver of the Law, and of Metteiya Bodhisatta, of the pre-eminent Natha Deva

netra-pinkama after giving over 25,000 fanams’ worth of things as remuneration to the
artists.”*
In 1801 Pilima Talava Adigâr built the Alut Vihàra at Asgiriya ; within it was an image
of Buddha, in the reclining posture, sculptured out of a solid block of stone, more than
forty feet long. Another stone image mentioned in a sannasa, is that of Urulevatte Vihara.
At Dambulla (Four Korales) there is a colossal clay image, a reclining figure of Buddha,
of which Mr. Bell-f- remarks: “this gigantic figure has been modelled so skilfully as to
give that impression of well balanced proportion, and calm repose, always aimed at, but
rarely attained, by Sinhalese artists in the representation of the sleeping figure.” Mr.
Bell gives the following measurements of this image, here re-arranged for more convenient
comparison with the canon :— total length from top of head to feet, 48 ft. 3 in. ; hair to
chin, 5 ft. 4 in.; nose, length 20 in.; across nostrils, 15 in.; each nostril, 5 in.; each knop
of hair, i ft. in circumference; mouth, 20 by 5 in.; eye, 14 in.; foot, 6 ft. 6 in. long.
The total length, 48 ft. 3 in., is 18# carpenters’ cubits. The figure is thus exactly twice
the standard size of nine cubits. The correspondence with the canon is very evident.
The face measure is two cubits : the whole figure up to the hair on the forehead is nine
‘ faces ’ : the top of the head is two thirds of a ‘ face ’ more. The other measurements given
correspond as nearly as could be expected, having regard to the vagueness of their exact
application, and their not having been made with the immediate object of comparison
with the canon. The foot is apparently too long. It is most desirable that measurements
of older images should be made in Ceylon and India, as they may be expected, when
compared with the canons, to throw light on the history of sculpture. At Embekke
Dévale there is a painted clay image of Kataragama Deviyo seated on a peacock, and a
painted wooden image of Devata Baijdara, about five feet high, kept in the Palle Dévale.
The Portuguese, as we have seen, destroyed in 1587 a.d., the Vishnu Dévale at Devundara ;
they destroyed ‘the idols, of which there were more than a thousand of divers shapes, some
of clay, some of wood, some of copper, and several of them gilt’ (p. 10, above).
It may be remarked the wood is but very rarely used for images of Buddha, but more often
for images in dévales.
fmages of crystal are rare. They are naturally always fairly small. There is one such
image at the Mâligâva, where it is kept in an elaborate silver and ivory shrine, suggestive
of Italian Renaissance work.
Ivory images of Buddha are not abundant. They were always painted. Kandyan crafts­
men are still skilful in making ivory figurines of drummers, Ratemahatmayas, and other
Kandyan characters, and the workmanship of these is superior to that of the ivory figures
shown on PI. XXXVI., where their chief value is in the illustration of eighteenth century
co stume. Such figures were not wholly coloured, but generally details of dress and features
picked out in red, and the hair blackened.
It should be understood that it is not possible to tell by inspection of what material the
larger statues are made. 'Whether of stone, brick or clay, they are always plastered and
painted or gilt. The same was, no doubt, true of the older statues at Anuradhapura and
Polonnaruva.

Figure Images in low relief are commonly found against temple walls, usually they represent
sculpture deities such as Vishiju, kings or heroes, or benefactors of the temple. The plastered
makara toraifa above a seated image (PI. VIIa.) is similarly modelled in clay, plastered
and painted. At the door of a vihara on each side of it, these are usually represented door
guardians (doratu-pala-rupd), with swords or clubs, symbolising the spiritual guardianship
of the shrine.
One is at a disadvantage in describing only the eighteenth century work ; for it represents
the old age of a great art, rather than its beginning or its prime. The earlier stone sculptures
of Ceylon, of various dates, and early bronzes are adequate examples of Indian art; but the
eighteenth century images, though possessed of dignity and other qualities, are generally
not beautiful, and are sometimes even grotesque.
Image making in Ceylon in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries was at a comparatively
low level, though not so low as that now reached in the low-country by artists unfamiliar
with the canon, or in the weak alabaster images that are imported from Burma. The
matter is that the canon has been used, not as a guide merely, but quite slavishly by artists
who, in spite of their strong decorative sense and capacity for ordinary drawing, had little
or no feeling for the human figure as such, though they felt the symmetry, passivity, and
grandeur of the symbol they made stand for it. “The image must exemplify a person with
an unfettered, quiescent, and absolutely pure mind, pre-eminent from head to foot.” The
artist did actually work with such ideals before him, and they could not but be reflected
in it. The traditional work, despite the decay of the tradition, is still in restraint, dignity
and religious feeling vastly superior to the sensuous and eifeminate work of ignorant
craftsmen in the low country, influenced by European art, but with no taste or real
knowledge of drawing.
I proceed now to a description of the artistic canon, and method of making images.
APPENDIX TO CHAPTER VIII.
SARIPUTRA.
Griinwedel’s work on ‘Buddhist Art in India,’ while specially lacking in reference to
ancient or modern Sinhalese art, nevertheless makes mention of the interest attaching
to works containing formulas for the construction or drawing of Buddhist images, giving
detailed dimensions. These he speaks of as modern and as specially characteristic of
the northern school. It is therefore of special interest to be able to give some account
of the work known in Ceylon as Sariputra, which deals with the dimensions of images
in general and Buddha in particular.
I am indebted to my learned friend Mudaliyar E. R. Gooneratne of Galle, for a translation
of the Sariputra, based on a transcript of the copy in the Colombo Museum, compared
with three copies which he with difficulty secured in the Southern Province and which
were deficient in the first and more general part which appears in the Museum ms.
Before proceeding to give some idea of the contents of the work, I quote a part of the
learned Mudaliyar’s remarks upon it:—
ISO

“The work takes its name from the author, who says at the end of the work that he heard Silriputra
it, from whom he does not state, though the inference in such cases, is that he must have
heard it from one of the fishis. From the style of the verses, though they are presented
to us in an incorrect form, it is plain that the work is the production of a master hand.
The author must not only have been well versed in Sanskrit, but (it is clear) that he was
also a thoroughly efficient artist.
“ Sàriputra is a common name in Buddhist history. One or two distinguished disciples
of Buddha owned it, and subsequently at various periods, several distinguished authors
and grammarians went by this name. The meaning of the term is, the son of Sari
(Sari-putra). . . .
“The making and painting of images have been in the hands of a particular section of
the Sinhalese ; not being versed in the Sanskrit, and not understanding the texts, it is
plain that they only took care to have the paraphrase jotted down, to enable them to
take the measurement, regardless of the accuracy of the Sanskrit verses. Hence the work
is full of errors, and I have had great trouble to get the verses corrected and put into proper
metre before commencing the translation.
“ In the first part which treats of images in general, in the paper copy sent me, all the
Sanskrit stanzas were omitted and by the aid of the gloss I had to recast them.
“The second part which is confined to the making of images of Buddha, is more complete ;
only a few of the verses are missing, but those that were found were full of errors and
omissions, and were deficient in metre. I had them collated with three copies which
I procured. It is curious, however, that the missing verses and omissions in one copy
were nearly the same in the others, leading me to infer that they must be copies of one
original work. . . .
“ In conclusion I have to acknowledge with thanks the very great assistance rendered
me by Talamalagala Somànanda Thera, of the Simhall Avasa, Galle. But for his willing
support . . . I am doubtful whether this translation would have seen the light of day.”
Mr. Gooneratne also remarks, “ (i) I have confined myself to translating the original
literally. (2) In some places the text is so vague, as regards the exact positions of the
parts of which measurements are given, and the terms used are so uncommon, I am not
sure whether my rendering is quite correct. (3) Several of the verses had to be recast,
of course embodying the exact meaning of the gloss, nevertheless there may be
deficiencies, . . .”
Regarding the date of the Sinhalese gloss {sannaya) which constitutes the most important
part of the mss. regarded from the imager’s point of view, the following staternent, an
annexure discovered in one of the old copies, is supplied by Mr. Gooneratne :
“About A.D. 1165, after the translation of the Sinhalese commentaries into Pali, the pious
and illustrious King Sarvajna Parakrama Bahu ascended the throne of Laftka. Having
noted with concern the corruptions that had crept into the Saògha since the sway of
the great King Vaftagamini Abhaya he took action to purge it from its corrupt adherents,
w ith the aid of the illustrious Maha Kasyapa of Dinibulagala (Dambulla), and he
thoroughly renewed the Cètiya at Purvarama and other temples (Anuradhapura) and
the Uposatha hall, and embellished the parapet around the Bodhi tree with various beautiful
paintings. Maha Kasyapa then approached his Majesty and prayed for a translation of
the Sariputra, a portion of the old Vedanga, which treats of the dimensions of the images
of Buddha for the guidance of lay artists. The King deputed this work to a pupil of the
Maha Thera Kasyapa, who was competent to undertake it.”
I do not give the text and translation of the Sariputra in full, as they deserve separate
publication elsewhere. The parts of the translation omitted are the astrological details,

Sariputra some of the more minute measurements, and some of the verses of which the exact meaning
is not clear. The second part of the work (as found in the Colombo Museum ms.) treating
in particular of standing, seated, and reclining images of Buddha, is here first dealt with;
afterwards the first or general part and a further gloss accompanying it. The work is not
now well known either by imagers and painters or by the priesthood in the low-country,
but is familiar to the best craftsmen in tbe Kandyan districts. The diagram (PI. XXVII.
and Fig. 95) of a seated image is drawn by D. S. Muhandiram to illustrate the use of plumb
lines, and to show the appearance of a correctly measured image. The chief point to be
comprehended is the use of the lines: a framework, of which a plan appears in the top
left hand corner of the figure, and another (Fig. 94), taken from an actual example given
to me by the same artist and now in my possession, in the text, is fixed horizontally over
the place where the image is to be made, and the plummets suspended from it. The
plumb lines so hung serve as axes of reference, determining the position of the chief parts
of the body. They act as a simple ‘pointing machine.’ The lines shown in the diagram
are those generally relied upon by Kandyan workmen, but others are available if still more
exact work is required, or if the size of the image is so great as to make their use advisable.
The ‘karifa stttra’ of the diagram is the ‘parsva sUtra' of the text, which latter is probably
correct. The height is reckoned at 5 ‘faces’ from top of forehead to throne, i.e. 67J
inches, an approximation used, it is said, in small work instead of the 62 inches of the
canon.

The ordinary architect’s cubit {^a u riyana), the foot {puda), and span [viyata) are scarcely
4
mentioned. The angala or ‘inch’ is presumably the va u angala, (distance from first to
to second joint of forefinger when bent), the twenty-fourth part of a va4u riyana., and
measures English inch (see p. 142). The '■ angala' of the text, however, is not merely
a fixed measure, but also may be translated ‘unit,’ as the instructions are intended to
provide for the construction of images of all sizes, both large and small. But there has
been much discussion as to the exact dimensions of the images in the case of images of
Buddha,* and special books have been written on the measurement of his person, usually
considered to be twelve cubits'f'; his span is usually considered much longer than the
span on which calculations are at present based; but such views are purely mythical.
The other units employed are technical and not in common use. The most important
is the mukha, or ‘face.’ This is the equivalent of 13I inches when images of Buddha are
spoken of. It is an unit corresponding to, but not identical with, the ‘head’ of European
artists. It is measured from the base of the hair on the forehead to the chin and is thus
less than a ‘ head ’ by the height of the crown of the head above the forehead. The standard
height of an image of Buddha, including the crown of the head, is 124 angal, as stated
in verse 22 of the canon, or more exactly 9 ‘faces’ and half a bhaga, making I23f inches
(about E. 13 feet 4 inches). The detailed measurements given actually add up to 121§
angal (9 ‘faces’) + 3I angal for the crown of the head. It will be seen that this canon of
proportion corresponds to about heads, in the terms of European art.
Some words are perhaps needed as to the purpose and use of artistic canons of proportion.
Probably they have been in use from the earliest times in the East, as we know that they
were in the West. But there is a tendency, not altogether unreasonable, to regard them
as purely mechanical devices, reliance upon which is a fetter upon free artistic expression,
and characterises rather the decline than the flower of a great tradition. But it is the
abuse, not the use, of canons .of proportion that does this, and it is therefore worth while
to enquire into the rationale of their use by Indian craftsmen and imagers. It is in drawing
from the life that a canon is likely to be a hindrance to the artist; but it is not the method
of Indian art to work from the model. Almost the whole philosophy of Indian art is
summed up in the verse of Sukracarya’s ‘Sukranitisara’ which enjoins meditation upon
the imager:
I “ In order that the form of an image may be brought fully and clearly before the mind,
the imager should meditate; and his success will be proportionate to his meditation. No
other way—not indeed seeing the object itself—will achieve his purpose.”
I The canon, then, is of use as a rule of thumb, relieving him of some part of the technical
difficulties, leaving him free to concentrate his thought more singly on the message or
burden of his work. It is only in this way that it must have been used in periods of great
achievement, or by great artists. It must also be remembered that the use of some such
device was always absolutely essential in the case of the many colossal images made, and
oft en executed in a relatively cramped space, such as the interior of a rock vihara. Further,
only a few of the measurements given are used in the case of the smaller images; all the
minuter details are necessary only in the case of colossal statues. And the fact that the
canon is now used mechanically by mere craftsmen is no contradiction of its value, for

SARIPUTRA, Part I.
The first part of Sariputra treats of images in general, not as above, exclusively of images
of Buddha. Here the mukha or ‘face’ consists of 12 angal only, instead of 13I, and the
bhaga of 4 angal instead of 4|. The other units are unchanged.
Verses i— 30 give very detailed measurements of the head and features, body and limbs,
hands and feet. The dimensions are slightly less than those above detailed: thus the
breadth of the back between the armpits is two faces (of twelve angal each only), the
middle finger six angal long instead of six angal and four barleycorns, and so on. Verse 30
concludes; “all the rest not described may be suitably supplied.” Verses 30—43 treat
of the plumb lines and measurements to be made thereby. Reference is made to the part
‘slightly slanting,’ this seems to refer to a slight bend in the waist, which, like the ‘sway'
in thirteenth-century Gothic work, gives grace and delicacy. I do not think that reference
is here intended to the markedly curved figures known as trivanka* (triple-curved).

It is évident that the universal Indian standard is one of nine ‘faces,’ which in the
terminology of European canons of proportion would be just over seven ‘heads.’ The
figure of Buddha is made only relatively ‘heroic’ by increasing the unit, without altering
the proportions to any appreciable extent. But there appears to have been some variation in
the standards ; the Rûpâvaliya (pp. 112,113, above), for instance, gives the height of a man
or a woman at eight, and an Asura at nine, Devas and Buddhas at ten ‘faces’; but verse
129 gives proportions agreeing with those prescribed in Sariputra for figures of the Buddha.
Slightly conflicting statements are also made by craftsmen ; as ten for Buddha, nine for
gods, eight for men, and seven for women. One craftsman reversed the last, explaining
this on the ground that tall women were considered beautiful.
Age of the canon, and the Silpa éastra generally.
Owing to the systematic neglect of the Silpa Sastra by English and Indian Sanskritists,
it is difficult to give any adequate account of the technical literature of Art and Craft in
India. This literature has evidently remained for centuries in the hands of craftsmen,
* Sukranltisâra, or Elements of Polity, by Sukracarya, ed. Calcutta, 1890.
•f- Brihat Samhita of Varaha Mthira, English 'Trans, by N. Chidambaram Iyer, Madura, 1884,
Pt. IL, Ch. XL
m I 161

Sariptttra whose knowledge of Sanskrit as a language was usually slight, though they might know
the text by heart. They relied on verbal glosses in the various vernaculars, Tamil and
Age of the Telugu in Southern India, and Sinhalese in Ceylon. It is quite clear that the Silpa Sastras
Stlpa are the remains of a very carefully systematised and complete literature, and it is certain
&astras that it must have taken many centuries for them to have become so imperfect and corrupt
as they now are.*
The golden age of Indian art and literature, when India was most herself, I conceive to
have been the period dating from the time of the Upanishads and of Buddha, to the close
of the fifth and sixth centuries a.d. The civilisation of this time found its ultimate literary
expression in the Ramayaija (about 300 a.d.) and the Mahabharata (about 400 a.d.) and
is in popular tradition centred round the court of Vikramaditya (about 375 a.d).
I have above (p. 63) referred to the now isolated occurrence of special crafts widely
scattered in different parts of India, and suggested that this indicates a once more universal
distribution. The study of Indian Art and Craft, in its profound unity in variety, suggest
that its present remains are but the wreck of its former grandeur. If so, this must have been
the case long ago, before the Hindu culture of the North was overrun by the Muhammadans.
It may well have been in the brilliant era of the Gupta rulers, culminating in the rule of
Vikramaditya. The great iron pillar at Delhi, erected in his reign, witnesses still to a
knowledge of metallurgy enabling the craftsmen of that day to forge a bar of iron larger
than any that could have been forged in Europe before the end of the nineteenth century.
It is probable that the Silpa ^astras were written down towards the close of this period.
They had previously been handed down orally by the hereditary craftsmen, amongst whom
their secret was jealously guarded. The brevity of the memory verses and their technical
language further preserved their meaning from common comprehension. The craftsmen
are reluctant to allow their technical books to be made public.
A certain parallel may be drawn between the writing down of the materials of the Silpa
Sastras, and those composing the epics of the Ramayaija, the Mahabharata and the
Mahavaipsa. There seems to have been a tendency at this time to put into permanent
form, traditions and accumulated learning previously transmitted orally in memory verses.-j'
There is a close correspondence between the literary and the artistic phenomena. Compare,
for example, a memory verse from the Rapavaliya (e.g. vv. 3 and 4, p. 112, above) with
this verse from the Dlpavaijisa, in which the history of the satsatiya is summarised: “The
throne, the Animisa (sanctuary), the cloisters, the Gem-court, the Ajapala (tree), and the
Mucalinda (tree) together with the Khirapala grove as the seventh.” In both cases wje^
have mnemonic verses of great brevity, evidently adapted to oral transmission; the artist
in each case had to fill in the meagre details, and make the story or the image live.
I suggest a parallel between the literary impulse which led to the writing down of these
mnemonic verses, and their expansion into epic history, and the impulse which led to the
writing down of the orally transmitted verses of the Silpa Sastra, and suggest also the
probability of these two processes having taken place about the same time.

or the pundits of the present day, that it requires no ordinary exertion to comprehend and explain the

select, then, the fifth century as a probable date for the writing down of the Silpa Sastras, Sariputra
but in doing so I do not attach, of course, importance to the exact figures, and do not forget
that not all the works in question are necessarily contemporaneous.
It is clear that the artistic canons and memory verses cannot have been formulated at a
very early period, for they imply the development of Hinduism from and through
Buddhism, such as could hardly have taken place before the close of the second century a.d.
They appear to be in the main independent of Buddhism ; we cannot suppose that any
vital tradition, or one concerned mainly with Hindu representations could have been
formulated in connection with the weak and effeminate sculpture of the Gandhâra school,
perhaps the least truly Indian and artistically least important of all sculpture in India.
There is some indication that the Silpa éâstras date from a time subsequent to the decline
of Buddhism as the complete expression of national religion. Thus in the Rûpâvaliya,
Buddha appears only as one of the ten avatars of Vishpu ; and as Ram Râz suggests,* there
is evidence in other works to show that the worship of the Jainas and Buddhists, though
still tolerated and provided for in these works, occupied a position of very minor importance
in them. But a purely Buddhist canon like the Sariputra would not have been preserved
in India at all after the complete extinction of Buddhism as a separate cult ; and it is not
likely to have been composed in Ceylon ; so that by this line of reasoning also we are thrown
back to the fifth century. Another piece of evidence is afforded by the Sukranltisara,'h
or ‘Elements of Polity,’ by Sukracarya, which was translated into Tibetan in the seventh
century a.d., and must therefore have been well known in India for a considerable time
previous to this. This work contains important chapters on the measurements of images,
summarised in part in the table given above, and also a clear presentation of the artistic
ideal of the imager himself.
The truth is that we have to consider in all probability two stages in the history of the
works in question, the first that of their formulation at the close of the fifth century in
Northern India, the second that of their subsequent use and final decay in the North,
finally completed as the result of Muhammadan conquest and influence. During this
second period, the traditions flourished in the South, where most of the remaining works
are Still to be found ; new recensions of them were made, with additions and interpolations
relating to representations of local deities and saints. Artistic expression in the South
culminated in the sculpture and architecture of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries,
after which there followed a gradual decline, rapidly accelerated in the nineteenth century,
uqtil now there are but few craftsmen who understand their own books, and but few copies
of these books procurable, and those imperfect and exceedingly corrupt.
Essay on the Architecture of the Hindus’ London, 1834. Lhis valuable book contains the
fullest account in English of the Silpa Èastras [so far as they relate to architecture) and some
discussion of their age.

CHAPTER IX. PAINTING.
OWING in a large measure to the activity of Kirti èri Raja Sirfiha, who was such
an eager friend of religion and of art, we find preserved a sufficient amount
of eighteenth century painting, to enable us to form an accurate idea of its scope
and capacity and methods, in which we are aided by a study of the good work which
can still be done by the hereditary painters when the opportunity is given them. The
few really good painters, now living, are equal to any but the very best eighteenth century
men, such as Silvatenna, who painted jatakas at Ridi Vihara and at Degaldoruva. The
eighteenth century work may be best studied in old and unrestored vihàras, such as
Degaldoruva, Ridi Vihara, Danagirigala, Dodantale, and in the low country at Kelaijiya.
Examples are also afforded by old painted furniture, like the book-box at Ridi Vihara,
and in the rare paper mss. of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries ; but I do not
know of any old paintings on cloth surviving.
The technique and character of Kandyan painting will first be described in detail.
The pigments were prepared as follows :
White {sudu pdta).—This is prepared from hydrous magnesite {makul, or kova makul)
obtained from a cave known as the makul gal-kna at Vetekgama near Maturata. It is
often mixed with other pigments to make pink, grey, etc.
Red {ratapafa).—^This is sadilingam or cinnabar, which is not known to occur in Ceylon
and must always have been imported. In all cases it forms the ground colour.
Yellow {p.aha pita).—This is gamboge from the gokatu tree (Garcinta morella)-, but the
material preferred for painting on wood or earthenware is orpiment (hiriyal, or mada
hiriyal) and this is now often used even when gokatu would be preferable.
Black (kalu pafd).—This is lamp-black,-to make which, jak-milk (ior-iiW, i.e. juice from
the fruit of Artocarpus integrifolid), kekuna oil (oil of Canarium zeylanicum), and rosin {hdl-
dummala, from the hal-trcs. Vateria acuminata) are ground up together and mixed with
shreds of cotton cloth, then set over a small fire in a clean earthen pot with a second pot
inverted above it. The soot is deposited in the upper pot and thence collected. Its oily
nature makes it difficult to mix with water.
Blue {nlla pafa).—This colour is very rarely seen; it was obtained from the leaves of
the indigo plant, nil-gas, but only in small quantities ; possibly some was also had from
the Dutch. In the great majority of old paintings blue and green are absent altogether.
Green [fiacca* fiatò).— Made by mixing blue with yellow.
Gold [ratram paid).—Gold is used in an old pattern-book of the eighteenth century which
I have, and in the baifadaham book (breviary) from which pages are reproduced on PI. XX ;
but I have seen no other examples. The gold prepared for use is said to have come
from Siam, which is quite possible. The use of gold leaf, however, applied to gild stone
or other statues is a common and ancient practice.
Shades of colour.— Red, black, and blue are mixed with white to form pink (imbuì sivi),
grey (sudu kalu or nil sivi) and pale blue (nil sivi). The grey is generally used to represent
blue or green or brown in nature and in representations of Vishnu, the ‘Blue God.’ A
little yellow added to the grey gives it the usual greenish tinge. The use of shades of
colour is very limited, and never such as to produce relief or interfere with the flatness
of the decoration.
A characteristic feature is the outlining of all forms with a clear black line : this outlining,
* It may be noted that the word pacca in ’■ pacca heffaya' (a chief ' s jacket, as in Fig. i) has little
or no colour significance, indicating rather the kind of jacket than the colour of it.
164

and the occasional use of small quantities of green or white in the detail of ornament, Painting
gives just the necessary softening required to harmonize the strong reds and yellows, and
reduce their extreme brilliancy. The whole range of colours may seem very limited, technique
but it will be found that a varied use can be made of them, and the very limitation was a
safeguard and a stimulus to the inventiveness of the painter. Regarding the exact meaning
of the names for colours, it may be noted that kalu means ‘black,’ but also ‘dark blue’
when applied to cloth ; nila means either blue or green, properly the former, it is applied
in poetry to the colour of parrot wings and compared with that of young rice. The
use of few colours in Sinhalese art is a point of importance, as also the fact that the
same word is sometimes used in different senses, as kalu, black or indigo; nila, blue or
green. The appreciation of shades of colour is even in Europe a comparatively modern
matter, and has gone to great extremes. The old appreciation of pure bright colour is
almost lost, a fact not generally realised hy persons who regard pure colour as barbaric.
One of the most important things needful to secure good colours, is long and careful
grinding. This work, often done by the pupils, may occupy as much as a month before
a large undertaking, such as the decoration of a vihara, is begun. The pounded colour
is ground with water in a stone mortar again and again until it is fine and smooth enough.
According to the best method, the pigments are mixed with dkml látu (gum of the elephant
apple tree, Feronia elephantum) and water, and thus used. The work is thus in no sense
fresco, but should be called tempera painting. Gum arabic is now successfully used when
the latu cannot be had. The use of dorar}a oil (oil of the doraija tree, Dipteroearpus
glandulosus) as a medium is said to be entirely a modern innovation; the effect is coarser
and altogether inferior. But some say that doratia oil was used for outside work, and
even in interiors when the lafu could not be'had. Certainly if oil was not used as the
medium for outdoor work, such as that above ifie vihara at Ridi Vihara, it is difficult
to understand how it can have lasted. The paintings at Ridi Vihara were executed in
the reign of Kirti árl Raja Sirpha. Siddhattha, the incumbent who had charge of the
works, after completing the viharas and their decoration, “caused a delightful picture to
be made of the Sage, seated amidst his five hundred disciples with Sariputra at their head,
above the image house, in the convenient hollow of the rock” (Mahavarpsa, Ch. G.).
There are external paintings also at Maniyangama and Lenagala. Mr. Bell (Regalía
Report, p. 30) says of the latter, that above the lean-to tiled verandah there “is still visible
a coloured representation of a perahfra, much faded, in which riders on elephants and
horses, with flag-bearers, escort a five-tiered karanduva on a car.” These paintings, at any
rate those at Maniyañgama, date from the time of Kirti árl Raja Sirpha. Ordinary interior
painting is sooner or later destroyed by even partial exposure to damp.
The brushes used for flat colouring of small spaces are made of cats’ or squirrels’ hair, and
are small and delicate. Larger brushes are made from the frayed $rial roots of vftakeyiya,
a species of Pandanus. Long stiff brushes for drawing fine lines are made from the awns
of the tell taifa grass (Aristida adscensionis). The tell taifa grass and the brush (tell kura)
are so-called from the resemblance to the snout of the teti fish. The tell taifa brushes
are very easily and rapidly made; the grass spike is wetted, and the awns stripped off
between the finger and thumb nail, shaken down to a level and tied on a pointed stick;
the longest awns form the fine point of the brush. Graphite pencils were unknown, but
actual lead pencils were used—but very sparingly, however, as the painter relied almost
entirely, perhaps altogether, on his brush.
The materials on which eighteenth century paintings were executed, were plaster (on
walls), wood (ceilings, furniture, etc.), cloth and paper and earthenware, as at the present
day. Accounts of paintings on cloth are quoted on pp. 72,73, above, from the Mahavarpsa.
m3 165

'Painting They refer, no doubt, to ordinary pigment painting, as dye-painting was not, at any rate
in the eighteenth century, a Sinhalese craft. I have seen no drawings on paper of Sinhalese
paper, which was very coarse and rough.* Such old drawings or paper ms. as have been
preserved are found to be on Dutch paper, or at a later time on English paper. No doubt
paper of Indian or Sinhalese manufacture was used at an earlier period.
Methods of Vihara walls were made sometimes of stone or brick, more often of mud mixed with sand,
wall laid on a wooden framework as in ordinary domestic work; the wooden framework was
painting filled with a mixture of puddled earth and sand, covered with a layer of finely ground clay
and sand, mixed with rice water. The surface was then covered with a layer of kirimetiya
(‘ milk clay,’ viz. kaolin) made very smooth, and then a coat of Maturata makul (magnesite).
The surface was thus made pure white. The sapu or bamboo wooden framework of
such walls lasts well; but some are riddled with white ants. In the case of the roof of
a rock temple, the plaster of clay, sand and rice water was applied direct with a coconut-
fibre brush, and then the kirimetiya and makul were laid over. The proportion of clay to
sand is one part to two. When there have been many successive redecorations the thick­
ness of plaster becomes considerable, and is sometimes heavy enough to fall away by its
own weight. According to the statement of good modern craftsmen, lime plaster was
not used as a basis for painting upon, but only for external surfaces not intended to be
painted. But a verse from the Gaija Devi Hella, quoted on p. 89, indicates that lime plaster
was sometimes painted on, as one would naturally have expected.
Painting is commenced upon the makul-covtvt& surface. The work is first sketched in
{lakuifu kald) with a fine brush and black paint, then the background filled in with pink,
leaving the figures white. The latter are then filled in with yellow, carefully outlined in
red, and the background filled up in pink exactly to the outline. Part of this work is done
by pupils. The pink is covered with a coat of red; and two or three alternate coats of
pink and red may be necessary to ensure a fine red at last. The final background is
invariably red, as in PI. I. Detail of features, etc., is added in red on the figures, which
are finally cleanly outlined with a firm black line, which at once defines, harmonizes and
unites the whole composition. All the line work is done with the fine teli tai}a brush.
The use of yellow for the face and figure is explained by the frequent comparison of the
colour of beautiful persons to that of gold. It is a fact that the most beautiful Indian
skin colour is golden brown, going with a very satiny texture, and this is recognized in
the Indian ideal of beauty, which demands a ‘fair’ skin. A very dark skin is despised,
and is actually more usual amongst persons of low caste, than those of high. The
elephant-keeper, in PL I., is accordingly represented as dark, in contrast to the goviydvatpsa
people attendant on the king. Trees, leaves, and water are usually represented in grey;
buildings are yellow, tiles red, and rocks black. The use of blue or green is most
exceptional.
Pattern work is done in a corresponding manner. It is usual to determine first the position
of the most important elements, such as flowers or animals, then to connect them together,
and last to add the leaves and detail on the stems. The black outline, and occasional use
of a little green, black, or white detail, temper any hardness of contrast between the red
and yellow. When a particular flower or animal is to be repeated several times, a paper
pattern {accuvd) is made, and the outline traced from it wherever required. Pouncing
seems to be unknown, although a familiar practice in India and Siam. When a limited
space has to be filled with a repeating pattern, it is carefully subdivided with compasses.

The methods of painting on wood are similar, except that hiriyal is preferred to gokafu,
and the work is usually protected by a layer of varnish {valicciya). The whole is first
covered with an even coat of pink, the design sketched on this, and the background filled
in with red, and detail as before. Painting on earthenware is done in the same way.
The varnish is made as follows: powdered dummala (which must be white and clean. Varnish
not dark) is mixed with dorarfa (oil) and boiled for half an hour or more and then allowed
to cool, when it is ready for use. The varnish so prepared smells strongly of turpentine
and dries quickly.* The yellow gokatu (gamboge) paint is said to be itself a valicciya
and not to require any other varnish. A superior method of varnishing small wooden
articles is to cover the painting with a thin coating of carefully cleaned and strained lac
(keppettiya laka^a), applied with! heat. Old book covers will always be found to have
been thus treated.
One great merit of the old Sinhalese painter is the thoroughness of his knowledge of the
preparation and properties of the pigments and tools at his disposal; their natural limitations
moreover tended to restraint and gravity. The readiness with which excellent implements
are made from the commonest and simplest materials is very striking. The old methods
are still well understood and sometimes followed by the best workmen ; but, unfortunately,
those responsible for modern vihara decoration rarely take the trouble to secure their
services; and the majority of inferior painters run riot with Aspinall’s enamel and Rickett’s
blue, with which they depict designs more like those to be looked for on second-rate
Christmas cards than suitable for temple walls.
Vihara walls are usually covered with jataka subjects, in long panels of continuous narration, yataka
set close together, one above the other (Pis. I. and VIIIa), the narrow space between paintings
sufficing for a short explanatory note; or a label may be inset in the picture itself; both
methods are illustrated in PI. XVIII. The ‘continuous narration’ should be specially
noted. In this primitive method, the same figures are repeated frequently in continuous
pictures, in fresh situations revealing the progress of the story; so that the result is a
panorama, where, however, the observer and not the picture itself must move. Thus
in PI. I. the one elephant appears twice, first ridden by King Vessantara, afterwards as
being given by him to certain Brahmans who in the original are shown on the right;
below again, Madri Devi and the two children are twice depicted, once passing along the
highway, and then arriving at the hermitage.

vihara. I have already quoted from the Degaldoruva sannasa some account of the
decoration of the vihara there; it is stated that twenty-four images of Buddha were painted
on the walls and ceilings, beside other workmanship. Of these paintings, the jataka
paintings on the outer surface of the wall of the pilima-ge are the most interesting and

the left of the main door, Sutasoma Jataka between the doors, and the Sllava Jataka on the
right. The little iron-barred window referred to above, p. 134, separates the Sattubhatta
and Vessantara Jatakas on the left. Mr. Cave in his ‘Book of Ceylon’, Fig. 489, gives a
good picture of Degaldoruva, showing the doors and the painted wall; in the same picture
may be observed the twelve monolithic pillars with their cushion capitals, the painted

The value of these paintings lies not merely in their beauty and charm as decoration,
but in the fact that they are priceless historical documents that could not be reproduced
under modern conditions. The gorgeous trappings of the elephants, the king’s and the
attendants’ dresses and the royal insignia ; the hermitage ; the village scene at the well in
the Vessantara Jataka, are all most faithfully drawn, and these pictures, like the medieval
manuscripts of Europe, are invaluable records of past manners and customs. In the
Sutasoma Jataka, the most interesting pictures are perhaps those in which the king’s sons
meet in an ambalam ; the representations of the king’s kitchen, with the gahoniya hanging
from a hook on a pillar, covering the provisions brought in from some royal manor ; the
king’s expulsion ; and his offerings of human victims as a sacrifice to the tree deva.
