In the Sllava Jataka, perhaps the most interesting scenes are those showing Senaka Paij it
expounding the dimrma to men and women, and a school scene showing a seated paijdit and
a row of respectful scholars, of whom the first is repeating his lesson to the master. Of
the other paintings at Degaldoruva, the most noteworthy are the Buddha and Maitri
Buddha on the rock ceiling within the pilima-ge.
Another temple which may be briefly described is the Kelaijiya Vihara. The main
building consists of an image room with a large reclining image and an antechamber
(PI. VIIa., below) with four doors, the walls and ceiling elaborately painted. Upon the
walls are depicted many jatakas, such as the Vessantara and Kiodura, a representation
of Mara’s battle, where the figure of Mihikata rising from the earth at the Buddha’s feet
. should be noticed, and also decorative panels of nari-Iata, flowers in pots, and portraits of
royal benefactors and successive incumbents. These paintings are not in the best manner,
but for nineteenth century low-country work are very good. Most of the characteristic
features of Kandyan painting can be recognized, such as ‘continuous narration,’ and
many of the details of pattern work on the walls, and especially the ceiling, are excellent
(PI. XIV., 3, 4, 5, and 7). It is instructive to examine the wall paintings critically and
determine the degenerate features. It will be found, for example, that the trees are more
slovenly in treatment than at Degaldoruva, often mere daubs ; there is also a tendency
to more relief and realism, and variety of colour. But the sprays and branches and birds
are well done, and the treatment of the makara toraifa and branches within the image room
could hardly be improved upon.
Other temples where good eighteenth century Kandyan painting is to be seen, include
Dodantale, Danagirigala, Lankatilaka (PI. VIIa), Ridi Vihàra, Gaijegoda (PI. XV.), and
many others. Almost all the painting at the Dalada Maligava has been renewed in recent
times, and although the designs are for the most part traditional, the colours are gaudy and
varied to an intolerable degree. One of the few remaining good paintings (PI. XVI.)
has been restored and altered very recently.
t©. In Kandyan painting there is an entire absence of perspective and shading. The
primary object is to tell an edifying story in an attractive way. The work is thus rather epic
in character, than artistic in the modern sense. It has a great deal in common with the
mural painting of Egypt ; in its pure gay colour, decorative flat treatment and restfulness,
168

it is most admirable as wall painting. As in Egypt, “ the wall is a wall still and not Fainting
a window; nay a book rather, where, if you will, you may read the stories of the gods
and heroes, and whose characters, whether you read them or not, delight you always with
the beauty of their form and colour.” Beside jstakas we find other subjects on walls,
particularly the sai-satiya, suvisi-vharana, rows of arhat priests, mara-yuddhaya, etc. Large
wall spaces are not usually covered with mere pattern work, which only appears as an
accessory (PI. VIIa). If the religious subjects are not depicted, beautifully designed
pictures of trees may be found, as at Danagirigala (PI. XIV., 8). Portraits of royal or other
patrons are sometimes painted flat on the walls, as at Doflantale, where there is a valuable
costume representation of Kirti érl wearing the famous kurulla bendi malaya now in the
Maligava, and carrying a jewelled cane ; but more often the figure of the patron is modelled
in low relief. All figure subjects, whether images of Buddha in the round, or Gods or
patrons in low relief on the walls are invariably painted, the costume of the Gods or men
covered with fine diaper and other pattern work (PI. XIV., 5 and 6).
Figures are represented in full, three-quarter or side face, never as seen from behind.
This fact is remarked by the medieval poet, Totagomuva (see p. 10), in a verse of the
Sela Lihiiji Sandéáaya: “True friends, alike when adverse fortune comes or when success,
like painted images upon a wall, show not their backs.”
The off eye is foreshortened in three-quarter face presentations, but the near eye is drawn
as if seen in front view, and the same is true of profiles. Lines to indicate the eye socket
are drawn above and below the lines of the eye itself. The four lines just mentioned
are drawn in red, the eyebrow black. The pupil is a black spot. In large paintings
the white of the eye on either side of the pupil is barred by vertical red lines, curved
concentrically with the limit of the pupil.
In small paintings by good artists, and particularly in renderings of jataka subjects, the
figure and features are sufficiently well done to allow even a critical observer to enjoy
the work as a whole, as one decorative construction. But in larger paintings it very
often happens that the distortion of the features and misproportion of the limbs is painful.
Paintings of Buddha are usually carefully and correctly drawn in accordance with the
measurements of the canon, but hardly show any appreciation of the physical beauty of
the figure.
The figures have a good deal of vivacity and dignity, but are rarely drawn with any feeling
for the beauty of the human form; they are sometimes almost grotesque. The canon of
rneasurement (Sáriputra) is not made use of in drawing figures in jataka scenes, but only
in representing Buddha or figures of the gods. The absence of perspective is so much a
part of the style that we can hardly call it a fault. We can imagine an improvement in
the drawing, but the introduction of perspective and relief and division of the picture into
several planes would so alter the work—not necessarily for the better—that it could no
longer be called Kandyan painting.
The most essential character of Kandyan painting, as of Kandyan design in general, is Idealism
it s idealism. This idealism belongs to all Indian art; but in Kandyan art it appears in
almost an extreme form. Some of the maguí lakum, for example, are little more than
hieroglyphics. But the idealism is very marked also in design and picture. Observe,
for example, the trees on PI. I. and XIV., 8; these are not portraits of particular trees,
but abstractions, representing the artist’s generalised conception of all such trees. When
I say ‘the artist,’ I do not refef to any individual, but imply the whole body of artists
who together worked out the language long ago; and I say language because traditions
and conventions are to the artist what words and metre are to the poet, and these no one
man made. The idealism of Kandyan art is part of its inheritance from India; but as
169

Painting we have already observed, Kandyan art does not represent Indian art at its greatest or even
at a very great period, but rather Indian art at the level of a great and beautiful scheme
Idealism of peasant decoration. Kandyan art as we see it represents a tradition handed down from
the earliest stratum of Indian art, modified and enriched by subsequent influences but in
many ways primitive; just as the original manner of building in wood, and of making
images in impermanent materials, survives in spite of the work in stone of Anuradhapura
and Polonnaruva. Could the sculptors of Barahat have come to life in eighteenth century
Kandy, they would have found little that would have seemed strange or unfamiliar in the
style or subject of the paintings on its vihara walls. The sculptured trees at Barahat differ
only from those painted at Danagirigala in their more intense feeling for beauty and the
deeper emotion which inspires them. This we should expect in work so much nearer the
beginning of a great tradition.
We shall understand the idealism of Indian and Sinhalese art as well from a study of the
Barahat or Kandyan trees, as in any other way. There are two ways of seeing a tree;
at first glance or in a photograph, it strikes us as an irregular growth of branches and
leaves, producing a confused effect of light and shade. We soon learn to distinguish more
than this, and to tell one kind of tree from another. But as we consider more deeply
a number of trees of different kinds, we realise that each has, as it were, a law of its being:
its leaves have a certain form, with a certain range of variation, its branches a certain
manner of growth, its flowers a particular symmetry. Each actual tree seems to be an
incarnation or embodiment of some more perfect and rhythmical idea of the tree. This
idea it is the aim of art to reveal.
A good example of the idealistic treatment is afforded by the lotus. The lotus to Indian
art and for the Indian mystic, is all that the rose was to Mediasval Europe. As English
medieval art is one long ‘Romaunt of the Rose,’ so Indian art is a romance of the
many-petalled flower that is the throne of all divinities, and whose ideal form continually
re-incarnates in every vessel and in every design. The simple lotus form represents the
ideal, form of all lotuses, as does the Tudor rose for all roses, it carries the emotion of
all lotuses compressed into one abstraction. This is the secret of the constancy of art
forms, that the ideal form they represent is eternal and immutable, a thought in the heart
of lávara; that is why the trees at Barahat and the trees in a Kandyan vihara are expressed
by the same formula. The impulse to the expression of emotion in art, is born of the
sense of the unity of all life, the recognition of the many in the one. The representation
of ideal forms, the reduction of various complex appearances to their simplest terms is
an expression of the desire to see the one in the many.* There is here a great affinity
between art and science; what natural law resuming the sequence of phenomena is for
phenomena, ideal art is for the expression of emotion. Scientific drawing is concerned
with the appearance of things as they seem to be in themselves; art with things as they
really are within ourselves: in other words science is objective, art subjective. It is most
important that their aims should not, as is now usually the case, be confused.
* This impulse in its extremest art form produces such hieroglyphs as many of the maguí lakunu, as
shown in Fig. 69. In religion it results in a corresponding asceticism. We feel that the hieroglyphs
or symbols are scarcely any longer to be classed as art., so slight is their intrinsic manifestation, arid so
entirely does the emotional value depend on association. We get a glimpse here again of the nature of the
antipathy between religion and art. Theformer must in the end transcend the latter. Of the golden
crowns which must be offered at the throne of truth, before the truth itself is known, art like all else
related to time and space, is one. Butfor most of us, the time is not yet arrived, when we are prepared
not merely to refine, but to transcend this life.

The memory element is in Indian art almost as characteristic as its consistent idealism. Painting
As already remarked, the Kandyan artist carried in his head the elements of his art, and
composed them as occasion required. His fault lay in becoming the slave rather than Idealism
the master of the tradition thus transmitted ; there have been many times in the history of
Indian art when it has been otherwise, but eighteenth century Kandyan was not one of
these high-water marks.
The essential points in the traditional representations were summarised in mnemonic
verses, for example, “This is the appearance of Vishiju, two hands, a chank, a discus, a
head-dress, a crown, ear-flowers, a golden garment, his colour blue, his vehicle xhtgaruia"
(Rupavaliya, v. 57). Such mnemonic verses correspond to the memory verses of the
early literature, and may once have been transmitted orally in the same way. Thus the
Dlpavaipsa, I., 29, describes the satsatiya thus: “The throne, the sanctuary, the cloisters,
the gem palace, the ajapala (tree), the (naga) mucalinda, together with the Khirapala
(grove) as the seventh.” But all this is subservient to the idealism and the living tradition.
From the verse alone, a quite inadequate figure of Vishiju would be drawn, just as from
the verse alone, a very poor idea of the satsatiya would be gathered. Each had to be filled
in by the artist, whether painter or reciter, as best he knew.
In some verses of the canon the idealism is more evident. The Buddha, for example,
is one with “an unfettered, quiescent, and absolutely pure mind” (Sariputra); of the horse
it is said that “his neigh has the sound of the storm, ... he is swift as the wind, stately
as the lion and has the gait of a dancer” (Rupavaliya). The expression of these abstract
ideas is of more value than the exact imitation of natural forms.
We are not told, and do not want to be told, what the animal itself was like, but what it
meant to the men who painted it, what it was like for them, and so what they were like.
As I have said above (p. 87), the artist’s lion need be like no lion on earth or in any
zoological garden ; the artist is not preparing the plates of a work on natural history; but
makes his lion at once a portrait of the universe and an expression of the whole theory
of his national existence. At the same time it must be recognized that the eighteenth
century craftsman in Ceylon was merely making use of such expressions already formulated,
and was not himself a creator. The same applies to the imager, who used the formula,
and was influenced, no doubt, by the suggestions of such verses as those just quoted, but
can hardly at this time have been accustomed to practise meditation and mental visualising
as truly great Indian artists have always done.
It must not be supposed, however, that tradition, by its very nature, fetters the expression
and production o( great art; on the contrary it enables the great artists to speak in a
language uhderstanded of the people, and without that necessity for explanation which
reduces the value of more individualistic art; and the existence of an art language is no
more a fetter to the true artist, than the existence of a word language is to the true poet.
And what did tradition mean to the lesser craftsmen, for whom art was but a craft? It
gave them a conception so defined as to avoid all danger of the sacred subjects being treated
ab surdly or irreverently. How well this aim was attained is shown by the vulgarity and
stupidity that do appear in Indian art, where the tradition is rudely and contemptuously
broken with. But while the tradition lasted, it saved the man of small capacity from
his own folly, and made it possible for him to work acceptably within its limits.
If, for example, the spiritual conflict of Buddha with the powers of evil had been depicted
by some great artist, in the shape of a strong man whose face was torn by conflicting
emotions, a wonderful picture might have resulted; but it would not have been peaceful,
impersonal, ideal. Such a rendering of ‘expression’ in the face would be quite foreign
to the aesthetic and philosophic conceptions of Indian art, which is not at all concerned
171

Painting with the interpretation of individuality. It would not be possible for many such personal
individual pictures to be made; and one essential of religious art, is that there shall be
Idealism a possibility of the work being done fairly well by average craftsmen. This does not at
all rule out the genius, who has a greater, not a less, opportunity than has such a man
nowadays who can only do good work, in conscious opposition to the spirit of the age.
Furthermore, only great individual artists could depict the mental struggle adequately as
such; but the concrete symbolism made it possible for average workmen at all times to
produce a sufficient result; without preventing the great man from throwing all his genius
into the expression of peace in the seated figure.
The serene seated figure, surrounded by vainly attacking devils, is a most assuring and
peaceful promise of final victory over the passions. The Buddha is not represented in his
painful struggles, but with the calmness of perfect victory and peace. So, too, in earlier
Christianity, representations of Christ in glory, or transfigured, were much oftener made,
than of Christ upon the cross.
In times of great artistic expression, we have both the work of men of genius, and that
of ordinary workmen. Their work is united by the bond of a common tradition, or means
of expression, just as the work of contemporaneous poets is united by a common language
and association of ideas. But in eighteenth century Kandyan art we have to deal not
with the work of men of individual genius as well as that of ordinary workmen, we have
only the work of the latter. The value of the concrete traditional symbolism in this case
can hardly be overestimated, a point which those who are acquainted with the extraordinary
vulgarity and unsuitability of modern vihara decoration, often executed by low-country
painters who are not hereditary craftsmen, will understand.
References To enable us to judge of the light in which art, and especially painting, was ordinarily
to Sinhalese regarded, an examination of some literary references will be useful. There was at this
literature time no great philosophy of art; it was regarded almost entirely as decorative in aim.
Here is the translation of a verse in the Nllakobo Sandeiaya (eighteenth century); the
writer, addressing the parrot messenger, “ Sit quietly on the fruitladen kaduru tree, and
behold the ambalam built at Polonnaruvavela, adorned with paintings of lions and leopards,
as if by the advent of Viivakarma with his mighty power.”
Again in the description of the building of a palace for the youthful GatfSia, in the Gaifa
Devi H^lla, “After the walls were daubed with clay, and smoothly plastered with lime,
an artist was engaged, who painted pictures of makaras and hamsas, gavaras, leopards
and lions, peacocks and parrots, ringdoves and cocks, pigeons and pretty kovulas.”
Verse 205 of the Gira Sandeiaya (fifteenth century) speaks of “ the monks reaching
the different parts of such a great vihara (Pepiliyana), and opening the painted covers
of the books of sacred doctrine to investigate the meaning of the Abhidhamma text.”
Verse 91 of the Sevul Sandeiaya (late sixteenth century) describes the paintings in a Hindu
Temple near Sitavaka: “Beholding with a heart filled with boundless joy the paintings
representing in detail the war between Rama and Ravaija, the war of the Mahabharata, the
wars of the auspicious Skanda, and the wars waged by Hvara against the Asuras in ancient
times.”
Other quotations could be given, but these show that the mediaeval poets did not fail
to notice and appreciate the paintings of their time.

is quite distinct from that practised by the craftsmen proper, and represents an historically Painting

Fa Hian (a .d. 400) states that on a certain occasion during his visit, both sides of a
procession road were decorated with representations of Buddha in the five hundred

beautifully painted in divers colours, and have a very life-like appearance ” no doubt they
were made of impermanent materials somewhat similar to those used in bait ceremonies.
(©k A few words may be said as to the history of painting in Geylon. Naturally there are no History of
surviving examples of primitive work of this character where earth and leaves supply the painting
pigments and materials. We are forced to rely upon inference and literary evidence for
anything even as old as the oldest stone sculptures, at which time.an equally developed
school of painting must also have existed. Painting was one of the 64 arts and sciences
practised in ancient India. It is frequently referred to in the Mahabharata and Ramayaija.
It may have been known in a primitive form to the original inhabitants of Ceylon before
the arrival of Vijaya. The first mention of it in the Mahavarpsa, is the reference to the
use of ‘painted vases’ in the reign of Devanam Piyatissa (307 b.c.). It is very likely
indeed that the foundation of the craft as now surviving in Ceylon, dates, like so much
else of Hindu-Buddhist culture, from the time of the settlement of Anoka’s missionaries,
and the great intellectual stimulus resulting from the contact of the art of Barahat with
the more primitive art, of which we have no remains, but which may have existed in
Ceylon. In connection with the building of the Ruvanveli Dagaba, we are told of the
mixing of orpiment (mistranslated vermilion in the English edition) with oil for use in
cementing the foundations; this has been taken as evidence of a practise of oil-painting,
but without the least justification. But we hear also (p. 5, above) of the decoration
of the relic chamber with representations of jatakas, and it is probable that tempera
painting (in water colour) is here meant, though not expressly indicated.
The artist king, Jettha Tissa (a .d. 330), has been referred to above, p. 7. The earliest
paintings actually surviving in Ceylon are those at Sigiriya. These differ in character and
in technique from all modern work, but very closely resemble the famous Ajanta paintings
of the same century. This period was one of great artistic activity, which began in India
in the fourth century under the Gupta dynasty, and absorbed Dravidian tradition into its
own.-f- The character of the art of this period may be judged best from the Ajanta wall
paintings, and the Ellora sculptures. The Sigiri paintings show that Ceylon was in close
tou ch with the art growth of the time. The early Chinese historians speak in raptures of
i mages made in Ceylon ; and it is clear that the fourth and fifth centuries were one of the
great periods of Sinhalese art. But they stand isolated from the historical development
of the later art, which possesses far less capacity for drawing the human form. The Sigiri
paintings are somewhat sensuous, and though apparently representing goddesses and
* Beal, '■ Buddhist Records’ I., p. lxxv.
•f' Okakura, ‘ Ideals of the East’ p. 78.
177
n I

Painting attendants, are not markedly religious in feeling. They appear to have left no trace on
later Sinhalese art. Were they not thus an isolated landmark, it would be easier to fit
them into the historical evolution of Sinhalese art as we know it.
Sigiriya It will be worth while to give a brief account of them. They are executed on the plastered
tempera surface of the Sigiriya rock, those remaining being only found in an almost inaccessible
paintings cave; probably the whole rock surface over the gallery was once plastered and painted.
The plaster consists of a groundwork of earth (white ants’ nest ?) and kaolin, half an inch
in thickness, strengthened with an admixture of paddy husk, and perhaps coconut fibre,
and covered with white chunam (lime) smoothed with a trowel. Only three pigments
are used, yellow, red, and green, but these are varied by shading and mixture, unlike their
use in modern work; blue is absent. Mr. Bell* thinks that the paintings are portraits
of Court ladies proceeding to the vihara with flower offerings. To me the fact that the
figures are cut off at half-length by conventional clouds suggests that they represent divine
beings; who are always so represented in modern work.
The work is much freer and shows much greater knowledge of the human figure than
any work now done; but is equally less ideal in character and less religious. Perhaps
we cannot judge much from this single surviving example of what must have been a great
school, working over a very extended area, and partly affected by Chinese influence.-f-
Their one great value is the demonstration of the fact that the work of the Ajanfa school
was so widespread. A controversy has arisen as to whether the artists were Sinhalese
or Indian. "The point is of little real importance. The Chinese and others at this time
thought exceedingly highly of Sinhalese images, which goes to show that art of a high
type flourished in Ceylon ; and suggests that the painters may also have been indigenous;
but if so, it can hardly be claimed that the school was so,—only that it was so widespread
as to have representatives even in Ceylon. The fact that the work differs so much from all
modern work suggests that special conditions made it possible. As regards technique it
is true that the work is much more enduring in character than any now done; but I do
not know that it was necessarily oil colour. The painters of to-day have a method of
varnishing water colour work, so as to make it very durable. There are outdoor paintings
at Ridi Vihara; the rock wall over the vihara is covered with remains of paintings of
priests on a plaster surface now much broken away (see p. 165, above). I do not know
in what manner these were executed, as they were inaccessible; they date from the
eighteenth century.. The problems raised by the Sigiriya paintings are many and hard,
but lie mainly outside the scope of the present volume; the chief concern is the place
of the school in relation to the historical evolution of modern Sinhalese art.
Passing on to later times, we find at Polonnaruva in the Maha Demala Saya certain jataka
paintings, more like the Sigiriya work than modern work; and on certain of the dagabas
(Ruvanveli and Abhayagiriya) at Anuradhapura, paintings (patterns) in a very bad state
of preservation, but which also incline to the earlier type in their free and almost careless
. execution.:];
Subsequently we find in the Mahavaipsa frequent references to paintings on cloth and the
painting of temples, evidently of the same character as the eighteenth century work known
to us. The modern work seems to represent the continuous tradition handed on from the
earliest times; for it has much in common with the Barahat sculptures, and the style of
painting which we may suppose to have existed in Anoka’s times. There are many

primitive features, such as the method of continuous narration, where the same figure Painting
or figures are repeated again and again without separation into different scenes, but in

continued more or less independent of the other schools of more developed art which
existed at various times; just as building in wood has always been the truly indigenous
style of architecture, apart from exceptional periods of important work in stone, mainly
under Indian inspiration.

I. PAPER MANUSCRIPTS.
Of paper manuscripts I am acquainted with two only, and am indebted to the owners for the
loan of them. The oldest is a small ba^a daham pota, containing a selection of sutras or
discourses of the Buddha, and said to have been used by the Kuij(Jasale king (Narendra
Sirtiha) as a prayer book or breviary; it now belongs to Indajoti Unnanse of the Meda
Pansala, Malvatte. It is written on i68 leaves (two blank) of Dutch paper measuring
5 inches by 3^ inches. There are twenty-seven lines to a page, rubricated throughout,
with stops (kundali) in blue and red and the words separated by red marks. Each stltra
is separated from the one following it by a tail-piece very delicately drawn in colour
(Pis. XVII. and XX); there is also a page of pure pattern work at the beginning and end.
The colours used are red, yellow, black, blue, emerald green and gold. The writing
is in a fine hamsa tipi hand, on lines ruled feint with a stylus but not marked in any clearer
way. The book is bound in brown leather, gold tooled with a pattern, the elements of
which are identical with those of one of the tail-pieces; two very finely worked silver
clasps are still perfectly preserved. Pages of the book are reproduced on PI. XX., and
in Fig. 3 ; the clasps and binding are shown in PI. LII. This little book is so very beautiful
and complete in every way as to give cause to regret the absence of others like it. It
may be supposed that the binding was executed by some Dutchman or Portuguese resident
in Kandy, who must also have explained to the silversmith the form of clasp required;
the silver work being typically Kandyan, and the best of its kind.
The other book is both larger and later; it was written in a.d. 1811 by Iriyagama
Dhammadassi at a cost of 200 ridls, at the request of a certain official and court favourite
w ho wished to perform a meritorious action for the benefit of the soul of the late Queen
Mother who had been his patron. Full details of the many lands and offices held by this
man are given in the long colophon, translated below; affording an interesting side­
light on Kandyan court life 100 years ago. The book is written on 150 leaves (two blank)
of Dutch paper measuring 13|- inches by qf inches, thirty-three lines to the page, and
is plainly bound in leather; folios 1-146 are numbered consecutively, the text beginning

II. HOW TO PREPARE COLOURS.+
1. Take equal parts of hiriyal and ran-hiriyal, and grind with the juice of milla \¡zr)s.,gammalu
bark, and goka(u bark, and roast it; the colour of gold is produced.
2. Take badulla milk, k(ppitiya lakada, hal-dummala, and old jak milk in equal parts, grind
these four together, and warm-; apply to what you will; this is black badama.
3. For red badama grind sadilirigam and warm with juice of ratmal bark; apply it to any
work you will; the colour is red.
4. For yellow badama take gokafu juice, hiriyal, and ratukaha in equal parts; collect old
jak milk and grind with dorai}a oil; apply it to any work you will, polish it with a cheetah’s
tooth ; this is yellow badama.
5. For a good effect take sea sand, roast and sift it; apply it with arrack where required,
polish it with a cheetah’s tooth; this is blue badama.
6. Take equal parts of hiriyal, gokofu milk, quicksilver, alum, sal-ammoniac, borax and
white lead {sudu iyan) and grind in dorarta oil; apply it to whatever work is needed, polish
it with a cheetah’s tooth ; this is gold coloured badama.

III. HOW TO MAKE GLUE.
“Whensoever they have occasion to use Glew, they make it after this fashion. They take
the Curd of milk, and strain the water from it through a cloth. Then tying it up in a
cloth like a Pudding, they put it into boyling water, and let it boyl a good while. Which
done it will be hard like Cheese-curd, then mixing it with Lime, use it. If it be not
for present use, they will roul up these Curds into a Ball; which becomes hard, and as they
have occasion will scrape some of it off with a Knife, and so temper it with Lime. This
Lime with them is as soft as Butter.”*

CHAPTER X. IVORY, BONE, HORN, AND
SHELL.
IT is remarkable that nowhere in India has ivory in mediæval or modern times held
a really prominent place amongst the arts and crafts, although its use must date
back to a remote antiquity, and where practised, was so well understood. No
collection of strictly Indian ivories can compare with that in the Colombo Museum,
although individually finer pieces of work are to be found on the mainland. An explanation
of this may be found in the Hindu reluctance to make use of animal products, and their
vid^v of bones, leather, and other remains of the dead body as unclean. The worship of
the tooth-relic, for example, would be quite impossible to a Hindu. With the rarest
exceptions, ivory has not been used in India for the fabrication of Hindu images ; and even
for domestic purposes ivory has not been used as extensively as might have been expected.
The Buddhists had no such scruples ; we know that they were willing to eat even the
flesh of animals slain by others, and in the same way to use animal products. Ivory has
always been a comparatively rare and costly material. That ivory was valued very long
ago by Buddhists is suggested by Chadanta Jataka, where a great elephant was robbed
of its tusks, and died from the suffering ; but this was regarded as a great sin, and held
up to execration in the story. In the ordinary way no elephant would have been killed
for the sake of its ivory ; indeed, the elephant alive would be of greater value.
It is, then, not altogether surprising that even in India, the traditions of ivory carving
“centre round the early Chalukyan and Buddhistic traditions rather than the more recent
Dravidian and Indo-Aryan schools of South Indian decoration.”* The same thing is, of
course, much more obvious in Ceylon, and we are again reminded of the value of late
Sinhalese art as preserving something of the Buddhist Indian art which preceded the more
definitely Hindu art of the seventh century and onwards.
Whilst in Africa and India elephants of both sexes have tusks, in Ceylon not more than
one in a hundred possess them, and those exclusively males; and these are particularly
valued, as the tusks are of so much use in enabling them to perform any work required
of them. But nearly all Ceylon elephants have ‘tushes’ or tusks not more than a foot or
so in length and an inch or two in thickness. The tusks of those elephants which possess
them rarely exceed fifty or sixty pounds in weight. Large tusks are highly valued and
gçnerally form part of the treasure of the greater viharas and dévales ; it is usual to place
a pair of tusks on either side of temple doorways, either permanently or on special occasions.
They are to be found in the dévale storerooms still, and were kept in reserve, ready to
be given to the temple craftsmen whenever work in ivory at or for the temple was required.
In a vihara at Badulla may be seen a large pair with an inlaid inscription in silver letters.
Ceylon ivory is valued in the East above African on account of its density of texture and
delicacy of tint ; but the quantity obtainable must always have been small. It is indeed
surprising that under the circumstances, so large an amount of work in ivory should exist
and such great skill in its manipulation attained.
But few references to Sinhalese ivory are to be found in works on Indian art. Mr. Maskell,
in his ‘Ivories,’ devotes a chapter to ‘India, Arabia and Persia,’ in which, after a violent
attack on Indian ivories in general, he does some justice to those of Ceylon. He perceives
that for true Hindu art, that is. Early Hindu in feeling, we must go to Ceylon. He
reproduces in his PI. lxxii. two beautiful fragments from a door jamb, one representing

Kinissa The beautiful kinissa here reproduced on PI. XLI., 3, has been illustrated in colours in
the ‘Journal of Indian Art,’ Vol. X., PI. 86, to accompany Mr. Andrew’s paper on ‘The
Elephant in Industry and Art.’ It is there, and also in the South Kensington ‘Portfolio
of Indian Art,’ incorrectly described as a ‘Sacrificial Ladle.’ Mr. Andrews describes the
typical liya pata decoration of the handle as follows:— “There is a distinct method of
conventional elaboration in the scrollwork, very striking and quite unmistakeable. The
general form of the scrolls may be likened to the upward flow of smoke and flame ; and as
thin threads of smoke rising beside heavy ones are curled over as they meet the downward
roll of the greater, so we see in this ornament innumerable lines flowing along the general
direction, but terminating in tiny volutes under the shadow of larger ones. Sometimes
two masses will divide and join higher up, and in the hollows so formed, sparks like pearls
may be seen to rise. And with all the scrolls and sparks and ripples the balance of the
gently waving mass that issues from the jaws of the grinning fire-breathing yali in this
example is perfect.”
The crafts of ivory carving and ivory turning are distinct. The ivory carver is usually
an all round craftsman of the highest rank, a galladda, used to practise both painting and
building also; the ivory turner does no other work, and belongs to the va^uvo. These
distinctions have been explained on p. 54.
Statuettes The ivory carver’s chief tools are his saws and gravers and chisels. The work he does is
varied in character, covering a wide range of objects required for religious, architectural
and personal use. The statuettes and images are of special interest. Ivory statuettes of
Buddha are not very rare ; good examples are to be found in the Colombo Museum. They
appear to have been usually painted; traces of paint can still be seen on some. I have
seen only standing figures in ivory, none seated or reclining. Statuettes of kings, and
ordinary men and women are also common, and are sometimes excellently done. Some
figures of Rafemahatmayas, drummers and other characters executed in the twentieth
century are superior to any old ones I have seen. The figures (from the Colombo Museum)
shown on Plate XXXVI. are of the eighteenth or early nineteenth century and more
useful as records of the costume of the royalty and nobility, than remarkable as works of
art; the costume is explained in the description of the Plate.
The Mahavaijisa speaks of a park made at Polonnaruva by Parakrama Bahu (a.d.
1164-1197), which was railed “ with pillars decorated with rows of images made of ivory,”
of which the ivory-railed palanquin of PI. IX. reminds us in a smaller way. Parakrama
Bahu also built in the ‘Island Park,’ a pavilion named Samimaijdapa ‘wrought with
ivory.’
Panels Next to the statuettes may be mentioned plaques and panels such as those figures of devas
representing the guardians of the threshold, which are seen at the base of the door jamb
at the doors of viharas and devales. These are illustrated in PI. XXXV., 5 and 6. The
head-dress, robes and jewellery are those traditionally given to figures of devas or kings.
It will be seen that the treatment is stiff and conventional, but not without dignity and
184

beauty. The right hand of the deva of PI. XXXV., 6, is especially fine. The figures are Ivory
enclosed within carved arimbuva border, carrying Itya pata crockets on the inner side.
We sometimes find that the ivory plaques of door jambs represent not devas, but dancing- Doors
girls, animals or other subjects. Thus at Ridi Vihâra, the figures at the dévale store-room
door are those of dancing-girls (PI. XXXVIII., 2), those at the side entrance to the lower
vihâra verandah are gaja-simhays. Probably such secular subjects are only represented
in the case of decorated doors, which are not the actual doors of a sanctuary ; for the
guardian devas are for the protection of the spiritual atmosphere of the sanctuary, and
this kind of guardianship is not needed for verandah or store-room doors, where a good
lock and key suffice for more worldly guardianship. But it is mainly sanctuary doors
on which decoration is lavished without stint ; and so magnificent a secular door as that
of the dévale store-room at RidI Vihâra is not to be seen elsewhere. It is shown on
PI. XXXVIII. in Figs. I and 2, and represents an extraordinarily high level of attainnient
in the application of ivory carving to architectural decoration. The contrast of the
comparatively plain door, with its ivory and ebony-covered frame, with the once gaily
painted wall could not be better conceived ; it will be many a long day ere anything so
fine is done in Ceylon again. Not all the efforts of the Department of Public Instruction,
aided by all the technical schools and Public Works Department’s draughtsmen can do
what Kirti éri and the royal craftsmen did so easily a hundred and fifty years ago. Indeed,
they do not want to do the same thing, and hardly know that they could not. If we
consider a capacity for producing and understanding literature and art to be any test of
‘civilisation,’ then, even though we know that Sinhalese art in the eighteenth century
is no more than a great and beautiful scheme of peasant decoration, we are driven to feel
that in the possession of such skilled craftsmen and in their organic relation to the life of
the people, a higher and more beautiful life is indicated than that of which the railway
goods-yard and the Governors’ Residences are visible evidence. The purchase of xylonite
combs made in Birmingham does not indicate any real advance upon the days when the
local craftsmen spent days and weeks on the elaboration of ever varied and beautiful design.
It is difficult sometimes to see where the advantage of the modern conditions lies, either
economically or ethically.
But it is necessary to return to the immediate subject before us, and in so doing, we may Combs
speak next of combs. The number and variety of Sinhalese ivory combs is surprising.
Their general characteristics are well shown in Pis. XXXIX. and XL. and need little
further detailed description beyond what is given in the explanations of the Plates. The
combs are most often elaborately carved, and often fretted, but occasionally more severe
and plain. Figure and genre subjects, plant and geometrical ornament abound. In the
case of figure subjects we find two ways of treating the back : either the back and front
are identical, so that the figure faces both ways ; or the back of the figure is treated as such,
and figure faces one way only. Of the combs illustrated on PI. XXXIX., No. 4 is of a
very unusual form. No. 6 is almost unornamented, but none the less finely designed, and
N o. 2, perhaps the most beautiful, is of bone, as is also No. 11 on PI. XL. The comb
shown in Fig. 10 on PI. XXXIX. shows traces of colouring.
A piece of ivory sawn for a comb {panava), but not finished, is called pana-katuva \ thé
same name is given to the central part of an old comb, when all the teeth are broken or
removed ; such pieces are often repaired by rivetting into a groove a thin strip of ivory
cut into new teeth.

Ivory The ivory carving already described is done by craftsmen of the upper group, the same man
turning being often a painter and an ivory carver. Ivory turning is done by men of the lower
division. The ivory carver is called from his work, çt-dat-kçfayan-karaya ; the turner, like

the turner of wood, Uyana-va uvâ. The chief articles fashioned on the lathe are fan handles,
handles of knives, and various implements and tools, boxes, book-buttons, {pot-saki), scent-
sprays, pacisi pieces. Fan handles and boxes of horn are also made. Most of these are
decorated with dots and circles incised and filled with coloured lac applied on the lathe.
This decoration is an excellent instance of the good effect produced by simple means directly
adapted to the material, and arising out of the method of manufacture and the nature of
the materials available. The dots are made with a pointed tool; the circles with one
having two points, used like a pair of compasses, one point being stationary, the other
describing a circle about it. Fan handles so decorated are illustrated on PI. XXXVII.,

box is shown on PI. XXXVI., 8, and horn pill-boxes on Plate XL., 15 and 16. The Ivory

One of the most remarkable feats of the turner is the manufacture of scent-sprays. The
simidiya, or ivory scent-spray consists of a hollow cylindrical base, and a long neck. The
base, holding the scent, is so thin that it is easily compressed by slight pressure of the hand.
The method of turning ivory to this extreme thinness, almost that of paper, is kept a secret,
but would seem to depend only on great patience and delicacy of handling.
The ivory turner’s lathe is shown on PI. VI., 4. It is extremely simple, and in principle Ivory lathe
identical with the carpenter’s lathe. The essential parts of it are the wooden spindle
{liyana kandd)\ the two supports embedded in the ground, the one in the figure furthest
from the observer being the pifa-kariuva, the nearer, the vftna-katfuva; the andina-larjuva or
string for turning the lathe; and the hand-rest, the faftala-l^lla. The other tools used,
an adze, saws, rasps and graver are seen in the foreground. It will be seen that the ivory
to be turned is attached to the end of the lathe, outside the v?ma-kai}uva, instead of between
it and the pita-katfuva; this is very convenient for hollowing out boxes and the like.

CHAPTER XI. METAL WORK; IRON,
BRASS, COPPER AND BRONZE; GOLD
AND SILVER; JEWELLERY.
‘ ‘the smith also sitting by the anvil, and considering the iron •work.'—Ecclesiasticus.
A KNOWLEDGE of iron is of great antiquity in India; the metals gold, silver,
iron, lead, copper, and tin were known in the Vedic period, and are mentioned in
the Vedic literature. Megasthenes at a later period noted the occurrence of
these metals, and states that they were “employed in making articles of use and ornament,
as well as the implements and accoutrements of war.” There is abundant evidence that
the ancient Hindus were skilled in manufacturing and working iron and in making and
tempering steel. “ Indian steel has been celebrated from the remotest antiquity, and the
blades of Damascus, which maintained their pre-eminence even after the blades of Toledo
became celebrated, were in fact of Indian iron. . . . The ondanique of Marco Polo’s travels
refers originally, as Colonel Yule has shown, to Indian steel, the word being a corruption
of the Persian Hund’waniy, Le., Indian steel. The same word found its way into Spanish,
in the shapes of alhinde and alfinde, first with the meaning of steel, and then of a steel mirror,
and finally of the metal foil of a glass mirror. The ondanique of Kirman, which Marco
Polo mentions, was so called from its comparative excellence, and the swords of Kirman
were eagerly sought after, in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, by the Turks, who gave
great prices for them. . . . Arrian mentions Indian steel, as imported into the Abyssian
ports; and Salmasins mentions that among the surviving Greek treatises was one ‘on the
tempering of Indian steel.’”*
Of monuments remaining in India, the most famous is Chandragupta’s wrought-iron pillar
near Delhi, which weighs ten tons and is about fifteen hundred years old. Of this pillar,
Ferguson-f wrote that “it opens our eye to an unsuspected state of affairs to find the
Hindus at that age capable of forging a bar of iron larger than any that have been forged
even in Europe up to a very late date, and not frequently even now. ... It is almost equally
startling to find that after an exposure to wind and rain for fourteen centuries, it is unrusted,
and the capital and inscription are as clear and as sharp now as when put up fourteen
centuries ago.” There are other monuments, such as the huge iron girders at Puri; the
ornamental gates of Somnalli; and the 24 ft. wrought-iron gun at Nurvar, that bear witness
to the metallurgical skill of the Hindus.
Iron and steel are still made in India, but the industry is dying out. In 1880 the Duirdusti
mines on the Godavari were still worked; the iron sand being “melted with charcoal,
without any flux, and is obtained at once in a perfectly tough and malleable state, superior
to any English iron, or even the best Swedish. . . . Excellent steel is also still fused for
gun barrels and sword blades.” A more detailed account of iron and steel manufacture
in India in still more recent times is given by V. S. Sambasiva Iyer in a lecture on “ Iron
Smelting in Mysore,” published in Madras in 1902. Mr. Iyer thinks it possible that with
improved methods it may be possible to continue and revive the industry in Mysore, where
there is still some market for the local iron and steel, though these cost rather more than
imported materials. Even in Ceylon there is a decided preference for the local product.

Metalwork while for making steel, the country-made iron is said to be altogether superior, probably
on account of its freedom from phosphorus.
Iron Seeing that a knowledge of iron is so ancient and widespread in India, it is not surprising
smelting to find it also in Ceylon, which is, strictly speaking, no more than a part of India. The
oldest specimens of iron in Ceylon are probably those found by Mr. Parker at Tissa-
maharlma.* Heaps of slag which are found in every district show how widespread an
industry this smelting of iron has been. At present the industry survives only near
Balangoda, where a certain amount of iron is made as a service rent, and where there still
live two very old men who understand the method of conversion to steel. With these
two men the latter craft will become a thing entirely of the past. One can hardly help
regretting the decay of so ancient and interesting a craft; nor is the change quite unmixed
gain, for comparatively little of the European iron is of the fine quality of Indian. But
with Mr. Vredenburg,-f- “ I doubt whether the iron industry can ever be revived in India
by smelting according to the native methods. . . . To try to smelt iron on a small scale
at the present day is probably equivalent, from an economic point of view, to attempting
to prepare galvanized or corrugated iron, or lead pipes, or soda water bottles on a small
scale or by manual labour.” The steel industry in Ceylon is already dead, for steel has
never been made of late years in the ordinary way of trade, and the old men who make
it cannot live many years more; a few families, however, are still partially occupied in
iron smelting, and though it is likely that even by them it will be abandoned sooner or
later, I see no reason why the smelters should be discouraged or laid under any unnecessary
disability in connection with obtaining wood for charcoal, or otherwise.
The methods i of the few remaining smelters are unchanged. Iron is still smelted at
Hatarabage, near Balangoda,by men oflow caste {yamannu). The photographs reproduced
on PI. LIIL, Figs. 1-3, show the workshop of an old man named Kiri Ukkuva, and his
sons. The furnace is beneath the thatched roof of a shed open on all sides; it is quite close
to the house occupied by the smelter and his family; for it is generally more convenient
to collect and bring the ore to the furnace, than to establish the furnace near the ore. But
smelters used also to erect the furnace near the ore, as in the case of those who used to
visit Nuvara Eliya to work the iron ores there found. The ore is generally the nodular
hematite or limonite which arises as a decomposition product of the country rocks, and is
widely distributed in small quantities. Before smelting, the ore is broken into small
pieces, and roasted to drive off water. In some districts it appears that the ore used has
been magnetite. The analysis § of a typical hematite is as follows :

It is of interest to note that there was evidently associated with the iron smelters’ furnace,
as with all agricultural and craft operations, some idea of ceremonial purity and of religion.
I have not been able to obtain any songs relating to the subject, but it is noted by Lawrie
(Gazetteer, p. 686) that in 1811 when some villagers had gone, as they often did, to Nuvara
Eliya to smelt iron, that one of their companions fell sick, whereupon he was at once carried
away, lest by death he should defile the furnaces. Some hint of a survival of primitive
j religious ideas is also found in the two cobras which may be seen moulded on the wattle-
and-daub wall of the steel furnace, PI. LIIL, 5 and 6.
Steel The manufacture of steel, even as a service rent is quite extinct ; but two very old men
manufacture at Alutnuvara still keep up the tradition, and are able to demonstrate the process when
required ; with these men a knowledge of the process will be gone, so that a record of
their methods is of much value. The steel makers are smiths {navandanns), thus of much
higher caste than the yamannu from whom they buy the iron required. Thé process of
steel making is more delicate than that above described. The furnace (PI. LIII., 5 and 6,
and Fig. too) is smaller, and at the ground level, instead of being raised three feet above
the ground ; it is a semi-circular hearth filled with charcoal, into which air is conducted
from the bellows, which rre identical with those of the iron furnace. The hearth is defined
by a low clay wall, rising about six inches above the ground. The steel is made in clay
crucibles, each about eight inches long, two inches
oO oO in diameter, and a quarter of an inch in thickness.
Into the crucible is put a piece of iron, with some
chips of ranavara {Cassia auriculata); in the pro­
portion of I2| oz. iron to 5 oz. wood,* in the case
examined. The crucible is covered with a lid,
having small holes pierced for the escape of gas;
six crucibles thus prepared are embedded in the
charcoal, and a fire started. Very soon the gases
burn off, and while this goes on the blowing is
stopped. Then the blast is kept up continuously,
while the tubes are turned about and more char­
coal added, the great object being to keep up a
constant and even distribution of heat. When the

The steel is thus very free from sulphur and phosphorus and very rich in carbon. It is Steel
stated to resemble somewhat the older forms of Sheffield tool steel, which, however,
seldom contained more than i'5 per cent of carbon. The high percentage of carbon is
characteristic and interesting, for it has been pointed out by Ritter Cecil von Schwarz*
that “it is well known by every manufacturer of crucible cast steel how difficult it is *
sometimes to get the exact degree of hardness to suit certain purposes, especially with
reference to steel for cutting blades, &c. With the ordinary process endeavours are made
to reach the required degree of hardness by selecting such raw materials as on an average
have the required contents of carbon in order to correspond with the required hardness as
far as possible. The natives [of India] reached this degree by introducing into their cast
steel an excess of carbon, by taking this excess gradually away afterwards, by means of
the slow tempering process, having it thus completely in their power to attain the exact
degree by interrupting this decarbonising process exactly at the proper time in order to
cast steel of a quality exactly suitable for the purpose.”
The work of the blacksmith falls to be considered next. The general duties of a smith Smiths'
are enumerated above, on p. 25. We have seen that he purchases iron from the smelter, services
This rough bloom he prepares for use by repeated heating and hammering ; or makes steel
from it in the manner already described. But the chief part of his work is the manufacture
of tools and implements. We have seen that for each royal manor, a smith was appointed
whose duty it was to make the tools required by the tenants ; and certain fees and perquisites
were due to the smith for this work, viz. a certain rate of corn in harvest time, according
to ancient custom, and extra presents in the case of special work. These smiths were
‘protected,’ for the tenants of each manor were compelled to go to their own smith, and
none else ; and any smith working out of his own district was liable to pay damages to
the smith whose rights were thus infringed.
Beside the smiths of the royal manors, who should probably be included under the Koftal-
badda group of state craftsmen (p. 55, above), there were the king’s craftsmen working
in the Four Workshops ; and the smiths who were tenants on private manors, or tenants
of religious foundations. The last named owed service rent to the proprietors, of which
services examples may be quoted. Thus, at Nàyakunjbura, Mátale North, tenants held
land s from the Dambulla Vihára ; the services, commutable for the considerable sum of
Rs. 54'20, were to supply the vihara with nails and keys at the Nànumura Mañgalya ; to
give one vahun-kctta and five hiramana (kitchen knives and rasps), iron being supplied ; to
give thirty days’ work in iron ; to appear before the incumbent at the Old and New Year
and eat each time, to give him six arecanut sheers and chisels or some such small articles,
and the same to the Vidáne ; to give fourpence as sivurumila ; to contribute one day’s share
to the dan-kada in common with the other pangu of the village (Lawrie’s Gazetteer, p. 638).

The blacksmith’s forge is somewhat similar to the smelter’s hearth, having a wattle and
daub wall between the hearth and the bellows. The latter may be of several kinds, either
like the English form, or the iron-smelter’s bellows already described, or consisting of
two bullock-hide bags, with a bamboo nozzle, and at the other end a wide slit with wooden
lips; air is admitted through these lips, which are then dosed and the bellows compressed;
the blower sits between the two bellows and works each in turn so as to keep up a continuous
blast. The blacksmith’s tools consist of hammers,
tongs and pincers, files, punches, etc., beside the
gal-toraparfaya (Fig. 91), or instrument for boring
holes, shown in use on PI. V., 6.

Metalwork is elaborately damascened. PI. IV., 3, shows a blacksmith at work damascening a handle-

Damascen- A digression is made here to explain the nature of the damascening. This takes in Ceylon
ing three forms; the simplest is that known in Northern India as koftgari, where the surface
of the iron is roughened by fine crossed scratching, and the silver wire pressed into these,
engaging firmly with the rough surface. This method is only employed in inferior work,
and is not very often met with. The two other forms, which are generally combined in
the same piece of work, are those of inlay and overlay. In the case of inlay, a very narrow
groove is cut in the steel, and the silver or brass wire laid in this; the surface is then
hammered, causing the two sides of the groove to grip the silver wire very tightly; and
when the surface is smoothed and filed, the design shows up brightly in clear outline.
In the case of overlay, the surface to be covered is first slightly excavated, and round its
circumference a groove is undercut in the matrix; then the brass or silver plate is fitted
into the groove, and the overhanging edge of it beaten down so as to hold the overlaid
plate quite firmly. In most cases the surface of the matrix is carved before the overlay
is applied, and then the design appears in relief through the overlay, the silver or brass
being beaten down on to the carved matrix until closely moulded to its surface. The
overlaid metal may also be chased after its application to the matrix. These various ways
of damascening are known as ridi-ketayan-ve^a. The work is for the most -part done by
blacksmiths; but the finer knives and boxes are made by silversmiths.
Colouring Kandyan blacksmiths frequently make use of a method of colouring their wrought iron
iron work, the effect of which is to darken the surface and make it look like European ‘blued’
steel; the process is adapted to show up damascened work well against the dark surface,
and also to check rusting. The process is by way of being a trade secret. The recipe
is as follows :—Take three parts of sinakkdran (alum), one part of pal-manikkan (copperas),
two parts of the leaves of (hm^ fmbul-fmbiliya [Oxalis corniculata, L.) and grind together
and allow to stand three days; add the juice of one lime, and spread over the iron to be
coloured ; place carefully in the fire till the right colour is attained. The process is called
4
yaka a pafa ganava or yakaia kalu karai}ava (to colour or blacken iron).
Apparently the oxalic or other organic acid in the preparation reduces any higher oxide
of iron to the ferrous state, and when applied to the steel and heated, slight etching takes
place and a probable reduction of part of the sulphate to sulphide of iron. The temperature
employed would affect the amount of reduction and oxidation. The blue colour is probably
due to an uneven distribution of oxide and sulphide of iron.

Brass casting is a craft as important or more so than that of wrought Brass
■ Mahavalatenna.
brass ; but the lokarmo or founders belong to the lower division of casting
the craftsmen. A brassfounder’s workshop is shown on PI. V., 6.
Three furnaces with crucibles are seen in the foreground, and some moulds on the left
hand at the back. The method of casting is that known as ciré perdue. In the case of
solid articles such as images, a mould is first made in wax, then covered with fireproof
clay prepared from white ants’ nests and other ingredients ; the wax is then melted out
(through a hole in this covering of clay, and replaced by molten metal. In the case of
hollow vessels, a solid model of the fireproof clay is first made, and a wooden rod being
driven through the centre of the mass, it is turned smooth on a lathe. The model is then
covered with wax, again turned smooth, and covered with clay. When dry, the wax
is melted out through a hole in this outer layer, and replaced by metal. Objects so cast
in brass are afterwards turned smooth, or carved or repoussed or damascened.
Various vessels are cast in brass and bronze. Perhaps the commonest of these is the kotalaya. Brass
or water vessel found at every vihara, where it contains the water used to sprinkle flowers vessels
laid upon the altar ; these are open spouted vessels, and are also used for drinking from,
the water being poured from the spout to the mouth, with the hand held below the lip
to form a cup, thus avoiding contact of the vessel with the mouth ; but the vessels so used
are generally made of earthenware. A vessel much less often seen is the tel-kulava, with
a narrow grooved spout ; these are used to hold coconut oil for replenishing lighted lamps.

Clepsydras or water clocks {pMefl) were of copper. These instruments were used Water-
only by thè king and by the astrologers. “ They have,” says PCnox, “ no Clocks, Hour-glasses, clocks
or Sun-Dials, but keep their time by guess. The King indeed hath a kind of Instrument
to measure time. It is a Copper Dish holding about a Pint, with a very small hole in the
bottom. This Dish they set a swimming in an Earthen Pot of water, the water leaking
in at the bottom till the Dish be full, it sinks. And then they take it out, and set it empty
on the water again, and that makes one Pay. Few or none use this but the King, who
keeps a man on purpose to watch it continually. The people will use it upon some
occasions, as if they are to sow their Corn at any particular hour, as being the good lucky
Season, then they make use of the Copper Pan, to know the time exactly.” The piya, or
'■ Pay' as Knox calls it, is an ‘hour’ of twenty-four minutes, thirty making a day; the
pi-tefiya usually measure one p?ya, but there are others larger and smaller.
The tragic Story of Dilavati, the learned daughter of the great Indian astronomer. Dilavati
Bhaskaracarya, is called to mind by these water clocks. It had been foretold that Dilavati
would lose her husband soon after marriage, unless the ceremony were performed at a
certain auspicious moment. Her father prepared the wedding ceremonies accordingly,
and set the water clock to sink at the auspicious moment and so give the signal for tbe
ceremony to be performed. The child, however, in her play, found the dish, and leaning
over the basin in which it was floating, a pearl fell from her necklace and blocked the hole
by ^hich water was filling the bowl ; and it was not till long after the set time that the
distracted father found that his precautions had been taken in vain ; and it was after this
that he determined that she, even if widowed, should at least be the great and learned
woman she afterwards became.
A remarkable alloy, used as a niello, and also in the manufacture of certain small articles
such as nails used in superstitious ceremonies, is pas-ls or ‘ five metals.’ It appears to have
consisted of gold, silver, copper, lead and iron. The following couplet details its com­
position in the above sense: ‘PaHca lohan hema raupyan, tamrayah sisakan matam.’ It is
said that lokada (bronze or bell-metal) is sometimes used instead of lead.

craft must not be regarded as the mere amusement of an idle monarch ; the proper compre­

The ran-avudha-kkam-mahâtmaya, or keeper of the armoury, had charge of the royal arms,
of which he kept a register, and it was his business to see that they were kept in good order
by the different smiths attached to the department. Attached to this department were
forty-eight young men of rank who assisted the kkam-mahatmaya (Davy “^Travels in
Ceylon,’ p. 153).
Sannas or charters are generally engraved on copper, less often on silver or gold. The Sannas
Mahâ Devale possesses a gold sannasa, which is kept in a silver-mounted ivory box
(PI. XL., 7). Copper sannas are much commoner, and are to be found in the hands of temple
representatives, and lay grantees of lands or villages. In some cases they are very beauti­
fully engraved and ornamented, as may be seen from the reproductions of sannas in Bell’s
‘ Report on the Kegalla District.’ The Molligoda sannasa, for example, is a silver-mounted
copper plate, 19^ by 3! inches, smooth and polished, the letters small, close and beautifully
engraved. The royal sign manual, ÈRI, which heads every such grant, is inlaid in gold,
within a plain space, having an embossed fluted gold framing raised upon the surface of
the plate. This sannasa, dated áaka 1736 (a.d. 1814) was perhaps the last sannasa obtained
from a Kandyan king ; in workmanship it must be one of the most beautiful.
Another fine sannasa is the Gefaberiya sannasa (a.d. 1760). It also is a copper plate
with ornamental silver framing ; the ÈRI is inlaid in gold, with a sun and moon face,
sixteen stars and fourteen flower ornaments. These and other sannas are figured by
Mr. Bell.

‘Tools The tools used by goldsmiths are very simple. The gini-kabala is a
low earthen vessel or dish, generally a common nsmbiliya, filled with
chaff, covered by a little charcoal fire (see PI. VI., 6). With this fire
is used a small b^boo or metal blow-pipe, and a short earthen no2zle,
which is set in the fire and through which the blast is directed ; also
small crucible made of the clay of white ant hills. The other tools are
tongs and pincers, hammers and anvil (a square of steel or bronze
embedded in a heavy log, before which the jeweller squats), files,
gravers and chasers, doming blocks, bead punches, and sometimes one
or two bronze moulds for special purposes. The heat obtainable in
the simple furnace is very great, more than enough to melt silver or
gold pretty quickly. It is remarkable that with such a rough blow­
pipe such fine work can be done ; for the work to be soldered is placed
on the fire and covered with charcoal and heated through, instead of
directing a fine flame to one part alone. Different solders are used,
melting more or less readily ; and parts which must not be disturbed
writing style are also covered with a resistant preparation (powdered china paste)
{ran-panhinda), before the object is laid in the fire. The loose pieces to be soldered
length 14I inches. are kept in place by a sticky paste of olinda seed rubbed down on a

Those worn by others consist of a plain gold plate of similar outline but smaller and without

the Nàlalpate, on which the name was inscribed, was tied to the prince’s forehead by a
member of the Pilamë Talawë family, which being of royal descent, enjoyed this privilege
and that of putting on the regal sword, which was attached to a belt that passed over the
shoulder and came round the waist. The sword having been girded on the prince, the
Kapuralle presented a pot of sandal-powder, in which the prince, who may iiow be called
king, dipped his fingers and touched the sword ; and this ceremony was performed in the
Maha, as well as in the Nata-dewale.”

The general character of Sinhalese jewellery may be gathered from Plates XLVII.— LI.
The examples illustrated belong for the most part to the finer kind of jewellery worn by
the ladies of rank. But a good deal of jewellery was also worn by men, and especially by
the king. “When the king,” says Davy, “appeared on state occasions, he was either
dressed in the most magnificent robes, loaded with a profusion of jewellery, or in complete
armour of gold,* ornamented with rubies, emeralds, and diamonds.” He almost always
carried a jewelled cane. A special officer {lekam-mahâtmaya) had charge of the jewels
which the king wore habitually. Davy states that but few others were permitted to wear
ornaments of gold : “ those only who have been honoured with presents of the kind from
the hand of royalty, to whom, according to their sumptuary laws, this precious metal is
peculiarly confined.” All gems were also reserved to the use of royalty. But splendid
jewellery was also worn by the chiefs and their families, and even the ordinary govi-vanisa
families had generally one or two gold chains and rings, and a good many of silver.
t©kGems were almost invariably cut ‘en cabochon,’ never facetted. Coloured gems so
cut produce rich colour effects, rather than the flashy brilliancy characteristic of so much
European jewellery. Many a ring or pendant set with rubies or comparatively small value,
has all the glow of an enamel ; whereas facetted stones reflect a much larger proportion
* The Maiigalagama galladds still possess old designs for such gold ^ armour d
209
P *

Metal work of white light, and cannot be used in the same way to produce a generally decorative and
harmonious effect. The Sinhalese lapidaries are very skilful in turning the smallest speck
'Jewellery of colour in a stone to good advantage, so that a good effect when set is produced. Stones
are also sometimes set over coloured paste or foil to enhance the colour effect; glass and
crystal are sometimes similarly treated.
The decorative principles so well understood by the old Sinhalese and Tamil jewellers are
now generally abandoned, and almost all make use of European trade catalogues as the
sources of their designs, to meet the demand of the ‘educated’ Sinhalese who want
‘improved jewellery,’ and the demand of tourists, whose only idea of unfacetted stones
is that they are ‘uncut’ and ‘barbaric.’
Degenera- At one time it occurred to me to lay considerable stress in this volume upon the degeneration
tion of modern Sinhalese craft; but it would have been a thankless task, and it will suffice to s»y
that nowhere is it more conspicuous than in jewellery, and in general, it could hardly be
more complete. It is a compliment to true Sinhalese art to say that the jewellery now
made has nothing characteristically Sinhalese about it. With the loss of the tradition-
of good design, has gone the capacity for fine work ; not only is it impossible to get fine old
work copied, but modern settings in particular are so insecure that the stones frequently
fall out in a few days. Sinhalese jewellery to-day has indeed sunk “ to the level of the
extravagantly hard and vulgar trinketry of Birmingham, Paris, and Vienna.”
Bezels It may be remarked that bezels with teeth or claws were unknown to Sinhalese jewellers
until modern times. When first introduced they were not ineffectively used, but are now
reduced to pin-like and hardly effective teeth which, as explained, fail to hold the gem
firmly. Old settings rather resembled damascening, in that the gem was held by the
undercut surface of the metal, as in a ‘gipsy’ ring. But the most characteristic setting
was that known as tahaiu kola bemma, where the gems are set in soft gold over wax, the
gold being moulded and pressed into shape around the gem as the work proceeds. Work
so done is extremely rich and decorative in effect, but difficult to repair.
Charms Not much is known of Sinhalese jewellery in relation to its talismanic and protective
character. The children’s pendant called divi niya fota, cheetah’s claws ornament, consists
of two cheetah’s claws, mounted in silver, and suspended by a chain about a child’s neck.
Examples are illustrated on PI. XLVIII., Figs. 9, 10, and 14-17. Many specimens have
on the reverse side, representations of the ‘Five Weapons’ of Vishiju (spear, sword, discus,
bow, and chank). A navaratna muduva is a ring set with nine stones, said to be those
associated with the influence of the nine planets. Amulets to hold charmed oil or written
mantrams are worn on armlets and waist belts. An armlet carrying such an amulet is
called keccagama (PI. XLIX., 13).
It will be observed that gems are used not only in actual jewellery, but also in the decoration
of copper, silver and gold plate (Pis. XLIL, 2, 3, and 5, XLIIIa, i), the handle of a staff
(PI. XXIII., 4), and even on furniture or on a door-leaf or jamb. The eflects produced
are decorative and harmonious.
A dat-katuva (toothpick) and kan-henda (ear-spoon, PI. XLVIII., 13), the former of silver
or ivory, the latter of silver, are almost universally carried. In the low-country it is not
Low-country unusual for women to carry silver chatelaines, based on European models, often consisting
Jewellery of a large bunch of sham keys. There is also a large group, comprising the Dutch forms
made at Matara, chiefly combs, brooches, buttons, rings. Matara diamonds (white zircons)
are largely used. PI. XLIX., i, shows a typical example of this work; Figs. 2 and 3
on the same Plate illustrate examples of a brooch and part of a hair pin set with facetted
coloured stones. Though generally poor in effect, this low-country ‘Indo-Dutch’ or
‘ Indo-Portuguese’jewellery is sometimes beautiful, and it is possible to meet with ear-rings,
210

brooches and buttons strongly reminiscent of seventeenth century Italian or Portuguese Metalwork
jewellery, and exceedingly beautiful.
It is, however, with Kandyan jewellery that we are specially concerned. As might be 'Jewellery
expected, much of it shows strong Tamil influence ; but many forms are distinctive, and
experience enables the collector to judge with some certainty of their origin. The jewellery
worn by men consisted of gold chains, pendants, girdles, and especially rings ; by women,
ear-rings, chains, pendants, and girdles, bracelets, and finger rings. It will be found that Design
much of the gold jewellery is of South Indian design ; there is also much having a distinct
local character. The principal forms have distinctive names. In the case of the chains,
these are the names of flowers or seeds, as pol-mal-malaya {‘coconut-flower-garland’,
PL XLVIII., i), aralu-malaya (‘«ra/a-seed-garland,’ PI. XLVIIL, 4), peti-malaya (‘flower’
• ; oc ‘petal’ garland, PI. XLIX., 4 and 12), ge^i-malaya (garland of fruits). These names are
reminiscent of the garlands of real flowers which play so important a part in Indian festal
• dress, and which are the origin of the more permanent garlands wrought by the jeweller,
in gold and silver. It is highly characteristic of Indian art that these ‘garlands’ should be
in design entirely suggestive, and in no way imitative of the forms suggested. The naïve
realism which is so characteristic of all modern Western art, in jewellery producing the
wholly unimaginative elaborate imitations of flowers, leaves, and animals by the school of
Lalique, is never apparent in Indian design. The passion for imitation may be taken as
prima facie evidence of the lack of a true artistic impulse, which is always a desire, conscious
or sub-conscious, to express or manifest Idea. Why, indeed, imitate, where you can never
rival ? Nor is it by a conscious intellectual effort that a flower is to be ‘conventionalised’
and made into applied ornament. No Indian craftsman sets a flower in a vase before him
and worries out of it some sort of ornament by taking thought. If the flower has not meant
so much to him that he has already a clear memory picture of its essential characters, he may
as well ignore it in his decoration ; for a decorative art not intimately related to his own
experience can have no intrinsic vitality, nor would the appeal of some rare plant conven­
tionalised as ornament be strong for others. It is true, of course, that the original memory
pictures are now handed on as crystallised traditions ; but the force of their appeal is thereby
strengthened by association of ideas—artistic, emotional or religious. The traditional
forms have thus a significance not merely foreign to any imitative art, but dependent on the
fact that they represent rather race conceptions than the ideas of one person or one period.
They are a vital expression of the race mind ; to reject them, and expect great art to live
on as before, would be to sever the roots of a forest tree and look then for flowers and fruits
to appear upon its branches. And so the goldsmith’s chains are not like real flowers ; but
they mean flowers to himself and to the wearers of them.
The same principles apply to the treatment of birds in jewellery. The bird pendant of
PI. L., I, is pure ornament, without that descriptive character which would be as much out
of place as a didactic motif. To wear a real bird, as this pendant is worn by a Kandyan girl
in PI. II., would be barbarous ; to imitate a real bird very closely in the manner of Lalique
would be idle ; but all that is beautiful in the general idea of a bird, colour, form and poise
can be suggested.
Lastly we have wholly imaginative forms, such as the makara and bherunia used as chain
and pendant motifs. On PI. XLIX., ii, is shown a beautiful makara malaya\ on PI.
XLVIII., 6, a bheruifda pendant.
