CHAPTER XII. LAC-WORK.
1
T he lac-workers, or -vaiuvo, literally arrow-makers, belonged to the lower
division of the acariya, being essentially turners. They generally did both the
wood-turning and the ornamentation necessary for the work expected of them,
such as bows, arrows, spears, staves, bed-legs, handles of cressets, banner poles, etc. Some
idea of their relative numbers may be gathered from the fact above mentioned (p. 55) that
amongst ninety-eight craftsmen forming the Koftal-badda contingent of the Four Korales
4
there were fourteen l-va uva, of whom two worked in the armoury, presumably as assistants
to the regular craftsmen of the pattal hatara.
Ceylon lac* is the product of two species of the lac insects, both different from the Indian.
One called kfppitiya or kcn-lakada {‘Tachardia albizzice. Green) occurs on several trees,
amongst which are the k?ppifiya {Croton aromaticus), kon {Schkicheria trijuga), and hinguru
{Acacia ccesid). The other species {Tachardia conchiferata. Green) is called telakfriya lakada,
and is found on an euphorbaceous plant called telakiriya {Excascaria agallochd); this is a rarer
species, but produces lac of a brighter and clearer quality. Beside these, small quantities
of imported Indian lac are sometimes used.
Lac-work is now carried on in Kandyan districts at Hapuvida (South Matale), Pallekasda,
near Balangocfa, and Hürikatjuva in Pata Dumbara, and in the low-country at Áñgalmaduva,
nearTañgdla.
The Matale work is by far the most distinctive, and may be described in detail, after which»
the Hürikaduva and Añgalmaduva methods will be referred to.
Both types of lac-work differ fundamentally from painting in that brushes are never used ;
in this respect the work differs entirely also from the lacquer varnish work of Japan, with
which it is sometimes compared and confused. Plain lac is, however, occasionally used
as varnish, especially for painted wood (see p. 167, above). The technique differs also
from that of the Maidive Islands, where the lac applied by turning is afterwards incised,
a process also characteristic of the well-known Sindh boxes.
4
The Matale work is called niyapoten v( a or finger-nail work; this name is given because
the work is done chiefly with the finger or thumb nail, and no lathe is employed. The lac
pigments are prepared as follows: the freshly collected twigs bearing the lac insects are
dried in the sun; the resin is then removed, pounded, and winnowed or sifted. The
crushed lac is enclosed in narrow bolster-shaped bags of thin cloth; the bags are heated
over charcoal fires and twisted till the melted lac oozes through the cloth. The lac is
scraped off; a part of it is next softened over a fire and attached to the point of a small stick,
and then again warmed and a second stick attached. The softened lac is then drawn out
between the two sticks, worked about, doubled up, and redrawn many times until it assumes
the form of a long stout ribbon of glistening fibrous lac of a bright golden brown colour.
The pigments are now mixed into the lac by softening it and pounding the coloured
powders into it. The four colours used are red, yellow, green and black; of these the red
is vermilion {sadiliñgam)-, the yellow, orpiment {hiriyal); the green is yellow with the
addition of “dhobies’ blue,” formerly '■ panir (indigo); and the black is prepared in the
same way as the black used in painting.
The lac thus prepared is used for the decoration of a large variety of articles, especially
wooden sticks of various kinds, such as staffs (/ífrá«?//), handles of ceremonial spears, banners,
fans, &c., ceremonial pingos, &c., and also to many other things such as powder horns

Lac-work [ve ibehet karaka), oboes (horan?), book covers (^pot kambi), &c., and it is also used as an
inlay in ivory, horn, and chank work. For the last purpose the ivory is incised with lines
and circles which are filled up with the coloured lac. In the case of turned ivory or horn,
this is effected by holding a piece of lac against it, while revolving on the lathe; the lac,
heated by friction, is softened and fills up the incised grooves. Such ornament in Kandyan
districts is almost invariably confined to incised lines and circles similar to work from
Jodhpur in India*; but flat plates of ivory inlaid with scroll and floral ornament are used
in the fittings of calamander boxes made in the low-country, particularly at Matara, and

instruments still made at Tanjore. Examples of lac-work are illustrated in PI. XXIV., and

Returning to a consideration of the ordinary niyapoten ve a, it will be best to describe the
process in its simplest and commonest form, namely, in the decoration of a staff. The
stick having been shaped and smoothed, the workman squats on the ground, having before-
him a chatty {gii}i kabala) containing a charcoal fire. The lac-worker’s tools consist of
short sticks with a lump of coloured lac at one end of each and a short strip of puskola (talipot
leaf, Corypha umbracultfera). The stick is first coated with the ground colour, usually red.
To effect this, the stick is warmed over the fire and lac applied, which lac is pressed and
smoothed out with the piece of talipot leaf, while still kept warm over the fire; in this way
the whole stick is gradually covered with a coating of red lac. It now remains to add the
tpattern, which may be very elaborate. For this it is needful to draw out the lac into strips
of the desired thinness. To do this, the lump of lac is well warmed, and then, a small piece
being held between finger and thumb, the rest is pulled away, leaving a long thin connecting
thread which is wound round the bent knee, into a skein. After passing four or five times
round the knee the lac becomes cold and must be warmed afresh.
Now to apply a narrow band of coloured lac to the stick, the stick
is warmed gently, while kept continually turning by a small boy
^ ^ who squats behind the operator, and one end of the string of lac is
attached to the stick by pressure, and the rest likewise as the stick
turns; the thread of lac is nipped off by the thumb nail when a
revolution is complete. The stick is then warmed again and
smoothed with the leaf. For more complex patterns (and some
are very elaborate) string lac is applied in just the same way, and
nipped off with the nail;' dots are thus formed by applying the
end of the thread of lac and cutting off a tiny piece with the nail;
such dots are consequently square or diamond-shaj>ed.
The lac-work is usually limited to a small number of good con­
ventional patterns admirably adapted to the nature of the material;

is necessarily not quite so satisfactory. Most of the work, how­

The Ahgalmafiuva and Hurika uva process differs from that above described in that the
lac is applied to the wood while revolving on a turning lathe, the heat of friction softening
the lac and causing it to adhere. This process is more limited, being only applicable to

of the finger-nail process. In fact, the ornamentation can only consist of concentric bands
of colour applied to the different parts of small, usually ricketty, tables, chairs, tom-tom
frames, and walking sticks. The old Kandyan lac-striped round boxes (abhararfa heppu),
bed legs {?nda kakul), betel stands, &c., were handsome and substantial.
Hones {kana If lid) were also made by lac-workers, and consist of lac mixed with powdered
kurmdugala, properly corundun, sometimes garnet.

CHAPTER XIII. EARTHENWARE.
T he rather simple types of earthenware made and used by Sinhalese for ceremonial,
architectural, and domestic purposes are more varied than might at first sight be
supposed, and, apart from any question of painted pottery, will be found to possess
much excellence in respect of beauty of form and adaptation to the end in view. This
last consideration it is which determines the primary form of the vessels. Hardly any
work of a merely ornamental character falls to be considered in the present paper. It is,
however, this primarily utilitarian character and aim which give so much charm to the
elegance of form and very simple decoration which accompany it ; it has been said, indeed,
that ugly pottery can only be made by an exertion of the cultivated intellect, and has only
been so made in comparatively modern times. Much the same is true of India, where
unglazed pottery is everywhere made for domestic and other purposes. Says Sir George
Bird wood : “Truest to nature in the directness and simplicity of its forms, and their adapta­
tion to use, and purest in art, of all its homely and sumptuary handicrafts, is the pottery of
India, and the forms of it shown on ancient Buddhist and Hindu sculptures, and the ancient
Buddhist paintings of Ajanta, are identical with those still everywhere thrown from the
village hand-wheels.” We do not, however, find in Ceylon the more elaborate types of
glazed pottery made in some parts of India ; but it will be found that Sinhalese pottery
fulfils the requirements of good workmanship in earthenware; viz., first, the vessel must
be of a shape convenient for its purpose; secondly, that shape must be one that arises
naturally from the mode of manufacture and exhibits to advantage the plastic properties of
clay, without becoming weak or fanciful ; thirdly, ornament should not interfere with
usefulness and should be appropriate in amount and character in relation to the purpose
of the vessel and the material it is made of ; fourthly, smoothness of surface and elaborate
refinements (however good in their right place) are not to be thought of as ends in them­
selves, and may appear unsuitable if striven for in vessels meant for ordinary daily use and
made of a material not over fine. Nevertheless, the application of some simple glaze would
not be out of place, and it is perhaps rather strange that it is never met with in Ceylon.*
The Sinhalese potters {baiahçlayo') are found all over the country in every village affording
the necessary clay, but often aggregated in greater numbers in places where an especially
good supply of suitable clay is available. Thence the potter carries his pots for sale to
more remote districts in huge pingo loads. Nowadays a good deal of pottery is taken in
carts along the cart roads ; in this way the fine red pots made by a settlement of Tamils at
Nikapata near Haputale travel down the road to Balangocja, and the Kelani pots with their
white incised patterns come up to Ratnapura and Kegalla and even Kandy. Some pottery
is also imported from Southern India.
The general duties of potters have been enumerated on p. 25, above. Like other craftsmen,
potters held land either directly from the Crown, from the proprietor of a nindagama or
the grantee of a royal village, or from a vihara or dévale. Every manor had not only its
smith to make and mend the tools of the grantee, a washer to wash the clothes, and other
service tenants, but also a potter, ‘ to fit them with Earthen Ware.’ He, like other tenants,
supplied the king or lord with earthenware as service rent, but was paid for work done for

The potter may be found at work in the verandah of his house, or sometimes in a separate
sh ed wholly devoted to the work. His appliances are, as may be supposed, simple enough.
His wheel {poruva) is a circular board about 2| feet in diameter mounted on a stone pivot
which fits into a larger stone socket embedded in the ground, the horizontal surface of
the wheel itself standing not more than six inches above the ground (Fig. 134). The
wheel is turned by a boy (PI. V., i) who squats on the ground opposite the potter and keeps

plan, and has three or four openings along one side for the insertion of fuel, and on the other
sides smaller openings for the escape of air. Long sticks are used for fuel, pushed through
the openings by degrees as they burn away. The kiln is usually protected from the weather
by a rough shed.
The clay used is alluvial material such as is obtainable in most valley rice fields. The
best kind is very dark and stiff ; the colour after firing varies from a fine terracotta red to a
rather unpleasant yellowish gray.

Beside the above-mentioned four types there are other vessels, of which the nsmbiliya Earthen-
(= nambu + heljyd) is the most important. This is a shallow dish with a rim projecting ware ;
inwards and completely covered inside with an elegant arrangement of deep furrowings
(PL XXV., lo). These are scored before firing by means of a rough wooden comb Nembiliya
iirigahana katuva), a process illustrated in PI. V., 4. The rtfmbiliya is used for washing rice
to remove stones and dirt, very much as a gemming basket is used to separate the heavier
gem minerals from the common lighter constituents of the gravel. The fragments of grit,
&c., remain behind in the grooves of the nfmbiliya, or are held back by its inwardly pro­
jecting rim, as the rice is stirred up in the water and gently poured over the edge; this
vessel is in daily use in every household. A similar vessel made to stand by the addition
of a ring foot is called a koraha; the ring foot is not made in one piece with the rest of
the vessel, but is added after the completion of the underside of the vessel as if for a
nsmbiliya ; this vessel in this stage is inverted on the wheel and the ring of fresh clay added
to form a foot.
A more typical koraha, however, is the larger type sometimes called polkoraha and shown Koraha
on PI. XXV., 7. These large pots are used for various general purposes, but especially
by dhobies for washing clothes, and by mothers for washing their children. A vil-koraha
is a large vessel used for soaking seed paddy.
A shallow dish with a ring foot (thus resembling the smaller type of koraha, but without
internal furrowing) is sometimes used for eating rice from, and is called a batvalanda.
A vessel rarely seen is the psrnuva, or oven (PI. XXV., 6), a large three-legged affair with a Pornuva
big lid ; the interior is half filled with sand, and the oven is said to be very efficient; the
sand (as in the “sand bath” of the chemical laboratory) both retains the heat and preserves
an even temperature.
Large wide-mouthed vessels with lids, formerly used for storing cloths and garments, are Pilt-heliya
called pili-hfliya (PI. LII., 4), or if smaller halu-h(liya. Clothes in such vessels were better
protected from white ants than if stored in wooden boxes.
The name kalaha (kal,asa, kalayd), equivalent to Sanskrit kalasa, is strictly applicable to all Kalaha
vessels with only one opening, especially those of the kalagediya type; but it is more
specially applied to a kind of vase open at both ends, but otherwise resembling a kalageiiya
with an extended neck (PI. XXVI., 12), and used for holding sprays of coconut flower on
auspicious and ceremonial occasions (weddings, mahgalya, &c.) a pair being placed on the
two sides of the doorway, or as lamp stands, especially at festivals.
A taliya is a large wide-mouthed vessel similar to a patra. A pin-taliya is such a vessel of 'T'aliya
water set by the wayside for the use of travellers. Such vessels are to be seen everywhere,
usually supported in a forked branch, often roofed over. The vessel has usually a wooden
lid, and a ladle {kinissa). It is not customary in the East to apply the lips to the rim of such
a common drinking vessel, but the water is poured from the bowl of the ladle (or from
the spout of a kotalayd) into the hollow of the left hand held against the mouth. This
admirable sanitary precaution might with advantage be adopted in the West.

domestic pottery is thus exhausted. It will be seen that it faithfully reflects the simplicity
and lack of luxury characterizing the typical old-fashioned household. The vessels are
few, and each serves some simple purpose for which it is specially adapted. The ordinary
price of a kalageiiya is about 20 to 25 cents, of a nlmbiliya 6 to 15 cents, of a koraha 25
to 50 cents. The value of this rough earthenware is thus so small that breakages are not of
very serious consequence. Pieces of earthenware may remain in use for many years, and
are occasionally even found to be mended. On the other hand, Davy stated that there
was an ‘extraordinarily great’ consumption of earthenware amongst the Sinhalese inasmuch
as “ after a feast at which people of different castes have been entertained, all the earthen­
ware vessels used on the occasion are destroyed.-f”
Ecclesias- The vessels used especially in connection with viharas and dëvàles may be spoken of
tical collectively as ecclesiastical earthenware. Of these vessels the most common and most
characteristic is the kotalaya ; this is a spouted vessel for holding the water with which
flower offerings are sprinkled. Either an earthen or a bronze kotalaya may be found in

the case of a kotalaya of the common form, but closed above, and then yatura kotalaya,
‘secret jug.’
Very large wide-mouthed earthen vessels called patra are found in most viharas and are
used to hold water or to receive offerings of rice, &c., from worshippers. A very fine
painted example is to be seen at Dodantale Vihâra, but most specimens are plain or with
very simple decoration of simple lines or of ¿ff-leaves in red. Besides the big patras used
in viharas, smaller earthen alms-bowls are made, though the alms-bowls actually used by
priests are usually metal. Some potters (at Kelaijiya) make an alms-bowl for presentation
to a priest, with every batch of pots turned out. Earthen incense burners \dummala kabal) ,
often of very elegant form and skilful execution, are used in dévales and viharas, the incense
(powdered dummala resin) is sprinkled on burning charcoal carried on the dummala kabala.
Two of these incense burners are shown on PI. XXVI., 4 and 5.

Earthen-: used also for ridge or coping tiles. These semi-cylindrical tiles are leis characteristic than

The new-fashioned Basel Mission and Mangalore tiles are perhaps slightly more convenient,
especially in respect of leakage, but of course far less cool ; in addition to which their rigid
form and mechanical effect are distinctly unpleasant. Instead of the slight curves and
irregularities of a roof covered with ordinary tiles, we see what is practically a plane surface
crossed by strictly parallel lines which are wearisome and uninteresting. The ordinary
tiles if well burnt and well laid are much to be preferred in respect of appearance and
comfort ; though requiring slightly more attention, for in the services due to temples we
see regular provision made for the annual shifting of tiles.

Kandyan eaves-tiles, ¿¡j-leaf form, decorated The addition of ornament on the
with simha (A) and harrisa (B). A., Length 15I inches. reverse is more difficult. The
B., length about 8| inches. figure, usually a hanisa, is prepared ,
in the same way by pressing soft
clay into a suitable mould, but instead of the whole tile being so pressed against the mould,
only the actual animal form is made, and when this is lifted off the mould it is applied to
the back of the tile (the obverse of which has already been ornamented). The result of ,
this pressing of both animal forms into hollow moulds is that when they are applied together
back to back on the obverse and reverse of the tile there remains a hollow space within
the tile, and between the two animal shells. It is usual to pierce a small round hole on the
animal’s body on the reverse side to admit of the escape of heated air when the tile is fired.
The decorated tiles so made stand out in high relief, and show up well in brilliant sunshine.
A simpler method results in the production of similarly decorated tiles with less relief.
This result is attained by merely pressing the clay tile between the two wooden moulds.
It is obvious that equally high relief cannot be obtained in this way, as there is no way of
pressing the clay into the hollows of a deep mould.

In describing the ordinary methods of ornamenting earthen vessels, I refer only to such Ornament
decoration as is applied before firing. What is ordinarily known as ‘painted Kandyan
pottery’ is painted with oil colours (formerly with water colour varnished) after the pots are
fired, and this work will not be referred to in the present section. Leaving that oil-painted
pottery aside, the decoration of pottery may be classed as incised, stamped, and slip-painted.
Thfe'simplest form of slip-painting is the application of concentric bands of red, to apply
which the vessel is inverted on the wheel, which is revolved slowly while the brush is held
against it (see PI. V., 3, where a kalage^iya is being thus treated). The red paint is made
by grinding up with water certain ferruginous nodules and concretions called gurugal, while
white paint is similarly made from kaolin. Beside the plain stripes, simple geometrical
ornaments in red or white is sometimes seen, as on the porijuva (PI. XXV., 6). Black
stripes are sometimes done with graphite.
Incised ornament, if more than a mere concentric line, is usually combined with the red Incised
.striped painting. The pot is allowed to get very hard and dry and the pattern then engraved Ornament
on the red bands with a sharp tool. PI. XXV., 2, shows a kalage^iya so treated. This vessel
is ornamented with alternate concentric stripes of red and gray; the incised ornament
(Fig. 137, a) is cut on the red bands, of which the uppermost has geometrical forms only.

The general subject of painted pottery lies somewhat outside the scope of the present Painted
chapter; for the painting is of the same character as that applied to book covers, woodwork, pottery
and other objects, and is applied to earthenware only after it has left the potter’s hands,
q 2 227

Earthen- The best work has been done in the Kandy District, but comparatively little of real delicacy
<ware is now met with, while a great deal of careless gaudy stuff is to be seen. Tall classical
amphors*, too, are now largely made and painted, usually very badly, and considering their
Painted exotic form and poor decoration are not very pleasing.
pottery The only colours properly used in painting pottery are red, yellow, white, and black, i.e.,
the ordinary pigments of the Kandyan painter. The designs and decoration are also
identical with those found in other paintings, so that there is no need to describe them in
further detail upon the present occasion.
c©kThe subject of Sinhalese (especially Kandyan) pottery has now been reviewed in some
detail, although there are many points on which fuller information would be desirable.
A full account of early types of earthenware found at Sigiri, Anuradhapura, and elsewhere
would be of great value and interest. It is also possible that I have overlooked some forms
of earthenware to be found in other districts than those (chiefly Sabaragamuva and the
Central Province) which I have especially studied. I have found, however, that once a
familiarity with the typical forms had been obtained, I scarcely ever met with aberrant
or unusual forms ; in other words there is great fixity of type, and we do not find individual
potters experimenting on their own account, probably because the fixed types exactly fulfil
the purposes for which they were required, and it would not occur to the potter to work
for mere amusement or for the production of beautiful forms apart from practical ends.
Nor was the material available, or the potter’s skill sufficient, to so interest the leisured
or more wealthy classes as to lead to a demand for decorative pottery considered apart from
ordinary household requirements.
The most elaborate earthenware we meet with is made for use in connection with religious
buildings, for the needs of which the king or other rich patrons were willing to secure the
services of all the best workmen, or for which the potter was willing to work unpaid, or
to which he had to supply earthenware as a service rent.
The art of pottery has degenerated far less than the other Sinhalese industrial arts, and
though there is nowadays little demand for good work in decorated finials, imposing lamp-
stands or moulded eaves-tiles, the potter’s ordinary wares have not changed much, either
lately, or probably even for a very long time. We may congratulate ourselves then that
Sinhalese pottery has so far degenerated very little; this is mainly because it is so cheap
and so intimately adapted to local requirements as not to invite the competition of imported
machine-made wares. Unfortunately, however, the kerosine tin has made some progress,
and is commonly seen in use instead of a kalage^iya. This is pitiful, but less fatal than a
degeneration of form in the kalagediya itself. The growing use of Basel Mission and
Mangalore tiles is more to be regretted, no less on the score of comfort than of appearance ;
an ancient building re-covered with such tiles, perhaps subscribed for at considerable cost
by poor village contributors to some vihara funds, is robbed of most of its distinctive
character. Is it too much to ask those concerned to take a little trouble and exercise some
thought in dealing with such buildings ? Now that the old sumptuary laws forbidding
tiled roofs to any but Disavas are no longer in force, the builder of a new house might even,
ifhe cared to do so,make it beautiful by giving due consideration to its roof. Unfortunately,
the elements of beauty or dignity, which may enter into even such homely matters, are the
last which are likely to influence him; and at the same time the capacity for good work
in making and laying tiles is dying out, so that it is increasingly difficult to get it, and a
majority of persons are scarcely aware that good work ever was done, or can recognize it
when they see it.

APPENDIX TO CHAPTER XIII. POTTER’S
SONG.
The following is the translation of a very interesting craft song, the text of which was
kindly forwarded to me by Mr. S. D. Mahavalatenna:
1.
Waking before the dawn, carrying the basket, (the potter) fares to the place-of-clay ;
After cleaning the basket and clearing the place-of-clay, he worships his guardian god;
Wearing (only) a loin cloth, and gladly taking (the basket) in hand he goes down into the pit;
Not breaking down the two sides (of the pit) he digs the clay from the middle and fills
the basket.
2.
Breaking up the clay, he takes a yoke-load and heaps it in the potter’s yard ;
Separating the pieces of clay he breaks them to an equal size and spreads them on a big mat
in the sun;
After having dried the clay, and removed the stones, he pounds it in a mortar and in a
kulla winnows it;
Then taking up the powder, he adds an equal quantity of water and makes it into balls.

The following are some Sinhalese proverbs connected with pottery:
“The devil broke the koraha as he went away” (Eng. ‘The cat did it’).
“ Six months’ labour of the potter, is one stroke to the man with the cudgel.”
“A pot filled to the brim does not shake.”
“ The water in a half-filled pot shakes.”
“When an elephant gets thin, it cannot be bathed in a koraha."

CHAPTER XIV. WEAVING.
WE have seen above (p. 54) that there were two groups of weavers in Sinhalese
Ceylon, the saldgamayo from Southern India, who made fine and gold-woven
cloths, and the beravsyo, or caste of indigenous weavers, who were also
musicians, astrologers, etc. The history of the salagamays, or ‘ chalias,’ is briefly as follows;
Vijaya Bahu III. of Daajbadeijiya, to revive the art of weaving fine cloth, sent letters and
presents by a Muhammadan Tamil named Pati Mira Lebbe to Southern India; and he
brought back eight master weavers, and these were given villages, wives and honours by
the king. Their descendants incurred the disfavour of the Kandyan kings, and were
ultimately compelled to leave the interior, and settle on the south-west coast, where they
were allowed to occupy royal lands where cinnamon grew, on condition of peeling and
preparing the same for the requirements of the king. They came thus to be cinnamon-
peelers by trade, and were employed as such by the Portuguese and Dutch.
The Janavaipsa records many previous importations of Indian weavers *; but in every
case the industry decayed, and fresh blood had to be imported. With the detailed history
of these weavers we are not here concerned, as they seem never to have become an integral
part of the Sinhalese population as the imported Indian smiths have done.
The indigenous weavers, the beravays, on the other hand have probably made their plainer,
homespun cottons, much as they are still made in one Kandyan village, from time
immemorial, unaffected by changes of fashion at court or the influence of Indian weavers.-^
With their work the descriptions given in this chapter, and the pictures in the Plates,
are exclusively concerned.
The weaving of homespun cotton cloths was once universal in the Kandyan provinces. It
is now done only at Talaguije, Uda Dumbara, and perhaps occasionally near Vellassa in
Uva; and not long ago near Balango^a also. Remains of looms, ginning machines and
other accessories may be met with in other districts. At Talaguije the industry still
flourishes a little; two families have looms, and a number of the village women are skilled
in spinning. The villagers themselves still use some of the cloth made, but the industry
would hardly survive were it not for the demand for ftirili made through the Kandy Art
Association.
The weavers, as we have seen (p. 25, 26), were of low caste, and had other duties to perform
beside weaving. Their annual petfuma consisted of a taiuppu cloth or a lensuva or similar
piece of woven cloth. I have not been able to find any mention of cloths given as a regular
service rent, but this must have been quite usual; service at the loom was called al-gi
rnjakariya.

of whole pieces of cloth as woven on the loom; hence the necessity for making cloths of
different shapes and sizes. The following different kinds of cloth were made: napkins

Of these cloths, some may be more particularly described. A tuppotiya is a white cloth, Tuppotiya
eight or nine cubits long, made in two pieces neatly joined up the middle; single widths
are calledit, and measure six or seven cubits in length, and four to six spans in breadth,

wear narrow cloths. Women of low caste were obliged to substitute for the ohoriya, or the
skirt and bodice, of the higher castes, two short cloths, one to be wrapped round the loins,
and the other to be thrown over the shoulder.
Pieces of blue cloth were called kalu kdftgan; they were sometimes as much as twenty or Plain cloth
thirty cubits long, and used as hangings on occasions of mourning; the material was also

indeed) only the three colours, red, white, and blue are found even in the most ornamental
woven cloths. The other cloths mentioned are usually woven in pattern work. The
ftirilla is the equivalent of the Indian dart, and serves the same purposes, though thinner,
and less often used as a mat. The greater part of the cloths made now at Talaguije are

Diya kacci are undergarments or drawers made in one piece, having a large apron to hang Piya
down in front, a narrower flap with less ornament behind and a woven tape to tie round the kacciya
waist. They formed the most essential undergarment of old Kandyans, and were also a
bathing or running costume; diya kacci were worn also by watchmen and messengers ; on
PI. V. will be found a photograph of a Sinhalese man dressed as a watchman or guard
{murakdrayd), showing the manner of wearing the diya kacciya. Some of these garments
are quite plain, others most elaborately ornamented. Diya kacci are said to have been made
on special looms with double heddles {alu-vel). Such looms were called afa-vel-aluva.
There can be no doubt that special small looms were also used for making braids. The belt
i^papya) of a diya kacciya was sometimes made in one piece with the rest. Diya kacci so cut
as to be much narrower behind than in front were called pat kapapu (leaf cut). Diya kacci
are from five to six feet in full length, the apron averaging about one and a half by two feet.
Gahoni are bell-shaped or skirt-shaped cloths used to cover baskets or pots of food or other Gahoniya
offerings when carried on a yoke along the road for the king or any temple. The effect is
th at of a small three-flounced skirt, each flounce with a pattern border (PI. XXIX., 6).
The ‘skirt’ is really made of a single straight piece of cloth, joined up with one seam and
left open at both ends; one end is turned over and gathered in upon a string, thus forming
the waist and two of the flounces, and the third flounce is a separate piece of cloth sewn
on between the two others. A wall painting at Degaldoruva (about 1786) shows a yoke
[kada) and pair of gahsni suspended from a post in the royal kitchen. Every day the
country people brought in such tribute of food, betel, sweetmeats, etc., to the king, the
chief, or temple where their service was due ; as, for instance, when bringing first fruits
{alutsdl) from the temple lands to the temple or pansala. Even nowadays men may be

The loom So much for homespun cottons; the manner of their weaving is as follows t' ^he loom
(aluvd) and the manner of working it are identical in all essentials with the looms and
methods in use all over India and Burma. It is set up in an open shed (al-ge% sometimes
used as a name for the loom itself), on a platform {al-ptla) continuous with the outer
verandah {pila) of the weaver’s house, in one room of which are stored all materials and
accessories. A reference to the pictures will explain the general appearance of the loom,
and the manner of working it. For plain cloth, all that is needed is to throw the shuttle
(nadavd) to and fro, while alternate threads of the warp (nal-heda) are separated by the
heddles [alúcela; or aluva* the essential part of the mechanism, the loom itself) these are
moved by pedals [pa-medumd) of coconut shell {pol-katuva) which hang down into a hole
(al-vald) beneath the loom, in which hole the weaver’s feet move up and down. The
heddles are attached to narrow slips of wood {alu-kampaha), resembling the beam of a scale,
and these are suspended by the middle (about which they move) to a beam above. In
the Sinhalese looms which I have seen, only two heddles are employed, to separate alternate
warp threads; it is said that more were sometimes used formerly. The weft is pressed home
by a sleay or reed-frame, suspended like the heddles from a beam above. The sleay {rodu
Iplld) consists of three parts, the upper piece [poruvata) held by the weaver, the lower piece
{yatfinan gal l^lla) below the web, and the teeth [a¡u-karala), thin slips of cane, through
which the warp threads pass.
Patterns To make geometrical patterns, the necessary warp threads are picked up (PI. VI., 1) with
a narrow lath or weaver’s sword {sfma l(lla), and a wider lath is then inserted and turned up
sideways so as to form a ‘shed’ for the passage of the shuttle. Before the sword is pulled
out again, slips of cane are passed between the separated warp threads behind the heddles;
there they accumulate and preserve the pattern, as seen on PI. XXIX., i, making it easy
to pick up the threads again when the pattern is repeated or reversed.

names which I have obtained are pannan küra, hln ratava, maha ratava, gal-piyum, doniba

Irregular patterns such as birds, cobras, ¿ff-leaves and large flowers are put in by hand work
(atev^id), i.e., tapestry. The whole is thus a combination of weaving and tapestry.
As the work progresses it is wound by quarter turns on a square cloth-beam {pn-kandd) next
the weaver, the tension of the warp being regulated by a cord which passes round a post
{man-kanuva) at the remote end of it, and thence to the weaver’s right hand, near which it
is fastened. This rope is passed through a bird-shaped block [‘kurulla’), between the post
and the web ; this wooden bird bobs up and down while the work is going on. There is
no thread-beam, only a rod on which the warp threads are strung, so that the warp must be
stretched out at full length while work is going on (PI. XXIX., i). The web is kept tightly
stretched at the near end by an arrangement of two crossed canes {kaiumal-hedd), of which
the two ends next the weaver are connected by a tight thread, and the other two have pin
points which pass into the web and keep it stretched; moveahle thread loops regulate the
tension. The warp is supported at a point not far behind the heddles, by a horizontal bar,
called alkatiuve lella. A cloth fresh from the loom is called alvala redda.
We may now turn to the preparation of the thread and laying of the warp. Cotton was
extensively grown on hen (‘chenas’) or dry fields in Kandyan districts, so much that cotton
yarn could be traded thence to Anuradhapura and those parts where cotton was not so much
grown; as we gather from Knox, who himself traded in cotton yarn, on the occasion of his
escape. The cotton is of two sorts, a large kind which lasts several years, and a dwarf,
annual sort (bala kapu).
An interesting tale of a cotton field is related in the Ummagga Jataka, in a Sinhalese prose Ummagga
version of the early fourteenth century; it is a rather charming picture of a little village Jataka
episode. A certain woman, watching in a cotton field, had spun some cotton into fine
thread, and made a ball of it. On her way home she bathed in a certain tank, leaving the
ball of cotton with her cloth on the bank. Another woman took it up as if only to admire
it, hut walked off with it altogether. The first woman followed, and as they passed by a
certain pandit’s hall, quarrelling, he sent for them. They agreed to abide by his decision.
He asked one, around what she had rolled the thread, to which she replied that she had
rolled it round a cotton seed; the real owner replied to the same question, that she had
rolled it round a timbiri seed; and when the ball was unrolled, such was found to be the
case, and so the thief was discovered. The judgment of a Solomon.
The cotton is not usually, however, spun in the field, but taken home and dried and cleaned Tarn
in larger quantities. It is freed from seeds by passing through the rollers of a small machine
(kapu kapana yantrayd) resembling a mangle (PI. XXIX., 3). It is next carded by whipping
with a bow (pulun-talanavd), and lightly rolled into tufts ready for spinning from. The
action of spinning is a charming and graceful one; it is woman’s work, but weaving is
done by men and women alike. A tuft of cotton is held in the left hand, and thread spun
from it on to a long weighted spindle (idda), the end of which rests in a pod or coconut shell
on the ground; it is kept turning by the motion of the right hand against the thigh, or by
the fingers (PI. VI., 3); the thread winds itself round the big end.
It is very usual for a number of women to meet together for a spinning bee, when the work
is done to the accompaniment of songs, those most favoured being Vessantara, Magamana
and Vidhura Jatakas, YasOdharavata, Mara Yuddhaya, and Maha-hhinishkramaijaya, all
religious songs.
The thread so spun is unwound on to a conical reel (hulu d^d) of split bamboo, thence on
to another large reel (madavd) made of bamhoo and string (Fig. 140) and thence on to
a bobbin (Jiarassald), ready to be laid in the shuttles. The winding on to bobbins is accom-

plished with the aid of a winding machine (harassal ambarana

rod carrying the bobbin; when'the wheel is turned, the bobbin
revolves rapidly, and the reel is discharged on to it.
Laying the So much for the weft thread. That required for the warp is wound
•warp off the bamboo and string reel directly, to form a skein. This skein
is laid (process called dig-gahanavd) on a temporary frame of sticks,
and is the length of the warp required. The weaver walks up and
down along this framework, disposing the thread upon it with the
aid of a little forked stick (/«</« kulé). When completed, the skeins
Fig. 140. Madava, are lifted off, and rods passed through the ends, the whole laid
spool for reeling horizontally a couple of feet above the ground, and kept on the
cotton. stretch by strings attaching the rods to posts at each end. Strung
bows [h(t-li) are passed through the warp, to prevent tangling and to
preserve the lease or plane in which it lies. The warp is next well
sized on both sides with a starchy decoction (process called nul velanavd), after which
the threads are well brushed, and then carefully separated and arranged (process called
palal lanavd). The number of threads, of course, depends upon the width of cloth required.
Ordinarily, 120 threads are reckoned to the span. When finally dry, the warp is lifted
up and re-adjusted on the loom itself, the cloth beam of which has a groove into which is
laid the rod carrying the warp, which is held tightly when a turn is given to the beam.
The most troublesome part of the process is passing the threads through the heddles and
reed, for which purpose they have to be broken one by one, and rejoined after being
threaded through the loops and teeth. The length of the warp is often made sufficient for
two cloths in order to reduce this labour.
Kafhina Spinning, but not weaving, was sometimes done by women of high caste. A particularly
robes meritorious act is held to be the presentation to the Sañgha, at the close of Vas or Buddhist
Lent, of kafhina robes, i.e., priests’ robes, spun, woven, and made up in a single day. Even
kings frequently performed this ceremony, “employing hundreds of thousands of persons in
all such work as picking the cotton, after it is extracted from the fruit, weighing, converting
it into balls, spinning, weaving, washing, cutting into pieces, stitching, dyeing” (Rtlpa-
valiya, trans., p. 48). Thus on a certain occasion, Parakrama Bahu II. offered no less than
eighty such robes to the priesthood, in memory of the eighty chief disciples of the Buddha.
“The learned king gathered together the inhabitants of Lanka—a great multitude of men
and women— and set them all to work to prepare the cotton and other things, and speedily
finished the work of the robes. And he caused the eighty kafhina robes to be given in the
course of a single day” (Mahavaipsa, Ch. LXXXV.) And so he did on many other
occasions, nor was he alone in this practice. Private individuals acquired merit in the
same way; and it was on such occasions that the ladies of the household lent a hand in
spinning.
No yarn is now dyed locally, except occasionally with an aniline green. It seems, however,
natural to suppose that the red and blue dyeing, with madder and indigo, used to be done
by the weavers themselves, but evidence to that effect is very scanty. Nowadays, the red
and blue yarn are purchased in Batticaloa, where they are imported from India for use by
the Tamil weavers there. The blue has been difficult to obtain lately and black has been,
substituted, but the effect is not nearly as good. Good blue yarn is obtainable in Jaffna,
and I lately supplied a quantity of this to the Talagupe weavers. For further remarks on-
dyeing see Chapter XVI.

CHAPTER XV. EMBROIDERY.
Em broidery ¡s one of the least known of Sinhalese crafts, or at least remained
so until the publication of an account written by Mrs. Coomaraswamy in the
“Ceylon National Review,” No. 2, 1906. “This,” says Mrs. Coomaraswamy,
“is how I first came to hear of such embroidery. I was staying at Haldummulla ; we had
a visit from an ex-Àracci of a neighbouring village, who brought with him some of his
household treasures to show us. Among them was a large bag, made of fine blue cloth
with embroidered work on it in red and white cotton. He explained this was a precious
possession which no money would make him part with, and that it had been in his family
for generations. This was my first experience of this kind of work and I thereupon made
up my mind to get to know more about it. Some months after this I saw another bag,
and then found out that although this kind of work is now almost unknown, yet here and
there in out of the way villages old men can be found who know the stitches, although they
have almost given up making anything now. Many other things I also found out— how
that it is owing to modern conditions of life that this fine art has fallen into decay; that
now, even if people would work at it, they cannot ; the cloth cannot be got, the colours
cannot be got, the cottons cannot be bought, and the things that used to be made have gone
out of fashion. The cotton was grown by the people themselves, they used to dye it with
home-made dyes, and weave it into the cloth they wanted. Now all this is past ; the fine
blue hand-made cotton cloth that used to be universal, is now to be obtained only with the
greatest difficulty, if at all. It is no longer made and dyed by the Sinhalese themselves.”
There seem to have been, as in the case of weaving, two classes of work done, the first
limited in amount, for the Court and aristocracy, and Indian in style, the second more
strictly indigenous. The hannali, or tailors proper, were few in number, and held lands
in respect of which it was their duty to make “ the splendid and barbarous dresses of the
king and his court” (Davy). As tenants of dévales and viharas they had to prepare sacred
vestments, curtains, flags, etc., and to assist in decorating the car. As tenants of lay proprie­
tors, they had to make up the pacca hçftaya (brocade jacket), gold embroidered toppiya
(square hat of the chieftain), and to embroider jackets for the wives and daughters. The
materials used by such tailors were largely of Indian origin, as red felt, velvet, tinsel, the
brocades used for jackets, or the gold thread for embroidering hats and ceremonial fans.
The chief examples of the more elaborate ‘tailor-made’ embroidery now met with, are
hats and ceremonial fans {sesat). Mr. A. Ratvatte has a four-cornered toppiya worn by
Migastenna Adigàr, made of red velvet, with gold passing. On PI. XLL, 2, is illustrated
a similarly embroidered large sesata or processional ‘ banner ’ or ‘ fan ’ from the Maha Dévale,
Kandy. The basis is red velvet, with gold and silver thread passed over cords, and applique
of green velvet in enclosed areas. The reverse is of blue velvet, with sun, moon and stars
in metal. Diameter 34 inches.
The more purely Sinhalese embroidery, corresponding to the homespun cotton manutacture,
and executed in the home-made materials, appear to have been done mainly by the dhobies
{radav, washermen) who had charge of all matters connected with cotton cloth, not merely
its washing, but also the ‘getting up’ of Kandyan hats, preparation of decorations {rçH-

some of the old stitches, and who make small betel-bags out of such materials as they can

Materials The materials used were the white, blue, and red cotton cloth made in the villages, and
cotton thread of the same colours, also very rarely a small amount of coloured silk. The
most characteristic work is entirely executed in the blue, red, and white cottons.
Tilings em­ The embroidered objects most often seen are betel-bags (bulat-payi) of all sizes ; less common
broidered are kerchiefs or napkins (Jensu), caps [ispay), jackets {hettd), pillow cases {koffa ura),
pacisi cloths, saddle cloths {palas). The betel-bags (Pis. XXX.— XXIII.) vary in size
from small ones carried in the waist belt, to very large ones, four feet or more in length.
The latter were carried by a servant in processions or on journeys, slung over the shoulder.
Noblemen were never without an attendant carrying their betel-bag (see above, pp. 33, 34)
and lime-box ; less important personages carried their own. The large bags are exactly
the same in construction as the small ones— a bag of oval shape made of blue cloth lined
with undyed cotton cloth, which opens nearly half way down the whole length at the sides ;
the inner part is separated into two divisions. The inner division, again consisting of .a
double piece of cloth, is also used as a pocket, called horapayiya,'-hiààen pocket' ; it has a
very small opening at the upper end, through which spices, money and other valuables
are put. Larger things were carried in the two outer pockets. The handle is made of
embroidered cloth, or of a band of plaited cord, and is finished off at the end with a beauti­
fully and ingeniously worked, and very hard, ball (vsge^i-borale) and tassel {pohottuvd). The
outside of the bag is embroidered on both sides in red and white cotton with conventional
designs, sometimes very elaborately. Bags of later make are often done in red cloth,
probably because the blue hand-made cloth could no longer be obtained ; some of these
are equally good, the tradition both in design and stitches being for some time well main­
tained. Few or no good bags are now made, partly owing to the lack of proper materials.
One of the most perfect small bags I have seen was of red hand-made cloth embroidered
entirely with silk, the use of which is very exceptional. I have referred to the plaited cord
of which the handles are sometimes made ; for this, cotton cord of two colours is plaited
into a thick stout flat braid which is very handsome and durable. It may be mentioned
that similar plaited cord strings, but round, of two or three colours are made by priests
for ola book strings {pot-lam).
The embroidery of bags consists generally of a centre design, floral or otherwise, framed
by three or more borders parallel to the edge of the bag. Of these borders the innermost
4
is almost always pala peti, the largest liya-Vfla, the others a variety of hava iya or gal-bmdu
pattern. A limited amount of coloured silk is sometimes used ; the small bag of PI. XXX., i,
is exceptional in having embroidery entirely in silk. It may be noted that silk is frequently
mentioned in the Mahavarfisa, but never with any suggestion of its being an indigenous
product. The edges of bags are either bound with woven braid, which was made in a great
variety of designs, or stitched over with the peculiar ‘centipede’ binding stitch described
below.

consisting of four cords instead of the two of oval bags.

Jackets worn by devil-dancers in Sabaragamuva and the low country are often well em­
broidered, either with thread in the style of the betel-bags, or with appliqué. On
PI. XXIII., 1-3, are illustrated a fine embroidered dancer’s jacket, the ‘ Gard-yakshaya’*
costume. This consists of a red hand-made cotton cloth skirt and jacket, the skirt with
three flounces. The jacket fastens behind. The whole is covered with very elaborate
blue and white cotton appliqué embroidery, the edge of the applied cloth being turned in
and sewn with white cotton. The design on the chest (‘flower in vase’) might almost be
called ‘braided,’ as it is executed by sewing down very narrow strips of applied cloth
following the pattern. In the photograph the blue appliqué hardly shows, but follows
the white outline just inside it.
Appliqué work is also found on a larger scale, on flags and pillow cases. Appliqué flags
are not often well made, and may represent an attempt to find a substitute for the more
satisfactory dye-painted flags formerly used. The embroidered flags done for the Kandy
Art Association recently, have been of very poor workmanship.
Very few pillow cases {koffa ura) have remained to us, but those that have are generally of Pillowcases
one type— a centre piece of blue cloth, embroidered with a design, and a border three or
four inches wide, of a patchwork of red, white, and blue squares of cotton cloth. Probably
an earlier type was one with an embroidered border instead of the patchwork, just as the
later type is thé kind completely made of patchwork ; but I have never seen one. But as
we find woven pillow cases of the same shape and size with patterns all over, it is very
probable that the better examples used to be embroidered all over.
A saddle cloth {palasa) in red cloth, embroidered in white and blue cotton, was exhibited by
Nikaveva Disava at the Exhibition of Kandyan Art in January, 1906.
The only embroidered caps met with, are those known as ispayya (PI. XXX., 3). These are Caps
the “Countrey Caps” described by Knox as resembling mitres (p. 34, above). The flaps are
thinly quilted, and the cap finely embroidered in coloured silks. There is one of these caps
in the Kandy Museum ; the one illustrated was lent by Mr. T. B. Kçppitipola.
‘On occasions of ceremony,’ says Davy, ‘when full dressed, the men cover the body with a
short jacket; and those who have the privilege, lay aside the handkerchief for a capi and
dec orate themselves with gold chains and girdles.’

Embroidery alternately in blue and red. The flowers of the outer border are red, with a gold centre;
the leaves outlined blue. The shawl appears to consist of linen. Smaller kerchiefs or
napkins are not so rare (Pis. XXVIII., 2, 3, and XXXIII., 4, 5); there are at the Maligava
a considerable number, ranging in size from 13 to 24 inches square. They are embroidered
in red and blue. The material is usually cotton, occasionally linen. Fine drawn thread-
work resembling lace is sometimes found, and round the outer edge there is sometimes
a fringe of needlework ‘lace’ (PI. XXVIII., 2 and 3). Very characteristic of these napkins
is a peculiar style of embroidery in which both sides are made exactly alike (as in certain
types of Kashmir shawl). The effect is evidently obtained by working in even stitches
equal on back and front, with spaces between, which are afterwards filled when going over
the work a second time. Many of the designs so worked resemble, and are perhaps copied
from, the elaborate interlacing patterns of the woven cloth. The purpose of the small
napkins was for use in covering offerings, and similar ceremonial purposes. On PI. I., the
left-hand figure represents an officer carrying some ceremonial object under an embroidered
napkin, with tassels. So used, the napkin is called pesa lensuva.

Stitches The stitches most used are illustrated in Fig. 141. Most of the work is done with chain
stitch. If the background is blue, the pattern is outlined in white and red chain stitch, the
red inside, the white outside. The double outline is a very characteristic feature. The
borders of betel-bags are also separated from each other by three rows of chain stitch, red
or blue between two white lines. The stitch is often complicated by intertwining red or
240

blue threads, or one thread of each colour, as the work proceeds, as indicated in Fig. 141,6. 'Embroidery
Binding stitches are especially characteristic and well developed. Fig. 141, No. i, shows
a stitch used for binding together the outer cloth and the lining of the upper part of a betel- Stitches
bag, along the opening. It gives a firm edge, and is easy to work. The first stitch goes
straight through the edge of the stuff; the second catches up the threads where they cross
in the middle, as shown in the figure, without going through the cloth again. The stitches
shown in Fig. 141, Nos. 1-4, are all binding stitches, and must be imagined as binding over
the raw edges of cloth, or covering a seam ; they are drawn quite flat for the sake of clearness.
In these figures, small Roman figures indicate the order of making the stitches. Thus in i,
the needle, inserted at r., goes from i. to ii. in front, then from ii. to m. through the thickness
of the material, and then between iii. and iv. two buttonhole stitches are made, looping into
the first stitch. Each loop of the succeeding stitches embraces the loop immediately
preceding. In 2 and 3, the single loop is replaced by two and three loops respectively.
The two last especially make a very firm and useful edge. They are sometimes strengthened
and elaborated by intertwining a coloured thread along each side, below tbe edge of the
material. No. 2 is called amu karala, ‘amu ear’ (ear of corn).
No. 4 is the most complicated of all, and appears to be peculiar to Sinhalese embroidery. Centipede
It is called pattfya (centipede) or mudum m^sma (back-bone stitch); it is an elaborated stitch
herringbone. Two needles are in use together; sometimes even the three colours are
worked together. This stitch is most often used for binding the outer edges of large and
small betel-bags.
The method of working is as follows; at i. the white thread is brought to the front, the
needle is again inserted at ii. and brought out at in., on a line with i. on the other side of the
seam; it then goes back to iv. on a line with ii. on the right-hand side, and is brought out at
V., at a little distance below i. vi., vii. and viii. are the same repeated, but after vin. the
needle is brought out at ix. at some distance below v., leaving space for two other stitches
between; these stitches are begun below v., with a different coloured cotton, generally red,
and worked exactly the same as the first four stitches; after they are completed the first
needle is taken up again, the thread of which comes out on the right-hand side, at ix., just
below the two stitches of the red colour. The next stitch is a little different, in that the
needle does not go back to the extreme outside on the left but catches down a stitch at about
a quarter the width of the whole, as can be seen in the diagram. It then takes a slanting
direction behind the material, coming out below the red stitches, still on the left side; the
needle is shown in this position. Exactly the same is done on the right-hand side, and so on.
The thread always goes back to its own colour, that is if the white thread is being worked
it catches down a white stitch on the opposite side and so with the red. The backs of the
stitches are seen in No. 4A. If three colours are used, then more space must be left for the
insertion of four stitches between v. and ix. instead of two only.
No. 5 is the ordinary chain stitch which is used so much in this work. Chain stitch
No. 6 is also a chain stitch, but with coloured threads intertwined, one on each side of the
needle as it is worked. Sometimes a red thread is used on one side and a blue on the other.
No. 6 a shows the back of Nos. 5 and 6.
No. 7 is a very usual combination of two kinds of stitches; it consists of two Y-shaped
stitches held down by a stitch at the top and bottom, thus forming a square, this is then
filled in with a satin stitch of a different colour. This satin stitch is often used for filling
in small squares and other spaces.
A buttonhole stitch is often used for the conventional foliage when it needs filling in as can Buttonhole
be seen in the beautiful border of PI. XXXII., 9. The design of this particular border stitch
r I 241

Embroidery is outlined in white and filled in with a red buttonhole stitch which widens or narrows
according to the space needed to be filled. It has a very rich effect.
Seams No. 8 is a feather stitch used occasionally for filling in a space ; 8a is the back of the stitch.
No. 9 shows the method employed in joining the seams of a tuppoftya. The seams are sewn
close together though not overlapping, and at each end the seam widens out into a kind of
gusset, the space being filled up with a buttonhole stitch worked as shown, though often
with much thicker and closer stitches. At the end of the seam this gusset may be one
or two inches wide. It is a most satisfactory way of joining two pieces of cloth ; there
is no puckering and it is extremely strong. A simple cross stitch is rare.
In appliqué work there are two or three ways of stitching on the applied cloth ; the edges
are always carefully turned in, and may then be bound by hemming, by an even running
close to the edge, or by chain stitch.
APPENDIX TO CHAPTER XV. REVIVAL
OF SINHALESE EMBROIDERY.
Through the efforts of Mrs. Coomaraswamy, there has taken place of late some revival of
interest in Sinhalese embroidery. Mrs. Coomaraswamy has taught a class of Kandyan
girls at the Clarence Memorial School in Kandy, and a class of Sinhalese ladies in Colombo.
Great interest was shown, and some very excellent work resulted. Prizes were offered
through the Ceylon Society of Arts, and a good display of work was shown at the annual
exhibitions in 1905 and 1906. But the best evidence of the value of such work, was the
interest awakened in old traditions and designs, as, for example, in the case of the daughter
of a Kandyan chief, who brought to the class a highly valued memorial of the past, the
jacket referred to above (p. 239), and made the very excellent copy of part of the sleeve,
reproduced on PL XXX., 2.
At the same time, the Department of Public Instruction, through Mrs. Evans, the newly-
appointed Inspectress of Needlework, has abolished some of the worst abuses in connection
with the teaching of embroidery in schools. It may perhaps be hoped that the day of
gaudy Berlin woolwork, and gold-embroidered mottoes to be framed under glass and hung
on the wall, is now passing away, even in Ceylon, where all things Early Victorian linger
still.

CHAPTER XVI. MAT WEAVING AND
DYEING.
I. MAT WEAVING BY KINNARAYO.
T he well-known Dumbara mats, called kalalaya (PL XXXIV.), are made by men
and women of the Kinnaraya caste, practically the lowest of Kandyan castes,
excepting the Rodiyo. The fibre of which the mats are made is niyayda, the
bowstring hemp, Sansevkria zeylanica. The rounded green leaves of this common xerophitic
plant are gathered, and scraped against a log {niyandaporuvd) with a wooden tool [gl-valld)
shaped like a spokeshave. This scraping removes the fleshy part of the leaf, leaving the
white fibre, which is oiled and brushed, and then ready for use almost immediately. Part
of the material is left white, the rest dyed red, yellow, or black in the manner explained
below.
The warp thread {kalal heda) is spun like cotton on a spindle [iddd) (as shown on the right
of Plate IV). The weft elements are not spun at all, but consist of parallel fibres, of the
width of the mat.
The loom (PI. IV.) is a low horizontal contrivance, something like the loom used in cotton
weaving, but much more primitive. There is no ahala, or pit for the weaver’s feet; the
operator squats on the mat itself, supported by a few flat logs between it and the ground.
The pattern is picked up with a weaver’s lath (vemd); this lath, having an eye at one end,
serves as a bodkin * with which to draw the weft threads through the warp. A sleay [alu
karald) similar to the cotton weavers’, but not suspended, is used to drive the weft home.
The raising and separation of alternate warp thteads to form a ‘shed’ is effected by a very
44
primitive type of heddles {yo(la-ka uvd). The loops of the heddles, through which the
warp threads pass, do not move. Every alternate warp thread passes through a loop. The
separation of alternate threads to form the shed, is effected by the movement of two wooden
rods, placed on the far side of the tripod ; of these rods one (uttara-pata or kontaliyd) rests on
the warp, the other i^pannam-bate) passes between alternate threads of it. Relative move­
ment of these rods raises and separates alternate threads on the near side of the heddles.
The warp is carried on two rods, kofta kura and andina kanda. The first of these, on the
left in PI. IV., is tied to a stouter rod {heda kandd), and this is fastened to sticks firmly
driven into the ground. At the other end, the andina kanda is tightly strained by two
4
cords {ka u-pa-lanu) attached to two posts {kalsl-kai}u) in the ground. The heddles are
supported by a tripod arrangement of sticks {tun-pa kolk), which is shifted along as the
work progresses.
The warp is hid {dig-gahanava or h(da lanavd) in two operations. The spun thread {nal)
is first unwound from the spindle, then broken, and passed through the heddles and through
the teeth of the sleay or reed; the short ends left projecting through the teeth are tied
temporarily to avoid slipping out. The remainder of the warp is then laid to the required
length, and the threads broken off and joined on to the short ends projecting through the
heddles.
When the weaving is finished the projecting ends of fibre at each end of the mat are turned
up over a thread drawn tight along the edge (like a piping cord) and knotted each one to it
by another thread which catches up each projecting end in a slip knot, forming a neat
binding.

2. GRASS MATS AND BASKETS.
Grass mats [pMuru) are made by the PannayO or grass cutters, and also, but more particularly
for their own use, by women of all castes, inchiA.mg govivamsa; and the making of decorated
grass mats, dishes, and baskets was a domestic accomplishment which even the daughters of
a chief did not despise. The mats here referred to are made from various grasses {hfvan,
Cyperus dehiscent, gal(hi, C. corymbosus, etc.) and palm leaves {indi-kola, Phoenix zeylanica;
coconut; talipot, Corypha umbraculifera ; and palmyra). The best are those made of iudi-
kola or hfvan. Beside mats, baskets are made, also betel pouches {bulat main), boxes, etc.,
of dyed grasses. The grass-weaver uses a grass knife having a point at one end, and a
cutting edge at the other. A combined sickle and point for weaving, like that shown in
PL XLV., 11, is called pan ketta; a tool consisting of a small straight blade only, and a point
at the other end, is called hembili-katuva.
Country housewives take a pride in the variety of patterns they may know, and their skill in
making mats. The mats are in constant use for various purposes, especially for drying
grains in the sun ; they are also ofiered to any visitor to sit upon. An inferior, but not of
low caste, would receive a mat to sit on, and would be insulted if it were not offered; an
equal would be given a kolombuva; and a superior, especially a priest, a larger stool or chair,
covered with a white cloth. In large country houses, a number of mats are kept in store,
arranged in a ‘mat-rack’ {pfduru-ana) on the wall.
Dyeing Patavgi {Ccesalpinia sappari) is the most important dye used for grass. It produces a fine red.
The proper process is rather complicated, and the practice varies in different districts. At
Niriella (Sab.) I found the following methods in use:
On the first day two handfuls of korakaha leaves {Memecylon umbellatum, Burm.) are pounded
in a mortar, squeezed out in water by hand, and the resulting liquid, resembling pea soup,
strained; two handfuls of patangi chips are added and the whole left to stand. On the
second day the solution has become red. The patangi chips are removed, pounded, and
replaced, and the whole boiled with the indi-kola which is to be dyed, tied up in little
sheaves. The pot is allowed to cool and left till next day. On the third day leaves of
bombu-kola {Symplocos spicata), hln-bovifiya {Osbeckia octandrd), and korakaha, pieces of kebella
244

bark {Aporosa Lindleyana), and a handful of chips of a yellow wood called ahu {Morinda Mat
tinctorid), together with a small bundle of roots of ratmulgas [Knoxia platycarpa, Arn. var.) weaving and
are pounded and added to the solution in which the /sif« leaves remain; the whole is boiled dyeing
and then allowed to cool and stand till next day, when the leaves are removed and dried,
after which they are ready for use.
I have another receipt from Velimada. To a pound of galfhi (another grass used for mats)

slow fire during the day, and again strong fire in evening and slow fire during the night.

4. CANE.
Cane or rattan (vi-v^i. Calamus Roxburghi) is extensively used for making baskets, for

I. KINNARAYA’S SONG.
I. Early in the morning, when the wife has cooked and given food, set out to pluck niyanda;
scrape and wash it, and from that niyasda take three handfuls.

CHAPTER XVII. HISTORY OF SINHALESE
ART.
Materials are not yet available for the detailed history of Indian art or of any
off-shoot or branch of Indian art. It is only possible in speaking of the history
of Sinhalese art, to indicate its main sources, and the influences that seem most
to have affected it.
Accepting the general outline of the history given in Chapter I., it is clear that we have to
consider the following elements which have, or may have, gone to the building up of the
traditions of Sinhalese arts and crafts as they existed in late mediasval times:—the art of
indigenous peoples, pre-Vijayan ‘ Yakkhas’; the art brought by the Vijayan immigrants ;
the art brought with Buddhism and the Aiokan culture from N. India; the influence of
Dravidian art in early times, and at subsequent periods; the influence of Muhammadan
art; of Chinese and Malayan ; and finally of Portuguese, Dutch, and English.
Probably the most widely exerted influence in all Oriental art, is that which accompanied
and followed the A§okan Buddhist missions. To this rule Ceylon formed no exception.
It must, of course, be understood that the culture which was thus carried was not Buddhist
in the sense of being non-Hindu, but was rather what we ought to call Early Indian. It is
this fact which explains the perfectly true statement* that for Hindu art proper, one must
go to Ceylon. Mediaeval and modern Sinhalese art is essentially Indian art, but it is not
modern Hindu, rather it is such an art as might have survived in some yet Buddhist part
of the mainland, if Buddhism had not there been entirely merged in Hinduism.
Early Indian art of the Aiokan period can be best
studied in the Barahat sculptures (200— 150 b.c.).
There are, as might be looked for, many motifs in
Sinhalese art directly comparable with those character­
istic at Barahat; of these survivals, it will be worth
while to notice some of the most important or con­
spicuous. One of these survivals, is the use of rosettes
(lotus flowers), not as an essential part of a design, but
to fill awkward spaces, and so preserve the flatness and
evenness of the whole design, as, for example, in PI.
XVIII. Fig. 145 shows a lotus rosette similarly used at
Barahat. There are, moreover, significant resemblances Fig. 145. Lotus rosette (with
and survivals in the forms of the lotus rosettes them­ makard), Barahat.

may trace them, perhaps, to Northern India, and thence, not to Greece (where they did not
so much originate as develope), but to the common sources of all Indo-Aryan decorative art. Common
It is perhaps hardly possible to say more than that there survive in Sinhalese art a large sources
number of decorative motifs of archaic character. The most striking group of these occurs
on the decorated pottery made at Kelaijiya, Matara, etc. The most characteristic of these
forms are shown in Fig. 137, b-e. With these riiay be associated the lac-work design of

m otifs have a common origin in an art which we may call Early Asiatic or Indo-European;
they are the decorative analogues of the community of primitive religious conceptions in
East and West, and of the fundamental common motifs in Aryan folklore. The subject of
their origin is again referred to in the Appendix to this chapter.

parts of the world, and not necessarily traceable to a common centre of distribution. Such
forms are the plaits resembling basket-work (pp. 107, io8, above); simple cross-hatchings,

B^rly Analogous to the survival of primitive patterns, is the maintenance of the once universal
methods (pre-Aiokan) practice of building in wood. In spite of the repeated construction of stone
buildings at Anuradhapura, Polonnaruva, Yapahuva and elsewhere, the indigenous style
of architecture has remained to this day one of wooden construction. Another survival
from the earliest time is the continued practice of constructing images of impermanent
materials as clay, brick, etc., that has continued side by side with the more familiar, but
actually rarer, use of stone. The use of mud and primitive colours in the construction of
¿«//images is a survival of primitive methods, exactly analogous to the corresponding beliefs
that have survived side by side with the clear-cut non-animistic philosophy of Buddhism.
Later motifs Few decorative motifs are of later origin. The elaboration of simple motifs must always
have continued ; but most of them, such as the continuous branch, were already developed
at Barâhat,* and awaited only such an extension of their use as is illustrated in the pro­
gression from a simple border, to a design covering a large space as in Fig. 52. One
definitely Buddhist decorative motif is the ¿S-leaf, and the form of triangle derived from it
(see p. 106, above). Apparently post-Aéokan must be most of the patterns used for filling
space, or rather most of the ways of so using patterns ; thus the ‘continuous branch,’ well
known at Barâhat, was afterwards used in carefully constructed patterns covering large areas
as in Fig. 52 and PI. XV. When or where such methods of design originated it would
be hard to say. From such constructed patterns to patterns based on an invisible framework
{parsemé) the transition must have been easy.
