In architectural matters the relation of Sinhalese art to the Early Buddhist art of Northern
India is too obvious to need a detailed commentary. ‘ The tasselled ornament of the Meda- Architec-
goda pillar in the Colombo Museum, goes back to the tasselled chakra of Barâhat ; and the turalsurvi-
makara torai}a arch, to the chaitiya windows of the Early Buddhist cave temples of India, vals
Again, the wooden torat)., ‘triumphal arches,’ characteristic of street and gateway decoration
for festival occasions, afford one out of many instances of a survival of the use of wood in
architectural details ; in the gaily ornamented torana at the gateway of a devale procession
path at perahçra time, we see the prototype of the stone gateways of Sanchi. The national
style of architecture has remained in Ceylon an architecture of wooden construction.
Instances of similar survivals of wood construction could be multipled. This fact, con­
trasting with the universally stone architecture of Southern India, and of what may fairly
be called Hindu buildings in Ceylon (Bereijdi Kovil, etc.) again illustrates the survival of
Early Hindu culture in Ceylon, better preserved than on the mainland. The influence of
later Dravidian architecture is also everywhere apparent.
The history of Sinhalese art in post-Aáokan and in mediæval times is mainly one of continual Relations
action and interaction with India. During the whole of this period, and until the close of with India
the period of mediæval conditions, the relations between Southern India and Ceylon were
similar to those obtaining in the Middle Ages between France and England ; continually
fluctuating intimate intercourse, now friendly, now hostile, migration of craftsmen to
centres of civic activity, or to abandoned sites rebuilt by victorious kings, sometimes with
the capture of craftsmen amongst other prisoners ; sometimes their importation. Through­
out this intercourse, India remained the exhaustless reservoir from which Ceylon was able
to draw, whenever it became necessary to renew the traditions which fell into decay in
Ceylon, as was from time to time the case. This process of renewal is well brought out in
the Janavaipsa accounts of the history of the crafts in Ceylon. Its results are equally evident
in the community of motifs in Sinhalese and Dravidian art. The system of teaching
drawing (pp. 64— 69, above) is Dravidian, and many common elements of design have been
noticed in Chapter IV. A striking instance is afforded by the tree of life in a garlanded
frame, PI. XIV., 4, which is identical in design with the decoration of South Indian
palampores. The forms of jewellery, as well as the ‘gold leaf’ technique {taha^u kola
bçmma) are of South Indian origin. It is by no means easy always to say whether a given
piece of jewellery is of South Indian or Sinhalese manufacture.
We have spoken so far almost exclusively of the history of decorative art ; but the art was Representa-
one whole, and must so be considered from a historical point of view. If we compare the tion of trees
Barâhat sculptures and the Kandyan paintings as regards style and subject matter, we shall
find that the conventions of ancient and modern artists are close akin. The ancient method
of‘continuous narration’ is equally characteristic of both. The whole picture is brought
into one plane, and there is little or no attempt at perspective. A delight in delicate detail,
as in the delineation of feathers, costume, etc., and in clear distinct outline is apparent in
both schools. The representation of trees is very characteristic ; the sculptured trees of
Barâhat and the painted trees of a Kandyan vihâra have much in common. The treatment
is entirely decorative and idealistic. The lost school of Barâhat painting, if such existed,
must have been very like Kandyan. Unfortunately we have few remains of the minor arts
dating from Aáokan times ; it is likely that a study of these would increase the impression
of similarity between Kandyan and Barâhat art.
With regard to figure sculpture, we do not know the date of the earliest stone figures of
Buddha in Ceylon. To judge from the remains at Barâhat the early Buddhist artists
253

History of represented the Buddha by symbols only. Hence it has been assumed, in view of the
Sinhalese art Greeko-Roman character of the Gandhara sculptures, that “The ideal type of Buddha was
created for Buddhist art by foreigners.”* The improbability of this is discussed in the
Appendix to this chapter. In any case, it is fairly evident that the first sculptors of
Buddhist Images in Ceylon must have been Indians, and they may not have come to Ceylon
until some time later than the Aáokan missions, and the beginning of the general influence
of Northern Buddhist Art in Ceylon.
Sigiri The fifth century Sigiri paintings have already been referred to. They are almost certainly
paintings the work of Indian craftsmen. They were probably related to an indigenous school of
painting, much as the building in stone, and the fine weaving, were related to the indigenous
style of building in wood, and home-spun weaving; that is to say they were exotic products
of an art, never permanently naturalised in Ceylon. They are in every respect different
from modern Kandyan painting, which there is good reason to regard as the lineal
descendant of an early formal style similar in feeling to that of the Jataka sculptures at
Barahat. Into such a line of descent the Sigiri paintings would nowhere fit.
iEarly We may gather, however, that in the fifth century, as well as at other times, a school of
sculptures highly skilled craftsmen existed in Ceylon, and if of Indian origin, at least were much at
home in Ceylon. We have the Sigiri paintings; and with respect to figure sculpture
Tennent states that the “early historians of China speak in raptures of work of this kind,
obtained from Singhalese sculptors in the fourth and fifth centuries.”'}' It is possible that
the very beautiful small bronzes of somewhere about this date which are sometimes met
with in Ceylon, may have been the work of Sinhalese sculptors. This was a period of
culmination of Indian culture, both in the mainland and in Ceylon (see above, p. 162) and
the province was more intimately related to the mainland than is now the case. Perhaps
it would be correct to say of such a period, not so much that its productions in Ceylon were
the work of Indian craftsmen, as that in India at that time, of which Ceylon was a part,
there existed a common school of craftsmen great in artistic achievement; but that these
in Ceylon were unable to maintain a continuous tradition, owing to the disturbed state of
the country and other causes.
Polonna- We know from the recent discoveries of bronzes at Polonnaruva that fine Hindu art
ruva flourished there in the twelfth century still; and the better known stone sculptures,
bronzes especially the figure of Parakrama Bahu, show that here too a high level of attainment was
again reached. But the work is much rather Hindu than Buddhist, and there can be little
doubt that many or most of the craftsmen were of Dravidian origin.
Conclusions The sum of the conclusions so far drawn then is, that there exists in Sinhalese art an early
stratum of indispensable barbaric decorative motives, such as are found in savage countries
still, and survive everywhere in the art of civilised lands; then a main stream of North
Indian Buddhist influence; and thereafter the influence of continued reliance upon and
intercourse with India, especially Southern India, accounting at every period for the strong
admixture of purely Hindu with Buddhist motifs. The independent influence of China
may have been considerable at certain periods, and was also exerted at second hand through
India. Malayan influence is suggested in the elongated triangles described on p. 106.
Muhammadan influence on Sinhalese art has been of the slightest, J and on this account
Sinhalese art is of particular value as preserving Early Hindu feeling which in most parts of
the mainland has been obscured by Muhammadan or later Hindu motifs. Sinhalese

In later mediseval times, we have to consider Portuguese and Dutch and finally English Portuguese
influence on Sinhalese art. The influence of Portuguese and Dutch in the low-country and Dutch
in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, on art, costume, and manners was extremely Influence
marked ; but as regards the unconquered inland districts, comparatively slight. We trace
it in the forms of furniture; but here again it is almost entirely in the low-country that
almirahs, four-post beds, chairs and tables came into use, and only in the nineteenth century
that these spread rapidly into the Kandyan districts. In building, the same is also true;
the round pillared open verandahs, romanesque arches and other details of nineteenth
century domestic architecture have mainly spread from the low-country, and are often the
work of low-country architects and masons. The direct influence of the Portuguese and
Dutch on Kandyan culture was limited to that of the presents sent to the Kandyan kings;
the influence of the prisoners at the Kandyan Court, some of them having been, it is said,
employed as builders, and one, at least, appointed Kottalbadde Nilame; and the influence
of articles of commerce, principally cotton materials, metal ware, etc. Portuguese influence
is, for example, traceable in the type of chest called Indo-Portuguese, with iron or brass
fittings with Renaissance ornament. It is evident in many specimens of iron work; hinges
seem directly based on European forms. There is much repoussed and chased ornament of
metal work that seems also to show traces of Renaissance influence, yet may almost equally
well be quite indigenous. The silver and ivory casket of the Crystal Buddha at the Dajada
Maligava is suggestive of Italian workmanship. I have seen also old brocades that may
have been of Italian or Spanish origin. Dutch influence is seen in the brass tobacco boxes,
of which Dutch examples are still common, beside the Sinhalese imitations; and in certain
methods of representing lions, as in the corners of the Flag of the Four Korales figured
by Bell (Kegalla Report, p. 126). A similar lion rampant holding a sword is carved on a
jaggery mould in my collection. These forms are quite distinctly European, and diiferent
from typical Sinhalese lions.
Of English influence on purely Sinhalese art, the less said the better. It is been character- 'English
ised, from the English side, by almost complete indifference to indigenous culture, the result influence
of an ideal of purely material prosperity; the destruction of indigenous crafts by the
competition of cheap machine-made materials and luxuries; the neglect of surviving
architectural tradition and capacity for building; and by an entirely false and unnatural
system of education, the result of which is to make the ‘educated,’ strangers in their own
land. The immediate effect of British rule, was to destroy the system of State support of
the arts and crafts; the links that bound the Kottalbadde and the Pattal-hatara craftsmen to
the national life were snapped at a blow; by the withdrawal of support from the national
religion, it came about that funds formerly available for building and decoration of temples
were misappropriated. From the Sinhalese side, the history of the nineteenth century
has been one of continual and snobbish imitation of the external features ofWestern culture,
misunderstood and misapplied. . The results have been even more disastrous than is yet the
case in India; it is, indeed, almost a matter for surprise that so much of the indigenous
traditions of art and craft still survive. If it is so, if there are still devoted and skilled crafts­
men of the old school, this is thanks neither to the patronage of the Sinhalese themselves
nor to that of their British rulers; it is due to the vitality still latent in the old tradition,
the effectiveness of the caste system in conserving, if somewhat forlornly, some of the best
part of the old life, and lastly, and not least, to the affectionate devotion of the hereditary
craftsmen to their art and its traditions.

APPENDIX TO CHAPTER XVII. THE IN­
FLUENCE OF GREEK ON INDIAN ART.
The consideration of the origins of Sinhalese Art carries the enquirer back through Indian
Art to a remoter past, and raises the question of the origins of the Early Indian Art which
we have seen to be an immediate ancestor of Sinhalese. In the following notes I consider
briefly a special aspect of this question, viz., the Influence of Greek on Indian Art, without
limiting the scope of the enquiry to the facies of Indian Art preserved in late Mediseval
Ceylon.
When I first met with types of ornament, such as those reproduced in Figs. 133,137 and 150,
forcibly recalling early Mediterranean forms, I assumed the common view as to the extent,
permanence and importance of the influence of Greek on Indian Art, and endeavoured to
explain the presence of these decorative forms in Ceylon on those lines.* At that time I
•accepted such statements as those of Griinwedel-f- that the ideal type of Buddha was created
for India by foreigners. T also assumed that decorative forms such as the continuous branch,
palmette, honeysuckle, etc., being known from the Mediterranean area long before their
earliest known occurrence in India must have originated where they are first found, and
travelled thence to India; accepting, for example, Riegl’s statement that neither intermit-
tirende norfortplanzende Wellenranke (‘interrupted’ and ‘continuous branch’) borders were
known in the East in pre-Hellenic times.J
I have since seen reason to doubt the somewhat simple solutions of the difficulties thus
provided, and to believe that the influence of Greek on Indian Art, however extensive at
a certain period, was ultimately neither very profound nor very important. It is the
concentration of attention upon the effeminate and artistically unimportant work of the
Gandhara school that has given undue prominence to the Greek influence.§ It must be
admitted also that a certain prejudice has led European investigators to think of Classic
Greece naturally as the source of all art, and to suppose that the, influence of Classic Art must
have been as permanently important in the East as in the West. At the same time, it is to be
remembered that it is not generally realised by Western scholars, who are not always artists,
that Eastern Art, whether Indian, or Chinese, has a value and significance not less than that
of the Western Art of any time. ^The main difficulty so far seems to have been that Indian
Art has been studied only by archaeologists. It is not archaeologists, but artists, or at
any rate students of art rather than of archeology, who are best qualified to judge of the
significance of works of art considered as art, and to unravel the influences apparent in them.
No artist, familiar with the true genius of Indian art, could suppose that the work of the
Gandhara school was the real foundation of Indian figure sculpture, or that Indian art could
have been founded on such a decadent Greeko-Roman basis.
So far from foreigners having given to India the ideal type of Buddha, the Gandhara

The zenith of Greek art was in the fifth century b.c., if not earlier; the zenith of Indian
art, in times certainly later than the third century a.d. The sequence of cause and effect
would be hard to trace; it was not of the decadence of the one, that the achievement of
the other was born.
The question, however, depends essentially upon religious and philosophical considerations.
The philosophies of Greek and Indian Art are poles apart. Putting aside a few rare and
beautiful fragments of archaic art, the Greek representations of the gods belong entirely to
the Olympian aspect of Greek religion*; Greek art, as has been said, has in it no touch of
mysticism. The gods are but grand and beautiful men; sometimes, as in the case of many
Apollos, it is uncertain even whether the representation is of a god or of an athlete.
Indian art is essentially transcendental.-f- Indian art is concerned not with the representation
of perfect men, but with the intimation of Divinity. Its greatest manifestations have,
though perhaps not always so conspicuously as in Egyptian art, that sense of ‘ Being beyond
Appearance,’ which we miss in the Greek representations of beautiful Olympians. Without
saying that this or the other aim of art is the greatest, it is obvious to those acquainted
with both, that the genius of Greek, and the genius of Indian art, are so different that it is
difficult, and even impossible, to imagine a dependence of the one upon the other. Beside
the recognition of this fact, the question of just how far Classic influence can be traced in the
outward detail of Indian art, becomes of little moment.
The transcendentalism which is the essential character of true Indian art, is not of late
classic origin. That is not, of course, to say that Classic influence was non-existent, but
that its limits have not been defined, and that its importance has been over-rated. It would
be idle to deny that the Gandhara and the Amaravati sculptures exhibit the results of the
strongest classical influence. The Greek influence at Sanchi, Barahat, and Mahabodhi is
much less evident. It is, however, true to say that the early schools are compounded of
Assyrian, Persian, Hellenistic and Indian elements. The point is not that classic influence
was absent, but that itwas itself decadent, and at best un-Indfan,and that nearly all that is good
in later Indian art is there in spite of it.¿ Of course, if it be said, as Mr. Vincent Smith J says,
that “After a.d. 300 Indian sculpture properly so-called hardly deserves to be reckoned as

More than the merely negative evidence of the absence of surviving work in stone would

The Mahabharata and Ramayapa contain frequent references to “storeyed towers, galleries
of pictures, and castes of painters, not to speak of the golden statue of a heroine, and the
magnificence of personal adornment.” “ Indeed,” continues Okakura, “ it is difficult to
imagine that those centuries in which the wandering minstrels sang the ballads that were
later to become the epics, were devoid of image worship, for descriptive literature, con­
cerning the forms of the gods, means correlative attempts at plastic actualisation. This
idea finds corroboration in the sculptures of Aioka’s rails, where we find images of Indras
and Devas worshipping the ¿i-tree. These things point to the early use of clay, paste, and
other impermanent materials, as in ancient China.”J
Golden images, made by the ‘chief smith’ and the king, are mentioned in the Kusa Jataka,
in such a way as to suggest that such images were well known at the time of the composition
of the story,§ which in its present form has preserved the tradition of the third century b.c.
We pass next to references to the construction of images in Buddha’s own time. The
Kosala Bimba Varnanava states that a gilt sandal-wood image of Buddha was erected with
his consent, to compensate the disappointment felt by those who should come from afar
to visit him, if they should find him absent.
It is also related in the Divyavadana that Bimbisara, king of Magadha, desired to have a
representation of Buddha painted upon a cloth. Buddha let his shadow fall upon it, com­
manding that the outlines should be filled in with colour, and that the chief articles of the
faith should be written on it. This slender evidence Griinwedelcondemns, rightly enough, as
unauthentic, but he still claims it as showing that there was no desire to create an ideal type.H
It seems unlikely that a teacher such as the Buddha should have countenanced the con­
struction of images of himself in his own lifetime; and he is represented at Barahat and
Sanchi by the feet or the wheel.
There are also literary references to images in post-Buddhist and pre-Gandhara times.
Thus the Mahavaipsa informs us that in the relic chamber of the Ruvanv^li Dagaba, King
Dutiha GamanI (161— 137 b.c.) placed a resplendent golden image of Buddha, in the
attitude in which he achieved Buddhahood. The features and members of that image were
represented in their several appropriate colours, in gloriously resplendent gems. Figures
of the gods were also set in the relic chamber.

It will be noticed that the literary references speak always of precious metals,or impermanent Indian Art
materials such as wood or cloth. Had they spoken of early stone images the anachronism
would be evident. This adherence to actual possibilities is a point in favour of the literary
references.
A different line of argument may now be followed, based on observation of surviving Imper-
methods, where impermanent materials are employed. manent
The absence of images from ancient sites, as Barahat, is taken as proof of the non-existence materials
of an early school of sculptors or imagers. This negative evidence is, however, insufficient
to prove that images of impermanent materials or the precious metals were not made.
Even at Anuradhapura we find no statues of Buddha associated with the great stapas, the
only figure sculpture being in low relief on stelce as at Barahat. But it does not certainly
follow that wood; clay, or stone images were not worshipped in the neighbouring viharas.
Had wooden or clay images been worshipped in Aioka’s day, we should have no trace left
to show it, yet the negative evidence would be misleading. And even if, as is probable,
images of Buddha himself were unknown until several centuries after his death, this would
not in itself be a proof of the non-existence of images of any sort.
The use of impermanent materials is probably the true explanation of the difficulty. It can
be specially illustrated by survival in Ceylon. The Sariputra states that images may be
made from “gold, copper, clay, stone, wood, burnt clay* (brick) or lime.” And, in fact,
we find that a majority of images in mediaeval and modern viharas are of brick, metal, or
clay, very few of stone. Even when of stone they are always covered with plaster and
painted, so that one cannot tell by inspection, of what material the image is really made;
only metal images are, as it were, naked. How thoroughly this idea was associated with
images is suggested by the description of one of the 32 Maha-purusha-laksharja or superior
beauties or teches of the Buddha: “ His skin was soft and smooth, as an image polished by
the tooth of a tiger .”T One does not polish stone images with tigers’ teeth; the comparison,
moreover, has an air of antiquity; an early Chinese artist would have understood it. No
doubt the early stone statues of Ceylon (Anuradhapura, Kalaveva, Polonnaruva) were also
once under cover, plastered and painted. Contrast with their appearance, that of stone
sculpture intended to stand as it were naked out of doors, like the elaborately carved dvarpals
at Anuradhapura; or of statues executed in marble (like that of‘Duftha Gamani’ on the
Ruvanv?li Dagaba platform), which certainly were not intended to be covered by plaster,
but only to be painted; in both of these cases the detail and finish of the work is very
different and very much finer.
There are other examples of the survival of the early use of impermanent materials. In the
sixteenth century a.d. the Portuguese at Devundara in the Southern Province, “proceeded
to destroy the idols [of the Vishnu devale] of which there were more than a thousand of
diverse shapes, some of clay, some of wood, some of copper, and several of gilt.”.]; None of
sto ne are mentioned; what should we know of the existence of those idols, had we not the
P ortuguese record to inform us ?
The use of impermanent materials survives also in the most primitive form of image making

Indian Art An instance of the use of precious metal and impermanent material combined is afforded by

Thus we are able to trace in Sinhalese art as known to us, a survival of the Early Asiatic use
of impermanent materials (wood, clay, or brick), or of metal, but not stone, for making
images ; we trace it not only in the present use of those materials to construct entire images,
but also in the fact that even stone images are covered with plaster and painted. Similar
survivals, such as colossal mud images, floor diagrams, etc., can be traced in India also.
It becomes, therefore, unreasonable to say, as Grunwedel does,* that all Early Buddhist
sculpture was colossal and in stone, and only in the Middle Ages became “a miniature
manufacture in different materials—wood and clay in place of stone, and later in metal
casts.” It would be much truer to say that just as wooden building preceded stone con­
struction, so also the use of wood and brick and clay for figure sculpture must in general
have preceded that of stone ; and even in the case of images of Buddha, these materials
must have been made use of from the beginning, and also, as at present, contemporaneously
with the use of stone. The absence of stone statues is no more evidence of the absence
of statues of wood or clay, than the absence of stone buildings is evidence of the absence of
buildings of wood or mud.
Canon One interesting point of distinction between the technical methods of East and West is
found in the Indian canons of proportion. The ‘face,’ and not the ‘head,’ is taken as the
standard of measurement. The generally recognized standard for a human or divine figure
is a height of nine ‘faces’ (equivalent to about ‘heads’ in European terminology). The
whole artistic canon (Silpa lastra) of India appears to be independent of Western influence,
both in its insistence upon the importance of meditation, in the manner of describing the
details of the proportions, and in the technical methods of pointing (use of a horizontal
framework with suspended plumb lines, as a pointing machine).
Source of Certain conclusions drawn from the study of decorative art may also be referred to.
^branch' With reference to the important ‘branch’ (‘ Wellenranke’) motif, there is no reason to suppose
motif it to be of Greek origin in Eastern art. It first appeared in Mediterranean art on certain
Mykenean and Rhodian vases,-f in a very simple form still found in Sinhalese art (Fig. 53)
and not far removed from the most primitive possible forms of the kind. In the East, it
appears first at Barahat,J in a fully developed and quite un-Greek form, in the earliest Indian
art preserved in lasting materials. As its first appearance in Mediterranean art is in late
pre-historic times, a period of admitted Oriental influence on Greek art, the discovery of
this motif cannot be credited to classic Greece ; it is much more likely to be of Eastern
origin, like the lotus flowers and buds, palmettes, spirals, etc., and the mythical animals §
which first appear in Mediterranean art at the same time, succeeding the geometrical forms
which represented indigenous design.^It is not likely that the ‘branch’ was invented about

§ Griinwedel (p. 18) regards the mythical animals in Indian art as borrowings from Western Asia
or Greece ; and then proceeds to explain the success with which they were used, by supposing that
indigenous types of the same character already existed. No doubt they did; and if so, what need to
postulate a borrowing ? The sphinxes, griffins, chimaeras, and sirens, etc., in Greek art were as
much Oriental in origin as the lotus buds and rosettes and palmettes.

this time in more than one area. If it was invented in any one place, there is not sufficient Greek
evidence to show that this was not in Western Asia or Persia, whose art was the inheritor Influence on
and continuator of Egyptian. There need, however, be no antagonism between the claims Indian Art
of East and West. The Mediterranean in early times was so much an integral part of the
Oriental world, that it is easier and truer to explain resemblances by common origin, than
by borrowings.* The reason of the resemblances may be sought in the existence of a
“common Early Asiatic art, which has left its uttermost ripple marks alike on the shores of
Hellas, the extreme west of Ireland, Etruria, Phoenicia, Egypt, India and China.”-h The
real home of this art may have been in Mesopotamia. It owed much to Egyptian influence.
The sources of Mediterranean and Indian decorative art thus go back rather to a common
origin, than are borrowed in either direction. It might still be argued that Indian art had
borrowed from or been influenced by the later developments of Greek decorative art. As
regards Barahat and the decorative art generally, there is no evidence of this, and certainly
there was no need for it. For Greek decorative art, compared with Egyptian or Early
Indian, is unsympathetic in its treatment of vegetable form, “ a hopeless divergence from
any rational type,” as Flinders Petrie calls it..]: The Greeks invented nothing dynamic
in decorative art; the fact that the particular forms of their decorative art are still imitated
is by no means evidence to the contrary; what they did do was to take conventionalized
vegetable forms, and make them lifeless, changing lotus flowers into ‘honeysuckle’ and
‘acanthus,’ and lotus petals into ‘egg and dart.’
Their decorative art was so different in spirit from Indian, that it could have given little
to it; they regarded very little any aspect of nature except man himself; they had no
conception of ideal art in relation to any but the human form; whereas the Indian love of
nature, and sense of unity with it, led the Indian artist to cover surfaces with all sorts of
idealized vegetable forms, as well as animal. The idealistic rendering of trees at Barahat,
reached a perfection which the Greeks never at any time attained. Even the figure
sculpture at Barahat has little affinity with Greek sculpture of the same date, but only a
kinship! with the archaic Greek sculpture of centuries earlier. And history shows at the
same time how slight the intercourse with Greece at this time had been; Alexander’s
influence on Indian culture must have been of the slightest: “within three years of his
departure ... all trace of his rule had disappeared. . . . India was not Hellenized. She India not
continued to live her life of ‘splendid isolation,’ and soon forgot the passing of the Hellenized
Macedonian storm.”l|
It is such reasons as the foregoing, and especially a consideration of the fundamental
difference in the Spirit and aims of Classic Greek and true Indian art, that make it necessary
to reconsider the question of the extent and nature of Greek influence on Indian Art. The
result of such a reconsideration will be to show that the concentration of attention upon the
period of strongest and undoubted Classic influence, has magnified out of all proportion, the
importance of the foreign elements. Early India did not, alone in all the world, lack all
knowledge of the arts; the period of strong Greeko-Roman influence was not of great
arti stic importance; and it was not until this influence had largely, if not entirely, faded,
that the really great achievement of Indian art was attained.

APPENDIX I. THE KANDY ART ASSOCIA­
TION.
During the Agency of Sir John F. Dickson in 1882 an Association of those interested in
ancient art work was formed, and supported with the income derived from the annual sub­
scriptions of the members of the Association, The services of the best workmen in silver,
brass, and pottery were employed in making articles of Kandyan art and workmanship.
The Assistant Government Agent of the Kaccheri, subsequently Mr. H. Nevill, when
Fiscal C.O., undertook the supervision of the workmen, and as the object of the Association
became more widely known, orders were placed with him, and he arranged for them to be
carried out by the workmen in Kandy and Matale districts.
The work connected with the receipt of orders became entirely centred at the Kacceri, and
was conducted by the successive occupants of the office of Assistant Government Agent,
under general supervision of the Hon. the Government Agent.
The first home of the Association was in the rooms below the United Service Library, but
eventually a room was set apart at the downstairs of the Kacceri for the custody of the
articles made, and where parties could purchase and inspect them.
In 1893, the Association then known as the Kandyan Art Society being less prosperous,
application was made to Government for a loan of Rs. 2,000 to enable the Society to get
together a collection of Kandyan art work ; the grant of that amount was sanctioned by the
Governor, Sir A. E. Havelock. The whole amount of the advance has been repaid.
The necessity of having a place more suitable for the custody of these collections and the sale
of work was much felt, and there appeared to be no building more suitable for the purpose
than the building known as Palle Vahala which for many years in occupation of the Fiscal
C.O., was handed over for use in the future as a Museum and home for Kandyan art.

the duties which they had formerly been liable to under the Malabar dynasty), and which
had been enforced regardless of the ancient customs of the country, or the claims and
conditions of individuals” (‘Ceylon and its Capabilities,’ p. 423). See also the ‘Manual of
the North Central Province,’p. 140 : “although we continued the Rajakariya we omitted to
have it applied to agriculture. ... A more unfortunate system could hardly be devised
for agriculture, as it allowed the works to fall into ruin and discouraged cultivation.”
Rajakariya is often described as forced labour, and regarded as having been an intolerable
tyranny; but properly understoood, it was hardly more than a system of commanding
public assistance in works of public utility, analogous to the rates of a municipality. It was
only “the perversion of the compulsory labour from one of its chief original purposes, and
the neglect to enforce it for legitimate works under the later kings, and by the British
Government adopting their system, which occasioned the decay of agriculture and the
wasting of population.”
P. 20. A Government Agents report. This is a report by Mr. Liesching, quoted, ‘Manual
North Central Province,’ p. 43.
P. 21. Character of the Sinhalese. Cf. A. O. Brodie, J.C.B.R.A.S., III., p. 161 ; “The
people of Nuwara Kalawiya are the most gentle I have had the fortune to meet. . . . Serious
assaults, robberies, murders, are all but unknown, and during three years I have not had to
punish one native of the district for pilfering.” Also Davy, ‘Travels in Ceylon,’ 1821,
p. 289 : “Amongst few people, I believe, are family attachments more strong and sincere:
there is little to divert or weaken them; and they are strengthened equally by their mode
of life and their religion.” At the present day, it is mainly in the low-country, where
European influence has been long felt, and the social culture of the race has been destroyed,
that crime is prevalent.

Parakrama, afterwards Parakrama Bahu I. (1164— 1197 a.d.), an indication of the social
importance of these master craftsmen at the time.
The ‘five servants’ are also referred to (Mahavaijisa Ch. LVII.), as granted to a certain
ecclesiastic, together with workmen skilled in aU manner of works, to minister unto him.

P. 63. Former greatness and continuity of Indian art and craft. “Too little effort has been spent
in reconstructing the idea of that great splendour and activity which must have existed, in

good here also, for the surviving arts and crafts in India are indeed but the wreckage of a
former magnificence.
It may be noted in passing that Okakura’s reference to the cast iron pillar of ASoka at
Delhi is mistaken; the pillar referred to is of wrought iron, and belongs to the time of
Chandragupta II.

P. 69. 'Teaching of drawing in India. It is stated by Mr. Thurston (Journal of Indian Art,
Vol. X., p. 46) that the children of the Gudigars (sandal-wood carvers) “are early taught to
draw their beautiful scrollwork and designs on a slate.” It is of the utmost importance
that these old methods of training in design should be investigated before it is too late.
Indifference on the one hand, and ‘art schools’ on the other, are rapidly sweeping them out
of existence. Supposing there to be recogni2ed any excellence in Indian design, one would
have thought the first steps taken for the preservation of Indian art would have been to study
the methods of Indian designers; but so far from this, those methods have been completely
ignored.

were separate structures, the ‘iris’ of blue glass or enamel, the ‘sclerotic’ of quartz. There

in the grounds has eye cavities.

P. 79. Hands betokening {not sternness but) mildness and beneficence. Varada hasta : the hand
hanging down with palm towards the worshipper, the fingers slightly bent up— as if
granting the wishes of the devotee ; abhaya hasta : the other hand raised, as if signifying,
‘Do not fear.’ This is the usual position of the hands, or of two of the hands in Indian
sculptures representing the gods ; it is an attitude of blessing. There is in Indian art, both
sculpture and painting, as also in dancing, an elaborate symbolism of the hands and fingers.
P. 91. Fig. 28, E. Human svastika. Certain Celtic anthropomorphic designs closely
resemble this form ; see Romilly Allen, ‘ Celtic Art,’ pp. 294-295.

P. 119. Plaster. For other old recipes see Bfihad Saiphita, II., Ch, X. Bennett (‘ Ceylon
and its Capabilities,’ p. 338) states that the white stucco used in Ceylon and Southern India
is a mixture of fine sand, shell lime, green coco-nut water and coarse sugar or jaggery ; he
states truly that ‘when laid on by experienced plasterers, it displays the polish and appearance
of marble.’ The material now used, often a mere whitewash, is generally mixed with a
greater or less proportion of Reckitt’s blue, entirely destroying the value of milky whiteness.
------Pans ala. Mr. Lewis gives the following account of the small but typical pansala at
Huduhumpola near Kandy (Cave, ‘Book of Ceylon,’ p. 369) :
“The Huduhumpola pansala is built in the shape of a quadrangle opening into a spacious
verandah which occupies the whole of this side of the building. The roof is supported by
wooden pillars of the style already described. The usual small verandah surrounds the
other three sides of the quadrangle. Opening into it are the doors of the monks’ cells,
each of the usual Kandyan pattern, which is that of the main door also, only on a smaller
scale, each door about eighteen inches wide. Each cell has its own kitchen attached, and
there is also a larger kitchen for general use. There is a window of coupled lights with
carved tops in the room facing the main entrance. The whole of the centre of the quad­
rangle is occupied'by a preaching hall supported on carved wooden pillars more slender
than those in the vestibule.”

P. 124. Ceremonial purity associated with the gods. According to Davy (pp. 148, 149) the
Diva Nilame had on certain occasions to present offerings to the image of Buddha. On
these occasions he had to bathe, put on a clean cloth, and abstain from meat for at least
twenty-four hours, “not from the idea that these observances would be grateful to Boodhoo,
but from the persuasion that the gods, in whose keeping the temple is supposed to be, are
particularly attentive to bodily purity, and resent its neglect.”
P. 125. Erection of the Maguí Kapa. Compare Btihad Saiphita, I., Ch. XLIII., erection of
the Indra Dvaja. With the Mayamataya generally, compare also Brihad Sarphita, II.,

and XII., ‘The Entry into the Forest’ (to cut wood for images). Other parts of the
Brihad Saiphita (II., Chs. II., III., XL) correspond rather to parts of Sariputra, Rüpavaliya,
and Vaijayantaya.

P. 142. Vadu riyana. According to Knox, this is ‘ as much as will reach from one Elbow to
the other, the Thumbs touching one another at the tops, and so stretching out both Elbows.’
P. 147. Gem-cutting. Remains from the Piprahwa Stupa in India show that as long ago as
450 B.C., or at least in the third century b.c., Indian lapidaries were familiar with the use of
the lathe, and very skilful in shaping, polishing and piercing stones of extreme hardness.
P. 162. Zenith of Indian art. Mr. E. B. Havell would regard the seventh or eighth
centuries a .d. as probably the period of greatest achievement in Indian art. This would
tend to throw forward by some time the suggested date of writing down of the Silpa áastras.

P. 164. Archaological value of old paintings. This is well illustrated by Général L. de

P. 186. Dice. Clough gives’■ palaka^dice,particularly the long sort used in playing chaupai.’
The game of chaupai (==pacisi) has been so long forgotten, that though I have seen many
game-cloths and dice of Sinhalese make, I have not found any Sinhalese acquainted with the
game, or the name of it The game is commonly played by Tamils ; indeed, all the chief
games of this kind, olinda keliya, nerinci (a form of ‘noughts and crosses’ or ‘nine men’s
morris’), the cheetah and fourteen dogs, etc., are essentially Indian games, and not of local
origin.
------Ivory. In 1908 the Colombo Museum also acquired a'ceremonial ivory shuttle,’orna­
mented with lac, and said to have been granted as a sannasa or Royal Warrant to a family of
weavers. A warrant so given as a token, is properly called kçfa sakshiya (or sakkiya) ; the
word sannasa implies writing.
There is also in my own collection a lac-ornamented ivory spindle. Another object is an
ivory toy, consisting of a disc very deeply furrowed round the edge ; such toys are said to
have been played with on a piece of string by the Kandyan ladies. I have also a similar toy
in copper and silver.
At the Përâdçniya Exhibition in 1906 there was exhibited a beautiful ‘model’ of the
Dalada Mâligâva, made in ivory, with a brazen roof. The ‘model’ represented a typical
structural vihara, and not the Mâligâva in any detail. It is said to have been presented to
Veva Indasara Terunnânse, incumbent of the Hittettia Vihâra at Matara by Kirti 8rl Raja
Siipha in 1755 a.d. as a reward for a versified panegyric on the king’s rule.
P. 194. Knives of steel. Probably in most cases only the edge of a cutting instrument was
of steel, the remainder of iron. This is implied in a well-known Sinhalese proverb : ‘Like
the rustic who got his knife by imposing on the blacksmith ’— referring to a countryman
who went to a blacksmith to get a knife made, and gave him only the iron for it, keeping
back the steel, thinking by that means to cheat the smith, but actually cheating only
himself.
Other proverbs connected with smithing, etc., are :
‘To get the hand burnt in spite of possessing pincers.’
‘The dog that has been brought up in a blacksmith’s shop is not afraid even of thunder.’
‘ Like the silversmith’s father beating his son for undertaking an urgent work.’
Subjection to petticoat government is as bad as standing behind an adze.’
‘ The iron style of a man who is too lazy to write is heavier than the staff of King Gaja Bâhu ’
(a great iron rod).
‘The adze which straightens timber is itself not straight.’
P. 231. Pottery proverbs. Another well-known proverb, taken from a Buddhist rafra, is:
‘As all earthen vessels made by the potter break at last, so is the life of man.’

POSTSCRIPT.
Well-rings. A photograph of earthen well-rings in situ is given in the Ann. Rep. Arch.
Sur. India for 1903-4, Fig. 2.
Teaching of drawing. The method of teaching drawing on a primed panel closely resembles
that described by Cennini in his Treatise on Painting (trans. by Mrs. Merrifield, London,
1844, Chs. 5-8).
AvalokiteSvara. On PI. XXII. King Vimala Dharma Surya I. is represented wearing a
crown with a small image of Buddha upon the front of it. This was probably adopted from
the small Dhyani Buddha represented on the headdress of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteivara.
It appears also on the headdress of the very early alto-relievo figure of‘Kushta Raja’ at
Veligama. The cult of Avalokiteivara was well known in Ceylon in the ninth century.
It is just possible that the Veligama figure itself really represents Avalokiteivara.
Greek Influence in Decorative Art: p. 261. I do not mean to imply that the use of classic
decorative motifs (such as the acanthus) at Gandhara left no trace on later Indian decorative
art. On the contrary, such traces are not difficult to detect. But they no more inspired
Indian decorative art, than the Gandhara Buddhas inspired the Divine Ideal in Indian
sculpture; and the fundamental decorative motifs are of oriental (including Egyptian)
rather than classic origin. Such forms as those appearing on the woven belt of PI. XXIX.,
7, are much older than the period of classic influence at Gandhara, or even Barahat;
they are the common heritage of East and West.

DESCRIPTION OF PLATES.
PLATE I.
Details from jataka paintings at Degaldoruva Vihara, done between 1771 and 1786 a.d.
The pictures are chosen from those immediately to the left of the door of the image-room,
illustrating the Vessantara Jataka, of which a summary has been given above, p. 42. In the
original paintings, there is no division into separate scenes; there is instead ‘continuous
narration,’ the key to the events being only given by a few words of Sinhalese beneath the
principal scenes. The upper panel reproduced shows first Prince Vessantara, riding in
state upon the rain-giving white elephant. “Early in the morning,” says the jataka, “the
Prince, intending a visit to the alms-hall, washed himself with sixteen pitchers of perfumed
water, and broke his fast, and mounted upon the back of his noble elephant richly adorned
proceeded to the eastern gate.” Finally, near the southern gate, he met the Brahmans
from Kalinga, and in answer to their prayer gave to them the elephant, with all its trappings,
and this gift is represented on the right hand of the same panel.
Many interesting details should be observed. The Prince is dressed in the traditional royal
costume of a king or deva, not in the actual costume worn by the eighteenth century
Kandyan kings. In other respects the picture fairly represents a Kandyan State procession.
The five attendants, beginning from the left, carry respectively something, perhaps an
offering, covered by a napkin {pesa-lensuva) ; a sSsata with lacquered handle; sayda
4
koaya (?); mutu kupaya and vapana talatta. The sixth and seventh attendants are half
hidden; the eighth is the elephant-keeper, carrying the goad [heti4uva), his lower caste
indicated by his darker colour. The goad has a lacquered handle. The Prince has ready
to hand a smaller goad (amkusd). Then follow two attendants carrying emblems of
authority, and another with a white flag {sudu kodiya^, with a little streamer {savarama).
In the second scene, on the extreme right, the Prince is seen pouring water from a keifdiya
into the hands of the Brahmans, who come next in the original, in ratification of the gift;
immediately behind him is his chief attendant or minister, distinguished by the bsralaya
worn upon the vafa toppiya which the others wear alone. The elephant’s trappings,
described in the jataka as priceless, are also to be noted, especially the alternate red and
yellow cloth lappets in the form of ¿i-leaves, the jewelled anklets and ornament, worn
Hpop the frontal lobes and over the eyes. The lotus rosettes {nelum-mal) are used decora-
tively to fill out the space evenly, but have nothing to do with the picture. The first
of these is of the form in which the outer ring of petals is replaced by a whorl of cobra
heads.
The lower panel in two scenes shows us the arrival of Vessantara and MadrI Devi and
the two children at the hermitages prepared for them by Viivakarma at ^akra’s order at
Vangagiriya. On the left is thC'mountain Vipula, by the foot of which they passed, and
next the river Ketumatl where they rested and ate and bathed and drank before proceeding
further. The trees represent thick forest, through which they passed until they came
to the ‘four-square lake.’ Then Vessantara, seeing a path, knew that it led to a hermitage,
and going in front of the others, found indeed the pansala prepared, he entered, “and
putting oif his bow and sword, with the garments which he wore, he donned the garb
of a hermit, and coming forth entered the covered- walk and paced up and down and . . .
approached his wife and children. Madrl fell at his feet in tears; then with him entering
the hermitage, she went to her own cell and donned the ascetic dress.” This is the second
scene, shown on the right hand of the lower picture.
319

The hermit’s cave, with the couch, curtain and water-pot {ken^iya), and the hermit’s dress,
consisting of a cloth, a deer-skin and a girdle, should be observed. He holds in his hands a
rosary (nava-guna-v?ld) and a staff.

vaga\ i.e., “ Gift of the white elephant,” and “ Madrl Devi’s weeping and prostration
(before Vessantara).” (The syllable nu has been omitted in the reproduction.) ■

which is terminated by an earthen finial.

and earthen finials. Seep. 116.

PLATE XI.
WOODWORK.
1. Idi appan van-ge^iya, ‘string ‘hopper’ masher.’ The central part consists of a cylinder
in which a piston works up and down; cooked rice flour is placed in the cylinder and
squeezed out through the holes in a metal plate beneath, much as potatoes are wormed in a
masher. ‘Hoppers’ (a corruption of appd) are a kind of rice bread especially used at the
first daily meal; there are two chief sorts, the ordinary, and the ‘string’ hopper. Machines
for preparing the latter are not often so elaborately carved as that figured, which was lately
presented by Mr. T. B. Paraijatella to the Kandy Museum. It may have been used in the
Royal kitchen, or in that of some chief; but the use of ornamented tools and kitchen and
agricultural implements was equally characteristic of all classes. Measurements, 16 x 6|
inches, diameter of cylinder, if inch.

The spoon-rack used to be’a regular article of kitchen furniture; the long thin handles of
the coconut-shell spoons used in cooking are slipped through the holes in the rack. Racks
of plaited grass are also used in -some districts.

still commonly played by Kandyan women, but like all indigenous games is declining in
popularity. No. i, author’s collection, measures io^x6 inches; Nos. 2 and 3 from the
Kandy Museum. See also Plate XLL, 4.
